parts.what: Machines engine and drivetrain parts (engine blocks, cylinder heads, gearbox-related parts) for commercial vehicles, tractors/farm equipment, construction machinery, industrial engines and some passenger vehicles, including exports of truck engine blocks; it was about ₹1,558 crore of FY2024 revenue and ₹292 crore of EBIT, and management says it is still a core growth business but no longer the one the company depends on. A newer 'stationary engine' line tied to data-centre/AI power demand has a first order book of $100 million, expected to reach that revenue level around FY2029-30.

parts.name: Aluminium Products
parts.what: The largest segment (about ₹2,154 crore of FY2024 revenue and ₹322 crore of EBIT), formed in 2022 by merging the auto-aluminium and industrial-aluminium businesses; it die-casts and machines aluminium parts for two-wheelers, cars/SUVs and industrial uses, plus a fast-ramping alloy wheel business (Bhiwadi, Shoolagiri and Hosur plants, exiting March 2026 at a run rate of about 3 million wheels a year against 5.8 million installed capacity). It includes subsidiaries DR Axion (76%-owned, ₹1,246 crore turnover and ₹196 crore EBIT in FY2024) and Sunbeam, which is being restructured out of low-margin casting-only work; management's stated ambition is to take this business to $1 billion.

parts.name: Industrial and Engineering
parts.what: The smallest segment (about ₹740 crore of FY2024 revenue and ₹49 crore of EBIT), combining a storage-solutions business selling racking/storage systems to e-commerce and similar customers (about ₹88 crore of the segment's ₹157 crore quarterly revenue in Q1 FY2023) with general engineering work; it is material-intensive so its EBITDA margin looks low, but the ROCE is good, and management describes it as the 'backbone' supporting the powertrain and aluminium businesses.

overview.what_it_does: Canara Robeco Asset Management Company (CRAMC) runs a mutual fund business in India: it pools money from savers into 26 investment schemes across equity, debt and hybrid categories, and manages that money for a fee. Its customers are ordinary Indian households (individual investors are about 86% of assets, institutions 14%), reached through a network of over 56,000 empanelled distribution partners, 29 branches and its own digital platforms, with about 24% of assets coming from smaller 'B-30' cities beyond the top 30. It earns money mainly as an annual management fee charged as a percentage of assets under management — roughly 35-39 basis points overall, so revenue rises as AUM grows while costs (fund managers, operations) stay largely fixed; management targets a cost-to-income ratio of 38-42%. It operates only in India, manages about ₹1.2 lakh crore of assets, is owned 38% by Canara Bank, 37% by Japan's ORIX Corporation and 25% by the public, and listed on the NSE and BSE in October 2025.

parts.name: Equity schemes (active)
parts.what: Actively managed stock funds are the core of the business at roughly 91% of AUM and the highest-earning part at about 37 basis points of fee yield; management calls itself 'an equity-focused fund house' that will lag slightly in falling markets and outperform in rising ones.

parts.name: Fixed income / debt schemes
parts.what: Bond and debt funds make up about 9% of AUM alongside equity, earning around 30 basis points.

parts.name: Liquid funds
parts.what: Short-term cash-parking funds that earn a very thin fee of about 3 basis points, so they add assets but little revenue.

parts.name: Hybrid schemes
parts.what: Mixed equity-and-debt funds are part of the 26-scheme product basket, though the calls give no separate size for them.

parts.name: SIP book
parts.what: Recurring monthly investment plans are described as 'a key strength of our franchise' — over 21 lakh active SIP accounts contributing about ₹768 crore a month (SIP and STP combined), giving sticky, predictable inflows.

parts.name: Distribution and branch network
parts.what: The sales engine of over 56,890 empanelled partners, 29 branches (up from 23 a year earlier) and digital platforms, which management says is being expanded and is a source of rising cost.

parts.name: Treasury / investment book
parts.what: The company's own ~₹735 crore investment pot: about ₹110 crore of 'skin in the game' seed money that SEBI requires it to hold in its own schemes, with the remaining roughly ₹600 crore in debt, overnight and liquid funds; it produced about ₹29.6 crore of mark-to-market and realised gains in Q1 FY27, i.e. most of the gap between operating revenue and total income.

parts.name: New products / NFOs and future lines
parts.what: Roughly two new fund launches are targeted per year (subject to board and SEBI approval), with passive/index funds and diversification 'from the mutual fund into other spaces' flagged as a short-to-medium-term option rather than something the company does today.

overview.what_it_does: CreditAccess Grameen (CA Grameen) is an Indian microfinance lender that gives small, mostly unsecured loans to low-income households in rural and semi-urban India, traditionally to women organised into groups ("centers") who meet and repay together — management describes it as serving "the bottom of the pyramid" and notes it has historically financed "only one woman per household". It earns money the way a lender does: it borrows wholesale from banks, domestic markets (including NCDs) and foreign lenders at around 9.2-9.8%, lends out at a portfolio yield of roughly 21% (which it calls the lowest in the microfinance industry), and keeps the spread — an interest spread of about 11% and net interest margin of 14%, less operating costs (cost-to-income ~29-30%) and loan losses (credit cost, which swung from ~2.2% in good years to 6.74% in the FY26 stress year). It runs a branch-and-field-staff model: about 2,276 branches across 457 districts and ~22,000 employees serving roughly 44 lakh borrowers, with a loan book (AUM) of about INR 30,319 Crore as of Q1 FY27, up from about INR 15,615 Crore in mid-2022. It is concentrated in rural India with Karnataka and a small group of "top 3 states" historically dominant, and it is deliberately expanding into newer states and into larger, longer-tenure retail loans for its older customers.

parts.name: Group Loans (GL) / microfinance
parts.what: The core business — small joint-liability loans made to groups of rural women for income-generating activities, collected largely in cash at weekly/periodic center meetings; it was essentially the whole company (INR 25,542 Crore of a INR 26,304 Crore book in Q1 FY25) and even after diversification still makes up roughly 80% of AUM, with growth driven by adding ~1 lakh new borrowers a month, about 35-38% of whom are new-to-credit.

parts.name: Retail Finance (RF)
parts.what: Larger, individually underwritten loans sold to long-vintage microfinance customers who "graduate" upward — this is the fastest-growing part, going from a tiny INR 762 Crore book in Q1 FY25 (and 5.9% of AUM in March 2025) to 18.1% of AUM in March 2026 and 20.6% by June 2026.

parts.name: Individual business loans (incl. "Unnati")
parts.what: Unsecured business loans to individual borrowers rather than groups, given to seasoned customers — management cites Unnati borrowers averaging 7.7 years of relationship history and a 732 credit score; it is one of the three retail products launched in the last ~3 years and one of the company's three customer-acquisition channels.

parts.name: Mortgage-backed loans
parts.what: Secured loans against property to existing customers moving up the ladder (average vintage 6.2 years, average credit score 714), part of the push into "higher ticket secured retail products".

parts.name: Two-wheeler financing
parts.what: Vehicle loans, the newest of the retail products named by management; the calls give no separate size for it, only that it sits inside the retail finance expansion.

parts.name: Grameen Mahi (customer app / digital channel)
parts.what: A mobile app used both to collect repayments digitally and to source business — 15.4 lakh active users (34.5% of borrowers) by Q1 FY27, with digital collections rising from 14% to 24.2% of total collections; management intends it to become a channel for instant eligibility checks, small-ticket loans and lead generation.

parts.name: MMFL (Madura Micro Finance)
parts.what: A separate microfinance subsidiary being integrated into the parent in the earlier calls — in FY23 it ran on two technology platforms (73% of its book on CA Grameen's system, 27% on its own) and had weaker collection efficiency (93% vs 97% at CA Grameen); it is not mentioned as a distinct unit in the later calls.

parts.name: Borrowing / liability franchise
parts.what: Not a customer business but central to how it makes money — it funds itself from banks, private NCD issues (e.g. INR 425 Crore in Q1 FY27) and foreign lenders (24% of the liability mix), backed by an 'AA-/Stable' rating, INR 3,536 Crore of cash, capital adequacy of ~24.9% and equity of INR 8,347 Crore, with management stressing that 86% of net-worth growth since FY20 came from retained profits.

overview.what_it_does: Crisil sells credit ratings, research, benchmarking data, analytics and consulting — essentially independent opinions and data that help others judge credit risk and make business decisions, under the stated purpose of "making markets function better." Its customers are banks, NBFCs, asset managers, global corporate and investment banks, corporates, governments and multilateral institutions; by April 2026 it says it serves 11,400-plus clients across 40 countries with 5,000-plus professionals, having started in India as the country's first credit rating agency roughly 40 years ago. It earns money mainly from fees: fees for assigning new ratings on bonds and bank loans plus recurring annual surveillance fees on existing ratings, and subscription/mandate-based fees for research, benchmarking, risk and consulting work — including analytical work delegated to it by S&P Global Ratings. It is headquartered in Mumbai and listed in India, but the business is heavily international: management said in 2023 that about 65% of revenue was overseas business billed in US dollars, and the company has since added geographies such as Canada (via the PriceMetrix acquisition) and Australia (Peter Lee Associates).

parts.name: Rating Services (reporting segment)
parts.what: One of the company's two reported segments, combining Crisil Ratings and the Global Analytical Center; management describes Crisil Ratings as holding a market-leading position in Indian corporate bond ratings, and the segment grew about 20.2% year-on-year in Q1 2026.

parts.name: Crisil Ratings Limited
parts.what: Assigns credit ratings on Indian corporate bonds and bank loans and then monitors them for a recurring surveillance fee — revenue rises and falls with bond issuance volumes and bank credit growth, and calendar 2025 growth came from strong surveillance fees plus momentum in the mid-corporate segment.

parts.name: Global Analytical Center (GAC)
parts.what: An offshore analytical unit inside the ratings segment that does ratings work delegated by S&P Global Ratings — mostly surveillance of existing ratings plus newer support engagements — and management flags it as a consistent growth contributor.

parts.name: Research, Analytics and Solutions (reporting segment)
parts.what: The second reported segment, housing the global and India non-ratings businesses (Integral IQ, Coalition Greenwich and Crisil Intelligence); it is the part most exposed to global financial clients' discretionary budgets, and it was the main drag when overall revenue growth slowed to 3.8% in FY2024.

parts.name: Crisil Integral IQ (formerly Global Research and Risk Solutions)
parts.what: Outsourced research and risk work for global banks and asset managers — credit monitoring, model validation, risk and regulatory support — with recent momentum in buy-side (asset manager) offerings and Gen-AI-based client solutions such as a deployed Gen-AI credit assessment tool.

parts.name: Crisil Coalition Greenwich (formerly Global Benchmarking Analytics)
parts.what: Sells benchmarking analytics that let banks and asset managers compare their revenue, market share and client experience against peers, serving corporate and investment banks and commercial/community banks; it has been built out by acquisitions including Peter Lee Associates in Australia and PriceMetrix in Canada for wealth management.

parts.name: Crisil Intelligence (formerly Market Intelligence and Analytics)
parts.what: The India-facing research, consulting and data arm — industry research, infrastructure and sustainability consulting, and credit/risk products such as the Credit+ ICON credit assessment solution — and it also produces the public economic forecasts and reports (India GDP, inflation, bank credit) that Crisil is quoted on.

parts.name: Crisil Foundation
parts.what: The company's non-commercial CSR arm running financial-literacy and environment programmes such as Mein Pragati (over a million people reached in Assam and Rajasthan) and 669 RBI Centres for Financial Literacy; it is a reputation and community activity, not a revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: Crizac is a Kolkata-based, business-to-business company that recruits international students for foreign universities: it runs an online platform where independent education agents around the world submit student applications, and Crizac processes those applications end-to-end and passes qualified students to its partner universities. It earns a commission from the universities for each student who actually enrolls, so revenue follows the admission cycle — applications come in 6 to 9 months before the money is booked, making Q3 (application peak) and Q4 (enrollment/revenue peak) the big quarters. Management describes it as asset-light, tech-led and debt-free, funded entirely from its own cash; FY26 revenue from operations was about INR 10,422 million (up 22.7%) with PAT of INR 2,191 million and an EBITDA margin of about 27%. It connects roughly 15,000 registered agents (5,389 of them active) and more than 400 partner universities, sourcing students from 85+ countries into eight destination countries, with the UK by far the largest destination and India about half the application volume.

parts.name: Core B2B student recruitment platform (Crizac Limited / Crizac UK)
parts.what: The main business — the proprietary platform that takes applications from agents, quality-checks and processes them, and delivers enrolled students to partner universities; it is essentially all of the revenue today, with roughly 90% of applications going to UK universities and the top 10 university partners accounting for 66% of revenue, and it processed 3.94 lakh applications in FY26 (up 43%).

parts.name: Global Tree Careers (B2C counselling and immigration)
parts.what: A 51% stake bought in January 2026 in a direct-to-student counselling and immigration services business in India, which management says carries much higher margins than the B2B core (around 50%) and starts consolidating into the P&L from Q4 FY26 — a new, still-small direct-to-student arm.

parts.name: StudiesPlanet (Latin America)
parts.what: A Latin American student recruitment agency acquired in October 2025 to open up LATAM as a new source region alongside Asia and Africa; described as an early-stage contributor to a more diversified revenue mix rather than a material earner yet.

parts.name: New Zealand business / Medway Educational Consultant team
parts.what: A destination-market build-out operationalised in April 2026 by onboarding an entire consulting team, giving Crizac on-ground admissions capability in New Zealand — one of the newer destinations management expects to benefit as students shift away from the US and Canada.

parts.name: US business (including Raj Consultant)
parts.what: A small operation, acquired in FY25 to diversify into the US market, which management repeatedly called 'very small' and held back by tightened US visa policy, with the hope of benefiting whenever conditions stabilise.

parts.name: Ancillary / adjacent student services
parts.what: Newer add-ons around the student journey — an accommodation booking platform launched during FY26, plus stated plans for student loans, visa services and insurance — meant to earn extra revenue off the same agent and student flow at similar operating leverage; not yet quantified in the calls.

parts.name: EduMentor (AI technology investment)
parts.what: A commitment of USD 2.5 million over five years, made in March 2026, to an AI platform for matching students to universities and providing mentorship and decision support — an investment in technology and conversion rates rather than a revenue line today.

overview.what_it_does: Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals is an India-based consumer electricals company with an 85-plus year history that sells everyday household electrical and home products under the Crompton brand — ceiling and other fans (it calls itself the world's number one ceiling fan brand), water pumps for homes and farms, water heaters, air coolers, kitchen and small domestic appliances such as mixer grinders, air fryers and juicers, and LED lighting. It makes money mainly by selling these products to ordinary households through a pan-India dealer and retail network, plus faster-growing 'alternate' channels such as e-commerce, modern retail and rural, and it also sells lighting and solar projects business-to-business (street lighting, industrial projects, state government tenders). Much of the product is manufactured or outsourced to third parties and sold on brand, distribution and after-sales strength; profitability is driven by pricing actions against commodity-cost swings, premiumisation and cost savings, with heavy advertising spend behind the brand. Operations are essentially all in India (head office in Mumbai), and results are reported both standalone and consolidated with its majority-owned subsidiary Butterfly Gandhimathi Appliances; consolidated quarterly revenue was around Rs 1,860 crore in mid-2022 and Rs 2,283 crore in the March 2026 quarter.

parts.name: ECD (Electrical Consumer Durables)
parts.what: The largest part of the company — fans, pumps and appliances sold to households; it drives most of the revenue and profit (standalone quarterly revenue was about Rs 1,959 crore in Q1 FY25 with ECD growing 21%, and ECD EBIT margins were run at roughly 19-20% excluding advertising spend).

parts.name: Fans
parts.what: Ceiling and other fans, the flagship category where management says Crompton is the world's number one ceiling fan brand and has steadily gained market share; BLDC (energy-efficient) fans are the current growth push, growing 30%-plus, and the category went through the BEE 2.0 energy-rating regulatory change from January 2026.

parts.name: Pumps
parts.what: Water pumps for homes (residential) and farms (agri), plus a newer solar pump business sold largely into government/B2B orders — solar pump execution was around Rs 21 crore in a single quarter in FY25 and was called out again as a growth driver in FY26.

parts.name: LDA (Large Domestic Appliances)
parts.what: Water heaters (geysers) and air coolers — a seasonal business that benefits from both hot and cold weather; management says Crompton is now the number 2 water heater brand nationally in general trade, and air cooler volumes grew 68% in one strong summer quarter.

parts.name: SDA (Small Domestic Appliances)
parts.what: Small kitchen gadgets led by mixer grinders, plus newer launches like infrared cooktops, air fryers and high-end juicers; described by management as arguably the fastest-growing kitchen appliance business of its size in India and now a 'material' business with a step-jump in profitability.

parts.name: Large kitchen appliances / built-in kitchen
parts.what: A newer, still-small incubating line of chimneys, built-in ovens, built-in microwaves and dishwashers sold partly through 'Crompton Signature Studio' exclusive stores — entered in 2022 targeting a roughly Rs 2,200 crore market, but only about Rs 14 crore of revenue in a quarter and still loss-making at the EBITDA level as of FY25.

parts.name: Lighting
parts.what: LED lighting split into B2C (battens, panels, downlighters, ceiling lights sold to consumers) and B2B (street lighting, industrial and large project orders); it was restructured around FY24 after years of price erosion and recovered to what management called industry-leading 14% growth and industry-leading margins by Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Butterfly Gandhimathi Appliances (subsidiary)
parts.what: A majority-owned (81%) kitchen appliance company acquired in 2022 selling mixer grinders, gas stoves, pressure cookers and similar products, historically strong in south India with a plan to expand to non-south markets — running at roughly Rs 245-253 crore of revenue per quarter with EBITDA margins around 8-10%, and the carrying value was written down (impaired) in FY26 even as growth and profits recovered.

parts.name: Solar rooftop
parts.what: A recently launched business installing rooftop solar systems for homes, initially off state government tenders (about Rs 18-19 crore booked in Q3 FY26) and expanding into direct-to-consumer, with roughly 5,000 homes installed by May 2026.

parts.name: Residential wires
parts.what: The newest launch, announced February 2026 — house wiring products sourced from third-party manufacturers and sold through Crompton's existing dealer network, targeting a market management sizes at Rs 36,000-37,000 crore, with essentially no revenue yet as products only reached select markets in FY26.

parts.name: Alternate channels (e-commerce, modern retail, rural)
parts.what: Not a product line but a route to market management tracks closely — about 17% of Crompton's sales and growing roughly 30% a year, with e-commerce alone delivering over Rs 100 crore per quarter.

overview.what_it_does: CSB Bank is a small Indian commercial bank that takes deposits from the public (savings, current and term deposits, plus bulk deposits and borrowings) and lends that money out, mainly as loans secured against gold jewellery, alongside corporate/wholesale loans, SME and business-loan-group lending, and a small retail book. It earns most of its income from the spread between what it charges borrowers (yield on advances around 10.6%-11.3%) and what it pays for funds — a net interest margin that ran above 5% in FY2023 and around 3.7%-3.8% by FY2026 — topped up by fee and other income (about 21% of total income in FY2026) from insurance sales, processing and commission fees, LC/BG and trade fees, treasury/bond gains and priority-sector lending certificates. It serves customers through a branch-and-ATM network that grew from roughly 794 branches in mid-2024 to 868 branches and 835 ATMs by June 2026, expanding beyond its home region towards a pan-India footprint to cut concentration risk. Management describes it as being midway through an 'SBS 2030' plan — a build phase of technology and branch investment now moving into a scale phase — with the aim of becoming a full-service, mid-sized bank rather than mainly a gold-loan bank.

parts.name: Gold loans
parts.what: Loans given against customers' gold jewellery — the bank's largest and fastest-growing lending line (24%-26% annual growth in earlier years and about 54% of total advances by Q1 FY2027), described as low-risk with tight loan-to-value and price controls, and targeted to fall to roughly 30% of the book by 2030 as other businesses grow.

parts.name: Wholesale / corporate banking
parts.what: Lending to larger companies; management says it 'progressed as envisaged' and by Q1 FY2027 it is, along with gold, one of the two biggest and best-performing parts of the loan book.

parts.name: SME / BLG (Business Loan Group)
parts.what: Loans to small and medium businesses; growth has been deliberately held back ('calibrated and cautious') during a weak operating environment, with management saying it will resume scaling when conditions improve.

parts.name: Retail assets
parts.what: A comparatively small book of personal and other retail loans including LAS (loan against security) and some unsecured lending; it shrank when the bank deliberately ran off a roughly Rs.2,100 crore gold-repledge LAS portfolio down to about Rs.60 crore, and management plans to relaunch a full retail product range and 'kickstart' retail growth around Q4 FY2027/Q1 FY2028.

parts.name: Deposits / liabilities franchise
parts.what: The funding side — savings and current accounts (CASA, about 25% of deposits in 2024 falling to roughly 19-20% by 2026) plus retail and bulk term deposits, supplemented by refinance and overseas/FCY borrowings; deposits grew 20-26% a year recently, faster than the industry, and building granular retail deposits is management's stated priority.

parts.name: Other income / fee business
parts.what: Core fees from insurance sales, loan processing, commissions, letters of credit and bank guarantees, plus penal charges, treasury/bond profits and income from selling priority-sector lending certificates (PSLCs); this grew 21% in FY2026 and made up about 21% of total income.

parts.name: Transaction banking and technology platform
parts.what: Newer capability being built out — supply chain finance, cash management and trade products on a newly migrated Oracle core banking system with surrounding systems — described as the foundation that will let the bank scale into a full-service bank over the next few years.

parts.name: Branch and ATM distribution
parts.what: The physical network used to gather deposits and customers, expanded at roughly 100 branches a year in the early build phase and standing at 868 branches and 835 ATMs by June 2026, with expansion aimed at widening the bank's geographic spread.

overview.what_it_does: City Union Bank is an old private-sector commercial bank in India, incorporated on 31 October 1904 and headquartered in Kumbakonam, Thanjavur district, Tamil Nadu, with its shares listed on the NSE and BSE. It does plain, traditional banking: it collects deposits from the public — current and savings accounts (CASA) plus term deposits — and lends that money out, mainly as working-capital and business loans to small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), loans against gold (especially agricultural gold loans), and secured retail loans such as housing loans and loans against property. It earns most of its money from the spread between what it charges borrowers (yield on advances around 9.8%) and what it pays depositors (cost of deposits around 5.6%), giving a net interest margin of roughly 3.6%–3.8%, topped up by fees like loan processing charges and income from its investment/treasury book. Management repeatedly stresses that it deliberately stays away from large corporate consortium lending, infrastructure and unsecured retail, and by mid-2026 the bank had grown to about Rs. 67,645 crores of advances and Rs. 79,342 crores of deposits, with return on assets around 1.55%.

parts.name: MSME lending (core business)
parts.what: Loans to small and medium-sized businesses — described as the bank's core strength and the segment that 'will continue to dominate' the loan book, and the main engine behind the 24%–26% loan growth reported in FY26 and Q1FY27.

parts.name: Gold loans (including agricultural gold loans)
parts.what: Lending against pledged gold jewellery, with a particular focus on agricultural gold loans; it is named alongside MSME as one of the two traditional lines that carried growth, and management says gold loans still fetch 'a decent rate' that supports margins.

parts.name: Secured retail (housing loans, loan against property, micro-LAP)
parts.what: A newer vertical, built out from around FY25 with added staff, a retail team and Newgen loan-origination software; it contributed almost nothing at first ('incremental credit growth from retail are yet to start' in FY25) but by FY26 was described as an additional growth enhancer on top of MSME.

parts.name: Deposits (CASA and term deposits)
parts.what: The funding side of the bank — savings and current accounts plus fixed deposits from customers, Rs. 79,342 crores as of June 2026 and growing 21% year-on-year, with management tracking average CASA (Rs. 20,062 crores) and a credit-to-deposit ratio kept around 84%–85%.

parts.name: Treasury / investments
parts.what: The bank's bond and investment portfolio, which yields roughly 6.4%–6.7%; it can add trading profits in good years but produced almost nothing in FY23 when rates rose (only Rs. 51 lakhs of trading profit in one quarter), and in Q1FY27 included about Rs. 700 crores parked in mutual funds earning Rs. 12 crores.

parts.name: Other income / fee income
parts.what: Non-interest earnings, chiefly loan processing charges (which roughly doubled from Rs. 23 crores to Rs. 38 crores between Q1 and Q2 of FY25) plus items like mutual fund income and income-tax refund interest; small relative to interest income but a visible swing factor in the cost-to-income ratio.

parts.name: Recovery and asset-quality management
parts.what: An in-house effort to collect on bad loans, including technically written-off accounts, which management treats almost as a profit line — recoveries (Rs. 206 crores in Q1FY27) have exceeded fresh slippages (Rs. 195 crores) for several years running, pulling gross NPAs down from 4.65% in mid-2022 to 1.73% by mid-2026.

parts.name: Third-party / DSA sourcing
parts.what: Loans sourced through outside direct selling agents rather than the bank's own branches — explicitly kept small, at only 1%–2% of the overall bank book.

overview.what_it_does: Cummins India Limited (Pune-based, listed as CUMMINSIND) makes and sells diesel and gas engines, generator sets ('gensets') and the parts and service that keep them running. Its customers are Indian buyers of backup and prime power — data centres, infrastructure and construction projects, realty and residential, rental operators, pharma and biotech — plus equipment makers in rail, mining, marine, compressors and defence, and overseas distributors and OEMs. It earns money three ways: selling new engines/gensets in India, selling spare parts and after-sales service through its Distribution arm, and exporting engines (split into 'high horsepower' and 'low horsepower') to markets like the Middle East, Africa and Europe. In FY2025-26 it reported sales of ₹11,950 crore, up 18%, of which ₹9,961 crore was domestic and ₹1,989 crore exports, with profit before tax (before exceptional items) of ₹3,104 crore; it sources some products from Cummins group related parties (e.g. the QSK60 built by CTIPL, the QSK95 imported) while saying most content is localised in India.

parts.name: Power Generation (domestic)
parts.what: Sells generator sets in India across low horsepower, mid-range, heavy duty and high horsepower nodes, and is the biggest single line at ₹4,758 crore in FY26 (up 24%); management says data centres alone were 30-35% of this business in FY26 and that the whole line has just moved from CPCB-II to the tighter CPCB-IV+ emission norms, which added after-treatment content and helped pricing.

parts.name: Distribution
parts.what: The after-sales arm selling spare parts, service and support on the installed base of engines — including servicing GAIL's hydrogen installation, described as the country's largest working hydrogen setup — and the steadiest grower at ₹3,278 crore in FY26 (up 22%).

parts.name: Industrial (domestic)
parts.what: Supplies engines to Indian equipment makers and end users in construction, rail, mining, compressors and marine; the smallest domestic line at ₹1,650 crore in FY26 and roughly flat (down 1%) after a very strong prior run, with management tying its fortunes to Indian infrastructure spending.

parts.name: High Horsepower exports
parts.what: Exports of the larger engines, ₹984 crore in FY26 (up 20%), sold mainly into Middle East, Africa and European markets and described as volatile because of geopolitics and tariffs.

parts.name: Low Horsepower exports
parts.what: Exports of smaller engines, ₹807 crore in FY26 (up 3%), the weakest-growing line, having gone through several quarters of decline before bottoming out and partially recovering.

overview.what_it_does: Cupid Limited is an Indian manufacturer, based at a factory in Sinnar, Nashik (Maharashtra), that makes male condoms, female condoms, water-based lubricant jelly and In Vitro Diagnostic (IVD) test kits. It earns almost all of its money from exports — 89% to 94% of sales in the quarters discussed — mainly by winning bulk tenders from government health programmes and international agencies such as the United Nations Population Fund (its largest customer at about INR57 crore in FY23), plus buyers in South Africa, Tanzania and Brazil; it says it has shipped to over 104 countries. Revenue was INR164.1 crore in FY23 with an order book of about INR177 crore, and the business runs at roughly 94-95% of a 560 million pieces-per-year condom capacity. Under new management (the Halwasiya group, which took control in 2023) it is also trying to build a consumer-brand (B2C) business in India and abroad, and raised about INR385 crore via warrants to FIIs in early 2024 largely for an acquisition.

parts.name: Male condoms
parts.what: Latex male condoms sold largely into export tenders and institutional buyers; management guided to about 75% of revenue for FY24, making it the biggest single line.

parts.name: Female condoms
parts.what: The company says it was the first in India to make female condoms; this is the high-margin line at roughly 23% of revenue, but it is lumpy — sales swing quarter to quarter on South African lab-testing delays and tender timing (only INR1 crore in Q3 FY24 versus an expected INR21 crore in Q4), and a US FDA filing was pending that could open the US market.

parts.name: Water-based lubricant jelly
parts.what: A smaller product sold alongside condoms (INR10-15 crore expected in FY23 at 40-45% margins, about INR25 crore supplied to UNFPA in FY23), but UNFPA cancelled outstanding jelly orders in 2023 after a quality parameter deteriorated in transit and storage.

parts.name: In Vitro Diagnostics (IVD) kits
parts.what: A newer diagnostics line of about 16-17 test kits (including HIV and malaria) licensed by the Drug Controller of India, still tiny — roughly INR90 lakh of sales in one quarter versus INR20 lakh the quarter before — with management saying the big export tender opportunity (a INR300-400 crore market) only opens once it has three years of manufacturing history plus WHO and CE certifications.

parts.name: Domestic / B2C business
parts.what: A small home-market segment, about 6-11% of sales, that the new management wants to grow by adding a sales force and selling branded condoms and lubricant jellies through Indian retail channels.

overview.what_it_does: Cyient is an India-based (Hyderabad-headquartered) engineering and technology services company that gets paid by large industrial and technology companies to design, engineer and maintain their products, plants and networks — aircraft and rail systems, telecom and 5G networks, energy and mining plants, automotive systems, geospatial/mapping work and, increasingly, semiconductor chips. Most of its money comes from selling engineering manpower and project work on contract (billed in dollars, euros and pounds), plus a manufacturing arm that builds electronic hardware for customers and a newer chip business that is starting to sell its own chips and intellectual property. Group revenue in the quarters described runs at roughly INR 1,900+ crore (about USD 200+ million) per quarter, with the services arm the bulk of it. It operates globally — India, North America, Europe (including Finland and Portugal via acquisitions), Australia and Taiwan — and grows through frequent acquisitions.

parts.name: DET (Digital, Engineering & Technology) — reported before FY25 simply as 'Services'
parts.what: The core business: engineers designing and supporting customers' products, plants and networks on contract, and the biggest segment by far — about USD 175 million of revenue in a single quarter (Q3 FY25) at roughly a 13-14% operating margin.

parts.name: Transportation business unit (within DET)
parts.what: Aerospace and rail engineering work, including for Cyient's single largest customer (an aerospace company); one of the two largest units inside DET and a steady grower.

parts.name: Connectivity / Communications business unit (within DET)
parts.what: Helps telecom operators plan and engineer their networks, including 5G rollouts and smart infrastructure — strengthened by buying Portugal's Celfinet and one of the two largest DET units, growing about 5-6% in a quarter.

parts.name: Sustainability business unit (within DET)
parts.what: Serves energy, utilities, mining and other asset-heavy industries; described as flattish in the quarters discussed.

parts.name: Plant engineering and consulting (within DET)
parts.what: Designing and digitally modelling industrial plants (including 'digital twins') for manufacturers, built up through the Finnish acquisition Citec and consulting firm Grit, which specialises in metals, mining and plant engineering.

parts.name: Automotive (within DET)
parts.what: A growth area anchored by one very large customer that management expected to become a top-five client, for which Cyient bought a company outright to onboard about 500 ready-trained engineers.

parts.name: Cyient DLM (Design-Led Manufacturing)
parts.what: A separately listed manufacturing arm that designs and builds electronic hardware for customers; around USD 24-25 million of revenue per quarter in FY23, later boosted by the Altek acquisition, and by FY27 running at its highest-ever order book with a book-to-bill above 1.5 and double-digit EBITDA margins.

parts.name: Cyient Semiconductors
parts.what: A carved-out chip subsidiary aiming to be India's first large fabless chip company, with three legs — chip design services, custom ASIC turnkey design-and-supply, and its own power chips/IP (ASSPs) — running about USD 17.9 million of quarterly revenue after buying Kinetic Technologies for ~USD 85 million, with an ASIC pipeline over USD 100 million and outside funding from EAAA at a USD 500 million (INR 4,650 crore) valuation.

parts.name: Others
parts.what: A small residual reporting segment alongside DET, DLM and Semiconductor; includes items such as the 27.6%-owned associate Azimuth whose profits or losses flow into group earnings.

overview.what_it_does: Dabur India Limited is an Indian consumer-goods (FMCG) company that makes and sells everyday branded household products — hair oils, shampoos, toothpaste, air fresheners and mosquito repellents, skin creams, honey and Chyawanprash health supplements, digestive tablets and candies, ayurvedic/over-the-counter remedies, fruit juices and nectars, and cooking staples like spices and edible oils. Many of its products lean on an ayurvedic/herbal or 'natural' positioning, which management repeatedly cites as its main point of difference versus non-herbal rivals. It earns money by selling these low-priced, repeat-purchase items through retail trade, modern trade and e-commerce (emerging channels were around 20% of the India business by FY25), plus a HoReCa channel; growth is described as a mix of volume growth and price increases taken to pass on input-cost inflation. Most of the business is in India, with a meaningful international arm covering the Middle East/North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, Egypt, Turkey, Nepal, Bangladesh, the UK/EU and the US, which is exposed to currency devaluation, tariffs and geopolitical disruption.

parts.name: India / domestic FMCG business
parts.what: The core operation selling Dabur's branded products across India; it is the bulk of consolidated revenue (growing ~6-10% in recent quarters on 3-6% volume growth) and is split by management into Home & Personal Care, Healthcare, and Food & Beverages.

parts.name: Home and Personal Care (HPC)
parts.what: Hair oils, shampoos, toothpaste, home care and skin care — described as the strongest-performing portfolio in recent quarters (10.6% growth in Q3 FY26, 17% in Q4 FY26) and the pillar management invests behind for premiumisation.

parts.name: Hair Care (hair oils and shampoos)
parts.what: Coconut and perfumed hair oils plus shampoos and post-wash products (Vatika, Cool King/Toofani Thanda); a large HPC sub-part where Dabur says its volume market share hit an all-time high of 20%, though recent growth was heavily price-driven by coconut-oil inflation.

parts.name: Oral Care / Toothpaste
parts.what: Herbal toothpastes and tooth powder led by flagship Dabur Red, with Meswak as the premium brand, Dabur Herbal, and Babool at the economy end; management says Dabur oral care reaches 1 in every 2 Indian households and it is the #2 brand in South India.

parts.name: Home Care
parts.what: Air fresheners (Odonil), mosquito repellents (Odomos) and toilet cleaner (Sanifresh) — a consistently fast-growing piece, up 24% in Q4 FY26 with market-share gains in air fresheners.

parts.name: Skin Care
parts.what: Rose water and body washes (Gulabari), bleaches, facial kits and OxyLife; a smaller HPC line growing anywhere from mid-single digits to double digits depending on the quarter.

parts.name: Health Care
parts.what: Health supplements (Chyawanprash, honey, Dabur Glucose), digestives (Hajmola, Pudin Hara, Isabgol) and OTC/ethical ayurvedic medicines (Honitus, Lal Tail, Shilajit, ayurvedic health juices, baby care); a major portfolio that boomed during COVID on immunity products and then normalised.

parts.name: Food and Beverages
parts.what: Real-brand juices, nectars, fruit drinks, milkshakes and coconut water plus a foods/culinary line (Hommade, fats and oils); beverages are highly seasonal and summer-dependent, while foods grew from a ~Rs. 100 crore base in FY22 toward a stated Rs. 500 crore ambition.

parts.name: Badshah (spices)
parts.what: An acquired branded-spices business included in the India numbers, growing about 15% year-on-year in FY25 with strong volume growth, though its exports were hit by tighter overseas regulatory screening of Indian spice shipments.

parts.name: International business
parts.what: Sales in MENA, Egypt, Turkey (Hobi), Sub-Saharan Africa, Nepal, Bangladesh, the UK/EU and the US (Namaste); it has posted strong constant-currency growth (18.4% in Q1 FY25) but reported growth is often eroded by currency devaluation, and recently by Middle East conflict and tariffs.

parts.name: Emerging channels (e-commerce and modern trade)
parts.what: Not a product line but a route to market management tracks closely — e-commerce was ~9% of revenue in FY23 and together with modern trade reached about 20% of the India business by FY25, growing in double digits.

overview.what_it_does: Dalmia Bharat Limited makes and sells cement in India — it digs limestone from its own mines, burns it into clinker at its plants, grinds it into cement, bags it and sells it to builders, contractors, infrastructure projects and individual home-builders through a dealer network. The calls describe it as India's fourth-largest cement player, with capacity of roughly 46-50 million tonnes selling into over 23 states, historically strongest in the East, North-East and South and now pushing into the West and Central regions to become a 'pan-India' player. It earns money on the gap between the price per tonne it realises and its cost per tonne, so management talks almost entirely about volumes (7.4 million tonnes in a quarter), realisation per tonne, and EBITDA per tonne (around INR 901 to INR 1,055), with quarterly revenue of roughly INR 3,300-3,900 crores. Because it is essentially a one-product commodity business, its profits swing with cement prices, with fuel costs like petcoke and coal, and with freight — and management's stated levers are being the lowest-cost producer, selling more premium-branded cement, and adding capacity organically and by buying distressed assets.

parts.name: Cement (the core and effectively the whole business)
parts.what: Manufacturing and selling grey cement — mostly blended cement, which was 82% of the mix in FY23 — from clinker units and grinding units across the East, North-East, South and now West/Central India; this is the only revenue-generating line the calls discuss, at close to INR 3,900 crores of quarterly revenue.

parts.name: Premium products / premiumisation
parts.what: A higher-priced branded range aimed at retail home-builders and channel partners, including a new 'Weather365' premium-plus product launched in FY27; management says premium products had reached 25% of the portfolio and are a main way to lift realisation per tonne without relying on market price rises.

parts.name: Trade vs non-trade sales mix
parts.what: Sales split between the dealer/retail 'trade' channel — about 64% of volumes — and bulk institutional/project sales; trade is the better-priced channel, so the mix is managed deliberately.

parts.name: Captive renewable and waste-heat power
parts.what: Solar, wind, floating-solar and waste-heat-recovery capacity built or contracted (including 127 MW under group captive arrangements) not to sell power but to cut the power-and-fuel bill, which is one of the largest cost lines at around INR 1,000 per tonne; renewable share went from 35% toward a targeted 50%, and the company also targets carbon neutrality by 2040.

parts.name: State government incentives
parts.what: Subsidies earned for operating plants in incentive states, accrued at roughly INR 45-74 crores a quarter with a large uncollected balance outstanding (INR 683 crores in 2022 rising to INR 822 crores by mid-2026) — a real but slow-paying add-on to cement earnings, not a separate business.

parts.name: Capacity expansion and acquisitions
parts.what: An ongoing programme of new plants (Belgaum, Pune, Kadapa, a Chennai bulk terminal) plus buying the Jaypee cement assets, which added 5.2 million tonnes of cement and 3.3 million tonnes of clinker capacity in Central India; management guides capacity from about 50 million tonnes today to roughly 67 million tonnes by Q3 FY28 and an aspiration of 110-130 million tonnes by 2031, funded by capex of about INR 3,200-3,400 crores a year.

overview.what_it_does: Datamatics is a Mumbai-headquartered IT and outsourcing company that sells technology services, back-office processing and customer-service work to large enterprises, billing them under service contracts and, increasingly, licences for its own software products. Its work spans building and running digital systems (cloud, automation, analytics, AI, Salesforce), taking over clients' routine paperwork and data processing, and handling their customer support and experience programmes. It also builds and runs automated fare collection systems for metro rail projects in India, such as the Kolkata and NCRTC deals it says are worth about Rs. 350 crores. The United States is by far its biggest market at roughly 52-56% of revenue, followed by the UK and Europe at around 21-22%, India at 15-17% and the rest of the world at about 8-9%; quarterly revenue has grown from about Rs. 327 crores in mid-2022 to about Rs. 510 crores by the December 2025 quarter, and the company reports zero net debt with net cash and investments of around Rs. 540 crores.

parts.name: Digital Operations
parts.what: Runs clients' back-office and data-processing work for them, delivered on Datamatics' own automation platforms; it is the largest and steadiest segment at roughly half of revenue (Rs. 273.8 crores of Rs. 510.1 crores in the December 2025 quarter, Rs. 694 crores for FY24) with the best profitability, EBIT margins of about 18-24%.

parts.name: Digital Technologies
parts.what: Software and IT services work — cloud, DevOps, low-code/no-code, SaaS platforms, analytics and AI, plus the company's own 'Tru' product suite (TruBot robotic automation, TruCap+ document processing, TruAI, TruBI) and metro fare-collection platforms; it is about a third of revenue (Rs. 169.6 crores in the December 2025 quarter) and was the problem child for years, with margins that went negative in FY23 and only 0.7-4.6% in FY24 before recovering to around 10.8% by FY26.

parts.name: Digital Experiences
parts.what: Manages customer contact and engagement across channels on clients' behalf, covering the whole customer lifecycle; it is the smallest segment at roughly 13-15% of revenue (Rs. 66.7 crores in the December 2025 quarter) and has been soft recently because two clients moved the work to their own in-house centres.

parts.name: Dextara Digital (acquisition)
parts.what: A platinum-level Salesforce services provider bought for roughly Rs. 110 crores in FY24 to push further into the US market and 'hyperscaler' partnerships, aimed at the roughly 25% of Datamatics customers that already use Salesforce.

parts.name: AI and product investment
parts.what: Not a reported segment but a stated spending line of about Rs. 40-50 crores a year on new technology, including partnerships with Microsoft and Google, a small language model and copilot of its own, Gen AI built into the automation products for over 30 customers, and a Google Gemini Enterprise rollout with 200 employees certified in one month.

overview.what_it_does: Data Patterns (India) Limited is a Chennai-based defence and aerospace electronics company that designs, builds and supplies mission-critical electronic systems — radars, electronic warfare equipment, avionics (such as cockpit displays and mission systems for the LCA fighter), communication systems, test equipment and naval systems. Its customers are almost entirely Indian government defence buyers — DRDO, HAL, ECIL, the Ministry of Defence and the Army, Air Force and Navy — with a small but growing export business (repeat work in the UK and a precision approach radar delivered to a European country; export order book about INR53 crore as of May 2026). It earns money from contracts booked into an order book that is worked off over time: first paid development/design contracts, which then convert into higher-volume production orders and follow-on service contracts. Because it designs almost everything in-house rather than assembling imported parts, margins are unusually high — FY26 revenue of INR925 crore with 63% gross margin, 40% EBITDA margin, an order book of roughly INR2,062 crore, and a net-cash (debt-free) balance sheet.

parts.name: Development contracts
parts.what: Paid design-and-build work where the customer (usually DRDO or the MoD) funds Data Patterns to develop a new system or prototype; management calls these the seed of future revenue because they later convert into production orders — roughly 31–53% of revenue depending on the quarter (37% in Q3 FY26).

parts.name: Production contracts
parts.what: Serial manufacture and supply of systems already developed and approved, which is the larger and more repeatable revenue stream — around 50% of revenue in Q1 FY25 and the biggest contributor at 57% in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Service contracts
parts.what: Ongoing support, maintenance and related services on delivered equipment; the smallest of the three contract types at roughly 11% of revenue in Q1 FY25.

parts.name: Radars
parts.what: The company's flagship area — ground, airborne, maritime, fire-control, surveillance and precision approach radars, including a first-of-its-kind Indian deep-space surveillance radar (initial prototype contracts of about INR189 crore and INR173 crore in FY23, with the full-scale versions described as potentially worth thousands of crores).

parts.name: Electronic warfare (EW), including COMINT and ELINT
parts.what: Systems that detect, intercept and jam enemy communications and radar signals, plus self-protection jammer pods for Indian fighter aircraft; management calls it a core strength built over more than a decade with DRDO, and large EW orders from ECIL and the MoD were the headline wins of FY26.

parts.name: Avionics
parts.what: On-board aircraft electronics such as cockpit displays and mission systems, notably for the LCA Mk1A and the smart cockpit for LCA Mark 2 (expected to carry over to the AMCA fighter); early orders were in the INR60–183 crore range and it is described as a repeat-order, high-margin area.

parts.name: Communication systems
parts.what: Military radios, radio relays and related equipment for the armed forces, developed in-house to replace imported kit; listed as a focus area alongside radars and EW but no separate revenue figure is given.

parts.name: Automatic test equipment (ATE), naval systems and other strategic electronics
parts.what: Smaller lines covering ground test/support equipment, naval electronics, fire control systems (e.g. BrahMos), seekers and an autonomous battle-tank autoloader; individually modest orders (single-digit to ~INR31–60 crore) that round out the portfolio.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Direct sales to overseas defence customers — regular repeat business in the UK and transportable precision approach radars delivered and site-accepted in a European country — currently small at about INR53–63 crore of order book but flagged as a strategic long-term growth pillar.

parts.name: In-house / internally funded new product development
parts.what: Self-funded R&D (INR54 crore spent in Q1 FY25 alone out of QIP proceeds) to build products India currently imports, including drone detection/spoofing/jamming and airborne radars — no revenue yet, but management positions it as what moves the company from subsystem supplier to full-system provider and drives future growth.

overview.what_it_does: Dilip Buildcon Limited (DBL) is an Indian construction and infrastructure contractor, headquartered in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, that builds public infrastructure — highways and roads, irrigation systems, water supply schemes, urban development works, metro rail, special bridges and tunnels — almost entirely for government customers such as the national highways ministry/NHAI and state governments (management says roughly 90% of revenue over 20 years has come from the central government and states other than its home state of MP). It makes money mainly by bidding competitively for these projects and getting paid to build them (EPC contracts, where the government pays for construction, and HAM contracts, where DBL also puts in some equity and is repaid over time), booking revenue as work is executed; order inflows were about INR18,548 crores in FY26 against a bid pipeline of over INR80,000 crores. Alongside construction, it runs a contract coal-mining business — operating mines for owners as a Mine Developer and Operator (MDO) — which produced about 28.7 million tonnes of coal in FY26 and is targeted at ~57 million tonnes by FY29. It also owns completed road assets which it transfers into infrastructure investment trusts (InvITs) to recycle cash, and management expects roughly three-quarters of profits to come from these long-life mining and asset businesses by FY29, versus one-quarter from construction.

parts.name: EPC (engineering, procurement and construction)
parts.what: The core contracting business that physically builds roads, irrigation and water-supply schemes, urban infrastructure, metro, bridges and tunnels for government clients — historically the bulk of revenue (around INR10,000 crores a year in FY23 guidance), now described as a 'capital-efficient execution and incubation engine' that gives only 2-3 years of visibility and is expected to shrink to about a quarter of profits by FY29.

parts.name: Roads / highways (within EPC)
parts.what: The original mainstay — highway construction for NHAI and state road agencies — deliberately reduced from 65% of order intake in FY20 to about 37% in FY24 as part of a diversification and risk-reduction strategy.

parts.name: Irrigation, water supply and urban development (within EPC)
parts.what: The newer non-road civil verticals that management pushed into for diversification; in FY24 they made up the majority of new orders (42% irrigation, 35% water supply, 8% urban development), supported by programmes like the Jal Jeevan Mission.

parts.name: Coal MDO / mining vertical
parts.what: Long-tenure contracts to develop and operate coal mines for their owners — mainly the Siarmal mine (about 22.35 million tonnes in FY26) and the Pachhwara mine (about 6.37 million tonnes) — totalling roughly 28.7 million tonnes in FY26, described as high-margin, low-investment-risk, with most capex already spent, and increasingly the company's central EBITDA and cash-flow engine with 25-55 years of revenue visibility.

parts.name: Assets vertical — HAM road projects and InvITs
parts.what: Completed hybrid-annuity road projects that DBL part-owns and then sells or transfers into infrastructure investment trusts to release cash — 7 HAM assets already transferred, the rest to move in tranches through March 2027, with about INR1,600 crores of InvIT units held on the balance sheet (INR1,400 crores in the listed Anantam Highways InvIT and INR200 crores in Shrem InvIT), providing regular distributions and helping cut debt.

overview.what_it_does: DCB Bank is an Indian private-sector bank, listed in Mumbai, that takes deposits from ordinary savers and small businesses through its branch network and lends that money out mainly as small-ticket, secured loans. Its typical borrower is a self-employed person or small business owner taking a loan of roughly Rs. 28-50 lakhs against property or a home, plus farmers, tractor buyers, gold-loan customers and small firms. It earns money in two ways: the spread between what it pays depositors and what it charges borrowers (net interest margin, around 3.3-3.4%, on a yield on advances of about 10.75%), and fee income from things like third-party product distribution, forex, trade and account/overdraft charges (core fee income of about Rs. 198 crores in a quarter). Management repeatedly describes the model as 'secured, small ticket and granular' - a roughly Rs. 45,000-crore-plus balance sheet in 2022 growing at about 17-20% a year, with credit costs guided at 45-55 basis points and full-year profit of Rs. 732 crores in FY26.

parts.name: Mortgages (home loans and business loans / LAP)
parts.what: Loans against residential and commercial property to self-employed and small-business customers - the bank's biggest and most important product, once split roughly half home loans and half loan-against-property, now deliberately shifted to about 70:30 in favour of higher-yield business loans, with quarterly disbursements around Rs. 1,500 crores.

parts.name: Gold loans
parts.what: Small loans against gold jewellery given at branches at a conservative maximum 75% loan-to-value (versus the 85% RBI allows); a book of roughly Rs. 7,000-7,500 crores, about 20-22% of total loans, with low yield but very low cost and almost no actual credit loss.

parts.name: Deposits and CASA / branch banking
parts.what: The funding side - savings and current accounts plus term deposits gathered 'brick-by-brick' in small tickets from a wide base (top 20 depositors under 7% of deposits); CASA was about 25-26% of deposits, savings balances growing 27% a year, and deposit growth is deliberately kept ahead of loan growth.

parts.name: Agri and Inclusive Banking (AIB)
parts.what: Rural and farm lending including Kisan Credit Card (KCC) and tractor loans, which also helps meet priority-sector requirements; a regular contributor to growth and a periodic source of slippages that mostly get recovered or upgraded.

parts.name: SME / MSME lending
parts.what: Working-capital and term lending to small and medium businesses, including the short-cycle TReDS bill-discounting product (90-120 day tenor), where quarterly disbursals look large relative to the outstanding book.

parts.name: Commercial vehicle loans
parts.what: Financing for commercial vehicles, described as a big product alongside mortgages, with slippages tracked against pre-COVID levels.

parts.name: Corporate, construction finance and educational institution loans
parts.what: Lending to companies, builders/projects and schools and colleges; called out in FY26 as meaningful contributors to the 18% year-on-year advances growth.

parts.name: Co-lending partnerships
parts.what: Loans originated jointly with partner lenders under agreed limits - lower yield but also lower cost; used opportunistically and then deliberately shrunk to under 15% of the book (13.9% by March 2026).

parts.name: Microfinance
parts.what: Small high-yield unsecured loans, which the bank scaled back from 2024 after foreseeing a weakening microfinance environment, giving up the associated high yields.

parts.name: Treasury and financial institutions
parts.what: Manages the bank's investments, liquidity and forex; can produce lumpy gains (Rs. 154-155 crores in one year, Rs. 101 crores in a quarter) but contributed 'nothing' in some recent quarters, which management is offsetting with repeatable core fee income.

parts.name: Fee income / third-party distribution
parts.what: Selling third-party products, plus forex, trade and penal charges - the deliberately grown 'repeatable' earnings stream, rising from Rs. 114 crores a quarter in FY25 to Rs. 198 crores by Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Digital banking
parts.what: App and online account-opening products such as Zippi+, plus heavy investment in core systems (Finacle, FinOne lending system, TCS treasury system, AML and cyber-security tools) to support growth without adding staff - headcount actually fell from about 11,900 to 11,554 while business grew ~18% a year.

overview.what_it_does: DCM Shriram is an Indian diversified manufacturer that makes and sells industrial chemicals, plastics, sugar and ethanol, farm inputs, and branded windows and doors. Its customers are mostly other businesses — alumina, paper, textile, detergent and pharma makers who buy caustic soda; PVC and plastics processors; oil marketing companies that buy its ethanol under India's fuel-blending programme; and Indian farmers who buy its seeds, crop-protection products, specialty nutrients and subsidised urea — plus retail homeowners and real-estate projects that buy Fenesta windows. It makes money by processing raw materials (salt and power into caustic soda and chlorine, sugarcane into sugar and ethanol, natural gas into urea) and selling at prevailing commodity prices, so earnings swing with caustic/chlorine 'ECU' realisations, PVC prices, sugarcane costs and government policy on sugar, ethanol and import duties. Operations are entirely India-based — chemical complexes at Kota and Bharuch, sugar and distillery units in Uttar Pradesh (Ajbapur, Loni), window fabrication plants including Hyderabad and Bhubaneswar — with a small overseas seed business and some exports; quarterly net revenue was around Rs 2,700-2,900 crore in FY23-FY25 rising to Rs 3,811 crore in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Chemicals (Chlor-Alkali)
parts.what: Makes caustic soda and chlorine plus downstream products — hydrogen peroxide, epichlorohydrin (commissioned Oct 2025), aluminium chloride and calcium chloride — and management calls it a core growth engine, with revenue up 30% year-on-year in Q3 FY26 and the bulk of the Rs 3,500 crore capex programme (new 850 TPD caustic capacity, 120 MW captive power, green power projects) directed here.

parts.name: Vinyl (PVC and carbide)
parts.what: Produces PVC resin and calcium carbide sold into agriculture and construction end-uses; it is the most volatile part, repeatedly squeezed by cheap Chinese imports and 'suboptimal' at low PVC prices — revenue fell 53% year-on-year in one quarter (Q2 FY23) — and is reported together with Chemicals as the combined 'Chloro-Vinyl' segment, the company's largest revenue driver.

parts.name: Sugar and Ethanol
parts.what: Crushes sugarcane at its Uttar Pradesh mills (473 lakh quintals in season 2025-26 at 10.8% recovery) into sugar sold domestically and exported, and distils ethanol sold to oil marketing companies for petrol blending; roughly comparable in revenue to chemicals (Rs 617 crore in Q2 FY23) but margins have been under sustained pressure because state-set cane prices rise faster than sugar and ethanol realisations.

parts.name: Fenesta Building Systems
parts.what: The consumer-facing arm that makes and installs branded UPVC and aluminium windows and doors, and has moved into glass façades, selling to homeowners and real-estate projects; management describes it as a steady growth business expanding geographies and product range, with an aluminium extrusion plant at Kota being commissioned.

parts.name: Shriram Farm Solutions (Agri-Inputs)
parts.what: Sells seeds, crop-protection chemicals and specialty plant nutrition to Indian farmers, backed by an R&D centre in Ludhiana and tie-ups with global technology partners; it is a consistent double-digit growth contributor, with research wheat seed described as a market-leadership product.

parts.name: Fertilisers (Urea)
parts.what: Runs a natural-gas-based urea plant whose economics are set by government subsidy and gas costs; management describes it as a stable, low-drama business where the focus is energy efficiency and cost control, though subsidy receivables ballooned when gas prices spiked in FY23.

parts.name: Bioseed
parts.what: Breeds and sells hybrid seeds for crops such as corn, paddy, wheat and mustard in India and in international markets; it is the smallest and weakest agri unit — management said in 2022 it should 'turn around over a period of next 2 years' — and its sales track farmer income and monsoon conditions closely.

parts.name: Advanced materials / Shriram Polytech and Hindusthan Speciality Chemicals
parts.what: Subsidiary-level businesses extending the chemicals chain — Hindusthan Speciality Chemicals in epoxy resins (helped by anti-dumping duty from Nov 2025) and Shriram Polytech in plastic compounding, in which the company sold a 50% stake to form a joint venture with Teknor Apex in FY26; described as a growing 'glycerine to ECH to epoxy' value chain rather than a large current earner.

overview.what_it_does: Deepak Fertilisers and Petrochemicals Corporation (DFPCL) is an Indian manufacturer that turns imported/contracted natural gas (LNG) and ammonia into a chain of industrial chemicals, mining explosives chemicals and fertilisers, selling almost entirely to business customers in India — mining and steel companies, chemical and pharmaceutical manufacturers, and farmers through fertiliser dealers. It makes money on the spread between raw material costs (mainly LNG, ammonia and propylene) and the prices of finished products such as technical ammonium nitrate, nitric acid, isopropyl alcohol (IPA) and NPK fertilisers, so profits swing with input prices, monsoons, mining activity and government fertiliser subsidies. Management describes the group as running from gas to ammonia to nitric acid to downstream products, with 9 nitric acid plants and 4 ammonium nitrate plants and 45 years of customer relationships, and it is pushing from plain commodity products into branded, crop- or customer-specific 'specialty' grades and bundled services to earn higher margins. Operations are in India — plants at Taloja, Dahej and a new site at Gopalpur in the east — with consolidated FY26 revenue of about INR 11,506 crores and EBITDA of about INR 1,684 crores; the three businesses have been approved by NCLT to be demerged into separate legal entities.

parts.name: Mining Chemicals / Technical Ammonium Nitrate (TAN)
parts.what: Makes technical ammonium nitrate, the chemical used in explosives for blasting in coal mines, limestone/cement and steel-related mining, and is moving from selling the product alone to 'total cost of operations' mining solutions including an acquired explosives unit and last-mile delivery to mines; management calls it a core business running above 100% capacity utilisation in good quarters, targeting a top-3 global position once the new Gopalpur plant (91% complete as of Jan 2026) starts up.

parts.name: Industrial Chemicals
parts.what: Sells nitric acid (including specialty stainless-steel and solar grades) and isopropyl alcohol (IPA, including a pharma grade) to downstream chemical, steel and pharmaceutical customers; nitric acid also feeds the company's own ammonium nitrate production, and the calls describe it as Asia's largest acid position with a new Dahej acid project 79% complete as of Jan 2026, though pricing has been squeezed by imports and weak propylene/acetone economics.

parts.name: Crop Nutrition Business (CNB) / Fertilisers
parts.what: Manufactures and sells bulk NPK fertilisers plus branded specialty products (Bensulf, Croptek and Smartek crop-specific grades, and specialty fertilisers via a tie-up with Israel's Haifa Group) to Indian farmers, with revenue depending on the monsoon, Kharif/Rabi sowing and government subsidy support; it was the fastest-growing segment in FY26 (Q3 revenue up 26% year-on-year) and specialty plus Croptek grades made up about 30% of its revenue.

parts.name: Ammonia plant (raw material / value-chain backbone)
parts.what: A world-scale ammonia plant commissioned to feed all three businesses instead of buying imported ammonia, described as running at ~98% capacity and acting as a risk mitigator against raw material price swings, backed by a 15-year long-term LNG supply contract with a Norwegian supplier whose first cargo arrived in 2026.

overview.what_it_does: Deepak Nitrite is an Indian chemicals manufacturer that makes industrial and specialty chemicals in its own plants (sites named on the calls include Nandesari, Dahej and Vadodara/Savli) and sells them in bulk to other manufacturers rather than to consumers. Its two revenue engines are Phenolics — phenol, acetone and IPA, which are basic building-block chemicals — and Advanced Intermediates, a range of nitration, fluorination, diazotization and amination chemistries sold to agrochemical, pharmaceutical, dye and other downstream industries, with roughly 40% of DNL's topline and 20–25% of Phenolics under contract as of FY23. It earns money on the spread between feedstock costs (crude-linked inputs) and product prices, so profits swing with global chemical pricing, and management repeatedly stresses backward integration, high plant utilisation and cost control as the way to protect margins. It is overwhelmingly a domestic business — the India-to-export revenue mix was 82:18 in Q1 FY23 and 86:14 in Q4 FY26 — and for FY26 it reported consolidated revenue of ₹7,947 crore, EBITDA of ₹1,041 crore and PAT of ₹551 crore.

parts.name: Phenolics (Deepak Phenolics / DPL)
parts.what: Makes and sells phenol, acetone and IPA to Indian customers from a large plant run at high utilisation; this is the bigger and steadier of the two segments — ₹1,429 crore of revenue and ₹287 crore EBIT (20% margin) in Q4 FY26, and management calls it the domestic market leader and a 'consistent performer'.

parts.name: Advanced Intermediates (AI)
parts.what: The older specialty-chemicals business built on nitration, fluorination, diazotization and amination chemistries, plus products like sodium nitrite and nitrate, sold to agrochemical, pharma and other industrial customers; smaller and far more volatile — ₹708 crore of revenue but only ₹34 crore EBIT in Q4 FY26, squeezed for several quarters by cheap Chinese supply and global oversupply.

parts.name: Advanced Materials / polycarbonate (Deepak Chem Tech Limited, 100% subsidiary)
parts.what: A new, not-yet-operating business: an approximately ₹5,000 crore project to make polycarbonate resins in India under a technology licence from Trinseo, including relocating a 165,000 tonne-per-year plant from Stade, Germany — aimed at a ~240,000 tonne Indian market currently met entirely by imports, and pitched as the downstream extension of the phenol chain.

parts.name: Solvents and new capacity projects
parts.what: A pipeline of plants that either feed the existing businesses or add new products — nitric acid (WNA and CNA), nitration and hydrogenation blocks, photochlorination, acetophenone, an R&D centre at Savli, and MIBK/MIBC solvents plus multipurpose agrochemical intermediates due to commission in Q2 FY27 — described as completing vertical integration from ammonia-nitration to amines and cutting dependence on outside suppliers.

overview.what_it_does: Delhivery is an Indian logistics company that picks up, carries and delivers other companies' goods across India — everything from a single e-commerce parcel to pallets of factory freight — and calls itself the country's largest integrated logistics platform. Its customers are businesses: online marketplaces, direct-to-consumer brands, SMEs, and large manufacturers in autos, electricals, FMCG, paints and engineering, plus some consumer-to-consumer shipping through its own app; it had ~29,000 customers in FY23 and over 51,000 by Q3 FY26. It makes money by charging freight/service fees per parcel or per tonne shipped (and fees for warehousing and supply-chain work), earning more as volumes and per-shipment yields rise while spreading costs over a fixed network. It runs that network itself — about 21.9 million sq ft of hubs, gateways, automated sort centres, processing centres and delivery centres reaching ~18,838 pin codes across India, with a 71,000-strong team, 67,000 partner agents and a 21,000 fleet — and operates almost entirely within India, with cross-border services to and from abroad. FY26 revenue from services was about Rs 10,486 crore with PAT of Rs 347 crore, and it closed the year with over Rs 4,500 crore of cash after acquiring rival Ecom Express.

parts.name: Express Parcel
parts.what: Door-to-door delivery of individual e-commerce and D2C parcels (including same-day and heavier 'heavy goods' items) — the biggest business at roughly two-thirds of revenue, Rs 6,685 crore and over a billion shipments in FY26, at the top of its 16–18% service-EBITDA margin band.

parts.name: Part Truckload (PTL) / freight
parts.what: Consolidated business-to-business freight where several customers' loads share a truck, sold by the tonne — about 20–21% of revenue, Rs 2,254 crore and 2 million metric tonnes in FY26, and the segment whose margins management has been steadily repairing since the SpotOn acquisition and integration in FY22–23.

parts.name: Truckload (FTL / full truckload)
parts.what: Booking whole trucks for large single shipments, won largely through customer tenders (RFQs); a smaller, more opportunistic line that management says it bids on selectively rather than chasing volume.

parts.name: Supply Chain Services / Solutions (SCS)
parts.what: Running warehouses and end-to-end distribution for large manufacturers and retailers (autos, electricals, FMCG, appliances, luxury/lifestyle) under long-cycle contracts — Rs 729 crore of revenue in FY26, small but turned profitable this year with service EBITDA quadrupling to Rs 79 crore (10.9%) after exiting loss-making accounts such as a quick-commerce mother warehouse.

parts.name: Cross-Border
parts.what: Shipping goods between India and other countries, including ocean freight and a new 'Delhivery International' air economy product aimed at SME exporters — a small line whose results swing with global freight rates and volumes.

parts.name: Delhivery Direct (local / rapid)
parts.what: On-demand intra-city delivery and consumer-to-consumer shipping via the Delhivery app, recently extended to Mumbai and Hyderabad — an early-stage growth bet, not yet a material revenue contributor.

parts.name: Technology, data and engineering (incl. TransportOne SaaS)
parts.what: In-house software and data science that runs the network, now also sold externally — the TransportOne SaaS product, a Freight Index One benchmark, patented address/ID systems and R&D in automation, robotics and delivery drones; described as a competitive moat rather than a large standalone revenue line.

parts.name: Financial services (new vertical)
parts.what: One of the 'next growth pillars' management says it is now funding from core transport cash flows, alongside local, cross-border and rapid; described as a long-cycle bet with no revenue detail given in the calls.

overview.what_it_does: Devyani International (DIL) runs fast-food restaurants and coffee shops — it does not own most of the brands it sells under, but operates them as a franchisee, mainly KFC and Pizza Hut (Yum! brands) plus Costa Coffee, alongside its own brands like Vaango and Biryani By Kilo. It makes money by selling food and beverages directly to walk-in diners, takeaway and delivery customers, so revenue is essentially store count times average daily sales per store; the calls track gross margin (~69-71%), 'brand contribution' margin per brand, and pre-IndAS EBITDA. Its main market is India — 215 cities as of Aug 2022, expanding into non-metro towns, food courts and airports — with international operations in Nepal, Nigeria and Thailand (Thailand KFC acquired in Jan 2024). The network grew from 1,008 stores in June 2022 to 2,256 stores at the end of FY26, with consolidated quarterly revenue of about INR 1,441 crore in Q3 FY26; a merger with Sapphire Foods is proposed, targeted for completion by end of FY27.

parts.name: KFC (India)
parts.what: Fried-chicken quick-service restaurants and the company's biggest and healthiest business — 783 stores and INR 586 crore of revenue in Q4 FY26 with 17.0% brand contribution margin, and management calls it the anchor of growth.

parts.name: Pizza Hut (India)
parts.what: Pizza restaurants and delivery, the problem child of the portfolio — 639 stores at end-FY26 with same-store sales down 3.7% and slightly negative brand contribution, so management has stopped net store additions and is shutting loss-making outlets.

parts.name: Franchise Brands (Costa Coffee and others)
parts.what: Coffee shops run under franchise, a much smaller line — 192 Costa stores and INR 45 crore of quarterly revenue in Q1 FY25, growing about 3% year-on-year in Q4 FY26 with a 16.1% brand contribution margin.

parts.name: Own Brands (Vaango, Biryani By Kilo, Goila Butter Chicken)
parts.what: Indian-cuisine brands the company owns outright, acquired via Sky Gate Hospitality — small but improving, reaching break-even brand EBITDA in Q3 FY26 ahead of guidance and now expanding through smaller 'Express' formats.

parts.name: International business (Thailand, Nepal, Nigeria)
parts.what: KFC and related stores outside India — 363 stores and INR 390 crore of quarterly revenue in Q1 FY25, with Thailand the growth engine and Nigeria a drag from currency devaluation (an INR 22.5 crore loss in Q1 FY25).

parts.name: Institutional / high-footfall business
parts.what: Outlets in food courts, airports and similar captive locations, described as a focus area for making the brands more accessible rather than as a separately sized segment.

overview.what_it_does: Divi's Laboratories is an Indian pharmaceutical manufacturer that makes the active chemical ingredients (APIs) and intermediates that go into finished medicines, rather than selling branded medicines to patients itself. It sells to other drug companies: generic drug makers who buy its off-patent APIs, and large multinational innovator ("big pharma") companies who hire it to develop and manufacture the molecules in their own pipelines under contract — a business management calls Custom Synthesis or CDMO work.
