Revenue comes from selling these chemicals by volume, roughly split half-and-half between generics and custom synthesis (47%/53% in Q1 FY23, 51%/49% in Q1 FY25), with about 86-90% of sales exported and roughly 70-74% going to regulated markets like the US and Europe. It manufactures at its own plants in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh in India — Unit 1 at Choutuppal, Unit 2, and a large greenfield Unit 3 at Kakinada — which are inspected by the US FDA; quarterly consolidated revenue ran about Rs. 2,343 crores in Q1 FY23 rising to about Rs. 2,986 crores in Q4 FY26, with EBITDA margins around 40%.

parts.name: Generics
parts.what: Sells off-patent active pharmaceutical ingredients it makes in bulk to generic drug manufacturers; it is roughly half the business (51% of the product mix in Q1 FY25, 47% in Q1 FY23), with management repeatedly describing stable volumes but a competitive, deflationary pricing environment offset by backward integration and process efficiency.

parts.name: Custom Synthesis (CDMO)
parts.what: Develops and manufactures molecules exclusively for large innovator pharma customers across clinical Phase-II/III and commercial stages, and is the other roughly half of revenue (49-53% of product mix); management says existing major commercial projects with big pharma keep performing and the pipeline of RFPs, validations and near-commercial molecules stays active.

parts.name: Nutraceuticals (carotenoids)
parts.what: A separate 20-year-old product line making carotenoids/nutrition ingredients, running about Rs. 178-190 crores a quarter (Rs. 186 crores in Q1 FY23, Rs. 178 crores in Q1 FY25) — so a small slice of total revenue, under 10% — where capacity was doubled and management expects continued growth.

parts.name: Peptides
parts.what: A growing capability inside the business making protected amino acids, peptide building blocks and fragments used in GLP-1 and GLP-2 drugs, supported by investment in both solid-phase and liquid-phase synthesis; management describes customer programs across all clinical phases and several validated fragments, but gives no revenue figure.

parts.name: Contrast Media APIs
parts.what: A product family within the generics portfolio — imaging-agent ingredients — where the company filed a DMF for one new contrast media API and had several more under development as of Aug 2022; described as a new-product growth area, not sized separately.

parts.name: Unit 3 / Kakinada and backward integration
parts.what: A large new manufacturing site in Andhra Pradesh (200-acre Phase-I, on land the company waited years to receive) that mainly makes its own starting materials and intermediates instead of buying them, cutting input cost and supply risk; it absorbed Rs. 1,018 crores of spend through Q1 FY25 and now also frees up GMP space at Units 1 and 2 for generics and custom synthesis.

parts.name: Technology platforms
parts.what: Cross-cutting manufacturing capabilities management invests in to win more complex work — continuous flow chemistry, photochemistry, biocatalysis, process automation and high-potency antibody-drug-conjugate handling — funded out of a fairly modest capex budget (about Rs. 500-600 crores excluding Kakinada, per the Aug 2022 call).

overview.what_it_does: DLF Limited is an Indian real estate company that builds and sells homes and also owns commercial property it rents out. On the development side ("DevCo", largely through DLF Home Developers), it builds and sells apartments, floors and luxury/super-luxury residences to individual home buyers, mainly in Gurugram (NCR), plus Mumbai, Goa and other cities — booking sales up front and collecting cash in instalments as construction milestones are hit (record collections of about INR 13,500 crores in FY26 and new sales bookings of INR 20,143 crores). On the rental or "annuity" side (mostly held through DLF Cyber City Developers Ltd, DCCDL), it owns roughly 50 million square feet of offices, shopping malls and data centres that it leases to corporate tenants and retailers for recurring rent, at about 95% occupancy. Money therefore comes from two streams: one-off profits on homes sold (gross margins in the 40-50%+ range) and steady rental income (DCCDL revenue near INR 7,400 crores in FY26), with operations concentrated in Gurugram/Delhi NCR and extending to Chennai, Mumbai, Goa and Noida.

parts.name: Development business ("DevCo" / DLF Home Developers)
parts.what: Builds and sells residential projects — plotted floors, apartments and townships such as DLF City Floors, Privana in Gurugram and West Park in Mumbai — and is the group's main sales engine, delivering INR 20,143 crores of new sales bookings in FY26 and now run with zero gross debt.

parts.name: Super-luxury residential (The Camellias, The Dahlias)
parts.what: A premium slice of the housing business selling very large, very expensive homes (The Dahlias filed at roughly INR 26,000 crores of revenue with 70%+ margins, minimum unit size 10,300 sq ft) to wealthy buyers from across India and abroad; management treats it as a separate, slow-burn sales process and it drove most of Q4 FY26 sales.

parts.name: Rental / annuity business (DCCDL and DLF's own RentCo)
parts.what: Owns and leases income-producing property — about 50 million sq ft at ~95% occupancy generating roughly INR 7,400 crores of DCCDL revenue in FY26 — with management guiding to mid-teens growth in net operating income over the next four to five years; most of it sits in DCCDL, though DLF Limited's own smaller rental pool (under 10% of the total in 2024) is being grown.

parts.name: Offices
parts.what: The largest part of the rental business — campuses like DLF Cyber City Gurugram, Downtown Gurgaon, Downtown Chennai and the Atrium Place joint venture with Hines — leased to global capability centres and BFSI/technology companies, running at 98-99% occupancy in non-SEZ space and 88-89% in SEZs.

parts.name: Retail (shopping malls)
parts.what: Owns and operates malls at 97-98% occupancy earning rent from retailers, with income from existing malls growing about 10-11% a year; three new malls — Midtown Plaza, Summit Plaza and Promenade Goa — are being opened, and management has long aimed to roughly double the retail footprint, including a Mall of India in Gurugram.

parts.name: Data centres
parts.what: A newer rental asset class in Noida, where a second data centre building began earning rent in Q3 FY26 and a third is under construction; small relative to offices and retail but a growing use of rental capital.

overview.what_it_does: Avenue Supermarts runs DMart, a chain of large value-retail supermarkets in India that sell everyday household goods — food and staples, non-food FMCG items like home and personal care, and general merchandise and apparel — to mass-market, price-conscious shoppers. It makes money by buying in bulk and selling cheap at high volume through its own physical stores: roughly 35.3 crore bills (customer transactions) in FY25 on standalone revenue of about INR 57,790 crores, at an EBITDA margin near 8% and a PAT margin near 5%. Growth comes mainly from opening more stores — 50 in FY22, 41 in FY24, 50 in FY25, taking retail business area past 15 million square feet — using a 'cluster-based' strategy of adding stores densely in existing markets, mostly on owned rather than leased real estate, with no external borrowings. It operates only in India, across many states, with management calling the North of India its main remaining 'white space', and it supplements the stores with an online grocery arm and small in-store food and grocery-packing businesses.

parts.name: DMart stores (standalone brick-and-mortar retail)
parts.what: The core business: physically operated value supermarkets selling Foods, Non-Foods (FMCG) and General Merchandise & Apparel, which is essentially all of the company's revenue (INR 49,533 crores in FY24, INR 57,790 crores in FY25 standalone), with the non-grocery General Merchandise & Apparel piece running about 22%–23% of the mix versus 27%–28% before COVID.

parts.name: Foods
parts.what: Groceries and staples such as agri products and edible oils — the largest and growing share of the sales mix, helped in FY24 by unusually high agri food inflation.

parts.name: Non-Foods (FMCG)
parts.what: Everyday branded consumer products other than food, such as home and personal care; a steady but slightly shrinking share of the mix in FY24.

parts.name: General Merchandise & Apparel (GMA)
parts.what: Higher-margin discretionary goods and clothing aimed at mass-market buyers; it fell from the old 27%–28% of sales to roughly 22%–23%, was under stress in FY22 as lower-middle-class shoppers postponed purchases, and by FY24 apparel had become the fastest-growing category after internal fixes to leadership, teams and sizing.

parts.name: DMart Ready / Avenue E-Commerce Limited
parts.what: The online grocery subsidiary, deliberately expanded slowly — 12 cities in mid-2022, 24 cities by FY25, with the model pivoted from store-pickup-plus-delivery to mainly home delivery; sales grew to about INR 2,900 crores in FY24 (+32%) and about 21% again in FY25, but it still loses money (INR 185 crores loss in FY24, INR 247 crores in FY25).

parts.name: Avenue Food Plaza
parts.what: Small ready-to-eat / takeaway fresh-food stalls inside DMart stores, described by management as 'the cherry on the cake' for shoppers — tiny relative to the group (INR 177 crores of sales in FY24) and loss-making because it is still in an expansion phase.

parts.name: Align Retail Trades
parts.what: The in-house grocery procurement, processing and packing subsidiary that sells entirely to DMart's own stores; about INR 2,800 crores of sales and INR 33 crores of profit in FY24, growing roughly 19% in FY25.

overview.what_it_does: DOMS Industries makes and sells stationery and art supplies — pencils, crayons, pens, sketch pens, art materials, notebooks and paper products, school kits, pencil boxes and school bags — mainly under its own DOMS brand (plus smaller brands like C3, Amariz and Fixy Fix). It sells to ordinary consumers, mostly school children and their parents, and to offices, reaching them through a large distributor network covering all 28 states and union territories of India as well as exports to 44 countries. It earns money by manufacturing these goods in its own heavily backward-integrated factories at Umargaon (Gujarat) and Bari Brahmana (Jammu) and selling them at a markup; sales are seasonal, peaking around the back-to-school season. India is by far the main market at over 85% of sales, with exports (Nepal, Sri Lanka, Middle East, Africa, and newer markets served through its Italian partner FILA's network) making up the rest; group revenue was about INR 2,326 crores in FY26 with roughly 17% EBITDA margin and about 10% net margin.

parts.name: Scholastic stationery
parts.what: Core school-writing products such as pencils and, more recently, pens and mechanical pencils; one of the two biggest core categories management repeatedly names as driving growth, with capacity added for it almost every year.

parts.name: Scholastic art material
parts.what: Crayons, colours, sketch pens, acrylic markers and similar art supplies for school children; the other big core category, with growth in FY26 helped by added capacity and modernised processes.

parts.name: Paper stationery
parts.what: Notebooks and paper-based products, made partly through subsidiaries Pioneer Stationery and the proposed Super Treads acquisition (aimed at strengthening eastern India); management calls it a capacity-expansion priority rather than the largest category.

parts.name: Kits and combos
parts.what: Bundled gift/stationery packs sold as a single unit; described as doing 'pretty well' and a repeated growth driver, partly taking sales that would otherwise sit in the stationery and art categories.

parts.name: Office supplies
parts.what: Products for office use including newly launched stamp pads; called out as the fastest-growing category in Q3 and Q4 FY26 on the back of added capacity and good market reception.

parts.name: Hobby and craft
parts.what: Craft and hobby products for children and hobbyists; a smaller category but flagged as seeing 'robust demand growth' in FY26 from new, utility-focused launches.

parts.name: Fine art products
parts.what: Higher-end art materials for serious artists; listed as one of the seven categories but barely discussed on the calls, suggesting it is small.

parts.name: Baby hygiene (Uniclan Healthcare)
parts.what: Acquired subsidiary selling diapers and baby hygiene products — a meaningful new leg that added roughly 10 percentage points to FY25 group growth, is seasonal (strong in winter, weak in Q4), and carries lower margins that pulled group EBITDA margin down in FY26.

parts.name: School bags and pencil boxes (SKIDO Industries and the Seven SpA JV)
parts.what: A newer line launched in FY25/FY26 selling DOMS-branded school bags and metal pencil boxes, to be extended via a 50-50 JV with FILA group company Seven SpA for premium backpacks, bags and pencil cases; still early-stage but expected to be a future growth driver.

parts.name: Micro Wood (subsidiary)
parts.what: In-house supplier of wood/packaging inputs to DOMS — part of the backward-integration strategy rather than a separate consumer business; its consolidation helped lift margins in FY24.

parts.name: Exports / FILA distribution tie-up
parts.what: Direct export of DOMS-branded products to Nepal, Sri Lanka, the Middle East and Africa, plus newer markets like Chile, Mexico, Canada, Europe, Turkey, South Africa and Australia through partner FILA's network; grew over 15% in 9M FY26 but is under 15% of total sales.

overview.what_it_does: Dr. Reddy's Laboratories is an India-based (Hyderabad-headquartered) pharmaceutical company that manufactures and sells medicines — mostly generic copies of drugs whose patents have expired, plus the active chemical ingredients that go into them. It sells to pharmacy chains, wholesalers, hospitals, doctors and other drug makers across the US, Europe, Russia and other emerging markets, and India, with quarterly consolidated revenue running roughly Rs. 6,300-8,100 crore (about US$775-920 million) over the period of these calls. Money is made by winning regulatory approvals and launching new products (7 US launches in one quarter, 10 in Europe, 31 across emerging markets), then selling volume against steady price erosion; the occasional exclusive or 'complex' launch — lenalidomide capsules, semaglutide, bosutinib with 180-day exclusivity — can swing profits sharply in either direction. Alongside the core generics business it is building newer engines: consumer health brands, biosimilars, peptides, contract manufacturing services for other companies, and in-licensed innovative drugs it distributes in selected markets.

parts.name: Global Generics
parts.what: The main business — off-patent finished medicines sold under the company's own or partner labels, carrying gross margins in the 52%-65% range and made up of the four geographic units below.

parts.name: North America Generics
parts.what: Generic medicines sold in the US, the single largest unit at $351 million in Q2 FY23 rising to $463 million in Q1 FY25 per quarter, driven by new launches including lenalidomide, and the swing factor behind most of the company's growth and decline.

parts.name: Europe
parts.what: Generics across European countries, a smaller unit at about €52 million a quarter in FY23 growing around 10% year-on-year, with roughly 10 new product launches per quarter.

parts.name: Emerging Markets (including Russia)
parts.what: Generics sold across Russia, CIS and other developing markets, around Rs. 1,225 crore a quarter, with Russia the biggest piece and a source of volatility from currency swings and channel-stocking cycles.

parts.name: India
parts.what: Branded prescription medicines sold at home, around Rs. 1,150 crore a quarter and ranked #10 by value on IQVIA's moving-annual-total, where management is growing big brands, in-licensing drugs (Vonoprazan, toripalimab) and divesting non-core brands.

parts.name: PSAI (Pharmaceutical Services and Active Ingredients)
parts.what: Sells bulk active pharmaceutical ingredients and development/manufacturing services to other drug companies — much smaller (about $81 million a quarter) and far less profitable, with gross margins swinging between roughly 4% and 23%.

parts.name: Consumer Healthcare
parts.what: A newer over-the-counter/wellness business built by acquisition and partnership — the Nicotinell nicotine-replacement brands bought outside the US in 2024, and a nutraceuticals joint venture with Nestlé in India.

parts.name: CDMO / Aurigene Pharmaceutical Services
parts.what: A contract development and manufacturing arm that makes drugs for other companies, including a 70,000 sq ft biologics facility opened in Hyderabad in 2024.

parts.name: Biosimilars, peptides and innovation
parts.what: Future growth engines funded by R&D of roughly 7%-9% of sales, covering copies of biologic drugs (e.g. a denosumab partnership with Alvotech), peptide products such as semaglutide, and in-licensed novel therapies and devices like Nerivio for migraine.

overview.what_it_does: Dynamatic Technologies is a Bangalore-headquartered company that designs and manufactures highly engineered mechanical products, chiefly hydraulic gear pumps and complex aerostructures (metal parts and assemblies for aircraft). It sells to tractor and equipment makers on the hydraulics side, and to aircraft makers and defence customers on the aerospace side — Airbus for commercial work, Boeing for defence work, plus Indian programmes with HAL and DRDO such as the Sukhoi, the Tejas front fuselage and the Lakshya drone. It makes money by building parts and assemblies to customer specification under long-term supply positions, often as the sole source, with management calling the pump business a 'door opener' to selling higher-value systems (a Rs 1,800 single pump becoming a Rs 4,500 double pump, and Rs 25,000-30,000 power lift systems) — a shift they describe as going from market share to wallet share. Operations run out of Bangalore and Coimbatore in India plus significant manufacturing in the UK (Swindon and a plant near Heathrow) and Germany, with a very small facility in North America; the deliberate model is handcrafted assembly and engineering in India combined with robotic machining in the UK.

parts.name: Hydraulics
parts.what: Makes hydraulic gear pumps for tractors — management says roughly one in three tractors made anywhere in the world has a Dynamatic pump inside, spanning the world's smallest to biggest tractors — and is now extending into power lift systems and steering; it employs about a thousand workers, has plants in Peenya (Bangalore) and a large UK plant bought from a competitor, and sells UK-made units at around £2,000 (about Rs 1.8-2 lakh) each.

parts.name: Aerospace
parts.what: Precision manufacturer of complex aerostructures for both commercial and military aircraft — sole supplier of the flap track beam assembly for the Airbus A318/A319/A320/A321 family, in production on A220 emergency hatches, and recently awarded what management calls the largest order in India's history covering all A220 door variants (passenger, service, over-wing exit and cargo); it is the growth engine management is pointing to ('blue sky above us'), and the aerospace site alone gathers 3,000-4,000 people with families.

parts.name: Defence / military work
parts.what: Supplies defence programmes as a deliberate counterweight to commercial aviation — hydraulics for Indian battle tanks and the Arjun, structures from the Lakshya target drone up to about one-sixth of the Sukhoi airframe and the Tejas front fuselage, and defence work for Boeing including the F-15EX; management says this kept the company running when commercial jetliner suppliers went bankrupt during the pandemic, and it holds 90 acres at Sulur Air Force base for further military expansion.

parts.name: Automotive (residual)
parts.what: Described as 'the vestiges' of the old automotive business — the company still owns what it calls one of the world's best automotive foundries, located in Germany, and also provides material science capability, after selling its Chennai aluminium, steel and iron foundries and machine shops (which supplied Hyundai, Tata, Renault and Daimler India) because that work had become a commodity.

parts.name: Wind farm (monetised)
parts.what: A captive wind farm that supplied the company with non-carbon electricity for 18 years, now largely sold with the proceeds used to pay down debt, though management says a strategic piece has been retained.

overview.what_it_does: eClerx is an India-headquartered outsourcing firm that runs specialised back-office, data and customer-support work for large Western companies — banks and asset managers, telecom/cable and media firms, high-tech, manufacturing & distribution, retail and fashion/luxury brands. It sells ongoing operational services (trade and client life-cycle processing, KYC and regulatory remediation, customer care and field-technician support, product-content and digital-shelf work, data operations and market intelligence, and finance & accounting), increasingly bundled with its own analytics and automation platforms such as Roboworx CogniFlows, GenAI360 and Market360. It earns money mainly per person deployed and per seat used — hence the constant talk of headcount (~17,700 in FY25), utilisation, bench, seat counts and attrition — plus some transaction-volume-based BPaaS contracts, consulting/staff-augmentation billing and platform deals; revenue is billed largely in US dollars while most costs sit in rupees. Work is delivered mostly offshore from Indian centres (Mumbai, Pune, Chandigarh) with a growing nearshore/onshore footprint (Cairo, Manila, Fayetteville) and roughly a fifth of revenue done onshore at client sites; FY26 operating revenue was USD 469 million, up ~18%, with EBITDA margins in the mid-to-high 20s and the top 10 clients at 59% of revenue.

parts.name: Financial Markets / BFSI
parts.what: Runs trade life-cycle and client life-cycle operations for banks and capital-markets firms — onboarding, KYC, financial-crime compliance, regulatory remediation projects and change/BAU staffing onshore and offshore — historically one of the three core businesses and the main growth driver in FY25, though it had a softer Q4 FY26 as some consulting engagements wound down.

parts.name: Customer Operations / CMT (Communications, Media & Telecom)
parts.what: Provides customer care, inbound sales and field-technician operations support for telecom, cable and media clients; a large, steady business that grew over 7% sequentially in Q4 FY26 and is expanding into new delivery centres in Cairo, Manila and Fayetteville, with management watching proposed US rules on offshore call restrictions.

parts.name: Digital (including Fashion & Luxury / CLX)
parts.what: Handles digital commerce and marketing content work for consumer brands — product content, creative/digital-shelf and campaign operations, backed by the Market360 tool and a Gold-tier Adobe partnership; it had a sluggish FY26 as the fashion and luxury industry weakened, with management expecting a return to growth in H1 FY27.

parts.name: Analytics and Automation
parts.what: The cross-cutting higher-value layer sold across all verticals — data analytics, DataOps, market intelligence, automation tooling and AI platforms (GenAI360, Roboworx CogniFlows, agentic KYC and data-sourcing tools); it grew from about USD 17 million a quarter in FY25 to roughly a USD 90 million annual book by FY26 and is the area getting the most investment.

parts.name: Emerging business / Finance & Accounting (Personiv)
parts.what: Outsourced finance and accounting plus order-management services, largely under the Personiv brand acquired earlier and aimed at small and mid-sized businesses in the US; described as growing strongly for three straight quarters in FY26 and a key contributor to the faster growth in non-top-10 clients.

parts.name: Hi-Tech and M&D (Manufacturing & Distribution)
parts.what: Serves technology and industrial/distribution clients with transformation, automation and customer-satisfaction programmes, DataOps and market intelligence; both grew strongly through FY26 and hosted the company's first agentic-AI deployment wins, though M&D and retail softened in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: BPaaS (business platform-as-a-service)
parts.what: Contracts where eClerx is paid on transaction volumes rather than headcount, sitting mainly inside the client life-cycle work — smaller and more volatile, having been called out as soft in Q1 FY25 on seasonal volume dips.

overview.what_it_does: Cannot be determined from the material provided. All 12 conference-call transcripts for Edelweiss Financial Services (Nov 2022 through Apr 2026) came through with no extractable text — each is flagged as a likely scanned image PDF. Since the instruction is to use only what the calls state, and the calls state nothing readable, there is no basis for describing what the company sells, to whom, how it earns money, or where it operates. Re-supply the transcripts with OCR applied and this can be answered.

Eicher Motors Limited (EICHERMOT) is an India-listed vehicle maker whose main business is Royal Enfield, which designs and sells mid-size motorcycles — 350cc, 450cc and 650cc models such as the Classic, Meteor, Hunter, Himalayan and Guerrilla — to retail riders in India and in over 70 countries abroad, and which the calls describe as the oldest motorcycle manufacturer in continuous production, celebrating 125 years in FY26. It makes money mainly by manufacturing and selling these motorcycles through dealers (plus spare parts, apparel and accessories), and it dominates its niche, holding roughly 85%-89% of India's middleweight (above-250cc) segment; in FY26 it sold 12.27 lakh motorcycles and reported consolidated revenue of INR 23,408 crores, EBITDA of INR 5,785 crores and profit after tax of INR 5,515 crores. Separately, it owns half of VE Commercial Vehicles (VECV), a 50-50 joint venture with Sweden's Volvo Group that builds and sells Eicher and Volvo trucks and buses in India and for export; EML does not book VECV's sales as its own revenue but takes its share of VECV's profit (about INR 183 crores in one quarter), and management says EML and VECV combined crossed INR 50,000 crores of revenue in FY26. Production is based in India — Royal Enfield's plants include Cheyyar in Tamil Nadu, now being expanded from 1.4 million to 2 million units a year, with a new greenfield plant planned in Andhra Pradesh — while sales reach India, Brazil (its largest and fastest-growing overseas market), Latin America, Europe, the UK, Thailand, Nepal and beyond.

parts.name: Royal Enfield (motorcycles)
parts.what: The core business and by far the biggest profit engine: it makes and sells mid-size 350cc/450cc/650cc motorcycles in India and internationally, selling 12.27 lakh units in FY26 (1.1 million domestic, 120,634 export) with an 88.9% exit share of India's mid-sized segment.

parts.name: Royal Enfield international business
parts.what: The overseas arm of the motorcycle business, selling through distributors and exclusive stores in 70+ countries with 3,000+ service touch points; exports grew 20% in FY26 to about 120,000 units, with Brazil (up ~71%), Argentina, Thailand, Nepal and Europe called out as key markets.

parts.name: Allied businesses (apparel, accessories, lifestyle)
parts.what: Riding gear, clothing and lifestyle products sold alongside the bikes — apparel alone grew 21% in FY26 — plus branded collaborations such as the Vallon Moto Aviators eyewear range; a smaller but steadily growing add-on to motorcycle sales.

parts.name: Flying Flea (electric)
parts.what: Royal Enfield's new 'City Plus' electric mobility brand, whose first product, the Flying Flea C6, launched in Bangalore in April 2026 with a deliberate city-by-city rollout; still tiny and at the start-up stage, but management frames it as the company's entry into electric.

parts.name: VE Commercial Vehicles (VECV) — 50:50 JV with Volvo Group
parts.what: An 18-year-old joint venture making and selling Eicher and Volvo trucks and buses in India; it crossed 100,000 units sold for the first time in FY26, and EML reports only its share of VECV's profit (e.g. INR 175 crores in Q1 FY25, INR 183 crores in Q3 FY26) rather than VECV's revenue, which ran around INR 5,000 crores a quarter at roughly 7.7% EBITDA margin.

parts.name: VECV — heavy-duty trucks
parts.what: Large trucks sold under the Eicher brand, running around 4,700 units in a first quarter with roughly 8.4% market share — the segment where VECV is a challenger rather than a leader.

parts.name: VECV — light and medium-duty trucks
parts.what: Smaller haulage trucks, about 7,800-8,300 units in a first quarter and a commanding ~34% market share, making this VECV's strongest position; a small commercial vehicle programme was also under customer trials.

parts.name: VECV — bus division
parts.what: Buses including Eicher electric city buses (the first delivered to Chandigarh) and premium Volvo coaches such as the 9600 platform; volumes of roughly 5,200 units in a first quarter, a record for the division at that time.

parts.name: VECV — exports
parts.what: Truck and bus shipments outside India, a small but fast-growing line at about 1,192 units in Q1 FY25, up 57.5% year on year.

parts.name: VE Connected Systems
parts.what: A joint venture VECV formed with iTriangle Infotech to build connected-vehicle and digital telematics services for Eicher truck customers; an early-stage services add-on, not yet a meaningful earnings contributor.

parts.name: Proposed vehicle financing JV with Volvo (Volvo Financial Services India)
parts.what: Announced in May 2026: EML intends to invest up to INR 750 crores for a 50% stake in a financing, leasing and financial-services JV with Volvo that already has INR 1,806 crores of assets under management, acting as the captive lender to Eicher, Volvo and Royal Enfield customers in India.

overview.what_it_does: E.I.D. Parry (India) Ltd. is an Indian sugarcane processing company that buys cane from farmers in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and nearby states, crushes it at its own mills (Nellikuppam, Sankili, Haliyal, Pugalur and others), and sells the sugar plus everything else the cane yields. Most of its money comes from selling sugar in bulk to the domestic market (and some exports, both governed by government release quotas and export permits), from alcohol — industrial-grade ENA and ethanol sold largely to oil marketing companies for fuel blending — and from surplus electricity generated by burning bagasse and exported to the grid. Smaller businesses sell branded consumer staples and packaged sugar to retail shoppers, and nutraceutical ingredients (algae-based), which are partly exported to the US. It also ran a separate raw-sugar refinery subsidiary that bought imported/raw sugar and refined it for sale — a large-revenue but loss-making operation the company shut down in FY26. Prices and costs are heavily policy-driven: cane cost is set by the government's FRP, sugar sales are capped by monthly release quotas, and ethanol offtake prices are fixed by the government.

parts.name: Sugar
parts.what: Crushes sugarcane into sugar and sells it domestically and occasionally for export; the core business, running roughly Rs. 390-470 crores of revenue a quarter recently, with cane cost (Rs. 4,000+ per tonne under FRP) and government release quotas the main pressure points.

parts.name: Distillery (part of the Sugar and Biofuel division)
parts.what: Turns molasses from the mills (and bought-in molasses) into ENA and ethanol, selling around 400 lakh litres a quarter at roughly Rs. 64-68 per litre for about Rs. 275-290 crores a quarter — the second-largest business, but squeezed because ethanol prices have been flat for about three years.

parts.name: Cogeneration / power
parts.what: Burns bagasse left over from crushing to generate electricity, using some in-house and exporting the rest to the grid at roughly Rs. 4-4.6 a unit; small but steady, about Rs. 37-66 crores of revenue a quarter.

parts.name: Consumer Products Group (CPG)
parts.what: Sells branded retail packs — packaged sweeteners plus a branded staples range launched around FY25 — with turnover that peaked near Rs. 195-236 crores a quarter and then fell to roughly Rs. 115-143 crores as management deliberately restructured the distribution channel to chase better margins.

parts.name: Nutraceuticals (Nutra)
parts.what: Makes nutraceutical/algae-based ingredients sold in India and exported (notably to the US); the smallest business, around Rs. 6-13 crores a quarter standalone and roughly Rs. 50-65 crores at the consolidated level including overseas operations.

parts.name: Refinery — Parry Sugars Refinery India Pvt. Ltd. (PSRIPL)
parts.what: A separate SEZ-based subsidiary that refined raw sugar for sale, generating very large revenue (about Rs. 700-1,200 crores a quarter) but persistent losses; operations were closed as of 31 March 2026, with staff settlements done, an SEZ exit underway, and about $78 million of bank loans repaid using an equity infusion from EID Parry.

overview.what_it_does: Enviro Infra Engineers (EIEL) is an Indian engineering and construction company, set up in 2009, that designs, builds, and then runs water and wastewater treatment infrastructure — sewage treatment plants (STPs), common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) for industry, sewer networks, and water supply schemes. Almost all its customers are government: state government bodies, urban development corporations, and municipal corporations, with the money largely flowing from centrally funded schemes such as Namami Gange (100% central funding), AMRUT (25% centre / 75% state), Jal Jeevan Mission, and Swachh Bharat Mission. It earns money mainly by building projects on contract (EPC), plus long-term operation-and-maintenance fees on the plants it has built (management says O&M revenue runs at roughly 3%–5% of a project's execution value per year), and on a few 'HAM' projects it funds construction itself and is repaid through quarterly annuities from the government. It works across many Indian states — Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Karnataka, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Bihar — and since FY26 has added a renewable energy arm; FY26 revenue was about INR1,146 crores with profit of about INR188 crores, and the total order book stood at over INR6,814 crores.

parts.name: Water and wastewater treatment (EPC / execution)
parts.what: The core business — designing and constructing sewage treatment plants, common effluent treatment plants, sewer networks and water supply schemes for government clients (recent examples: a 100 MLD STP, 55 MLD STP at Varanasi, 80 MLD STP at Jaipur, 25 MLD CETP at Sarigam, a INR250 crore Bhopal sewerage project, INR348 crore BUIDCO Bihar project, and INR824 crores of Pune/Nashik sanitation work); its execution order book grew from about INR1,960 crores in Dec 2024 to over INR2,733 crores by FY26-end, and it is described throughout as the company's primary segment.

parts.name: Operation and maintenance (O&M)
parts.what: Long-term contracts to run and maintain the plants it has built, typically stretching about 10 years, which management values at roughly 3%–5% of a project's execution cost per year and calls a source of steady, visible revenue; the water/wastewater O&M order book moved from around INR750 crores (Dec 2024) to about INR951 crores by FY26.

parts.name: HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) projects
parts.what: A smaller set of projects where EIEL arranges the financing and is paid back in quarterly annuities rather than upfront construction bills — the three discussed are Bareilly (~INR230 crores, completed 71 days early in July 2024), Mathura (~INR190 crores) and Saharanpur (~INR267 crores), and management said it planned to bid for more such work.

parts.name: ZLD, tertiary treatment and water reuse
parts.what: A newer, more technically advanced line using ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis, MBR and MVR to clean water enough to be reused — entered in Q1 FY26 with a INR395 crore Zero Liquid Discharge CETP in Maharashtra, and management flags reuse of treated water by process industries and thermal power plants as a potential new revenue segment.

parts.name: Renewable energy platform (solar, wind, BESS)
parts.what: A diversification begun in FY26 covering solar assets in Maharashtra and Odisha, wind EPC via the acquisition of Suyog Urja Limited, and battery storage — including four NTPC BESS EPC projects totalling 930 MWh worth about INR1,070 crores plus a 150 MWh Bihar project — run under both EPC and IPP (own-and-operate) models by a team of over 250 people; by FY26-end it carried an execution order book of over INR2,051 crores plus INR1,079 crores of O&M/IPP, making it roughly as large as the core water business by order book.

parts.name: Waste-to-energy / circular economy add-ons
parts.what: Compressed biogas, biogas-to-electricity and solar generation built into its own treatment plants (for example at Jodhpur) so the plants can power themselves and cut running costs — presented as a feature that strengthens its core projects rather than as a separately sized business.

overview.what_it_does: EIH Limited (stock code EIHOTEL) is the Indian hotel company behind the Oberoi and Trident brands — it owns, builds and runs upmarket hotels and resorts, and also runs hotels for other owners under management contracts for a fee. It makes money mainly by selling rooms (the calls track it as occupancy x average room rate, giving 'RevPAR'), plus food and beverage, banquets/MICE events, and a separate non-hotel service line management calls OFS, which is lower-margin and tied to airport levies. Guests come through direct bookings, corporate accounts, MICE/social events (including weddings) and leisure/international travellers, with foreign arrivals concentrated in the October-March half. As of Q3 FY26 it had 4,209 rooms ('keys') — 3,801 in India and 408 overseas, of which 3,338 owned and 871 managed — with international properties in places like Mauritius, Al Zorah, Marrakech and Egypt, and a pipeline of about 30 hotels/2,450 keys over three to four years, including a 21-key luxury hotel in Mayfair, London.

parts.name: Oberoi Hotels & Resorts (luxury segment)
parts.what: The premium flagship brand — city hotels like The Oberoi New Delhi/Mumbai/Gurgaon and resorts like Amarvilas, Rajvilas, Vanyavilas and the new Rajgarh Palace and Vindhyavilas; it is the largest and most profitable piece, described in FY23 as roughly a third of net capital employed at a 45% return on capital, and it consistently prices at a premium to its competitive set.

parts.name: Trident Hotels (upper upscale segment)
parts.what: The step-down brand aimed at business and mid-market travellers, with a return on capital employed of about 22% in FY23; management says it has recently grown RevPAR faster than its industry segment (12.5% in Q3 FY26 versus 8.6%).

parts.name: Owned hotels
parts.what: Hotels owned by EIH itself or through its joint ventures and associate companies (for example EIH Associated Hotels, which is building Trident Vizag) — 3,338 of the 4,209 keys, and the source of most revenue since EIH takes the full room and F&B income and the capital risk.

parts.name: Managed hotels
parts.what: Properties owned by third parties but operated under EIH's brands for management fees — 871 keys, and the main way the pipeline is growing lately (all four hotels signed in Q3 FY26 — Kabini, Hampi, Coorg and one in Cairo — were management contracts).

parts.name: Food and beverage / MICE
parts.what: Restaurants, banquets, conferences and social events inside the hotels; F&B revenue including managed hotels rose from Rs 143 crore to Rs 222 crore (+55%) in Q4 FY23, and MICE is repeatedly named as one of the fastest-growing demand segments, lifting cities like Bhubaneswar and Hyderabad.

parts.name: OFS
parts.what: A separate, faster-growing but lower-margin service business linked to airports (the calls cite an airport levy as a cost); its rapid growth is repeatedly given as the reason consolidated EBITDA grew slower than revenue in FY26 — the calls never spell out the acronym.

parts.name: International hotels and cruises
parts.what: Overseas properties (Mauritius, Al Zorah, Marrakech, Sahl Hasheesh in Egypt, plus Nile cruisers/luxury boats such as Oberoi Zahra) totalling 408 keys, with a 21-key Mayfair London hotel approved at GBP 69 million funded roughly half debt/half equity and with a partner intended to cut EIH's own exposure to under GBP 18 million.

parts.name: Investment property / other assets
parts.what: Non-hotel property such as the investment property in Gurgaon, which together with hotel assets made up about 62% of net capital employed in FY23 at returns of 16-35%.

parts.name: Surplus cash and treasury
parts.what: A large net-cash position kept for expansion — Rs 592 crore in Q2 FY25 rising to Rs 1,335 crore by end-FY26 — which earned Rs 113 crore of investment income in FY26 and funds the capex pipeline (Rs 680 crore spent in FY26) alongside debt.

overview.what_it_does: Elecon Engineering is an Indian engineering manufacturer that makes two main things: industrial gearboxes and gear-based power transmission products, and large material handling equipment such as conveyors, wagon tipplers, stacker reclaimers, crushers, feeders and port equipment. Its customers are industrial and infrastructure companies — cement, steel, sugar, power, marine, mining, ports and fertilizer plants — plus OEMs that build machinery, so it is a business-to-business capital-goods supplier rather than a consumer company. It earns money by booking orders and then designing, manufacturing (management stresses everything from drawing and design through manufacturing, testing and quality control happens under one roof) and delivering equipment against them, with a reported open order book of about INR 1,518 crores as of June 2026 and consolidated FY26 revenue of roughly INR 2,341 crores. It operates from India with overseas subsidiaries serving customers in more than 95 countries (85+ in earlier calls); domestic sales were about 71% of Q1 FY27 revenue and overseas about 29%, with a stated goal of taking overseas to 50% by FY30 and a recently added step-down subsidiary in Mexico.

parts.name: Gear Division
parts.what: Designs and manufactures industrial gearboxes and gear/power-transmission products — both standard catalogue items and custom engineered ones — for steel, cement, sugar, power and marine customers; it is by far the bigger business, described as the company's cornerstone at roughly 85% of revenue in Q1 FY25 and still about 63-80% in FY26/FY27 quarters (INR 416 crores revenue in Q1 FY27), with management claiming a leadership position in India's organised industrial gear market and status as one of Asia's largest gear solution providers.

parts.name: MHE Division (Material Handling Equipment)
parts.what: Designs and builds large, complex, high-capacity bulk material handling systems — conveyors, wagon tipplers, stacker reclaimers, crushers, feeders and port equipment — for power, steel, cement, mining, ports and fertilizer customers; it is the smaller but faster-growing arm (around 15% of revenue in Q1 FY25, rising to roughly 37% in Q4 FY26 before easing to about 20% in Q1 FY27 at INR 105 crores), and management says it was restructured to focus only on equipment supply and aftermarket service after loss-making legacy turnkey projects were cleared, which returned it to profitability.

parts.name: Overseas / international business (subsidiaries and exports)
parts.what: Sells the same gear and MHE products abroad through foreign subsidiaries and a distribution network spanning 95+ countries, supported by OEM tie-ups and brand-building; it contributed about 29% of consolidated revenue in Q1 FY27 (INR 151 crores) versus roughly 27-34% in FY25, and the company targets 50% of revenue from overseas by FY30.

parts.name: Aftermarket and service
parts.what: Supplies spares, life-cycle support and aftermarket services alongside new equipment — management describes end-to-end life cycle support in gears and calls aftermarket services one of the two things the MHE division now concentrates on — though the calls give no separate revenue figure for it.

overview.what_it_does: Electrosteel Castings makes ductile iron (DI) pipes, cast iron pipes and pipe fittings — the large iron pipes used to carry drinking water and sewage — and is described by management as the leader in DI pipes and fittings in India. Its demand comes overwhelmingly from government-funded water infrastructure: the Jal Jeevan Mission (tap water to every household), AMRUT, urban water and sewage networks, with JJM alone said to be 50%-60% of industry demand, so revenue rises and falls with central and state fund releases. It earns money on the spread between selling price per tonne and raw-material cost (notably imported coking coal); management quotes volumes in lakh tonnes and a blended EBITDA margin that ran around 17% in FY24 but fell to roughly 9-10% in FY26 when JJM funds were frozen. Manufacturing is integrated (it makes its own coke, sponge iron, pig iron and ferroalloys and sells the surplus), with plants at Khardah in West Bengal and Srikalahasti, a registered office in Rajgangpur, Odisha, land being acquired in Odisha for a new plant, capacity growing from about 8.5 lakh to 10 lakh tonnes a year, and a growing export business plus an Italian subsidiary.

parts.name: DI Pipes, Fittings and CI Pipes (domestic)
parts.what: The core business — ductile iron pipes, cast iron pipes and fittings sold into Indian water supply and sewage projects; volumes were about 7.47 lakh tonnes in FY24 and 5.84 lakh tonnes in FY26 (down 25%), and this is what drives nearly all of standalone revenue of roughly Rs. 5,200-7,000 crores.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: The same pipes sold overseas, largely to the Middle East; volumes grew 11% year-on-year in Q3 FY26 and 7% for full-year FY26, which management repeatedly credits with partly offsetting the domestic slump — though it flagged an expected hit to Middle East sales from March 2026 due to the US-Iran conflict.

parts.name: Intermediary products (coke, sponge iron, pig iron, ferroalloys)
parts.what: Surplus output from its own integrated iron-making chain sold on the open market; a side line rather than the main event, but management says it "partly compensated" the top line when pipe volumes and prices fell in Q3 FY26, and pig iron sales were also called out as meaningful back in FY23.

parts.name: T.I.S. Italy (acquired manufacturing subsidiary)
parts.what: An Italian manufacturing arm whose revenue grew 15% in calendar 2025 to EUR 41 million with improved EBITDA margins; small relative to the group, but management wants to double its revenue in four years and is using it to start valve-castings production in India.

parts.name: Subsidiaries / consolidated operations
parts.what: Group companies beyond the standalone parent that add roughly Rs. 300-500 crores of extra income (consolidated FY26 income of Rs. 6,133 crores versus Rs. 5,228 crores standalone), with intra-group profit on unsold stock adjusted out at the consolidated level.

overview.what_it_does: Elgi Equipments is an Indian engineering company, founded in 1960 and based in Coimbatore, that designs and manufactures air compressors — the machines that supply compressed air, which management describes as a utility "just like electricity" that virtually every factory needs. It sells industrial and portable compressors, plus downstream accessories like dryers and filtration systems, to customers across essentially every industry (no single industry is more than 2-3% of revenue), partly direct and largely through a network of roughly 600 distributors, only about 60 of which are in India. Revenue comes from selling machines and related equipment and aftermarket accessories/service; it does business in 120-plus countries with direct presence in about 28 and manufacturing in three locations, and management notes it is a significant net earner of foreign exchange. In FY26 consolidated revenue was close to ₹4,000 crore, with the compressor business split roughly 50-50 between India and the rest of the world, and compressors making up about 90% of sales versus about 10% from automotive equipment.

parts.name: Compressors (industrial)
parts.what: The core business — a full range of air compressors (screw, reciprocating, high-volume machines) sold to factories on the strength of energy efficiency, reliability and service; roughly 90% of company sales sit in compressors, and management says about 80% of customers buy on efficiency rather than price.

parts.name: Portable compressors / construction and mining
parts.what: Portable and construction-and-mining compressors sold for infrastructure and rental use; in the US these are sourced from the group's Italian operation Rotair, and management calls this a structurally less profitable business that was hurt by tariffs on Italian imports.

parts.name: Accessories and downstream products
parts.what: Dryers (refrigeration, with desiccant planned), filtration and other downstream equipment that used to be bought in and are now manufactured under Elgi's own brand — described as a strategic area of focus for the future.

parts.name: Railways
parts.what: Compressors and equipment for Indian Railways — an India-centric, government-driven business that management calls "reasonable" rather than headline-grabbing, but which won a locomotive tender from Siemens that is running well and could open the door to locomotive OEM work worldwide.

parts.name: Automotive equipment
parts.what: Garage/automotive workshop equipment, a separate product line from compressors; the sales mix is described as stable at roughly 10% of total sales against 90% for compressors.

parts.name: North America — ELGi Industrial
parts.what: Supplies air compressors to independent distributors across the US; it drove record North American revenue in FY26 after the company doubled its sales headcount calling on distributors and converted many from competitors.

parts.name: North America — ELGi Distribution Operations
parts.what: Houses the two US distribution acquisitions, Patton's and Michigan Air, i.e. company-owned distribution rather than third-party channel.

parts.name: North America — Patton's Medical
parts.what: The medical air and gas business in the US, called a success story in FY26 and expanding into lower-presence regions like California, New York and the Northeast.

parts.name: Vacuum (licensed)
parts.what: A newer line added through a license agreement with DVP for vacuum products — mentioned as a recent addition to the portfolio rather than a material revenue contributor so far.

parts.name: Backward integration (foundry, motors, pressure vessels)
parts.what: In-house manufacture of castings, electric motors, pressure vessels and some of its own machining — not standalone revenue but described as a major competitive pillar, done for quality, safety and to remove sourcing risk from Chinese motors while cutting cost.

parts.name: Regions
parts.what: Management reports by geography: ISAAME (India, South Asia, Africa, Middle East) as the home base, North America as the second-largest market, plus Europe (a consolidation/cost-realignment story now sized to fit and profitable), Australia, Southeast Asia (a ~$700m annual market being rebuilt under new leadership) and Brazil.

overview.what_it_does: Ellenbarrie Industrial Gases makes and sells basic industrial gases — mainly oxygen, nitrogen and argon separated out of air, plus hydrogen and medical gases — to Indian industrial and healthcare customers, with steel and metals the biggest end market and chemicals, pharma, healthcare, solar and electronics described as growing ones. It earns money three ways: piping gas directly to a single large customer from a plant built at that customer's site under long-term take-or-pay contracts (so revenue is contracted from day one), producing liquid gas at its own 'merchant' plants and trucking it to many buyers in the surrounding region, and filling and distributing cylinders locally. The company owns and runs the plants, so it is capital-heavy — power is its single largest cost — and profitability turns on plant utilisation, power cost and the price of argon. It has historically operated in eastern and southern India (plants at Uluberia in West Bengal and Kurnool, a cylinder-filling operation in Bangalore), holds mid-single-digit share of an industry it sizes at about Rs 15,000 crore, and is building out to north India and west-central India to become pan-India; capacity was 1,370 tonnes per day at end-FY25, planned at 1,910 TPD by end-FY26 and 2,130 TPD in FY27.

parts.name: On-site gases
parts.what: Plants built at a large customer's own premises supplying gas under take-or-pay contracts — management says capacity utilisation is 'irrelevant' here because revenue is guaranteed from day one, and these carry a higher EBITDA margin; examples include the Tata Steel Metaliks plant already running and a 320 TPD East India on-site plant due around Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Merchant gases (bulk liquid)
parts.what: Company-owned plants producing liquid oxygen, nitrogen and argon sold to many customers across a region; each new merchant plant takes roughly 18–24 months to ramp to about 85% utilisation, and recent examples are the Kurnool plant (60–65% loaded in Q1 FY26) and the 220 TPD Uluberia 2 plant in West Bengal commissioned in Q4 FY26 at about Rs 160 crore capex with roughly Rs 100–110 crore of revenue potential.

parts.name: Packaged / cylinder gases
parts.what: Local cylinder filling and secondary distribution so customers who want gas in cylinders rather than bulk liquid can be served — the small Rs 5.5 crore acquisition of cylinder-filling assets in Bangalore is the example given, valued mainly because it adds value to Kurnool's output and lets the company serve nearby medical-oxygen customers who need a supplier close at hand.

parts.name: Argon
parts.what: The highest value-added product, a by-product of oxygen production sold from the same plants; it rose from about 7% of revenue a year earlier to roughly 9–10% and management targets 15%-plus, and its price swings matter a lot — a more than 25% drop in Q3 FY26, blamed on weak steel and oversupply from steel makers' captive plants, pushed group EBITDA margin from 38% down to 31% that quarter before recovering in Q4.

parts.name: High-purity and speciality gases (planned)
parts.what: A future product capability to be built alongside the planned west-India plant, targeted for FY28, aimed at customers such as solar cell manufacturers; management says it is still in discussions with no signed contracts to disclose.

overview.what_it_does: Emami Limited is an Indian consumer-goods (FMCG) company, headquartered in Kolkata and listed in India, that makes and sells low-priced branded personal-care and ayurvedic healthcare products — cooling hair oils and talc, antiseptic creams, hair-fall oils, men's grooming creams, prickly-heat powders, pain balms and ayurvedic health remedies — mostly to ordinary household shoppers. It earns money by selling these branded goods at high gross margins (around 68%-70% in FY26) through distributors into general trade and wholesale, plus fast-growing modern trade, e-commerce and quick-commerce channels, which together were about 32% of domestic sales by FY26; it spends heavily on advertising (now roughly half of it digital) to support the brands. Most sales come from India, with an international business selling the same brands into the Middle East/GCC, SAARC, CIS and Africa, including some manufacturing in the UAE. Full-year FY26 consolidated revenue was about INR3,780 crore with EBITDA of INR964 crore and profit after tax of INR775 crore, and the company describes itself as debt-free.

parts.name: Navratna (and Dermicool)
parts.what: Cooling hair oils, cool talc and prickly-heat powder — the core 'summer portfolio' and one of the company's biggest revenue drivers, so much so that a delayed summer in Q4 FY26 dragged the whole quarter's revenue down 4%.

parts.name: Healthcare range (Zandu / Zanducare)
parts.what: Ayurvedic health and immunity products sold under the Zandu brand, including digital-first launches on its own Zanducare D2C site and e-pharmacies; a consistently growing line (up 7%-11% in recent quarters) backed by two WHO-GMP factories.

parts.name: Pain Management range
parts.what: Balms and pain-relief products (the Zandu balm family) that sell mainly in winter — a swingy, seasonal category that fell 30% in one quarter in FY23 but grew 8%-11% in FY26.

parts.name: BoroPlus
parts.what: Antiseptic cream and related winter skincare plus a talc line; a large winter-season brand that grew 16% in Q3 FY26, though its talc part suffered badly in the weak FY26 summer.

parts.name: Kesh King
parts.what: Premium ayurvedic anti-hair-fall oil and hair care; a sizeable but volatile brand that fell 15% in one quarter of FY25 and returned to 10%-14% growth in FY26.

parts.name: Male Grooming (Fair and Handsome / Smart and Handsome)
parts.what: Men's face creams now being extended into sunscreens, deodorants and body washes; a discretionary category that has swung between 32% growth and 4%-5% declines.

parts.name: 7 Oils in One
parts.what: A light hair-oil brand that is one of the faster-growing smaller brands, up 34% in Q4 FY26 and also selling well in international markets.

parts.name: International business
parts.what: Sells the same brands plus Creme 21 across MENA/GCC, SAARC, CIS and South Asia, with about half of those goods produced in the UAE; it grew 9%-11% in most periods but fell 5% in Q4 FY26 on Middle East shipping disruption.

parts.name: Strategic investments / subsidiaries (The Man Company, Brillare, Axiom, IncNut)
parts.what: A portfolio of newer, premium, digital-first companies — men's grooming (The Man Company), professional hair and skin care (Brillare), fruit juice (Axiom, already profitable) and personalised beauty brands Vedix and SkinKraft (IncNut) — still small but growing 31%-34% and targeted to keep growing about 30% a year.

overview.what_it_does: Embassy Developments (EMBDL/EDL) is an Indian listed real estate developer that builds and sells homes — plots, villas, and apartments — plus office space, to individual home buyers and, on the commercial side, to institutional occupiers and investors. It was formed in 2025 by merging the erstwhile Indiabulls Real Estate with the Embassy Group's development arm, NAM Estates, and it develops mostly on land it already owns outright (a fully paid land bank of roughly 3,100-3,250 acres). It makes money by pre-selling units and collecting cash in instalments tied to construction milestones — FY26 pre-sales were about Rs. 4,631 crores and collections Rs. 1,673 crores — though accounting revenue is only booked when a project gets its occupancy certificate and is handed over, which is why FY26 showed a reported loss of Rs. 872 crores despite record sales. It operates across 8 cities with 40-plus projects and about 38 million square feet under development, with Bengaluru as its home market and Mumbai/MMR and NCR as the other two core markets.

parts.name: Residential development
parts.what: The main engine of the business — plotted developments, villas and apartments (Embassy Springs projects, Embassy Eden, Embassy Citadel in Worli) making up over 30 of the roughly 38 million square feet of portfolio and essentially all of FY26's Rs. 4,631 crores of pre-sales, tilted towards luxury and premium products.

parts.name: Commercial assets
parts.what: Office and business-park development such as Embassy East Business Park in Whitefield (2.7 million sq ft in Phase 1, roughly Rs. 3,100 crores GDV) and 109 Commercial in Gurgaon — about 7.4 million square feet today, small versus residential but something management says it wants to grow as a share of the portfolio.

parts.name: Development management (DM) projects
parts.what: Projects on land the company does not own where Embassy manages and sells the development under its brand — Juhu in Mumbai and Sky Terraces in Bengaluru, with combined GDV of about Rs. 6,000-6,100 crores and expected to add Rs. 2,000 crores of the Rs. 8,000 crore FY27 pre-sales target, i.e. roughly a quarter of guided sales.

parts.name: Legacy Indiabulls / completed (OC-received) portfolio
parts.what: The inherited older projects across MMR, NCR and Visakhapatnam that the company has been finishing and handing over (6 delayed projects, 3,300-plus families given possession); this completed inventory is now 98% sold and contributed Rs. 573 crores of FY26 pre-sales and Rs. 645 crores of collections, but its high costs (Vizag, Thane Phase 1) are a drag on reported profit.

parts.name: Land bank
parts.what: Roughly 3,250 acres of fully paid-up land that feeds future launches — management says it supports about Rs. 41,000 crores of gross development value over three years plus a further 20.4 million sq ft / Rs. 23,500 crores of planned pipeline beyond FY27, so it is the raw material behind multi-year growth rather than a separate revenue line.

parts.name: Joint ventures and specialised formats
parts.what: Smaller partnership and niche products such as Serene Amara, a senior-living project in Bengaluru with Columbia Pacific Communities (occupancy certificate for 239 apartments), Embassy Serenity managed residences in Alibaug (111 units), and a Whitefield JDA project where Embassy holds 68.5% — individually modest but adding second-home and lifestyle categories to the mix.

overview.what_it_does: Emcure Pharmaceuticals is a Pune-based Indian drugmaker that makes and sells prescription medicines — branded generics, specialty products and biologics/biosimilars — in therapy areas like women's health and anemia, cardiac, diabetes, anti-infectives, vitamins, CNS, nephrology, oncology and, more recently, dermatology and consumer wellness. In India it earns money by having a field force of over 5,000 medical representatives promote branded products to doctors (specialists account for about 70% of its prescriptions), and it supplements its own R&D pipeline by in-licensing or distributing other companies' brands, such as Sanofi's cardiac and oral diabetes portfolios, Novo Nordisk's semaglutide (Poviztra) and Roche's nephrology/transplant products. Outside India it sells generics and complex injectables through businesses it has bought and built in Canada (Marcan), Europe/UK (Tillomed, Manx) and emerging markets, including HIV/ARV medicines. FY26 revenue was about INR 9,204 crore (over $1 billion), split roughly INR 4,027 crore domestic and INR 5,177 crore international; the US business was demerged before listing, so US exposure is under 3% of sales.

parts.name: Domestic / India business
parts.what: Branded prescription medicines sold to Indian doctors and patients across women's health, cardiac, diabetes, anti-infectives, vitamins, CNS, nephrology and oncology — roughly INR 4,027 crore in FY26 (about 44% of revenue), the part management calls closest to its heart, with Emcure ranked 12th largest pharma company in India and 4th largest in its covered market.

parts.name: In-licensed / partnered India portfolio
parts.what: Brands owned by multinationals that Emcure markets and distributes in India — Sanofi's cardiac portfolio and oral diabetes brands Amaryl and Cetapin, Novo Nordisk's patented rDNA semaglutide sold as Poviztra, and Roche nephrology and transplant medicines from April 2026 — a growing profit driver that management says proves its commercial reach, though the Sanofi diabetes deal initially weighed on margins.

parts.name: International – Europe
parts.what: Generic and specialty medicines sold across Europe and the UK, built from the 2014 Tillomed acquisition and scaled about tenfold in a decade, with the recent Manx bolt-on in the UK and the Amphotericin B launch adding growth; revenue was INR 403 crore in Q1 FY26, growing 12.8% then and 29.6% by Q3 FY26.

parts.name: International – Canada
parts.what: A top-10 Canadian generics player built through the 2015 Marcan acquisition plus a second company for Quebec and the Cutimed derma buy, growing on market share gains and new launches; revenue was INR 342 crore in Q1 FY26, up 16.4%.

parts.name: International – Emerging markets / Rest of world
parts.what: Sells products developed in India, Europe and Canada into emerging markets, partly through its own front-end teams and partly via partners and distributors, split between HIV antiretrovirals (ARV) and a widening non-ARV range; the fastest-growing piece at INR 360 crore in Q1 FY26, up 42% year-on-year.

parts.name: R&D, biologics and biosimilars
parts.what: The in-house engine management credits for its differentiated products — chirality-based cardiac drugs, the Orofer anemia franchise, seven marketed biotherapeutics with two awaiting approval, plus a pipeline in complex injectables, biosimilars (including ophthalmic Bevacizumab), new delivery routes and antibody-drug conjugates, and a global voluntary licence for Gilead's lenacapavir.

parts.name: Zuventus
parts.what: An Indian subsidiary whose minority stake Emcure bought out in FY26 for full consolidation; its portfolio and team reorganisation caused attrition that made Q4 FY26 domestic growth softer, which management says was fixed by April.

overview.what_it_does: Electronics Mart India (EMIL) is a consumer-durables and electronics retailer in India — it buys branded goods from around 70 manufacturers and sells them to ordinary shoppers through large stores, mostly under the "Bajaj Electronics" name in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana and "Electronics Mart" in Delhi NCR. Its shelves carry air conditioners, televisions, washing machines, refrigerators, mobile phones, small appliances and IT products — over 6,000 SKUs — with easy EMI options, and management described the company at listing as the fourth largest such retailer in India and the largest organised player in the south. It makes money on the retail margin between buying and selling the goods, plus a sizeable stream of "other operating income" from brand incentives and commissions (about INR 2,021 million in H1 FY23), and the business is highly seasonal, peaking in the summer quarter (Q1) and the Diwali festive quarter (Q3). By FY26 it operated 223 stores across roughly four states, with revenue of INR 7,183 crores, EBITDA margin of 6.1% and PAT of INR 107 crores.

parts.name: Retail
parts.what: The core business — selling electronics and appliances to walk-in customers through company-run stores; it is essentially the whole company, contributing INR 11,105 million of the INR 12,277 million of Q2 FY23 revenue.

parts.name: Multi-brand outlets (MBOs)
parts.what: Large one-stop stores stocking many brands under one roof, branded Bajaj Electronics in AP/Telangana and Electronics Mart in Delhi NCR; they are the bulk of the network (157 of 170 stores in June 2024).

parts.name: Exclusive brand outlets (EBOs)
parts.what: Single-brand stores selling only one manufacturer's products such as Apple, LG or Samsung; a small part of the network, around 12-13 stores.

parts.name: Specialised store formats (Kitchen Stories, Audio & Beyond)
parts.what: Niche stores focused on high-end kitchen appliances and on home cinema/networking solutions respectively; only a handful of stores, including one Kitchen Stories outlet in Kerala.

parts.name: Wholesale (B2B)
parts.what: A small side business supplying stock to roughly 200 individual and mom-and-pop shops in AP and Telangana, mainly to help liquidate inventory; tiny at INR 92 million in Q2 FY23 versus over INR 12,000 million total.

parts.name: E-commerce / online
parts.what: Listing about 200 selected SKUs on major online marketplaces as an extension of the store business; the smallest channel at INR 21 million in Q2 FY23.

parts.name: Other operating income (incentives and commissions)
parts.what: Payments and incentives earned from the brands it stocks plus commissions — a meaningful profit contributor, at INR 1,050 million in Q2 FY23 and INR 2,021 million in H1 FY23.

parts.name: Large appliances
parts.what: Air conditioners, televisions, washing machines, refrigerators, dishwashers and coolers — historically the biggest product category at 53% of revenue in Q1 FY25, easing to roughly 42-43% by FY26.

parts.name: Mobile phones
parts.what: Smartphone sales, driven by new OEM launches; roughly 35% of revenue in Q1 FY25 and about 44% by Q3 FY26, growing 28% in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Small appliances / IT and other categories
parts.what: Smaller-ticket items such as kitchen and personal appliances and IT products; the smallest slice at about 12% of revenue in Q1 FY25.

parts.name: South cluster (Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala)
parts.what: The home market and profit engine, centred on Hyderabad where it claims very high market share; it held an EBITDA margin of about 6.5% in FY26 despite most new stores being opened there.

parts.name: North / NCR cluster
parts.what: The newer Delhi NCR expansion started with 8 stores in August 2022, growing to 24 by mid-2024; it turned EBITDA positive but at thin margins (around 0.5% for 9M FY26) as stores are still maturing.

overview.what_it_does: Emmvee Photovoltaic Power Limited is an Indian solar manufacturer based in Bengaluru, Karnataka, that makes and sells solar panels (modules) and the solar cells that go inside them, all using TOPCon technology. It sells in bulk to power producers and project builders — independent power producers (IPPs), utilities, EPC contractors, commercial and industrial customers and rooftop buyers — with exports described as part of the strategic roadmap; revenue comes from taking multi-gigawatt orders and shipping panels against them, typically over a 12-18 month execution window. The company is 'integrated', meaning it increasingly makes its own cells rather than buying them, which management says lifts margins and improves control over quality and supply. FY26 revenue was INR 5,049 crores with EBITDA of INR 1,734 crores and PAT of INR 1,082 crores; the company listed on the BSE and NSE in November 2025 and says it grew over three decades from a small solar water heater maker into one of India's leading integrated solar manufacturers.

parts.name: Solar module manufacturing
parts.what: The core, largest business — making finished solar panels; installed capacity rose to 10.3 GW by March 2026 with production of 2,999 MW in FY26 (roughly double FY25) and 970 MW in Q1 FY27, and the whole fleet is now 100% TOPCon, including new higher-power G12R format modules.

parts.name: Solar cell manufacturing
parts.what: Making the TOPCon cells that feed the module lines — capacity of 2.94 GW, production of 1,520 MW in FY26 (about 3x FY25) with utilisation climbing from 43% in FY25 to 70% in FY26 and 83% in Q1 FY27; FY26 was its first full year and management credits it with much of the margin improvement.

parts.name: DCR and non-DCR modules
parts.what: Management splits module sales into DCR (domestic-content-requirement panels using Indian-made cells) and non-DCR, and tracks EBITDA per watt separately for each; having its own ALMM List 2-approved cell capacity is what lets it serve the DCR market, which it expects to grow through FY27.

parts.name: 6 GW integrated cell and module facility (Devanahalli, Bengaluru)
parts.what: The main growth project under construction — about INR 5,500 crores of total cost with INR 3,300 crores of IREDA-backed debt tied up at under 8%; the module line is due by December 2026 and the cell line by March 2027, taking total capacity to roughly 16.3 GW of modules and 8.9 GW of cells.

parts.name: Ingot and wafer backward integration (planned)
parts.what: A future, not-yet-built step further up the supply chain: 9 GW planned in two phases (5 GW targeted in FY2029, 4 GW in FY2030), to be funded largely from internal cash and timed against clarity on ALMM List 3, intended mainly to protect margins and cut dependence on outside suppliers.

parts.name: Order book
parts.what: Not a product line but the key demand measure management reports each quarter — it grew from 4.9 GW in FY25 to 9.4 GW in FY26 and 9.9 GW by Q1 FY27, with about 7-plus GW to be executed over the next 18 months and average order size among the top 10 customers rising to 221 MW.

overview.what_it_does: Endurance Technologies is an Indian auto-components maker that manufactures and sells parts that go into vehicles — mainly braking systems (disc brakes, brake discs, ABS), suspension (front forks and shock absorbers), transmission parts such as clutches, and aluminium die castings and alloy wheels. It sells these directly to vehicle manufacturers (OEMs) under supply contracts won through a request-for-quote process, so revenue comes from per-part supply on programs that ramp from a 'start of production' date to peak annual sales a few years later; its Indian customers are chiefly two-wheeler makers — Bajaj Auto (its largest and anchor customer), Hero MotoCorp, HMSI/Honda, TVS, Royal Enfield, Suzuki, Yamaha and EV players like Ather — plus three- and four-wheeler makers such as Tata Motors, Mahindra, Hyundai, Kia and Isuzu. Roughly three-quarters of group income comes from Indian operations and about a quarter from European operations (largely Italy/Germany, serving passenger-car makers with castings and tooling). Manufacturing is concentrated in Maharashtra (Waluj/Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Chakan-Pune, AURIC Shendra and Bidkin) with newer plants in Tamil Nadu (Chennai, Vallam), alongside European plants.

parts.name: Braking systems (2W disc brake assemblies, discs, ABS)
parts.what: Makes disc brake assemblies, brake discs, master cylinders and calipers for two-wheelers, plus anti-lock braking systems; management calls it a key growth engine — capacity is being built toward 7.6 million disc brake assemblies and 8.6 million discs a year (including a new 3-million-unit Chennai plant), ABS capacity is being expanded from 0.64 million to 1.84 million units a year on expected regulations mandating ABS on smaller bikes, and the company is backward-integrating into in-house electronic control units to raise margins.

parts.name: Suspension (front forks, inverted front forks, shock absorbers)
parts.what: Supplies conventional and premium 'inverted' front forks and rear mono-shocks for motorcycles and scooters, including high-end units developed with partner KTM AG and exported to KTM Austria; it is one of the biggest repeat sources of new order wins, with individual OEM programs worth Rs 250–1,650 million a year from HMSI, Hero MotoCorp, Suzuki and TVS.

parts.name: Transmission / clutch assemblies
parts.what: Makes clutch assemblies for motorcycles and continuously variable transmissions (automatic clutches) for scooters, including a shift from cork-based to paper-based clutches and entry into 200cc-plus premium bike clutches using know-how from its Italian acquisitions; it is a smaller line than brakes and suspension and mainly a value-add/mix-improvement story.

parts.name: Aluminium die casting and machining (including four-wheeler castings)
parts.what: Casts and fully machines aluminium parts for two-, three- and four-wheelers, increasingly finished parts rather than raw castings; this is the main way the company sells into car makers, with the new AURIC Shendra plant alone carrying cumulative orders worth about Rs 513 crore of peak annual sales (from a large US EV maker, Jaguar Land Rover, Yazaki and Valeo), plus Chakan work for Tata Motors and Mahindra growing 35–40% in a year and Chennai/Vallam plants serving Hyundai, Kia, Isuzu and Ather.

parts.name: Alloy wheels (two-wheeler)
parts.what: A newer plant at AURIC Bidkin making aluminium alloy wheels for two-wheelers, which management says was 100% booked on capacity before it even started production in October 2025 — first for Bajaj Auto, with Royal Enfield, Suzuki, TVS, Yamaha and Ather following through FY27.

parts.name: Driveshafts
parts.what: A newer, higher-technology product launched at Waluj that transmits engine torque to the wheels for three-wheelers, four-wheelers and some light commercial vehicles; management describes it as a proprietary, 'EV-agnostic' additional revenue stream, with orders from Bajaj, Mahindra and TVS.

parts.name: Maxwell Energy Systems (electronics / Battery Management Systems)
parts.what: A subsidiary being bought out in stages (61.5% owned as of mid-2024, moving to 100% by FY27) that makes battery management systems and motor control units for electric two- and three-wheelers and battery packs, supplying over 70 OEMs and battery-pack makers across 15 countries; it had won about Rs 4,242 million of business since FY22 and was targeted to exceed Rs 2,500 million of sales in FY27.

parts.name: Electric-vehicle business (group-wide)
parts.what: Not a separate factory so much as EV-specific orders across brakes, suspension, castings and electronics, plus a new battery-pack assembly plant near Pune starting production around March–April 2026; cumulative EV order wins were Rs 8,421 million as of Q1 FY25 (from HMSI, Ather, Bajaj, Hero, Mahindra, Tata, TVS and Aptiv) on top of Maxwell's own wins.

parts.name: European operations (Endurance Overseas — Italy and Germany)
parts.what: Supplies aluminium castings and related tooling to European passenger-car makers, run under a separate CEO, and contributes roughly 24–25% of consolidated income; it has been bolted on to via Italian acquisitions — Gremica and Adler (2020, premium two-wheeler brakes and clutches), Frenotecnica (2022, brake friction materials with the 'Brenta' aftermarket brand) and Velcoli (fleet-efficiency software), intended to form a European centre of excellence for premium two-wheeler components and aftermarket sales.

overview.what_it_does: Engineers India Limited (EIL) is an Indian project-engineering company that designs and builds industrial plants for others — mainly oil refineries and petrochemical complexes for large Indian energy companies such as BPCL and IOCL (for example BPCL's refinery and IOCL's Paradip petrochemical project). It earns money in two ways: selling engineering brainwork (design, consultancy and project management, where it charges fees and keeps a segment margin of roughly 20-28%), and taking on lump-sum turnkey contracts where it delivers the whole physical project for a fixed price at much thinner margins (management cites about 3-7%). Revenue is recognised as projects are executed, so quarterly results are lumpy and cyclical, and the company works off an order book that stood at a record Rs 15,109 crore as of March 2026 against annual revenue of Rs 3,849 crore in FY26. It works mostly in the Indian domestic market, with an overseas arm serving the Middle East (about 30% of overseas business secured) and an ambition to grow in Africa.

parts.name: Consultancy and Engineering segment (also referred to as PMC / consultancy)
