parts.what: Sells engineering design, project management and consultancy services for refinery and petrochemical projects; it is the higher-margin half (20-28% segment profit) and contributed Rs 1,782 crore of FY26 revenue with roughly Rs 7,500 crore of the order book, and management expects it to grow 15-20% a year.

parts.name: Turnkey / LSTK segment (lump-sum turnkey, including OBE jobs)
parts.what: Takes full responsibility for delivering complete projects for a fixed price — procurement and construction included — which makes it the bigger revenue line (Rs 2,067 crore in FY26, about Rs 5,000 crore of order book) but at low margins of roughly 3-7%, and it is the main reason revenue and margins swing sharply between quarters.

parts.name: Overseas / international business (Middle East, Africa)
parts.what: Serves clients outside India, with the Middle East accounting for about 30% of business secured overseas; management flagged a slowdown there in FY26 with work shifting toward repair and revamp of damaged facilities rather than new greenfield projects, while Africa is being targeted for growth.

parts.name: CEIL (subsidiary) and other investments such as RFL
parts.what: EIL holds stakes in other companies whose earnings show up only in consolidated results — subsidiary CEIL earned Rs 24.71 crore in FY26, and consolidated profit of Rs 691.59 crore exceeded standalone profit of Rs 638 crore; an earlier call also cited a Rs 13.85 crore contribution from RFL that had previously been loss-making.

overview.what_it_does: Siemens Energy India Limited (ENRIN) is a "pure play" energy equipment and services company — it makes the hardware and provides the engineering and after-sales services that generate electricity and move it across the grid. Its customers are power utilities (generation, transmission and distribution), industrial companies such as cement, steel, sugar, paper, oil and gas and semiconductors, plus newer users like data centres and infrastructure such as railways and ferries. It earns money by winning orders for equipment (gas and steam turbines, transformers, switchgear, substations, grid-stabilisation systems) and for projects and long-term services like modernisation, upgrades and efficiency improvements on machines already installed, then executing that order backlog into revenue. It is based in India — eight factories, four service centres and four engineering/R&D centres, about 4,500 people, listed in June 2025 — selling mainly into the domestic market but with a growing export share, including transformers to the US data-centre market and switchgear to the Middle East. In the half year to March 2026 it reported revenue of about ₹43 billion (up ~27%), an order backlog of about ₹184 billion (up 22%), and profit from operations of 20.7% of revenue.

parts.name: Power Transmission
parts.what: Sells the equipment and services that carry electricity from power plants to users — high-voltage AC and DC substations, HVDC links, power transformers, switchgear, grid-stabilisation systems (STATCOMs) and related services; it is the slightly larger of the two segments by revenue and the faster-growing one, with backlog up from about ₹98 billion to ₹125 billion and revenue up about 30% to ₹24 billion in H1 FY26, and management says it holds roughly 30% of India's HVDC capacity.

parts.name: Power Generation
parts.what: Supplies equipment and services for making electricity — large gas turbines for the grid, industrial gas and steam turbines for captive power at oil and gas, sugar, paper, cement and steel customers, plus waste-heat-recovery systems that turn hot exhaust gases into extra steam and power; management describes it as a steady grower resting on a large installed base, with its Vadodara steam-turbine factory having shipped around 2,000 turbines and the company holding about 25% of India's gas turbines.

parts.name: Service business (within both segments)
parts.what: Maintains, modernises, upgrades and improves the efficiency of machines already installed — including refurbishing turbines at coal-fired plants (a 210 MW turbine in Orissa) even though the company does not sell coal-plant equipment; management calls this fleet the largest in the country and names service expansion as a key growth priority.

parts.name: Exports / global network role
parts.what: Manufactures finished products and components and does engineering and project execution out of India for Siemens Energy companies and customers abroad; exports rose about 500 basis points as a share of revenue year on year and helped lift margins through better price realisation.

parts.name: Green hydrogen (PEM electrolysers)
parts.what: The company says it is the market leader in PEM electrolysers, but treats this as a longer-term bet — it does not yet manufacture electrolysers in India and expects demand to pick up only around five years out.

overview.what_it_does: Entero Healthcare Solutions is an Indian wholesale distributor of healthcare products: it buys medicines, medical devices and related products from manufacturers and delivers them to retail pharmacies, hospitals and clinics across India. It makes money on the margin between what it pays manufacturers and what it charges customers, plus fees for commercial services like sales, marketing and supply-chain support that it provides to manufacturers wanting national reach. Started in 2018, it runs a pan-India network — by FY26 about 130+ warehouses serving over 100,000 retail pharmacies (roughly 1 in 10 in India) and about 3,600 hospitals across 523 districts, carrying ~97,500 SKUs from more than 3,300 manufacturers. Revenue grew from about ₹3,300 crore in FY23 to ₹6,591 crore in FY26, on thin distribution-style economics (gross margin ~10%, EBITDA margin 4%, PAT margin ~2.2%), with growth coming both organically and from buying up smaller local distributors in a highly fragmented market.

parts.name: Pharmaceutical distribution (core healthcare product distribution)
parts.what: The main business — warehousing and delivering branded medicines and other pharma products from manufacturers to pharmacies, hospitals and clinics nationwide; it is the bulk of the ~₹6,591 crore FY26 revenue and management says it consistently grows faster than the Indian pharmaceutical market (e.g. 1.6x IPM in FY26).

parts.name: MedTech (diagnostics and medical devices)
parts.what: A newer segment built up mainly through FY26 acquisitions (Anand Chemiceutics, Ace Cardiopathy, Bioaide Technologies) covering diagnostic reagents and equipment, IVD, cardiology, point-of-care devices and lab consumables; management says it now crosses ₹1,000 crore of annualised revenue and should add 70–90 bps to gross margin and 50–75 bps to EBITDA margin once integrated, and can grow via pan-India exclusive distribution deals rather than only acquisitions.

parts.name: Commercial / sales and marketing services for manufacturers
parts.what: Beyond just shipping product, Entero sells manufacturers access to its network and does demand generation — sales, marketing and promotion of their products using Entero's own field team — which management describes as a 'value-added commercial role' and a source of better margins, especially in MedTech.

parts.name: Technology platform (Entero Direct and business intelligence tools)
parts.what: Proprietary systems including the Entero Direct B2B ordering app, which lets pharmacy and hospital customers order 24/7 with live visibility of range, pricing, stock, order status and dues, and gives manufacturers data insights; it is presented as the efficiency and stickiness engine of the business rather than a separate revenue line.

parts.name: Acquisitions / consolidation engine
parts.what: A standing programme of buying small regional distributors (35+ since inception by FY24; 7 closed in FY26, usually 70–80% stakes leaving minority interests) to add cities, customers and product categories, then plugging them into Entero's technology, central procurement and manufacturer relationships — inorganic growth contributed about 16% of FY26's ~31.5% like-for-like revenue growth.

parts.name: Product adjacencies and private label (stated ambition)
parts.what: Management repeatedly flags expanding into adjacent products and own-brand/private-label lines as a future lever for margins, but the calls describe it as an opportunity being explored rather than a business of meaningful size today.

overview.what_it_does: EPL Limited makes flexible packaging — principally squeezable tubes — that consumer-goods companies fill with their products, selling to leading global oral care brands (toothpaste) and beauty, cosmetics and personal care brands. It earns money by manufacturing and selling these tubes in volume from 21 factories across 11 countries, with roughly half its business under contractual arrangements that pass raw-material cost changes (mainly polymers and aluminium) through to customers, and it uses price increases to protect margins when input costs rise. It runs as four geographic regions — AMESA (India, Middle East, South Asia, Africa), EAP (East Asia Pacific, including China), Europe and the Americas — and reported FY26 revenue growth of 13% with EBITDA margins above 20%. Sustainability is central to how it competes: 'sustainable' recyclable tube formats reached 38% of sales in FY26 and have helped it win wallet share from customers, and it holds an EcoVadis Platinum rating. In March 2026 it agreed to merge with Indovida, a rigid-packaging company owned by Indorama Ventures, to create a roughly $1 billion (INR 8,300 crore) emerging-markets consumer packaging group in which Indorama becomes the promoter.

parts.name: Oral Care
parts.what: Tubes for toothpaste and similar oral products — historically EPL's biggest category and still a core one, growing about 10% in Q4 FY26, though by FY26 management says Beauty & Cosmetics had become larger than Oral Care in most key markets.

parts.name: Personal Care and Beyond (including Beauty & Cosmetics)
parts.what: Tubes and newer formats such as Neo-seam for cosmetics, beauty and personal care brands; this is the company's declared growth priority, reaching 53% of the mix in FY26 with Beauty & Cosmetics growing about 30% for the year.

parts.name: AMESA region
parts.what: Asia Middle East South Asia and Africa, centred on the Indian business, which management reports separately as 'India standalone'; grew 10.4% in Q4 FY26 with India standalone up 11.5%.

parts.name: EAP region
parts.what: East Asia Pacific, including China, where COVID lockdowns badly hurt sales in FY23; it recovered strongly and grew 25% in Q4 FY26, and it now includes a new plant in Thailand serving that country's beauty and cosmetics market.

parts.name: Europe region
parts.what: European manufacturing and sales, which had the weakest margins (single digits) in FY23 due to energy and wage inflation but recovered to mid-teens margins by FY25 and grew 15.5% in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Americas region
parts.what: North and South America, including a new Brazil plant commercialised around FY24 that has added multinational and local customers; regional margins went from single digits to high teens, and the region grew 24.1% in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Sustainable tubes
parts.what: Recyclable tube formats (including the Platina line) that customers are switching to on their own sustainability commitments; the mix rose from 21% of volume in FY24 to 29% in Q1 FY25 and 38% of sales in FY26, and management treats it as a source of competitive advantage and wallet-share gains.

parts.name: Indovida merger (announced March 2026, pending)
parts.what: A share-swap merger with Indorama Ventures' rigid-packaging arm — INR 3,800+ crore revenue, 21.3% EBITDA margin, 19 plants in nine countries, mostly Southeast Asia and Africa — that would roughly double EPL to INR 8,300 crore revenue and add rigid packaging alongside EPL's flexible tubes, with $35-50 million of identified synergies.

overview.what_it_does: Equitas Small Finance Bank is an Indian bank that takes deposits from retail savers and lends the money out to small borrowers in what management calls the "informal and formalizing economy" — small shop and business owners, small fleet operators, first-time home buyers and low-income women borrowers. It gathers money through savings and current accounts, retail term deposits and NRI deposits (offering relatively attractive interest rates plus app-based service), and earns mainly the spread between the ~15.6% yield it charges on loans and the ~7.1% it pays on deposits, plus fee income from selling insurance, mutual funds and other third-party products. It operates through branches concentrated in South India (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka are named) with vehicle finance rolled out across India, and services NRI customers in 140-plus countries. As of March 2026 it had roughly INR46,165 crores of loans and INR46,533 crores of deposits, with quarterly profit of INR213 crores.

parts.name: Small business loans (SBL), including micro LAP, secured business loans and merchant overdraft
parts.what: Loans to small/informal business owners, typically against property, and small overdrafts to merchants — described as the bank's "flagship" and largest product at INR18,559 crores (about 45% of the book), growing 13-27% a year across the calls.

parts.name: Vehicle finance (new and used commercial vehicles, used cars)
parts.what: Loans to buy trucks and cars, with management increasingly steering toward used vehicles — used CVs at INR5,899 crores and used cars growing 31% year-on-year, while new CV lending is shrinking 20%; it is the second-biggest business and has been a repeated source of bad-loan slippage.

parts.name: Affordable housing loans (AHL)
parts.what: Home loans for lower-income buyers, a newer product that has grown steadily to INR5,782 crores and was said in FY26 to have finally turned profitable.

parts.name: Microfinance (MFI)
parts.what: Small unsecured group loans, historically 20% of the book in March 2024 but deliberately shrunk to about 8.5-10% (INR4,667 crores) after heavy defaults, and now capped at roughly 10% of lending on an ongoing basis.

parts.name: MSE finance
parts.what: Lending to micro and small enterprises, one of the newest lines, crossing INR2,000 crores and growing about 24-35% a year.

parts.name: Branch banking, liabilities, product and wealth
parts.what: The deposit-gathering and fee side — savings/current accounts, retail fixed deposits, NRI deposits (over INR2,000 crores), digitally-opened accounts, plus selling mutual funds/SIPs and insurance to customers; deposits were INR46,533 crores with CASA at 26% and retail deposits 68% of the total.

parts.name: Treasury
parts.what: Manages the bank's funding, liquidity and capital-conservation steps such as IBPC sell-downs (raised to INR2,000 crores) and buying loan pools through direct assignment; a support function rather than a customer-facing business.

overview.what_it_does: Eris Lifesciences is an Indian pharmaceutical company that sells branded prescription medicines — mainly for long-term (chronic and sub-chronic) conditions like diabetes, heart disease, skin disorders and kidney disease — which it promotes to specialist doctors in India through its own field sales force, tracking productivity as revenue per rep per month (YPM). About 90% of sales come from this Domestic Branded Formulations (DBF) business in India, with the remaining roughly 10% from an exports and contract-manufacturing arm (Swiss Parenterals) selling injectables into Latin America, other emerging markets and, increasingly, Europe on a CDMO basis. It makes money on high gross margins (historically around 80%, more recently 75-86% depending on mix) by owning and pushing well-known brands, and it has grown heavily by acquiring brand portfolios and companies — Oaknet, derma brands from Glenmark and Dr. Reddy's, two tranches of Biocon's India business, Swiss Parenterals — then lifting their margins sharply, funded largely by debt. In FY26 consolidated revenue was about INR 3,129 crore with EBITDA of INR 1,120 crore, and it manufactures in its own plants in Gujarat/Ahmedabad, Sikkim and a Bhopal insulin fill-finish site.

parts.name: Domestic Branded Formulations (DBF)
parts.what: The core India business of branded prescription medicines sold to doctors, worth INR 2,778 crore of revenue in FY26 at a 37% operating margin — roughly 90% of the company and more than 85% chronic/sub-chronic by turnover; management calls it a 'specialty plus super-specialty' business and says Eris now ranks in the top 20 of the Indian market, up from rank 29 at its 2017 IPO.

parts.name: Cardiometabolic (Oral Anti-Diabetes + Cardiac Care)
parts.what: The flagship therapy area of diabetes tablets and heart/blood-pressure drugs, which together with vitamins/minerals used to be 80% of revenue and had fallen to about 65% by 2023 as other therapies were added; oral anti-diabetes market share was nearing 6% in FY25, and a new hypertension molecule, Esaxerenone, developed in-house, is its big launch.

parts.name: Insulins / injectable diabesity
parts.what: Insulin and injectable diabetes-obesity products (Basalog, Insugen, Xsulin, Xglar), mostly bought from Biocon in 2023-24, where market share in the RHI-plus-Glargine market rose from about 9% at acquisition to 16% by FY26 against a 25% target; Eris also launched its generic Semaglutide brand 'Sundae' in vials and pens in March-April 2026 and claims the number-one volume rank in injectable Semaglutide in its first full month.

parts.name: Dermatology
parts.what: Skin medicines built almost entirely by acquisition (Oaknet for INR 650 crore, nine Glenmark brands for INR 340 crore, nine cosmetic-derma brands from Dr. Reddy's for INR 275 crore, plus Biocon's derma portfolio), covering both medical derma and cosmetic products like anti-acne, moisturisers and hair care; it became the fourth-largest therapy at roughly 15% of revenue by 2023, ranks number 3 in its covered market, and grew 14.2% in FY26 versus an 8.6% market.

parts.name: Super-specialty: Nephrology, Oncology and Critical Care
parts.what: Kidney, cancer and hospital critical-care products added through the Biocon deals, described as still-growing super-specialty segments; management says critical care 'did not take off as expected' in FY26 and it is discontinuing a basket of low-margin, non-core general injectables worth about 2% of DBF revenue.

parts.name: Other emerging therapies: CNS, Women's Health, VMN
parts.what: Central nervous system drugs (entered via the Strides acquisition), women's health, and the vitamins/minerals/nutrition range; together with dermatology these 'emerging' therapies rose from 12% to 28% of revenue by early 2023.

parts.name: International Business / Swiss Parenterals
parts.what: The exports arm acquired in FY24 (then under INR 300 crore revenue and INR 80 crore EBITDA), which makes sterile injectables for emerging markets and Latin America and is building an EU contract-manufacturing (CDMO) order book of over INR 1,000 crore; it did INR 348 crore revenue and INR 110 crore EBITDA in FY26 at ~32% margin, is guided to INR 550-600 crore in FY27, and targets INR 1,000 crore by 2029-30, with a third injectable unit due in 2028.

parts.name: Trade Generics
parts.what: A small unbranded-generics line that the company wound down and discontinued during FY26, contributing essentially nothing to FY26 revenue.

overview.what_it_does: Escorts Kubota Limited (formerly Escorts Limited) is an India-based machinery manufacturer, headquartered in Faridabad, Haryana, that makes and sells farm tractors and related agricultural equipment, construction machinery, and — until it was divested in FY26 — railway equipment. It earns money mainly by selling tractors to Indian farmers through a large exclusive dealer network (about 1,240 dealers in mid-2023, around 1,500 by late 2024) under the Farmtrac, Powertrac and Kubota brands, with quarterly tractor volumes running from roughly 26,000 units in 2023 to about 37,000 units by Q3 FY26 and a domestic market share of roughly 9.7% to 11.3%. Beyond India it exports tractors and, increasingly, components — a growing share routed through the global network of its Japanese partner Kubota (about 32% of exports in Q1 FY24, rising to roughly 68% by Q3 FY26) — and it has built an export hub in Faridabad to supply parts to Kubota group companies worldwide. Quarterly revenue has grown from about INR 2,328 crores (June 2023) to about INR 3,261 crores (December 2025), with EBITDA margins in the 10-14% range; the company describes itself as debt-free with liquidity to fund growth.

parts.name: Agri Machinery Business Division (Tractor Business Division)
parts.what: The core and by far largest business — building and selling tractors under the Farmtrac, Powertrac and Kubota brands to Indian farmers plus exports, contributing segment revenue of roughly INR 1,667 crores in Q1 FY24 rising to about INR 2,770 crores in Q3 FY26 (well over two-thirds of company revenue), with EBIT margins moving from roughly 9% to 13.5%.

parts.name: Non-tractor business within Agri Machinery (Agri Solutions)
parts.what: A range of farm mechanisation equipment — rotavators, harvesters, rice transplanters (including the Japan-engineered next-gen KA6 and KA8 models), balers and sprayers — sold under the Farmpower and Kubota brands; part of a non-tractor pool that grew from roughly 10-12% of agri machinery revenue before the 2024 merger to about 17-21% after it.

parts.name: Engine business (within Agri Machinery)
parts.what: Makes high-performance diesel engines — Escorts engines from 7.5 kVA to 58.5 kVA sold mainly to generator-set makers, and Kubota engines in the 10-55 kilowatt range supplied to construction machinery manufacturers — one of the three legs of the non-tractor revenue that is roughly a fifth of agri machinery sales.

parts.name: Service and spare parts business (within Agri Machinery)
parts.what: Supplies after-sales support and replacement parts across the agri machinery range so customers can keep their equipment running; counted alongside agri solutions and engines in the non-tractor revenue pool.

parts.name: Construction Equipment Business Division
parts.what: Makes and also trades cranes, backhoe loaders, mini excavators and compactors for infrastructure and construction contractors — roughly 1,100 to 2,000 machines a quarter and segment revenue of about INR 338-516 crores per quarter (a low- to mid-teens share of sales), with margins swinging widely (7.6% to 11% in good quarters, down to 3.8% in Q2 FY26) as infrastructure spending and emission-norm changes move demand.

parts.name: Railway Equipment Business Division
parts.what: Supplied products to the railways on an order-book basis (about INR 950 crores of orders as of June 2023) and was the highest-margin unit at times (20.9% EBIT on INR 298 crores of revenue in Q1 FY24), but the business was divested by Q3 FY26, prompting a one-time special dividend of INR 18 per share.

parts.name: Escorts Kubota Finance Limited (EKFL) — captive finance
parts.what: A newly RBI-registered lending arm, set to begin operations in FY25, whose job is to finance customers buying the company's own products; management also cites strengthened financing partnerships as a support to tractor sales.

parts.name: Global sourcing / component exports for the Kubota Group
parts.what: Using India's low-cost manufacturing and the company's vendor base to supply components and services to Kubota companies worldwide under a 'China plus One' strategy, anchored by a 58,000 square foot export hub inaugurated in Faridabad; described as an enormous long-term opportunity though still early.

overview.what_it_does: Eternal (formerly Zomato) is an Indian consumer internet company that runs delivery apps: customers order restaurant food or everyday grocery and household items on their phone and a delivery rider brings it in minutes. It makes money mainly by taking a cut (a "take rate") of each order's value from restaurants, selling advertising to restaurants and brands on its apps, charging customers delivery fees and paid-membership (Gold) plans, and, in quick commerce, by earning a margin on goods sold out of its own network of small neighbourhood warehouses called dark stores. It operates in India, city by city — starting from the Delhi/NCR region and expanding across other cities including the south — with roughly 3,000 dark stores targeted by March 2026 and over 30 million monthly transacting users on the quick-commerce app alone. Management measures the business on gross/net order value (GOV/NOV), contribution per order and adjusted EBITDA, and is targeting about $1 billion of EBITDA by FY29.

parts.name: Food delivery (Zomato)
parts.what: The original app that lets people order cooked meals from restaurants for home delivery, earning commissions, restaurant ad spend and customer delivery charges; it is the mature, cash-generating leg — it reached adjusted EBITDA breakeven back in FY23, was still growing order value about 20% a year in recent calls, and management targets a roughly 4-5% margin on order value.

parts.name: Quick commerce (Blinkit)
parts.what: Ten-minute delivery of groceries and daily-needs products from company-run dark stores, acquired and pivoted into quick commerce from January 2022 after an initial ~$320 million investment budget; it is now the main growth engine and the focus of most analyst questions, with a guided ~60% order-value CAGR over three years, a 3,000-store target by March 2026, and a long-term margin goal raised to about 6% of order value.

parts.name: Going-out / District
parts.what: A separate app and brand for dining-out and other going-out experiences (restaurant discovery, bookings, events), built to reuse traffic from the main app to keep customer-acquisition costs low; it is the smallest and newest leg, with management guiding only to profitability around FY30.

parts.name: Bistro
parts.what: A newer, smaller venture discussed as Eternal's answer to lower-priced, affordability-focused food ordering (compared by analysts to a rival's cheaper delivery model); the calls treat it as an early-stage option rather than a material contributor.

overview.what_it_does: Ethos Limited is an Indian luxury retailer that sells high-end wristwatches — mostly Swiss brands — through its own network of physical boutiques and its website, ethoswatches.com. It buys watches from luxury brands and resells them to affluent Indian customers at retail, so it makes money on the gross margin between purchase and sale price, earning better margins on the brands it has signed exclusive India retail rights for (about 31% of revenue) and on its certified pre-owned business, alongside servicing and after-sales support. It operates only in India (73 boutiques across 26 cities as of March 2025, targeting 100+, plus a 22,000 sq ft flagship 'City of Time' in Gurgaon), with a newly formed, exploratory UAE subsidiary. Revenue was about INR 1,252 crore in FY25, up roughly 25% year-on-year, with EBITDA of about INR 161 crore.

parts.name: Luxury watch retail (multi-brand boutiques + omnichannel)
parts.what: The core business — selling luxury and high-luxury watches through Ethos boutiques (multi-brand formats such as Ethos Summit and the newer Ethos Haute Horology) backed by a website, social media, HNI customer database and home/office delivery; this is the bulk of the roughly INR 1,252 crore FY25 revenue, and management said the digital channel alone contributed nearly one-third of billings back in Q1 FY23.

parts.name: Exclusive brand portfolio / exclusive brand boutiques
parts.what: Watch brands that have appointed Ethos as their exclusive India retail partner (35 brands as of 2022, with Jacob & Co., NORQAIN, Ulysse Nardin, Nivada Grenchen, Gerald Charles, Chronoswiss, ID Geneve, Singer Reimagined and Hautlence added since); management calls these long-nurtured relationships a competitive moat and says they carry higher margins, contributing about 26% of billings in Q1 FY23 and around 31% of revenue by FY24–FY25.

parts.name: Certified Pre-Owned (CPO) — 'Second Movement'
parts.what: Buying, authenticating and reselling second-hand luxury watches — increasingly on a consignment basis — through a dedicated lounge and the secondmovement.com website; described as a 'new growth pillar', it did INR 32 crore in H1 FY24 and INR 43 crore of billings in H1 FY25, growing 25–34% a year and over 30% in FY25.

parts.name: Luxury jewellery — Messika
parts.what: Retailing the French jewellery brand Messika in India, with the first dedicated boutique opened at Chanakya Mall, New Delhi in May 2025; it is an early-stage diversification that management says it is approaching cautiously with a long-term outlook.

parts.name: Premium luggage / lifestyle — Rimowa
parts.what: Retailing the LVMH-owned luggage brand Rimowa, starting with a roughly 500 sq ft boutique opened October 2023 at Jio World Plaza, Mumbai (their first non-watch luxury store), with a second Delhi boutique planned; small in size but positioned as a future growth vertical.

parts.name: After-sales service and watch servicing
parts.what: Repair, servicing and related customer support (including watch insurance and specialised luxury watch consultants) offered alongside sales; management repeatedly names it as a pillar of the strategy and a reason customers and brands trust Ethos, though no separate revenue figure is given in these calls.

parts.name: Favre Leuba (group-invested Swiss brand)
parts.what: A Swiss watch brand the promoter group has invested in and relaunched globally in Geneva in August 2024; Ethos has a long-term exclusive agreement to sell it in India, adding a brand-ownership angle on top of pure retailing.

parts.name: International expansion — Ficus Trading LLC (UAE)
parts.what: A wholly-owned UAE subsidiary set up as of May 2025 which management describes as purely exploratory at this stage, to understand what Ethos might do outside India.

overview.what_it_does: Eureka Forbes is an India-focused consumer appliance company that sells home health-and-hygiene products — water purifiers under its well-known Aquaguard brand, vacuum cleaners (including robotic and cordless models), air purifiers and water softeners — mainly to Indian households, at prices ranging from about INR 6,499 at the entry level to INR 79,999 for its most premium purifier. It makes money in two ways: one-time sales of the machines themselves (the 'product business'), and a recurring 'service business' of annual maintenance contracts (AMCs), repairs and replacement filters and spares sold to its installed base of 8 million-plus customers through a nationwide service technician network. Products reach buyers through an omnichannel mix of direct sales agents, retail/modern trade, distributors and e-commerce, all within India. Full-year FY26 revenue was INR 2,710 crores (up 11.3%) with adjusted EBITDA of INR 332 crores at a 12.2% margin, up from a 6.3% margin in FY23 after a multi-year turnaround management calls 'Project Udaan'.

parts.name: Water purifiers (Electric Water Purifiers / Aquaguard)
parts.what: Sells household drinking-water purifiers under the Aquaguard brand across economy to premium price points; this is the company's original and still largest category — management describes the business as having been 'a single category company' built on it — and says the category has grown at a 3-year CAGR of over 12% despite a soft patch in FY26.

parts.name: Vacuum cleaners / convenient cleaning (including Robotics)
parts.what: Sells vacuum cleaners, with growth coming from robotic, premium upright and cordless models; it is the second-largest product line and robotics is repeatedly called out as delivering strong growth and expanding into organized retail.

parts.name: Air purifiers
parts.what: Sells home air purifiers, pitched on worsening urban air quality; still small ('on a low base') but the fastest-growing line, up about 2.7x in FY26 and sold out at the end of Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Water softeners
parts.what: A newer category of water-softening equipment for homes, reported as delivering steady healthy double-digit growth on the back of rising awareness and investment in distribution.

parts.name: Service business (AMCs, filters and spares)
parts.what: The recurring-revenue arm — annual maintenance contracts, servicing visits by its technician network, and sales of replacement filters and spares — where AMC bookings grew in double digits in FY26; management calls the aftermarket filter opportunity large but slow to capture, and notes service carries a higher margin mix than products.

overview.what_it_does: Exide Industries is an Indian battery maker — it has been in the lead-acid battery market for about 75 years and calls itself a leading player in that space. It sells batteries for vehicles (both to auto manufacturers as original equipment and, in larger and more profitable volume, to vehicle owners replacing worn-out batteries) and for power back-up and industrial uses such as home inverters, UPS systems, solar installations, telecom towers, railways and traction. Money is made by manufacturing and selling these batteries through a pan-India distribution network and a strong brand, with some sales exported; quarterly revenue crossed Rs. 4,000 crores in Q3 FY26 at an EBITDA margin of about 11.7%, and profitability swings with lead and other raw-material prices. Alongside this core business, it is spending heavily to build a lithium-ion cell factory near Bengaluru airport through a wholly owned subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions, into which Rs. 4,802 crores of equity had been put by March 2026.

parts.name: Automotive – replacement / aftermarket
parts.what: Sells 2-wheeler and 4-wheeler batteries to existing vehicle owners through the trade channel; management calls this a consistently strong, higher-margin part of the business, growing in the mid-teens quarter after quarter and hitting record quarterly revenue in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Automotive OEM
parts.what: Supplies batteries fitted into new vehicles at the factory (for example, being 100% supplier on the Tata Sierra petrol and new Kia Seltos models); it is described as lower-margin, moves with car and two-wheeler production, and grew about 25% year-on-year in both Q3 and Q4 FY26 after a weak FY25.

parts.name: Home UPS / inverter batteries
parts.what: Batteries for household power back-up, sold through distributors and highly seasonal — hurt by early or extended monsoons, helped by early summer, and it posted its highest-ever Q4 sales in FY26.

parts.name: Industrial UPS (trade and OEM)
parts.what: Batteries for commercial and industrial back-up power systems, growing steadily at roughly 13%–15% year-on-year in recent quarters.

parts.name: Solar
parts.what: Batteries and related products for solar installations, a vertical incubated over the last few years that grew 25%–30% at times and crossed Rs. 1,000 crores of revenue in FY26.

parts.name: Industrial infrastructure (Railways, Traction, Motive Power)
parts.what: Large B2B orders tied to public and private capex in power, railways, traction and motive power; order inflow and execution have kept it growing at double digits year-on-year.

parts.name: Telecom
parts.what: Batteries for telecom towers — once around 10% of revenue during the 5G rollout, now a structurally declining business as operators shift from lead-acid to lithium-ion; together with exports it was about 7%–8% of turnover, with telecom (including some e-rickshaw sales) roughly 3%.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Sales to overseas markets including Central Asia, Western Europe and the US; it has fallen from about 8% of revenue a couple of years ago to roughly 5%–6%, held back by tariff barriers and geopolitical tension, and management expects recovery once tariffs settle.

parts.name: Exide Energy Solutions (lithium-ion cell manufacturing)
parts.what: A wholly owned subsidiary building a lithium-ion cell plant on about 80 acres near Bengaluru airport — two 6 GWh phases, roughly Rs. 6,000 crores of total capex, Rs. 4,802 crores of equity invested by March 2026 — with cylindrical lines starting customer samples around May 2026 and prismatic lines in trial, targeting 2-wheeler, 3-wheeler, 4-wheeler and stationary energy customers; it also already supplies lithium-ion battery packs to telecom tower operators.

overview.what_it_does: Federal Bank is an Indian commercial bank, headquartered at Federal Towers in Aluva, Kerala, with a legacy the management calls 90 years old and shares listed on the NSE and BSE. It takes deposits from the public through a branch network it keeps expanding (about 65 branches added in one half-year, six in a single recent quarter) and lends that money out to individuals, small and mid-sized businesses, and large corporates; a distinctive strength management repeatedly calls its "moat" is deposits from non-resident Indians (NRE deposits crossed INR 1 lakh crore by March 2026). It earns money mainly on the spread between what it pays depositors and what it charges borrowers — net interest income of INR 2,652 crore in Q3 FY26 at a net interest margin of about 3.18% — plus fee income (INR 896 crore in that quarter, growing ~19% year-on-year) from cross-sell and other services, with a treasury operation that manages investments and can swing results with bond-market moves. As of March 2026 total business was about INR 5.79 lakh crore (deposits roughly INR 2.98 lakh crore, gross advances INR 2.68 lakh crore), and quarterly net profit reached a record INR 1,145 crore; it also owns a listed subsidiary, Fedfina, and has agreed a strategic investment from Blackstone.

parts.name: Deposits / liability franchise (CASA, retail and NRI deposits)
parts.what: The money-gathering side of the bank — current and savings accounts plus term deposits, overwhelmingly retail in nature (management says "high 90s" percent retail), with CASA balances crossing INR 1 lakh crore and a CASA ratio of about 32.9% that management calls among the best in the industry; the NRI/NRE book, also above INR 1 lakh crore, is described as the bank's key differentiator.

parts.name: Retail banking
parts.what: Everyday lending to individuals — housing and personal loans, credit cards, and related products — growing about 15% year-on-year and one of the larger pieces of the loan book.

parts.name: Commercial banking (mid-market / medium lending)
parts.what: Loans to mid-sized companies; management calls it the "primary growth engine," growing roughly 26% year-on-year through FY26.

parts.name: Business banking
parts.what: Lending to smaller businesses; it was weak at the start of FY26 but turned around, growing about 4-6% quarter-on-quarter by late FY26.

parts.name: Corporate and institutional banking (wholesale banking)
parts.what: Large-ticket lending and banking services to big companies and institutions, headed by a dedicated country head, growing about 14% year-on-year.

parts.name: Gold loans
parts.what: Loans against gold, described as one of the bank's medium-lending portfolios, growing roughly 26% year-on-year even while part of the book was deliberately shrunk to fit new regulatory rules.

parts.name: Loan against property (LAP)
parts.what: Secured loans backed by property, one of the fastest-expanding books late in FY26 at about 8% growth in a single quarter.

parts.name: Agriculture and microfinance
parts.what: Farm lending and very small-ticket loans, both described as new-age/newer businesses that gained traction after COVID and grew 5% and about 7% quarter-on-quarter respectively.

parts.name: Commercial vehicle / commercial equipment (CV/CE) finance
parts.what: Loans for trucks and business equipment, another of the newer businesses management has been scaling, up about 8.5% in the March 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Treasury
parts.what: Manages the bank's own investments and funding; run by a dedicated group president and head, it can add to or subtract from profits depending on bond-market rates, which management flags as outside its control.

parts.name: Fee income and wealth management
parts.what: Non-interest earnings from services and cross-sell — a record INR 896 crore in Q3 FY26 — now being extended by a wealth management business launched in the March 2026 quarter to serve mass-affluent customers and deepen the fee pool.

parts.name: Fedfina (subsidiary)
parts.what: A separately listed subsidiary whose IPO management called a standout success and which reports its own quarterly numbers; it contributes to the group but is not the bank's core operation.

overview.what_it_does: Fedbank Financial Services (FEDFINA) is an Indian non-bank lender (NBFC) that makes small, mostly collateral-backed loans to self-employed people and small business owners — the segment management calls "emerging India" — whose income is hard to document and who larger banks generally won't underwrite with standard models. It lends against whatever the customer can pledge: gold jewellery (gold loans) or property (loan against property, both small-ticket and medium-ticket), and it previously ran an unsecured business-loan book that it stopped originating and fully sold down, so the on-book portfolio is now over 99.5% secured. It earns money mainly from the spread between the ~15-18% yields it charges and its borrowing cost, supplemented by co-lending tie-ups with banks and by direct assignment (selling loan pools), though management has deliberately shrunk direct-assignment income in favour of core interest income. It operates a branch-led, physically intensive model across India — 607 branches in 17 states at listing in late 2023, growing to over 750 branches by FY26 — with total loan assets (AUM) rising from about Rs. 10,000 crore in Sept 2023 to Rs. 21,136 crore by June 2026; it listed on the NSE and BSE on 30 November 2023 and is majority-linked to Federal Bank, which it refers to as its parent.

parts.name: Gold Loans
parts.what: Loans against pledged gold jewellery to small customers, including a fast-growing "doorstep" service where the loan is done at the customer's location; it is the company's largest and fastest-growing business, with AUM of Rs. 11,191 crore (about 53% of the book) by Q1 FY27 versus Rs. 3,969 crore in March 2024, and management calls it one of the two "twin engines."

parts.name: Small Ticket LAP (ST LAP) / Small Ticket Mortgage
parts.what: Small loans against residential or commercial property to self-employed borrowers at high yields; it was the company's stated focus area at listing, then hit heavy delinquencies through FY24-FY25 requiring new leadership, rewritten credit policy and a system-driven rules engine, and it disbursed Rs. 904 crore in FY26 while management described it as "stabilized" and again a growth business (as of FY27 it is being run together with Home Loans).

parts.name: Medium Ticket LAP (MT LAP)
parts.what: Larger loans against property, positioned as the lower-risk, lower-capital half of the mortgage book, run partly through direct assignment to conserve capital; it grew 44% in FY25 to Rs. 4,394 crore (28% of AUM) and disbursed Rs. 2,180 crore in FY26 with stable yields.

parts.name: Business Loans (BL) — unsecured
parts.what: Unsecured loans to small businesses, which management deliberately wound down: originations were stopped during FY25 (Rs. 1,656 crore, under 10% of AUM at March 2025), and the remaining Rs. 886 crore portfolio was 100% assigned away in FY26 to free capital and shield the company from stress in unsecured lending.

parts.name: Co-lending and Direct Assignment (DA)
parts.what: Rather than fund every loan itself, it partners with banks — a large private bank and a foreign bank were the first co-lending tie-ups, mainly for gold — and sells loan pools to investors; the gold co-lending book reached Rs. 2,127 crore by Q4 FY26, while DA income was deliberately cut 89% in FY26 to Rs. 7 crore and is now used as a capital-allocation tool rather than a profit source.

parts.name: Branch network / "Vyapar" branches and collections
parts.what: The distribution and recovery machinery behind the lending: over 750 branches by FY26 (148 new gold branches added that year), with 70 small-ticket LAP branches folded into gold branch premises as combined "Vyapar" branches selling both products, plus a collections organisation that was verticalized by product and roughly doubled in headcount over FY26 to bring credit costs down to 0.8%.

overview.what_it_does: Fiem Industries is an Indian auto-parts maker whose main business is designing and manufacturing lighting and related electronics — head lamps, tail lamps, number plate lamps, fog lamps, reflectors and similar parts — that go onto vehicles as they are built. It sells almost entirely business-to-business, directly to vehicle makers (OEMs), overwhelmingly two-wheeler brands: Honda (HMSI), TVS, Yamaha, Suzuki, Royal Enfield and Hero, plus 20-plus electric two-wheeler customers, and more recently passenger-car makers such as Mahindra & Mahindra. It makes money by winning parts on specific vehicle models and supplying them in volume from its own plants (Rai/Sonepat and Tapukara in the north, Hosur in the south, with an EMC/EMI test lab at Gurgaon), so revenue rises and falls with how many units its customers build; management credits its margins to an 'integrated manufacturing model' and operating leverage. Revenue grew from roughly INR 2,014 crores in FY24 to INR 2,790 crores in FY26 with profit after tax of INR 254 crores, EBITDA margin just over 14%, and it describes itself as a net-zero-debt company.

parts.name: Automotive lighting (two-wheeler)
parts.what: The core business — lamps and lighting assemblies fitted to motorcycles, scooters and mopeds for Honda, TVS, Yamaha, Suzuki, Royal Enfield and Hero; management discusses company results essentially as this business, and quotes total two-wheeler industry production (26.7 million units in FY26) as its main demand driver.

parts.name: LED lighting (share of automotive lighting)
parts.what: The higher-technology slice of the lamp business that management tracks explicitly and says is steadily replacing conventional lighting — 44% of automotive lighting in FY22, 52% in FY24 and about 60-63% in FY26, with 'most of the new business we are winning in LED'.

parts.name: EV / electric two-wheeler supply
parts.what: The same lighting and electronics sold to electric two-wheeler makers — more than 20 EV customers as early as FY23 (INR 18.5 crores of revenue in Q1 FY23), and by FY26 including TVS iQube, Honda's Activa EV platform, Royal Enfield EV initiatives and an approved new Hero EV platform.

parts.name: 4-wheeler / passenger car business
parts.what: A newer growth line started with an order from a European car maker and then Indian car makers; by FY26 Fiem supplies number plate lamps, rear reflectors and fog lamps to Mahindra & Mahindra across various models, with high-mount stop lamps for Bolero and Scorpio in development — still small but flagged as a major future growth driver.

parts.name: Hub motors and motor controllers (Gogoro project)
parts.what: A non-lighting venture to make electric-scooter hub motors and motor controllers for Gogoro; as of May 2024 it had produced almost nothing because Gogoro's launch volumes were tiny (about 5,000 vehicles), so it had made no meaningful contribution to revenue despite capex being planned for it.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Supply of lamps for models built in India for overseas markets — Yamaha models for Europe and the US, Hero's Harley-linked X440, and development work for TVS-owned Norton — described as a source of growth but lumpy, since fixed export order quantities finishing can dent a quarter.

parts.name: Electronics capability and new products
parts.what: In-house electronics manufacturing (a surface-mount / SMT line running since around 2006, plus a new EMC/EMI lab at Gurgaon) supporting products such as USB chargers and sensors and future technologies like laser lighting, touch interfaces and adaptive drive beam; presented as capability that lets Fiem move into higher-value lighting rather than as a separately sized revenue line.

parts.name: Fuel pump module joint venture (exited)
parts.what: A former JV making fuel pump modules that Fiem fully exited in June 2022 for INR 26 crores, removing an expected INR 150-200 crores of potential revenue from the portfolio.

overview.what_it_does: Finolex Cables Limited is an India-based manufacturer of electrical wires and cables, run from Pune and listed in Mumbai (BSE/NSE) and Luxembourg. Its bread-and-butter is copper electrical wire and cable sold mainly to Indian builders, homeowners, factories, farms and vehicle makers, alongside a second business making communication cables, including optical fibre cable and the fibre and preform that go into it, sold to telecom operators like Reliance and Bharti and to government broadband projects such as BSNL's BharatNet. It sells almost entirely through a distribution network — roughly 730 distributors and about 4,500 channel partners (around 2,000 buying regularly) — rather than directly to projects, so profits depend on volume plus the gap between copper/commodity input costs and the selling prices it resets every few weeks (14 price changes, about 24%-25% cumulative, in FY26 alone). Sales skew to South India (~45% of revenue) and West India (~30%), with North and East making up the remaining ~25%, and quarterly revenue has grown from about INR 1,222 crores in Q3 FY24 to roughly INR 1,600 crores in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Electrical cables (electrical sector)
parts.what: The dominant segment and main profit engine — a range of copper wires and cables that hit a record INR 1,697 crores of revenue in Q4 FY26, up about 22% for the full year, historically earning roughly 13.5%-14% margins though product mix has pushed this around.

parts.name: Building wire / construction wire
parts.what: House and building wiring, described as still the majority of electrical sales; growth was only marginal in FY26 because repeated copper-driven price hikes met customer resistance.

parts.name: E-beam cured premium wire and solar cables
parts.what: New products off an electron-beam plant commissioned January 2025 — a premium halogen-free, flame-resistant building wire rated for 25+ years of life, plus solar cables; management targets INR 500-600 crores of annual revenue from the two, and by FY26 solar was running at 80%-85% of capacity with more capacity planned.

parts.name: Auto cables
parts.what: Wiring sold into the automotive industry; one of the fastest-growing lines, up about 42% in volume in Q3 FY26 and about 30% in Q4 FY26, with plant utilisation in the late 70s percent.

parts.name: Industrial cables / flexibles
parts.what: Cables for industrial use, a many-SKU business that grew about 28% in volume in Q3 FY26 and about 17% in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Power cables
parts.what: A deliberately small presence — management sizes India's power cable market at INR 23,000-25,000 crores a year against Finolex's exposure of only about INR 150-180 crores — though volumes still grew 21%-22% in FY26.

parts.name: Agricultural applications
parts.what: Wires and cables for farm use, the one weak spot in FY26: volumes fell 15%-16% on an unfavourable monsoon, off-season timing and pricing problems.

parts.name: Communication cables
parts.what: The second-largest segment, roughly two-thirds optical-fibre-based products and the rest metal-based; revenue is lumpy because it depends on BharatNet tenders and on capex by Reliance and Bharti, and was flat for FY26 overall before a ~30% jump in Q4 as global fibre prices rose from under $3 to about $5.

parts.name: Optical fibre and preform manufacturing (backward integration)
parts.what: In-house fibre drawing and a new preform plant commissioned in March 2026, part of a capex programme lifting fibre draw capacity from 4 million to 8 million kilometres by around Q1 FY27, aimed at capturing demand management believes could reach 50 million km a year in India.

parts.name: Extra high voltage (EHV) JV with Sumitomo
parts.what: A joint venture in very-high-voltage cables (160kV+) serving a market management sizes at $400-500 million; it turned profitable in FY26 with about INR 21 crores of profit on roughly INR 450 crores of revenue and opened the next year with an INR 380 crores order book.

overview.what_it_does: Finolex Industries is an Indian maker of plastic (PVC) pipes and fittings, sold mainly to farmers for irrigation and water supply and, increasingly, to the building trade for plumbing and sanitation. It is unusual in that it also manufactures the key raw material itself — PVC resin — at its own plants (it imports the chemical inputs EDC and VCM and runs a captive coal-fired power plant), covering roughly 65-70% of its own resin needs in-house and selling the surplus resin to other buyers. It makes money on the gap between the cost of resin/raw material and the price of finished pipes, so profits swing with global PVC, EDC and VCM prices as much as with volumes. It operates in India, with plants in Maharashtra (registered office at Urse, Pune), sold about 333,000 tonnes for FY26 on revenue of roughly INR 4,113 crores, and carries a large net cash pile (about INR 2,563 crores) rather than debt.

parts.name: Pipes & Fittings
parts.what: The main business — making and selling UPVC and CPVC pipes and fittings, contributing almost all of company revenue in recent quarters (e.g. INR 1,123 crores of INR 1,140 crores total income in Q1 FY25).

parts.name: Agri (within Pipes & Fittings)
parts.what: Pipes sold to farmers for irrigation and farm water use — historically the biggest slice at roughly 65-70% of volumes, seasonal and dependent on the monsoon and the pre-monsoon kharif buying season.

parts.name: Non-agri / Plumbing & Sanitation (within Pipes & Fittings)
parts.what: Pipes and fittings for buildings and housing, the faster-growing and better-priced part of the mix, rising from about 25% of Q1 volumes in FY2020 to 36% by Q1 FY2023 and continuing to gain share.

parts.name: CPVC pipes (within Pipes & Fittings)
parts.what: A higher-value hot-water plumbing product line management tracks separately — around 3,600 tonnes and roughly INR 150 crores of sales in a single quarter in FY2023 — and one of only two pipe technologies (with UPVC) the company currently makes.

parts.name: PVC Resin
parts.what: The backward-integrated chemical plant that produces PVC resin from imported EDC and VCM, feeding most of the pipe business and selling the rest outside; it is the smaller revenue segment (e.g. INR 548 crores in Q1 FY25) but is the source of the company's cost advantage over pipe makers who buy resin on the open market.

overview.what_it_does: Brainbees Solutions, which trades under the brand FirstCry, is an Indian retailer of products for mothers, babies and kids — diapers, baby gear, nursery items, fashion, toys and similar — sold mainly to young parents. It reaches them through several channels at once: its own online platform, a chain of 1,000-plus (now about 1,200) branded stores, and distribution of its own in-house 'home brands' into ordinary general-trade retail shops; it also manufactures part of what it sells and runs its own delivery network. It earns money by selling merchandise at a margin (gross margin was about 37.8% in India in Q1 FY26), so profit comes from growing order volumes and widening that margin rather than from fees. Beyond India it runs the same model in the UAE and Saudi Arabia, owns a house-of-brands business called GlobalBees, and operates an asset-light preschool chain; consolidated FY26 revenue was ₹8,547 crore, up 12%, with adjusted EBITDA of ₹486 crore.

parts.name: India multi-channel
parts.what: The original and by far largest segment (started 2010) — the FirstCry online store, 1,000+ (about 1,200) offline stores including company-owned COCO stores, and a newer distribution arm that pushes FirstCry's home brands into general-trade shops; FY26 revenue grew 9% with adjusted EBITDA of about ₹505 crore, and management says it stayed profit-and-cash-flow positive all year.

parts.name: International (UAE and KSA)
parts.what: The same retail playbook run in the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, roughly ₹207 crore of revenue in Q1 FY26; it is still loss-making but management is deliberately shrinking the losses (adjusted EBITDA loss down 35% in FY26) rather than chasing growth against discounting by large horizontal e-commerce rivals.

parts.name: GlobalBees
parts.what: A separate company incubated in May 2021 that owns and runs a portfolio of consumer brands in home improvement and utilities, home appliances, health and personal care, and active/lifestyle and accessories; revenue was ₹426.5 crore in Q1 FY26 (up 31%), all growth organic since the last acquisition in September 2022, with FY26 adjusted EBITDA of roughly ₹92 crore after corporate costs, while weaker non-core brands are being pruned.

parts.name: Others (preschool)
parts.what: The smallest segment — an asset-light preschool business where FirstCry does not own the physical assets; FY26 revenue grew 11% and its adjusted EBITDA improved 21% over FY25.

parts.name: RocketBees (initiative within India multi-channel)
parts.what: FirstCry's own asset-light delivery network, where the company owns the technology and dedicated third-party regional couriers ship its orders, built after customer-experience problems with outside logistics firms; it went from 13 cities to 62 cities during FY26 and handled over 40% of online delivery volumes by the March 2026 quarter, improving delivery times about 20%.

parts.name: FirstCry Qwik (initiative within India multi-channel)
parts.what: A fast-delivery service promising under three hours across the full product range, fulfilled from company-owned stores, warehouses, stockists and dark stores; started December 2025 and already in 5 cities, where it accounts for over 20% of online orders in those catchments, with management expecting roughly 10% of all online business in FY27.

overview.what_it_does: Five-Star Business Finance is an Indian non-bank lender (an NBFC, listed as FIVESTAR on the NSE and BSE, with its registered office in Chennai) that has been making small-ticket loans for about 20 years to small shopkeepers, self-employed people and cash-salaried workers — borrowers who have no formal documentary proof of income or credit history, which management describes as a niche, less-crowded segment. Every loan is fully secured (management repeatedly contrasts itself with unsecured lenders), and the company builds its own capability to assess these borrowers' cash flows and integrity and to collect on their earn-and-pay cycle. It makes money on the spread: it lends at high fixed rates (about 24% yield historically, cut by 200 bps from 1 November 2024 to roughly 22.5% on new loans) while borrowing from banks, mutual funds, NCDs, market-linked debentures, securitisation/PTC deals and ECBs at far lower cost (about 10.35% in FY23, down to roughly 8.8–9.1% by 2026), leaving a spread near 13.9%. It runs a branch-heavy, feet-on-the-street model that grew from 369 branches and a INR 6,242 crore loan book in December 2022 to about 856 branches, over 500,000 active loan customers and an INR 13,722 crore book by June 2026, with newer branch additions coming largely from states such as Maharashtra.

parts.name: Small-ticket secured lending to small businesses / self-employed and cash-salaried borrowers
parts.what: The single core product — fully secured, fixed-rate loans averaging a small ticket size to shopkeepers, self-employed and cash-salaried customers with no formal income documents; the calls describe no other revenue line, so this is effectively 100% of the business, growing from INR 6,242 crore AUM (Dec 2022) to INR 13,722 crore (Jun 2026).

parts.name: Branch network (including "split branches")
parts.what: The distribution engine: physical branches do the sourcing, underwriting and collection, and management deliberately splits busy branches into smaller ones to cut concentration risk in any one location — count went from 369 (Dec 2022) to 856 (Jun 2026), with 113 opened in the September 2024 quarter alone (32 new plus 77 splits).

parts.name: Collections vertical
parts.what: A dedicated in-house collections organisation that management built out heavily after asset quality wobbled in FY26 — 678 business and collection officers added in the December 2025 quarter alone, taking collection officers from 1,329 (Dec 2024) to 2,452 (Dec 2025), plus a full collections hierarchy up to head-office level; it is treated as central to keeping collection efficiency in the 96–98% range and is the reason growth was deliberately slowed.

parts.name: Borrowings / liability franchise (treasury)
parts.what: The funding side of the spread, run as a deliberate diversification effort away from banks — roughly 50 lenders in FY23 with banks at 56%, later spread across NCDs, market-linked debentures, securitisation/PTC deals subscribed by mutual funds (Nippon, Kotak, HDFC, HSBC) and ECBs; ratings improved to AA- (India Ratings) and cost of funds fell from about 10.35% to 8.80%, with liquidity buffers of roughly INR 1,000–2,276 crore held on the balance sheet.

overview.what_it_does: Gujarat Fluorochemicals (GFL) is an India-based chemicals maker that turns basic chemicals into fluorine-based products — plastics and rubbers called fluoropolymers (PTFE, PVDF, PFA, FKM), refrigerant gases (R-22, R-32, R-125), specialty chemicals, and commodity chemicals like caustic soda and chloromethanes. It sells to industrial customers rather than consumers: semiconductor makers, auto and emission-control companies, air-conditioning and cold-chain players, solar and clean-energy users, and increasingly electric-vehicle and battery-storage manufacturers. It makes money by selling these materials by the tonne, mostly at higher margins in the specialty grades, and is heavily export-oriented — management repeatedly cites the U.S., EU, Japan, Korea and India as markets, and blames U.S. tariffs and Red Sea shipping delays for weak quarters. Manufacturing is in Gujarat, India (Ranjitnagar/Dahej), with a new greenfield battery-materials plant being built in Oman; consolidated revenue runs roughly INR 1,100–1,400 crore a quarter, and the company describes itself as virtually debt-free while spending heavily on capacity expansion.

parts.name: Fluoropolymers
parts.what: Makes PTFE plus the higher-value 'new fluoropolymers' (PVDF, PFA, FKM, micropowders) used in semiconductors, auto emission control and solar film — this is the biggest and fastest-growing part, at INR 848 crore of a INR 1,358 crore quarter in Q4 FY26 and growing 14–19% year-on-year.

parts.name: Fluorochemicals (refrigerants and specialty chemicals)
parts.what: Sells refrigerant gases (R-22, R-125, and R-32 whose production started March 2026) for air conditioning, commercial refrigeration, cold chain and AI data-centre cooling, plus specialty chemicals; it swings a lot with seasons, R-22 production quotas and Chinese competition, and was the main drag in Q3 FY26 when segment revenue fell 33% year-on-year.

parts.name: Bulk Chemicals
parts.what: The commodity base — caustic soda, chloromethanes/MDC and fluoromethanes — which feeds the company's own downstream plants (backward integration) and is described as low-growth and price-driven, with revenue falling when caustic and chloromethane prices soften.

parts.name: Battery Materials (GFCL EV Products Limited)
parts.what: A newer subsidiary building an integrated set of lithium-ion battery inputs — LiPF6 salt (commercial sales began December 2025), LFP cathode active material, fluoropolymer binders and a planned natural graphite anode — aimed at EV and grid energy-storage customers; it earns almost nothing yet but is the company's big bet, with INR 6,000 crore of planned capex through FY28, an IFC investment of INR 430 crore and an $82 million sovereign-fund commitment, and full earnings expected only around FY29.

overview.what_it_does: Force Motors is a 66-year-old Indian vehicle maker based in Akurdi, Pune, that today sells mainly vans and buses — its Traveller and Urbania passenger vans, 26-seater Travellers, 33- and 41-seater Monobuses, Trax delivery vans, and the Gurkha off-roader for the armed forces. It earns money by selling these vehicles to Indian customers (shared-mobility and fleet operators, delivery businesses, and the defence forces) and increasingly to export markets in the Middle East, Latin America and Africa, plus a steady stream of spare-parts sales through about 287 service touch-points in India and 23 abroad. Alongside vehicles, it runs a components/aggregates business that manufactures engines and parts for global carmakers Mercedes-Benz and BMW, which management calls a good 'ballast' to the vehicle business. It has exited tractors and stopped making small commercial vehicles to focus on these lines; FY2024-25 revenue rose about 16%, EBITDA about 21%, ROCE reached roughly 43%, profit was around Rs 1,200 crore versus Rs 100 crore three years earlier, and the company is now essentially debt-free after repaying about Rs 500 crore.

parts.name: Vehicle business — T1 (Traveller and Urbania vans)
parts.what: Its core and biggest product line: passenger vans used for shared mobility, where management says it holds roughly 77% market share; the premium Urbania currently runs at 500-600 units a month with a target of about 1,000, and the Traveller platform is undergoing a major upgrade due to launch around Q1 of next year.

parts.name: Vehicle business — T2 (26-seater Traveller)
parts.what: The larger 26-seat version of the Traveller, where market share has grown to close to 19%.

parts.name: Monobus platform (33- and 41-seater buses)
parts.what: Full-size buses that have been gaining share, reaching about 7% in the 33-seater segment.

parts.name: Delivery vans (Traveller and Trax platforms)
parts.what: Goods-carrying vans holding roughly 16% market share; new niche, higher-margin Trax variants are being developed to grow volumes.

parts.name: Gurkha / defence
parts.what: A rugged vehicle sold to the armed forces — already supplied as a light strike vehicle, and last year the company won a major contract for 3,000 Gurkhas as troop carriers, with Indian and international defence seen as a growth avenue.

parts.name: Automotive component / aggregates business (engines for Mercedes-Benz and BMW)
parts.what: Manufactures engines and components for Mercedes-Benz and BMW in India; it grew about 16% last year, has no seasonality, and specific engine volumes are confidential — India's luxury car market it feeds is around 60,000 vehicles a year and growing.

parts.name: Spare parts business
parts.what: Aftermarket parts sold through the service network; grew about 20% last year and is targeted to grow over 20% again this year.

parts.name: International / export business
parts.what: Exports of Urbania and Traveller vans started in the last six months into the Middle East, Latin America and now South Africa and wider Africa; management expects at least 100% growth this year off a small base.

parts.name: FMTU joint venture (referred to by a shareholder as the Rolls-Royce JV)
parts.what: A joint venture company that reached break-even last year after three years of ramp-up and localisation — described as a big milestone but no size figures were given.

overview.what_it_does: Fortis Healthcare runs a chain of private hospitals in India and, through its Agilus Diagnostics arm (earlier branded SRL), a network of pathology labs and sample-collection points. It earns money by treating patients — mostly paid-for hospital admissions and surgeries in specialties like oncology, cardiac sciences, neurosciences, orthopedics, gastroenterology and renal sciences — and by charging for lab tests ordered by consumers directly (B2C) and by doctors, hospitals and other labs (B2B), plus some government contracts. Patients are largely Indian, with a meaningful slice of higher-paying foreign 'medical travel' patients (INR639 crore, about 7.8% of hospital revenue in FY26). Operations are concentrated in India in cluster geographies such as Delhi NCR, Punjab, Maharashtra, Bengaluru and Kolkata; FY26 consolidated revenue was INR9,128 crore with operating EBITDA of INR2,085 crore (22.8% margin) and profit after tax of INR1,064 crore.

parts.name: Hospital business
parts.what: Multi-specialty and tertiary-care hospitals where patients are admitted, operated on and treated — by far the main engine, at INR7,773 crore of FY26 revenue and roughly 85% of both consolidated revenue and consolidated EBITDA, run at about 68% bed occupancy with revenue per occupied bed (ARPOB) of INR2.51 crore a year.

parts.name: Diagnostics business (Agilus Diagnostics, formerly SRL)
parts.what: A lab-testing business doing about 9.9 million tests a quarter through roughly 4,370 customer touch points with a balanced 52:48 B2C-to-B2B mix; FY26 gross revenue was INR1,527 crore (net INR1,355 crore), the smaller of the two businesses at roughly 15% of the group, and its earnings swung sharply with COVID testing in FY22-23 before recovering to about 23% margins by FY26.

parts.name: Focus / key specialties (within hospitals)
parts.what: Oncology, neurosciences, cardiac sciences, gastroenterology, orthopedics and renal sciences, which management tracks as the growth drivers — they grew 18.9% and contributed 62% of hospital revenue in FY26, helped by higher-value complex work such as robotic surgeries (up 66%) and radiation therapy (up 19%).

parts.name: International patients / medical travel
parts.what: Foreign patients travelling to Fortis hospitals for treatment, worth INR639 crore in FY26 (up 18.5%) and about 7.8% of hospital revenue — a small but high-yield slice management calls out every quarter.

parts.name: Digital channels
parts.what: Patient bookings and enquiries coming through the company's website, mobile apps and online campaigns, which management says now feed roughly 30% of overall hospital revenue, up from about 23% two years earlier.

parts.name: Preventive and specialized test portfolios (within Agilus)
parts.what: Higher-value wellness/health check-up packages and specialized tests rather than routine ones; preventive rose to about 12% of diagnostics revenue and specialized to about 35% by Q3 FY26, and management points to both as the route to better lab margins.

parts.name: Emerging care formats
parts.what: Newer, smaller-format offerings outside the main multi-specialty hospitals — such as the 12-bed oncology chemotherapy daycare centre in Delhi and Adayu, a 36-bed dedicated mental-health facility launched in Gurugram in November 2025 — described as pilots or new areas to scale rather than material revenue today.

parts.name: Bed expansion and acquisitions
parts.what: Growth comes from adding beds in existing hospitals (brownfield) and buying or leasing hospitals in its cluster cities — roughly 800 beds added in FY26 including People Tree Hospital in Bengaluru (INR430 crore), Shrimann Hospital in Jalandhar and a leased 200-bed Greater Noida facility, with about 1,800 more beds planned over four years and FY26 capex of about INR700 crore.

overview.what_it_does: Firstsource Solutions is an Indian-listed outsourcing company (Mumbai head office, listed on NSE/BSE as FSL) that runs customer-facing and back-office business processes on behalf of large companies — answering calls and chats, processing claims and paperwork, chasing overdue payments, and increasingly redesigning those processes with automation and AI. Its customers are mostly big US and UK firms in banking and lending, health insurance and hospital systems, telecom/media/technology, and utilities and retail. It makes money mainly from ongoing multi-year service contracts priced per transaction, per interaction or per seat/outcome (management calls a contract worth over $5 million of annual value a 'large deal'), plus newer platform-fee-plus-per-interaction pricing on its AI collections platform. Work is delivered from the US, UK, India and other offshore/nearshore sites (including Mexico, plus Australia and Canada more recently) by about 36,000 staff; FY26 revenue was about INR 95.6 billion (roughly $1 billion, up ~19.7% in rupees) at an EBIT margin of 11.7%.

parts.name: Banking and Financial Services (BFS)
parts.what: Handles lending and banking processes for US and UK banks, mortgage lenders, fintechs and card issuers — historically the company's most cyclical and heavily discussed vertical, and in FY26 still growing about 9% year-on-year with the strongest exit pipeline of recent quarters.

parts.name: Mortgage (within BFS)
parts.what: Loan origination and servicing support for US mortgage lenders — about $32 million of revenue in one quarter of FY23 when it collapsed (down 48% year-on-year) and dragged down group guidance; by FY26 it has been repositioned as consulting-led 'mortgage transformation' work aimed at cutting clients' costs while volumes stay weak.

parts.name: Collections (within BFS)
parts.what: Recovering overdue debts for card issuers, banks, fintechs and utilities across first-party, third-party and legal collections, increasingly through a digital/AI platform; management calls it 25-plus years of domain expertise and it is now being extended into the UK (a large regulated UK collections deal went live in FY26) and reinforced by the Pastdue Credit acquisition.

parts.name: Healthcare
parts.what: Serves both health insurers ('payers') — member and provider services, claims processing, digital intake — and hospitals/health systems ('providers') via revenue cycle management; described as a core growth pillar and a key differentiator because few rivals cover both sides, with 16% year-on-year growth in Q4 FY26 and bolstered by the QBSS and TeleMedik acquisitions.

parts.name: Communications, Media and Technology (CMT)
parts.what: Customer service and back-office work for telecom, media, education-technology and consumer-technology firms — including newer work like training large consumer tech companies' AI models — and one of the fastest-growing verticals, up 14% year-on-year in Q3 FY26 with three of that quarter's five large deals.

parts.name: Diverse portfolio (Utilities & Energy, Retail)
parts.what: Mainly UK utilities, energy and retail clients — the smallest but fastest-growing bucket, up 21% year-on-year and 37% sequentially in Q3 FY26, with the Pastdue Credit deal adding several large new utility logos.

overview.what_it_does: Gabriel India makes ride-control parts for vehicles — shock absorbers, struts, front forks (including newer inverted/upside-down forks) and dampers — and, through a subsidiary, car sunroofs. It sells mainly to Indian vehicle manufacturers (OEMs are about 86% of revenue) across two-wheelers/three-wheelers, passenger cars, commercial vehicles and Indian Railways coaches and locomotives, with named customers including Bajaj, TVS, Atul Auto, Mahindra, Ola, Ather, Ampere, Tata, Volkswagen, Stellantis, Hyundai, Kia, Piaggio and Hero MotoCorp; the rest comes from the replacement/aftermarket channel (roughly 11-13%) and a small but growing export business (e.g. cabin and axle dampers for DAF). It earns money by winning per-model supply programs and then selling parts by volume for the life of that model, so revenue tracks Indian auto production, with margins driven by cost programs such as "CORE 90" (EBITDA around 9%). Operations are in India (plants include the sunroof facility at Oragadam near Chennai), and it is part of the ANAND Group, which treats Gabriel as its automotive growth engine toward a Rs 50,000 crore 2030 group target; FY26 consolidated revenue was Rs 4,667 crores, up 15%.

parts.name: Two-wheelers and three-wheelers
parts.what: Shock absorbers and front forks for motorcycles, scooters and three-wheelers — the largest business at roughly 61-65% of revenue, with about 31-32% market share and near-100% presence on leading electric two-wheeler makers (Ola, Ather, TVS, Ampere).

parts.name: Passenger cars
parts.what: Shock absorbers and struts for cars and SUVs, about 22-25% of revenue, with roughly 35% share in the fast-growing utility-vehicle segment and program wins on platforms from Tata, Volkswagen, Stellantis, Citroen and Maruti's Jimny.

parts.name: Commercial vehicles (and railways)
parts.what: Dampers for trucks and buses at about 12% of revenue, plus supply to Indian Railways coaches, electric locomotives and the Siemens loco program; exports are being built here, notably cabin dampers and newly won axle dampers for DAF.

parts.name: Aftermarket (replacement market)
parts.what: Selling the same ride-control parts as replacements through the spares channel — about 11-13% of revenue, described as a consistent focus area, crossing Rs 400 crores for the first time in FY24.

parts.name: Sunroofs — Inalfa Gabriel Sunroof Systems (IGSS)
parts.what: A subsidiary making car sunroofs at the Oragadam (Chennai) plant, ramped from zero to about 10,000 units a month and reaching Rs 434 crores of revenue in FY26 at roughly 15% EBITDA margin — the highest-margin part of the group, with new wins at Hyundai and Kia.

parts.name: New/emerging lines
parts.what: Early-stage diversification management flags each call — solar dampers (samples under validation in Europe, North America and India), e-bike components (first European development order, plus an award-winning patented integrated dropper post with Supernova), and JVs in fasteners (Jinos) and lubricants; small today, positioned as future growth.

parts.name: Group restructuring / ANAND Group consolidation
parts.what: Not a product line but a stated strategy: automotive businesses of the parent group are being folded into Gabriel — the Anchemco/Asia Investment scheme took effect 22 May 2026 after NCLT approval, with more group businesses intended to follow.

overview.what_it_does: GAIL (India) Limited is an Indian company that buys natural gas (domestic gas and imported LNG/RLNG) and sells it to power plants, fertilizer plants, refineries, industries and city gas retailers, and separately owns and operates the pipeline network that physically carries that gas across India — over 18,000 km as of December 2025 — charging a regulated tariff per unit shipped (raised from Rs.58.61 to Rs.65.69 per MMBtu effective January 2026). It also uses gas as raw material in its own plants to make petrochemicals (polymers such as polypropylene) and liquid hydrocarbons like LPG, propane and butane, and it ships LPG through a separate liquids pipeline. Closer to the consumer, it sells CNG for vehicles and piped gas to homes and industry, both directly in six licensed city areas and through its wholly owned subsidiary GAIL Gas and various joint ventures. Quarterly standalone turnover runs around Rs.34,000-35,000 crore with quarterly profit after tax typically in the Rs.1,600-2,700 crore range, and the company is putting roughly Rs.1,600-2,200 crore of capex to work each quarter on pipelines, petrochemical plants, city gas and clean energy.

parts.name: Gas Marketing
parts.what: Buys and resells natural gas — around 104-105 MMSCMD sold per quarter in FY26 — and is the company's main profit engine, with management guiding to Rs.4,000-4,500 crore of profit before tax from this segment in FY26 (Rs.2,221 crore already earned in the first half).

parts.name: Natural Gas Transmission
