parts.what: Owns and operates the cross-country gas pipeline grid (18,000+ km, carrying about 123-125 MMSCMD, roughly 74% utilisation on the core integrated system) and earns a regulated per-unit tariff; the January 2026 tariff hike alone is worth about Rs.1,200 crore a year, and volumes are expected to reach 133-134 MMSCMD in FY27 as new pipelines like Mumbai-Nagpur-Jharsuguda and Jagdishpur-Haldia come on stream.

parts.name: Petrochemicals
parts.what: Makes polymers at its Pata plant and elsewhere — about 220 TMT a quarter — a swing business that made a Rs.116 crore profit in H1 FY25 but lost Rs.299 crore in Q2 FY26 when input gas costs spiked; new capacity is being added (60 KTA PP at Pata, 500 KTA PDH-PP at Usar, 1,250 KTA PTA at Mangalore).

parts.name: LHC (Liquid Hydrocarbons)
parts.what: Extracts liquid products including LPG, propane and butane from the gas stream, producing roughly 200-250 TMT a quarter, with GAIL hedging propane and butane prices from time to time to protect margins.

parts.name: LPG Transmission
parts.what: A separate liquids pipeline business moving about 1,100-1,190 TMT per quarter at essentially full utilisation (around 100%); the approved doubling of the Jamnagar-Loni line from 3.25 to 6.5 MMTPA is expected to add roughly Rs.700 crore of revenue and Rs.600 crore of EBITDA a year.

parts.name: City Gas Distribution (CGD) — GAIL's own six geographical areas
parts.what: Sells CNG at 215 stations and piped gas to about 4.64 lakh household connections in the six areas licensed directly to GAIL, a small volume business at roughly 0.55 MMSCMD, with 85 more CNG stations and 150,000 more connections targeted over two years.

parts.name: GAIL Gas Limited (100% subsidiary, with JVs and subsidiaries)
parts.what: The dedicated retail gas arm selling CNG, piped domestic gas, industrial gas and bulk gas — around Rs.3,292 crore of quarterly turnover and Rs.106 crore of quarterly profit on 7.8 MMSCMD — operating about 674 CNG stations and 12.46 lakh piped household connections including JVs such as Bengal Gas.

parts.name: Renewables and clean energy
parts.what: A small but strategically emphasised portfolio of 145 MW (118 MW wind, 27 MW solar) with larger wind and solar projects under development, plus compressed biogas plants (one 5 tonne-per-day plant commissioned at Ranchi, six more approved, 25-30 planned) and earlier-mentioned green hydrogen and biofuel work.

parts.name: Retail LNG
parts.what: An early-stage effort to build LNG refuelling stations for long-haul trucking, with 29 stations planned, five under development, and 13 LNG/LCNG stations already commissioned through GAIL's city gas entities.

parts.name: Other investments and new ventures
parts.what: Includes a small exploration and production (E&P) spend, the GAIL Global IFSC finance subsidiary (which lent Rs.290 crore to Bengal Gas), and a board-approved-in-principle plan to build two fertilizer plants along the Mumbai-Nagpur-Jharsuguda pipeline for about Rs.21,000 crore, partly to create anchor demand for that pipeline.

overview.what_it_does: Gallantt Ispat is an Indian integrated steel maker that turns iron ore into finished construction steel — mainly TMT reinforcement bars sold under its own 'Gallantt' brand — at two plants, one at Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh and one at Samakhyali/Bhachau in Kutch, Gujarat. It runs the whole chain in-house (iron ore pellets, then sponge iron, then billets, then TMT bars), so most of the intermediate products are consumed internally and only the finished bar is sold; management says the more it keeps in-house, the more value it captures. Sales are almost entirely domestic, into the UP and Gujarat construction and infrastructure markets where it claims roughly 25% market share and a price premium over peers, with no exports unless export realisations happen to beat domestic ones. In FY26 it earned revenue of about INR 4,419 crores with EBITDA of INR 776 crores (17.6% margin, INR 8,785 per tonne) and profit after tax of INR 484 crores; it is net-debt-free and is spending an INR 3,000 crore capex programme on more steel capacity (1.0 to 1.3 million tonnes), captive iron ore mines, and solar power.

parts.name: TMT bar
parts.what: The finished construction steel that is the company's main sellable product and revenue engine — 788 kilotonnes produced and 766 kilotonnes sold in FY26, i.e. virtually all of it goes to customers rather than being used internally.

parts.name: Billet
parts.what: Semi-finished steel made in-house and mostly rolled onward into TMT bars — 883 kilotonnes produced in FY26 with only 81 kilotonnes sold externally.

parts.name: Sponge iron (DRI)
parts.what: Direct-reduced iron made from ore and coal that feeds the company's own steelmaking — 915 kilotonnes produced in FY26, of which 125 kilotonnes was sold outside.

parts.name: Pellet
parts.what: The upstream iron ore pellet stage that feeds the sponge iron plants — 819 kilotonnes produced in FY26 with just 49 kilotonnes sold externally; management's stated goal is to keep shrinking these outside sales of semi-finished products.

parts.name: Captive iron ore mines (under development)
parts.what: Four iron ore blocks allotted in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, with about INR 1,500 crores earmarked and a target of FY28, expected to secure raw material supply and lift EBITDA by roughly INR 2,000 per tonne once running.

parts.name: Renewable (solar) power
parts.what: About INR 225–300 crores going into 18 MW near the Gujarat plant (Sidhpur, Q2 FY27) and 60 MW for the Gorakhpur plant (Prayagraj, Q4 FY27), all self-consumed in steelmaking, saving an estimated INR 30–40 crores a year — a cost lever rather than a separate business.

overview.what_it_does: The Great Eastern Shipping Company (GESHIP) is a Mumbai-headquartered, BSE/NSE-listed company that owns ocean-going ships and hires them out to move other people's cargo — crude oil, refined petroleum products, LPG and dry bulk commodities like iron ore, coal and grain — across global trade routes such as the Middle East to Asia, US to Asia and Atlantic to Pacific. It makes money from the daily hire rate its ships earn, either on the open 'spot' market (rates quoted in dollars per day, which swing widely with oil and commodity trade flows) or on fixed-period 'time charters' that lock in a rate for months or years; management repeatedly says a large part of its capacity sits on the spot market, which is why it refuses to forecast earnings. Through its subsidiary Greatship (India) Limited it runs a second, separate business renting out offshore oilfield equipment — jack-up drilling rigs and support vessels — mostly on time charter to oil companies in India and the Middle East. Alongside operating the ships, management actively trades the assets themselves, buying and selling vessels to time the cycle, and tracks a per-share 'net asset value' (the fleet's market value plus cash) as its main scorecard; the business throws off heavy cash, has paid 16 consecutive quarterly dividends, and by FY26 held over $500 million of net cash.

parts.name: Crude tankers
parts.what: Ships that carry unrefined crude oil (Suezmax-class is the size management quotes); a core earner whose rates swing hard with events — around $46,000/day in Q1 FY25 versus $5,500/day for the market in FY22 — and the segment behind the record March–April 2026 spike from the Strait of Hormuz disruption.

parts.name: Product tankers
parts.what: Ships carrying refined fuels such as diesel and other middle distillates (MR-class); comparably important to crude tankers, and the biggest single beneficiary of the Red Sea rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope, which lengthened voyages and pushed rates to roughly $36,000/day in FY23 from $6,000/day the year before.

parts.name: Dry bulk carriers
parts.what: Ships carrying iron ore, coal and grain (Capesize and Supramax sizes), driven mainly by Chinese import demand; a meaningful but more volatile leg — rates fell over 50% year-on-year in Q2 FY23 and were unusually strong in the seasonally weak Q4 FY26.

parts.name: LPG carriers
parts.what: A small fleet — four ships as of FY23 — carrying liquefied petroleum gas, kept entirely on fixed time charters, so the company collects steady contracted hire and deliberately does not participate in the spot market's swings.

parts.name: Offshore drilling rigs (Greatship / oilfield services)
parts.what: Jack-up rigs chartered out to oil companies in India and internationally, run through subsidiary Greatship (India) Limited; a predominantly time-charter business where a handful of rigs come up for repricing each year, and the main reason consolidated profit exceeds standalone (e.g. INR 813 crore consolidated versus INR 650 crore standalone in Q3 FY26 — so roughly a fifth of group profit).

parts.name: Offshore support vessels (OSVs)
parts.what: Vessels servicing offshore oil platforms, also under Greatship and mostly on time charter with a large share of days locked in ahead (about 80% of FY27 days already fixed as of May 2026); management describes a global fleet of ~3,000 ships with 500–700 in long-term 'cold layup', supporting a tightening supply picture.

parts.name: Ship buying and selling (asset play)
parts.what: Not a separate reporting segment but treated as a core profit driver — management times the cycle by selling older vessels and replacing them with newer ones ('switch transactions'), levering up when assets are cheap and staying net cash when they are dear, with net asset value per share compounding above 20% a year over five years.

overview.what_it_does: GHCL Limited is an Indian chemicals manufacturer whose core product is soda ash (sodium carbonate), a bulk industrial chemical it produces in India and sells mainly to domestic industrial customers — above all glass makers, including a fast-growing solar-glass segment, plus users like detergent and lithium-carbonate producers. It makes money by manufacturing large volumes at low cost and selling at prevailing commodity prices, so profits swing with soda ash realisations: FY26 revenue was about Rs 3,144 crore with EBITDA of Rs 769 crore (24.4% margin) and PAT of Rs 479 crore. Its main competitive pressure is cheap imported soda ash landing in India, against which management leans on cost leadership, customer relationships and the rupee's depreciation. Until FY23 it also ran a sizeable textiles business (roughly Rs 1,000 crore of revenue) which was demerged out, leaving the company essentially a single-chemical business now trying to diversify into related products (sodium bicarbonate, vacuum salt, bromine) while building a large new greenfield soda ash plant.

parts.name: Inorganic Chemicals (Soda Ash)
parts.what: The main business — manufacturing and selling soda ash to glass, solar glass, detergent and related industrial users; it was about Rs 1,096 crore of Rs 1,371 crore total revenue in Q1 FY23 and after the textile demerger it is effectively the whole company, with domestic demand growing around 5% a year but pricing depressed by global oversupply and rising imports.

parts.name: Sodium Bicarbonate
parts.what: A smaller downstream chemical made alongside soda ash, where management expanded capacity and guided to very high tonnage growth (roughly 20-25%) versus only 5-6% for soda ash, but off a much smaller base.

parts.name: Vacuum Salt
parts.what: A new value-added salt product line under construction through FY25-FY26, with first commissioning done and full commissioning expected in Q1 FY27; management calls it part of a 'new earning layer' meant to reduce dependence on the soda ash cycle.

parts.name: Bromine
parts.what: A second new diversification project being commissioned alongside vacuum salt in FY26-FY27, fed by the company's own salt operations and intended to add higher-margin, non-commodity earnings.

parts.name: Salt / Captive salt fields
parts.what: Raw-material operations, including 6,449 hectares of leased land at Zara Zumara, Kutch granted for 30 years, supplying salt for soda ash production and for the new bromine and vacuum salt projects; management treats it as a cost and self-sufficiency advantage rather than a revenue line.

parts.name: Greenfield Soda Ash Project
parts.what: A planned new 500,000 tonne-per-year soda ash plant described as the company's big long-term growth investment; approvals and groundwork were in place for first-phase commissioning beyond 2026, but by early 2026 management said progress had been slower than expected.

parts.name: Textiles (demerged)
parts.what: A yarn and home-textiles business selling into end-user segments, running at roughly Rs 275 crore of quarterly revenue and about Rs 1,000 crore a year with 20-year average EBITDA margins of 16%; it was separated from GHCL via an NCLT-approved demerger completed around Q3 FY23 and is no longer part of the company.

overview.what_it_does: GIC Re is India's government-owned reinsurance company: it does not sell policies to the public but instead insures the insurers, taking a share of the risk that general (non-life) insurance companies have written on motor, property, crop, health, marine and similar covers, in exchange for a share of their premium. Part of that business arrives automatically because Indian regulation requires every domestic insurer to cede a fixed slice of each policy to GIC Re (the 'obligatory' or mandatory cession, cut over the years from 30% down to 4%), and the rest is won competitively against cross-border reinsurers, foreign branches and new GIFT City players. It earns money two ways — underwriting (premium collected minus claims and expenses, tracked as the 'combined ratio', which has run above 100% and was 106.02% for FY26, meaning underwriting alone lost money) and investment income on the large float it holds (about INR3,059 crore in the March 2026 quarter alone), which is what makes the overall result profitable. Gross premium was INR44,007 crore in FY26 with profit after tax of INR8,392 crore, split roughly 75% from India and 25% from international business.

parts.name: Domestic business
parts.what: Reinsurance written for Indian insurance companies — the core of the company at INR32,979 crore of FY26 premium, about 75% of the book; management says it will keep running above a 100% combined ratio by design because the investment income earned on Indian business makes up the difference.

parts.name: International / foreign book
parts.what: Reinsurance written outside India, INR11,028 crore or about 25% of FY26 premium; it shrank sharply in the early years shown (down to 16% of the book by mid-2024) after old loss-making contracts, notably a US marine contract stopped in 2021 whose claims kept arriving for years, and management wants this book to get below a 100% combined ratio.

parts.name: Obligatory / mandatory cession
parts.what: The regulator-mandated 4% slice of every Indian non-life policy that must be passed to GIC Re — a proportional book an investor sized at roughly 38% of revenue; management says it performs reasonably but worse than the rest, and that if the cession were reduced or abolished it would not all be lost because much of it would come back through negotiated deals.

parts.name: Non-obligatory business
parts.what: Everything won on merit rather than by rule — proportional treaties, non-proportional treaties, facultative (case-by-case) covers and miscellaneous covers; management describes it as a diverse mix that should perform better than the obligatory book.

parts.name: Crop / agriculture (PMFBY)
parts.what: Reinsurance of the government crop insurance scheme; it was once a very heavy share of the book with a bad combined ratio, was deliberately pruned to about 25% of premium by mid-2022, and swung back up strongly in FY25 (around INR10,000 crore written the prior year).

parts.name: Health
parts.what: A line management called out as growing meaningfully alongside agriculture in the June 2024 quarter.

parts.name: Marine (cargo and hull) and motor
parts.what: Older lines whose overseas premium collapsed after the US contract was stopped in 2021 while claims kept coming, pushing the overseas marine combined ratio into the hundreds of percent; provisions have since been made.

parts.name: Investments
parts.what: The pool of premium held before claims are paid, generating INR2,000-3,900 crore of income per quarter across the period — described by management as an important earnings contributor and the reason the adjusted combined ratio (about 84.79% for FY26) is far better than the headline one.

overview.what_it_does: Gillette India Limited is an Indian consumer-goods company, part of the P&G group (registered at P&G Plaza in Mumbai, listed on the BSE and NSE), that sells everyday personal-care products in two categories: Grooming (mainly razors, blades and shaving-related products under the Gillette and Venus brands) and Oral Care (manual and electric toothbrushes under Oral-B). It makes money by selling these low-priced, frequently repurchased items to Indian consumers through distributors and retailers — traditional grocery and retail stores plus e-commerce and quick-commerce platforms — across a range of price tiers from mass to premium. Growth comes from launching improved products, advertising heavily to bring new users into the categories, and constantly cutting costs (management cites roughly Rs 40-45 crore of annual productivity savings) to fund that spending and widen margins. The business is India-focused and has grown steadily: sales of Rs 2,633 crore with PAT of Rs 412 crore in the year to June 2024, Rs 2,232 crore of sales and Rs 414 crore PAT in the 9-month transition period to March 2025 (after changing its financial year-end), and Rs 3,100 crore of sales with about Rs 650 crore PAT in FY ended March 2026 — a fifth straight year of both top-line and bottom-line growth.

parts.name: Grooming
parts.what: Men's and women's shaving and grooming products — razors and blades across price tiers (Gillette Guard and the new Guard 3in1 for value-seeking consumers, Mach 3, Fusion 5, and the super-premium Gillette Labs), plus shave preps, styling/shaping tools and electronic grooming; management calls it one of the company's two focus categories and says Gillette is the market leader in India after decades of serving Indian consumers, though the calls give no separate revenue figure.

parts.name: Female Grooming (Venus)
parts.what: The Gillette Venus line of razors aimed at women, including a Bikini Sensitive razor for intimate grooming, marketed largely through digital and social media to overcome myths and hesitation about female shaving; presented as a distinct part of the grooming portfolio, but no size is disclosed.

parts.name: Oral Care (Oral-B)
parts.what: Toothbrushes and oral-hygiene products split into a Manual Oral Care range (including Criss Cross technology, a new Sensitive Care range with softer bristles that management says is growing double-digit and is one of the fastest-growing segments in the category, and a kids line with Chhota Bheem designs) and a Power Oral Care line of electric toothbrushes (iO3, Vitality Pro Sensitive) pitched at more affordable entry prices; it is the company's second focus category, again with no separate revenue figure given.

overview.what_it_does: Gland Pharma is an India-based maker of injectable medicines — drugs given by needle or drip, such as vials, lyophilized (freeze-dried) vials, ampoules, prefilled syringes and cartridges — manufactured at plants around Hyderabad (Dundigal, Pashamylaram, Genome Valley) plus sites in France and Belgium. It makes money two ways: selling its own generic injectables (Enoxaparin, Ertapenem, Bortezomib, Pemetrexed, Dalbavancin and the like) largely to pharma partners, distributors, hospital group-purchasing contracts and government tenders rather than directly to patients; and, increasingly, manufacturing under contract for other drug companies (CDMO), which was 46% of FY26 revenue. Doing this requires heavy regulatory paperwork — as of mid-2024 it and its partners had filed 356 ANDAs with the US FDA and held 1,708 product registrations worldwide. The United States is by far its largest market (about INR 33 billion of FY26's INR 64.3 billion total), followed by rest-of-world markets (MENA, LATAM, APAC), Europe and other regulated markets, and a small India business; FY26 revenue was INR 64,307 million with a 26% adjusted EBITDA margin.

parts.name: Base business – United States (core market)
parts.what: Sells its own generic injectables in the US through partners and hospital GPO contracts; the single biggest piece of the company at INR 33,181 million in FY26 (+11%), with 31 new product launches during the year, though management repeatedly calls the market crowded and price-competitive.

parts.name: Base business – Europe and other regulated markets
parts.what: Sells the same injectable portfolio into Europe, Canada and Australia; much smaller, at INR 3,249 million in FY26 (+11%), and grouped with the US as 'core markets', which were 76-82% of revenue in the earlier years covered.

parts.name: Base business – Rest of the world
parts.what: Supplies partners across MENA, LATAM and APAC, largely through lumpy tender-led orders; INR 6,511 million in FY26 (+7%), roughly 12-20% of revenue over the period, and the segment most exposed to timing swings in tenders.

parts.name: Base business – India
parts.what: The smallest market at INR 2,672 million in FY26 (only about 4-6% of revenue), including a dedicated insulin line; management said in 2024 it was deliberately shrinking this business and weighing strategic options for it.

parts.name: CDMO (contract development and manufacturing)
parts.what: Makes drugs on contract for other companies — including monoclonal antibodies and plasma-based proteins at its Genome Valley biologics site, biosimilars, oncology products, peptides, GLP-1 cartridges and prefilled syringes — and is now the company's stated growth engine at 46% of FY26 revenue, growing 28%, with cartridge fill-finish capacity being expanded from 40 million to 140 million units.

parts.name: Cenexi (European CDMO subsidiary)
parts.what: An acquired French/Belgian contract manufacturer with plants at Fontenay near Paris, Hérouville, Osny and in Belgium doing ampoule and aseptic fill-finish work; roughly €43-45 million of revenue a quarter, it lost money for several years and only became EBITDA-positive by FY26.

parts.name: R&D and product filings
parts.what: Spends about 4-5% of base-business revenue developing new injectables and filing ANDAs (8 filed in one quarter of FY25), which is what feeds the launch pipeline that management credits for most growth.

overview.what_it_does: GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals Ltd. (GSK India) is the Indian arm of the global GSK drug maker, headquartered in Mumbai and listed on the BSE and NSE. It sells branded prescription medicines and vaccines in India — everyday primary-care drugs like antibiotics, skin treatments, painkillers and vitamins, plus preventive vaccines for children and adults, and newer 'specialty' drugs for asthma/COPD and cancer. It makes money by selling these products through pharmacies and doctors in the private, largely self-pay Indian market, with a field force of over 2,000 sales reps calling on doctors face-to-face plus digital outreach (roughly 4 million doctor touchpoints in a quarter); much of its manufacturing sits with contract manufacturers (a fire at one CMO disrupted supply through FY2026). It operates essentially only in India — where management says its products reach more than 270 million Indians a year — and is described as the second-largest contributor to global GSK's emerging markets; quarterly revenue first crossed INR 1,000 crores in Q3 FY2026, with full-year FY2026 revenue up 2%, EBITDA margin about 34% and PAT up 10%.

parts.name: General Medicines (GenMeds)
parts.what: The established primary-care drug business — antibiotics (Augmentin, Ceftum), dermatology (T-Bact), pain/paracetamol (Calpol), vitamins and thyroid (Eltroxin) — still described as the largest single chunk of the top line, with leadership positions in anti-infectives, dermatology, pain and vitamins and the number one spot in self-pay dermatology.

parts.name: Vaccines – Pediatric
parts.what: Children's vaccines sold outside the government immunisation programme (Boostrix, Varilrix, Havrix), growing 9-11% and holding the lead in the private vaccines market segments where GSK participates.

parts.name: Vaccines – Adult
parts.what: Adult immunisation, led by the shingles vaccine Shingrix, a newer space the company has been building for roughly three years; it was called a key growth driver in FY2026 and is now being promoted using a link between shingles prevention and cardiovascular/metabolic disease.

parts.name: Specialty – Respiratory
parts.what: Trelegy Ellipta (a single-inhaler triple therapy for COPD) and Nucala (severe asthma, adding 100-120 new patients a month), the first leg of a specialty business management says was 'almost non-existent' a few years ago.

parts.name: Specialty – Oncology
parts.what: The newest addition: Zejula for ovarian cancer and Jemperli for endometrial cancer, launched with their first full quarter in Q3 FY2026; a December approval extended Jemperli to first-line endometrial cancer, widening the eligible patient pool from about 800 to roughly 6,000.

parts.name: Innovative / new portfolio ('freshness index')
parts.what: Management's cross-cutting measure of newly launched innovative medicines and vaccines (Jemperli, Zejula, Shingrix, Trelegy, Nucala), which contributed about 6% of the top line at the end of FY2026 against a stated goal of at least 10%.

parts.name: Distributed / tail-end brands
parts.what: A portfolio of smaller, non-promoted brands the company distributes; it saw soft demand and was called out as one of the two main drags on FY2026 growth.

overview.what_it_does: Glenmark Pharmaceuticals is an India-based drugmaker that makes and sells finished medicines — both cheaper copies of off-patent drugs (generics) and its own or in-licensed branded medicines — mainly in skin (dermatology), breathing (respiratory) and cancer (oncology) treatments, plus heart and diabetes drugs in India. It earns money by selling these medicines to doctors, pharmacies, hospitals and distributors in about 80 countries, split across four regions: India, North America, Europe and Emerging Markets (Russia/CIS, Latin America, Middle East & Africa, Asia-Pacific); in some markets it sells through partner companies rather than directly. On top of product sales, it earns licensing income by discovering new drug molecules in its own labs and out-licensing them to larger drugmakers — management says it has earned over $300 million this way historically, including a deal with AbbVie in FY26 worth $700 million upfront. Full-year FY26 revenue was about INR 169,825 million (roughly INR 1.7 lakh crore-scale sales base of ~$1.5 billion when management last sized it), with the four regions each now contributing broadly similar amounts.

parts.name: India formulations business
parts.what: Sells branded prescription medicines to Indian doctors across dermatology, respiratory, cardiac, diabetes and oncology; it is the single largest region (about 37% of revenue in FY23 and roughly INR 10,000-13,000 million a quarter by FY26), ranked 13th in the Indian pharma market with ~2.3% share and second in both dermatology and respiratory.

parts.name: India Consumer Care (GCC)
parts.what: A small over-the-counter consumer brands arm selling products like Candid Powder, La Shield, Scalpe, Bontress and Elovera directly to shoppers; it is a modest but fast-growing piece, around INR 1,265 million in the March 2026 quarter.

parts.name: North America business
parts.what: Mainly a US generics operation selling copies of off-patent drugs — 214 approved generic products, plus a growing injectables portfolio (about 20 products sold through partners) and generic respiratory sprays/inhalers — running roughly INR 9,000-9,700 million a quarter, and it also books the out-licensing income from the AbbVie deal.

parts.name: Europe business
parts.what: Sells generics in Western Europe (Germany, Netherlands, Spain, Nordics) and increasingly higher-margin branded respiratory and dermatology products in Central & Eastern Europe (Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia); about INR 8,000-8,900 million a quarter and management is deliberately shifting the mix toward branded.

parts.name: Emerging Markets (earlier called ROW)
parts.what: Covers Russia/CIS, Latin America, Middle East & Africa and Asia-Pacific, where the company sells largely branded medicines in dermatology and respiratory; around INR 8,100-9,000 million a quarter and growing at high single to double digits.

parts.name: RYALTRIS (global branded product)
parts.what: The company's flagship self-developed nasal spray for allergic rhinitis, filed in over 90 countries and commercialised in 52 markets — sold directly by Glenmark in some countries and through partners (Menarini, Hikma, Grand Pharmaceutical, Organon, Yuhan) in others — with 50%+ yearly sales growth and described by management as transformational.

parts.name: Innovation R&D / Ichnos Glenmark Innovation (IGI)
parts.what: The in-house new-drug discovery arm working on novel cancer and other molecules using its BEAT antibody platform; it does not sell products but generates upfront and milestone payments plus royalties by licensing assets out, most notably ISB 2001 to AbbVie (up to $1.925 billion potential deal value), with innovation spend cut back to about $50 million a year.

parts.name: In-licensed specialty/branded portfolio
parts.what: Medicines developed by other companies that Glenmark buys the local selling rights to and markets in India, Europe or emerging markets — such as JABRYUS (from Pfizer) in skin disease, WINLEVI (from Cosmo) in acne, and TEVIMBRA/BRUKINSA (from BeOne) and envafolimab in cancer — used to move the sales mix up-market.

parts.name: Glenmark Life Sciences
parts.what: A separately reported subsidiary referenced in the earlier calls that supplies active pharmaceutical ingredients (the raw drug substances), reported on alongside the main formulations business.

overview.what_it_does: GMDC is a Gujarat state government-owned mining company that digs up and sells lignite (a low-grade coal used as industrial fuel) from mines across Gujarat such as Mata No Madh in Kutch, Bhavnagar, Tadkeshwar, Rajpardi and Valia/Bharuch. It sells this lignite in two ways: to power plants like ATPS and KLTPS at prices fixed by a conservative government formula, and to industrial and MSME customers in clusters like Morbi and Surat at market prices that management deliberately sets just below imported coal so lignite stays the cheaper option. Volumes have run around 8-9 million tonnes a year, with management targeting about 15 million tonnes from Gujarat lignite by 2030, and margins that were over 50% two years ago now around 30%. Alongside the core lignite business it is building out three coal blocks in Odisha, runs a small loss-making power plant, and is developing early-stage rare earth and copper projects.

parts.name: Lignite (Gujarat mining)
parts.what: The core and by far the biggest business — mining lignite at four operating mines plus six new ones under development, doing roughly 8-9 million tonnes a year with a target of about 15 million tonnes by 2030; Mata No Madh is described as 'the backbone of the organization' and the largest supplier to the power sector and market sales.

parts.name: Marketing and Sales
parts.what: The function that prices and sells lignite to industrial customers, benchmarked against imported coal, with stated pushes like 'Mission 2000' to grow active customers past 2,000 and 'Mission 18.0' to sell 18 lakh tonnes during the weak monsoon quarter.

parts.name: Coal (Odisha blocks)
parts.what: Three coal blocks won in Odisha — Baitarani-West (targeted at 15 million tonnes a year and set to become GMDC's largest mine), plus blocks in Angul/Sundargarh and the unexplored Kudanali-Lubri — with roughly Rs 5,000 crore of capex over the mine life, groundbreaking targeted in FY26 and first volumes of about 1 million tonnes ramping quickly to 3 and then 5 million tonnes.

parts.name: Power
parts.what: A small division running the ATPS lignite-fired power plant, described as running 'in the red' at about Rs 25 crore of revenue with Rs 11 crore of loss, delayed by imported spare parts; it burns GMDC's own lignite, which can be sold into the market instead when the plant is down.

parts.name: Rare Earth (Ambadongar)
parts.what: An early-stage project where GMDC has been named by the Government of India as the agency and preferred allottee to develop it, with management guiding to a roughly three-year horizon and declining to give details because the sector is regulated.

parts.name: Copper Project Ambaji (earlier called the multi-metal project)
parts.what: A renamed early-stage underground mining project that management calls the true value driver of that asset but flags as complicated — close to a residential area and ecologically sensitive land — with two to three years of clearances, RFPs and mine development work ahead and no near-term revenue.

overview.what_it_does: GMM Pfaudler makes and sells heavy process equipment — most famously glass-lined reactors and vessels, plus mixers/agitators, fabricated heavy-engineering equipment, mechanical seals and complete engineered process systems — to companies that run chemical plants. Its traditional customers are chemical, agrochemical and pharmaceutical makers (once about 70% of business, and management says roughly 60-70% of revenue as recently as FY25), but it has deliberately pushed into oil and gas, petrochemicals, fertilizer, nuclear, defence, space, semiconductors and metals/minerals, which by FY26 were about 50% of order intake. It earns money order-by-order: it books orders into a backlog (INR 2,205 crores at Dec 2025, the highest ever; FY26 order intake INR 3,714 crores), manufactures and ships against them, and adds a steadier stream of after-sales service and re-glassing work on equipment already installed. It runs as two halves — an India business and an International business — with plants and operations in India, Germany, the UK (since shut), the USA, Italy, China and Brazil, and FY26 revenue delivered EBITDA of about INR 403 crores at roughly 11% margin.

parts.name: Glass-lined equipment (glass-lined / GL business)
parts.what: The core legacy product — steel reactors and vessels lined with glass so corrosive chemicals can be processed in them; it is the historically higher-margin proprietary business but has been the weak spot lately, with pricing pressure and global capacity being consolidated (Hyderabad plant shut and land sold for INR 55 crores, UK plant shut, ~30 staff cut in Germany at a cost of INR 44 crores).

parts.name: Heavy Engineering
parts.what: Large fabricated equipment for oil and gas, petrochemicals, fertilizer and now nuclear customers; management repeatedly says it is structurally lower-margin than glass-lined and proprietary products, but it has been a big contributor to order intake and helped offset the chemical slowdown.

parts.name: Mixing
parts.what: Industrial mixers and agitators, built up from roughly INR 30 crores a few years before 2022 via the acquisition of Pune-based IMSD to INR 50-60 crores and then expected to double, with MixPro in Brazil also part of it; it won large fermentation/penicillin orders and is described as one of the higher-margin non-glass-lined lines.

parts.name: Systems
parts.what: Engineered process systems where the company supplies its own process technology rather than just hardware — the part management says moves it up the value chain and carries improving margins; it won a $6 million China order engineered in the US and built in India, and in FY26 saw a big order surge from European defence spending.

parts.name: Services (including re-glassing)
parts.what: Aftermarket work on installed equipment — repairs, spares and re-glassing of used vessels — supported by dedicated sites such as the GMM Pfaudler JDS facility in Georgia, USA opened in 2024; it is cited as a recurring revenue stream that helps fill the year alongside project shipments.

parts.name: Proprietary products (e.g. Interseal mechanical seals, acid recovery)
parts.what: Smaller specialist product lines sold into the same plants — mechanical seals under the Interseal brand (four new clients and a 20-25 seal order flagged in 2022) and acid recovery projects — grouped by management with glass-lined as the higher-margin proprietary end of the portfolio.

parts.name: India business
parts.what: The domestic half, led by its own CEO and CFO, serving mainly chemicals and pharma plus growing pharma, oil and gas and nuclear demand; in FY26 it grew revenue about 12%, EBITDA about 24% and PAT about 40%, and it also manufactures for the international arm (e.g. 25 vessels shipped to Germany under a 'stock and sale' programme).

parts.name: International business
parts.what: The overseas half covering Europe, the USA, China and South America (SEMCO and MixPro in Brazil), with its own CEO and CFO; Europe has been the problem geography with slow chemicals and pharma investment, the Americas and Brazil are recovering on metals, minerals, rare earths and oil and gas, and China remains challenging and is being cost-cut.

overview.what_it_does: GMR Airports Limited (GAL) is an Indian company that builds, upgrades and runs airports, and then earns money from everything that happens inside and around them. Its income comes in two main streams: regulated 'aero' charges paid by airlines and passengers for using the runway and terminal (tariffs set by the regulator AERA, with a big Delhi tariff revision from mid-April 2025 lifting Delhi aero revenue 161% in FY26), and 'non-aero' income from duty-free shops, food and beverage, retail, cargo handling, advertising and aircraft maintenance — which management says is now more than 50% of total income versus about a third from aero. It also monetises the land it controls around its airports through hotels, offices, retail and warehousing. Its main assets are Delhi (its biggest, ~20-21 million passengers a quarter), Hyderabad (74%-owned, ~8 million a quarter), Goa's Mopa airport, plus Nagpur and the under-construction Bhogapuram airport in India and an airport at Crete in Greece; total traffic was a record 121.6 million passengers in FY26 on total income of INR152 billion and EBITDA of INR61.5 billion.

parts.name: Aeronautical (aero) business
parts.what: The regulated core: charging airlines and passengers for landing, parking and terminal use at Delhi, Hyderabad and Mopa, with prices fixed by the regulator in multi-year 'control periods' — combined aero yield per passenger was about INR430-434 in FY26, and it makes up roughly a third of total income.

parts.name: Non-aeronautical (non-aero) business — described as the 'second platform'
parts.what: Retail, duty-free, food and beverage, lounges, advertising and other passenger spending inside the terminals; management says it now contributes over half of total income, with non-aero income per passenger of about INR640-666 and duty-free spend per passenger around INR1,033 at Delhi and INR769 at Hyderabad.

parts.name: Airport adjacency businesses (duty-free, F&B, cargo operations taken in-house)
parts.what: Rather than leasing these out to third parties, GAL has taken over running them itself — Delhi duty-free from July 2025, Hyderabad duty-free from Q2FY26, and the Delhi cargo terminal (whose concession it formally won in FY26) — which management calls turning GAL into a 'scaled consumer platform'.

parts.name: Commercial property development (CPD) / real estate — the 'third platform'
parts.what: Developing the land around its airports: Delhi Aerocity offices (first self-developed building handed over in FY27), hotels under Hilton/Waldorf and Taj Vivanta brands, four hotels at Goa, retail at Hyderabad, and warehousing via the wholly owned ESR GMR Logistics Park; still early but flagged as the next big growth leg.

parts.name: Cargo and logistics
parts.what: Freight terminals and warehouses — the Delhi cargo terminal (record monthly tonnage in December 2025) plus a separate 'Cargo City' being built at Delhi through GMR Cargo and Logistics with a INR7.5 billion loan, and a new 50,000-tonne Hyderabad cargo terminal two with a temperature-controlled pharma zone.

parts.name: MRO (aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul)
parts.what: Aircraft servicing at Hyderabad, including a three-year base-maintenance deal with Akasa Air for its ~30 Boeing 737 MAX fleet, a Boeing Defence India contract for Indian Navy P-8I aircraft, and a half-million-square-foot facility built for Safran.

parts.name: Airports under construction / new assets
parts.what: Greenfield and upgrade projects that are spending money now and will earn later — Bhogapuram in Andhra Pradesh (98.7% complete as of March 2026, opening targeted Q2FY27), Nagpur airport upgrade, and Crete in Greece (69% complete); these are the main reason consolidated net debt sits around INR340 billion.

overview.what_it_does: GNFC (Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers & Chemicals Limited) is a Gujarat-based manufacturer that runs chemical and fertilizer plants at Narmadanagar/Bharuch and Dahej, and has been operating for 50 years as of May 2026. It makes money two ways: selling industrial chemicals — TDI, nitric acid, ammonium nitrate, acetic acid, methanol, aniline, ammonia — mostly to Indian industrial buyers at prices set on an import-parity basis (with some exports), and selling fertilizers such as urea (including neem-coated and technical-grade) and complex fertilizers to the farm market, where realisations depend on government subsidy (NBS rates for complex fertilizer, fixed-cost and energy norms for urea). Its costs are driven by bought-in feedstock — natural gas, oil from IOCL, benzene, toluene and methanol — so profits swing with energy and raw-material prices; in FY26 it earned PBT of about Rs 1,065 crores and PAT of Rs 797 crores and paid a Rs 21 per share dividend. It is listed on BSE and NSE, is building out roughly Rs 2,800 crores of capacity projects, and also runs a small IT services business plus one consolidated subsidiary, Gujarat Green Revolution Company.

parts.name: Chemical segment (Industrial Products)
parts.what: Makes and sells industrial chemicals from the Bharuch and Dahej plants, and is described by management as the main driver of profit improvement — chemicals are where realisations and volumes lifted FY26 earnings while fertilizer lost money.

parts.name: TDI (toluene di-isocyanate)
parts.what: Its flagship chemical, made at two plants (TDI-1 and TDI-2 Dahej) with combined capacity of roughly 60,000-70,000 tonnes; GNFC holds about 60-65% of an Indian market of roughly 1 lakh tonnes used in flexible foam, is protected by an anti-dumping duty extended for another five years, and exports the balance — though TDI-2 at Dahej ran at heavy losses (Rs 259 crores in FY24, Rs 89 crores in Q1 FY25) before conditions improved.

parts.name: Nitric acid and ammonium nitrate
parts.what: Weak and concentrated nitric acid plus ammonium nitrate; a concentrated nitric acid expansion was expected to add about Rs 110 crores of revenue, and a new 200,000 TPA weak nitric acid plant (about 57% more capacity) was approved in 2024 to feed an ammonium nitrate project — demand management called out as nationally important during the Q4 FY26 war-related disruption.

parts.name: Acetic acid and methanol
parts.what: Methanol is both a product and the key input into acetic acid; in FY26 high gas and oil prices made in-house methanol production uneconomic and pushed up acetic acid costs, so management was weighing whether to keep making acetic acid or source it, and is in licensing talks with INEOS for added capacity.

parts.name: Ammonia and captive utilities
parts.what: Ammonia is produced in-house as feedstock (a 50,000 TPA additional ammonia loop was due around 2026) and supported by capitalised infrastructure — a double-wall ammonia tank, a 4 MW solar plant wheeled to Dahej, a desalination plant, railway track renewal, and a roughly Rs 613 crore power plant at Dahej expected to add about Rs 82 crores net contribution.

parts.name: Fertilizer segment
parts.what: Sells urea (neem-coated and technical-grade) and complex fertilizers through its own fertilizer marketing department; volumes have been stable to good, but the segment has been loss-making and widening, with management saying the overdue government revision of urea fixed cost and energy norms is what would fix it — subsidy receivables stood at about Rs 302 crores at end-Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Others (IT division)
parts.what: A small non-chemical business, mainly IT services, which management said grew revenue about 20% in FY26 with profit doubling from Rs 17 crores to Rs 35 crores.

parts.name: Gujarat Green Revolution Company
parts.what: The only subsidiary GNFC consolidates, described simply as a profitable operation.

overview.what_it_does: Go Digit General Insurance is an Indian general (non-life) insurance company, regulated by IRDAI and listed on the BSE and NSE, that sells policies covering vehicles, health and travel, property and business risks. Its customers range from individual retail buyers of car, two-wheeler and health cover to large corporates buying fire, marine, engineering and liability cover and group health for their own employees, reached mainly through a large network of distribution partners (66,000+ partners as of mid-2024, growing since) and a direct corporate team present across India, all run on an in-house digital platform with automated and predictive underwriting. It earns money in two ways: underwriting profit, the premium it keeps after paying claims and expenses (management tracks this as the combined ratio, around 105-107%), and investment income on the float it holds, an investment book of about INR23,000 crores by March 2026 that is mostly fixed income with a roughly 9.5% equity allocation. Gross written premium was close to INR11,300 crores in FY2026, with a full-year profit after tax of about INR179 crores in Q4 and an annual ROE of roughly 17.7%; it operates only in India.

parts.name: Motor - Own Damage (OD)
parts.what: Covers damage to the customer's own vehicle; it is one of the two halves of motor and made up 37% of Digit's motor premium in Q1 FY26 versus 41% for the industry, and management has deliberately cut back stand-alone OD and older private-car business where prices and commissions no longer pay.

parts.name: Motor - Third Party (TP)
parts.what: The legally required cover for injury or damage caused to others, priced by the regulator with no rate increase in five years; it is the larger half of Digit's motor book at 63% of motor premium, and management says rising wage-linked claim costs make aggressive TP growth unattractive.

parts.name: Private car
parts.what: The biggest slice inside motor at about 41% of the motor book, closely tied to new car sales, which management said were weak in Q1 FY26.

parts.name: Two-wheeler
parts.what: About 31% of the motor book and a fast-growing line (Q4 FY26 premium jumped to INR556 crores from INR365 crores); the long-tenure '1+5' policies push up the reported expense ratio because commission is booked upfront while premium earns over one year, but management considers it profitable and a good source of long-lasting investable funds.

parts.name: Commercial vehicle
parts.what: Cover for trucks and other commercial vehicles, about 28% of motor in FY26 but shrinking by choice - it was 65% of the whole book four or five years ago and had fallen to roughly 23-24% of motor by Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Health, travel and personal accident (PA)
parts.what: Retail and group medical, travel and accident cover; it grew 52% against the industry's 17% in Q1 FY25 and rose from 22% to 27% of gross premium, driven by retail personal-lines business.

parts.name: Group health (employer-employee)
parts.what: Health cover companies buy for their own staff; Digit has deliberately de-grown here (minus 2% in Q1 FY25) because management calls the segment volatile and under-priced and expects pricing discipline to return.

parts.name: Fire / property
parts.what: Cover for buildings, plant and corporate property, a strong growth area - up 40% against the industry's 17% in Q1 FY26, with Digit taking lead positions on very large corporate accounts, though it passes much of the risk to reinsurers (retention cut to 9% from 15%) to avoid concentration.

parts.name: Marine, engineering and liability ('others')
parts.what: Other commercial covers for goods in transit, projects and legal liability, grouped with fire as the corporate book; grew 23% in Q1 FY26 and is supported by increased reinsurance treaty capacity from 1 April.

parts.name: Crop
parts.what: Mentioned only as a line carrying different (corporate-style) commission rates than retail business, so it affects the reported expense ratio through mix.

parts.name: Investments (AUM)
parts.what: The pool of premium float invested until claims are paid, grown from about INR17,773 crores in mid-2024 to roughly INR23,000 crores by March 2026, primarily fixed income with about 9.5% in equity; it is a core profit driver, though management says it refuses to book capital gains just to smooth quarterly numbers.

parts.name: Reinsurance / retention
parts.what: Not a product but a lever management discusses constantly - the share of premium ceded to reinsurers, with net retention swinging from 76% to 65% in Q1 FY26 to lay off large fire risks, which worsens the optical combined ratio without changing economics.

overview.what_it_does: Godrej Agrovet is an Indian agriculture and food company that sells things farmers buy and things food buyers want: cattle, poultry, aqua and other animal feed; crop protection chemicals like herbicides, pesticides and plant growth regulators; crude palm oil and palm kernel oil pressed from oil palm fruit bunches; packaged milk and value-added dairy such as curd, buttermilk, ghee and milk drinks; and chicken and frozen foods under brands like Real Good Chicken and Yummiez. It makes money mainly by buying farm commodities (maize, soymeal, fish meal, raw milk, palm fruit) or making chemicals, then selling the processed product at a spread, so profits swing with input costs, monsoon timing and commodity prices as much as with volumes. It operates across India, with a plantation and mill footprint in the northeast (Mizoram, Assam, Tripura, Manipur), an export and contract-manufacturing chemicals arm (Astec LifeSciences), and a feed joint venture in Bangladesh called ACI Godrej. In FY26 consolidated revenue crossed INR 10,000 crore, at INR 10,233 crore, with profit before tax excluding one-offs of INR 569 crore.

parts.name: Animal Feed / Animal Nutrition
parts.what: Makes and sells cattle, poultry and aqua feed to farmers, earning a margin per tonne over grain and protein-meal costs; the calls treat it as the largest and most closely watched business, quoting volume growth and EBIT per tonne (for example INR 2,258/MT in Q1 FY25) every quarter, with Q4 FY26 volumes up 15% and cattle feed up 24%.

parts.name: Vegetable Oil / Oil Palm
parts.what: Buys fresh fruit bunches from oil palm growers and crushes them into crude palm oil and palm kernel oil, so earnings depend on palm oil prices, fruit arrivals and the oil extraction ratio; management calls FY26 a landmark year with record area expansion and an all-time-high extraction ratio, and it swings hard with prices — segment results grew 2.6x in Q1 FY23 when palm oil peaked.

parts.name: Crop Protection / Crop Care (standalone)
parts.what: Sells branded agrochemicals to Indian farmers through a dealer channel — in-house herbicides, pesticides and plant growth regulators plus co-marketed products — and is a high-margin but seasonal business (segment margins of 45% in Q1 FY25) whose sales hinge on monsoon timing, channel credit discipline and distributor inventory.

parts.name: Astec LifeSciences
parts.what: A listed chemicals subsidiary with two halves: 'enterprise' products (mainly triazole fungicide molecules sold in India and exported, hit hard by low prices and Chinese dumping) and a growing CDMO/CMO business making molecules to order for global agrochemical customers; it lost money for several years and only reached EBITDA break-even in FY26, with CDMO now driving its recovery.

parts.name: Dairy / Creamline Dairy (CDPL)
parts.what: Buys raw milk from farmers and sells packaged milk plus value-added products such as curd, buttermilk, ghee and milk drinks, mainly in south India; profitability turns on the 'milk spread' between procurement cost and selling price, and management keeps pushing value-added products, which rose from about 36% of sales in FY24 to around 40% in FY26.

parts.name: Poultry & processed foods / Godrej Foods Limited
parts.what: Sells live birds to traders plus branded chicken (Real Good Chicken) and frozen ready-to-cook foods (Yummiez); the company has deliberately shrunk the volatile live-bird trade in favour of branded sales, which were over 80% of this business's revenue in FY26.

parts.name: ACI Godrej (Bangladesh joint venture)
parts.what: A jointly owned animal feed business in Bangladesh selling cattle, poultry and aqua feed, reported separately as a growth add-on rather than a core segment — revenue grew 42% in Q1 FY23 but fell 13% in Q1 FY25 amid Bangladesh's political and economic turmoil.

overview.what_it_does: Godrej Consumer Products Limited (GCPL) is a Mumbai-headquartered, stock-exchange-listed FMCG (fast-moving consumer goods) company that makes and sells branded everyday household and personal-care products — mosquito repellents and insecticides, air fresheners, soaps and body wash, hair colour and hair care, laundry detergents, perfumes and deodorants, and sexual wellness products. It earns money by selling these low-priced, frequently repurchased branded goods in large volumes to ordinary households, routed through distributors and retailers (general trade, modern trade and e-commerce), with growth described in terms of 'underlying volume growth', price increases and market share; profitability is driven by gross margins (heavily exposed to input costs such as palm oil), advertising spend held at roughly 10% of sales, and cost-to-serve savings, producing consolidated EBITDA margins of about 20-22% and India margins near 25%. India is the core market, reported as the 'standalone' business, and management pushes rural reach through a van distribution programme. Outside India it operates in Indonesia; in Africa, the USA and the Middle East (which it calls GAUM); and in Latin America, including Argentina.

parts.name: Home Care (India) — Household Insecticides, Air Fresheners, Fabric Care
parts.what: Sells mosquito/insect protection (Goodknight liquid vaporizers, Hit aerosols, electrics and incense sticks — GCPL says it is market leader in India), air fresheners (aer, aer Matic, aer pocket) and laundry/fabric care including the fast-growing Godrej Fab liquid detergent, described by management as one of GCPL's most successful innovations; this cluster grew about 12% in value in the most recent quarters and is repeatedly called the main engine of India growth.

parts.name: Personal Care (India) — Soaps / Personal Wash, Hair Colour, Hair Care, Sexual Wellness
parts.what: Sells bar soaps and body wash (including Magic ready-to-mix body wash), hair colour and hair care, and sexual wellness products; soaps are a large, palm-oil-sensitive business that still earns roughly 20% EBITDA margins, while body wash is admitted to be a small, early-stage part of the soap market where GCPL says it is 'behind the curve', and powder hair dye has recently been under pressure.

parts.name: Perfume & Deodorants (India)
parts.what: A newer India business built partly on the acquired Park Avenue (Raymond) portfolio plus the KS99 perfume brand now sold pan-India; management says the market is shifting from deodorants to eau-de-parfums, where GCPL is growing fast and competing to be the number-two player, and it delivered strong double-digit growth in the March 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Muuchstac (men's face wash) — acquired November 2025
parts.what: A recently acquired, roughly INR 70 crore, high-margin single-SKU men's face wash brand sold mainly through one or two online channel partners, which GCPL plans to scale across e-commerce, modern trade and general trade in a men's face wash market of about INR 1,000 crore growing 20% a year.

parts.name: Pet food (new venture, India)
parts.what: A brand-new category launched as a test market in Tamil Nadu with a plant now ready in Nashik; results so far are called 'mixed' with market share below hopes, and management frames it as a deliberate slow-burn, multi-year investment rather than a current contributor.

parts.name: Indonesia
parts.what: A significant international market selling shampoo, hair colour, baby care and household insecticides; after a very weak stretch in FY2023 it recovered to mid-single-digit volume growth, then faced pricing pressure through FY2026 with flattish-to-3% revenue growth, and management expects a meaningful step-up from FY2027.

parts.name: GAUM — Africa, USA and Middle East
parts.what: Sells hair fashion / 'dry hair' products (wigs and extensions-type categories, with Nigeria a key market) plus a growing FMCG portfolio including air fresheners; it has been one of the fastest-growing pieces recently at 19-20% rupee sales growth with operating margins around 15%, and management targets double-digit revenue and profit growth.

parts.name: Latin America and others
parts.what: A smaller international business, including Argentina, that has recently grown very fast — over 25% volume growth and 26% sales growth — with EBITDA margins only lately reaching double digits and still exposed to weak local macros and one-off costs.

overview.what_it_does: Godrej Properties is an Indian real estate developer that builds and sells homes — mostly apartments in group-housing projects, plus some plotted (land-parcel) developments and a few luxury projects — to individual home buyers and retail investors. It makes money by acquiring land or tying up land through joint ventures and partnerships (what management calls 'business development'), launching projects, booking pre-sales, then collecting cash from buyers against construction milestones and recognising revenue and profit largely when projects are completed and delivered. It operates across India's major residential markets — Mumbai/Thane, NCR (Delhi, Noida, Greater Noida, Gurgaon), Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad, with deliveries spanning 9 cities — and says it was the country's largest listed residential developer by bookings and collections in FY26, with FY26 bookings of INR34,171 crores, collections of INR19,965 crores, total income of INR8,374 crores and net profit of INR1,850 crores. Management describes it as roughly a 4.8% share of the market in calendar 2025, doubled from 2.4% four years earlier.

parts.name: Residential group housing (apartments / homes)
parts.what: The core business — building and selling flats in large multi-tower projects such as Godrej Woodscapes (Bengaluru), Godrej Jardinia (Noida), Godrej Reserve and Godrej Ascend (Mumbai region); this drives nearly all of the 17,513 units and 27 million square feet sold in FY26, with 11 individual projects each generating over INR1,000 crores of bookings in the year.

parts.name: Plotted development
parts.what: Selling developed land plots rather than built apartments, mentioned as a smaller add-on with launches in places like Nagpur, Bhandup and Khalapur; the calls never size it separately.

parts.name: Luxury / premium projects
parts.what: A small number of high-value, low-area city projects such as Carmichael Road in Mumbai (about 1.2 lakh square feet of saleable area but roughly INR1,200 crores of revenue potential), plus Worli and Bandra developments — high value per square foot but a minor share of overall volume.

parts.name: Business development (land and partnership tie-ups)
parts.what: The land- and project-sourcing engine that feeds everything else — in FY26 it closed 18 deals covering about 33 million square feet and INR42,100 crores of future sales potential, over 200% of guidance, and management treats it as the main determinant of future growth and margins.

parts.name: Joint ventures / partnership projects
parts.what: Many projects are done with landowners or JV partners rather than fully owned, so profits from them are recognised only at project completion; the company has been steadily buying up more of the economics, raising its economic interest in booking value from 50% in 2021 to 87% in 2025.

parts.name: Commercial / office and retail
parts.what: A very small side holding rather than a real business line — the calls mention only the Godrej Two office building in Mumbai (whose revaluation boosted Q1 FY25 profit) and a possible retail component in one Pune project.

parts.name: Construction execution and delivery
parts.what: The in-house project-execution arm (run on a 'site head' model with external contractors) that completes and hands over homes — 12.1 million square feet delivered across 9 cities in FY26, 121% of guidance — and matters because collections, reported revenue and profit are tied to construction progress and handover.

parts.name: Geographic zones
parts.what: The business is run by regional zones, each material in size: in FY26 Mumbai contributed over INR10,000 crores of bookings, Bengaluru INR8,801 crores, NCR INR7,412 crores, Pune INR3,659 crores and Hyderabad (a new market) INR2,360 crores, with no single market above 30% of the total.

overview.what_it_does: Gokaldas Exports is an Indian garment maker that manufactures apparel on order for global clothing brands and retailers and ships it to them, mainly in the United States and increasingly in Europe and the UK. It does not sell its own brand at retail; it wins style-by-style orders each fashion season, buys the fabric, converts it into finished garments in its factories, and earns money on the spread between the price it charges the brand and its cost of fabric, labour and overheads. Its plants are in India (Karnataka base plus newer low-cost sites in Madhya Pradesh and Ranchi, Jharkhand, and a fabric mill in Tamil Nadu) and in Africa through the acquired Atraco business, so it can serve customers from whichever location has the better duty access. Total income was about INR 4,065 crore in FY26 (up 4%), and profitability swings heavily with trade rules — US tariffs on India cost it over INR 90 crore of discounts given to customers in FY26, and the lapse and later restoration of AGOA duty-free access drove the Africa order book down and then back up.

parts.name: India apparel operations (standalone Gokaldas Exports)
parts.what: The core garment manufacturing business in India — historically woven apparel — which is the largest part of the group, grew 10% in FY26 while Indian apparel exports fell 1.4%, and ran about a 12% operating EBITDA margin in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Africa operations (Atraco)
parts.what: Garment factories in Africa acquired in FY24 that ship mainly to the US and relied on AGOA duty-free access; revenue fell 19% in FY26 (roughly INR 180 crore) when AGOA lapsed, then grew 17% in Q4 after it was restored, with management targeting an 8%–10% EBITDA margin in H2 FY27.

parts.name: BTPL — fabric processing unit (Tamil Nadu)
parts.what: A knits fabric processing mill (initial investment a little over INR 120 crore) that supplies the group's own critical raw material — vertical integration for speed, quality and cost — currently running near 50 lakh metres a month against 70 lakh capacity, still loss-making but expected to turn an operating profit in H2 FY27, and being merged into the parent subject to NCLT approval.

parts.name: Other Indian subsidiaries (Matrix and others)
parts.what: Additional acquired garment units in India, including a factory at Ranchi in Jharkhand, positioned as low-cost locations meant to compete with Bangladesh; smaller than the core business and hit in Q4 FY26 when some of their customers shifted orders to other countries because of the 50% US tariff.

parts.name: New capacity — Madhya Pradesh and ongoing capex
parts.what: Greenfield and brownfield capacity added over the period (the Madhya Pradesh unit started in FY24 and contributed roughly INR 55–60 crore in its first year), with about INR 170 crore spent on new capacity in FY26 alone — the main reason net debt rose by INR 395 crore.

overview.what_it_does: Godawari Power & Ispat Limited (GPIL) is an Indian steel and iron-ore company based in Raipur, Chhattisgarh, that digs its own iron ore, converts it into iron-ore pellets, and then turns those pellets into sponge iron, steel billets and finished steel products such as structural rolled sections, wire rod, H.B. wire, MS rounds, ERW pipes and galvanized fabricated items. It sells iron-ore pellets to other steel makers in the domestic market and sells its finished and value-added steel products to industrial buyers and government-linked agencies such as Indian Railways and power distribution companies. It makes money mainly on the spread between cheap, self-mined ore and the price of pellets and steel — because it owns its Ari Dongri iron ore mine, its own captive power (waste-heat recovery, biomass and a large captive solar fleet), it keeps costs low, running EBITDA margins of roughly 20-30% and FY26 revenue producing INR 1,253 crores of EBITDA and INR 802 crores of PAT. Everything operates from plants in and around Siltara/Raipur in Chhattisgarh, India, and by FY26 the company was debt-light with a cash position of INR 837 crores, while expanding into cold-rolled steel and, newly, battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing.

parts.name: Iron ore mining (Ari Dongri mine)
parts.what: The company's captive iron ore mine, which feeds its own pellet plants and is being expanded from 2.35 million to 6 million tons a year (environment clearance received Feb 2026, full-scale operation targeted FY28) — management calls it the core of its raw-material security and backward integration.

parts.name: Iron ore pellets
parts.what: Its largest and most-discussed product line: high-grade pellets both sold to outside steel makers and used in-house, with capacity raised from 2.7 to 4.7 million tons after a 2-million-ton natural-gas grate-kiln plant was commissioned in December 2025; pellet realization was around INR 10,000-10,500 a ton.

parts.name: Sponge iron (DRI)
parts.what: Pellets are converted into sponge iron, the intermediate feed for steel making; capacity was expanded from 0.59 to 0.65 million tons and production exceeded 100% of target in FY26.

parts.name: Steel billets / steel melting shop
parts.what: Sponge iron is melted into steel billets, the semi-finished steel that feeds the rolling mills; billets hit 96% of targeted production in FY26.

parts.name: Finished and value-added steel products
parts.what: Rolling mills turn billets into structural rolled steel, MS rounds, wire rod and H.B. wire (H.B. wire capacity raised to 0.115 million tons); a strip mill feeds ERW pipes, and this group has been the fastest-growing sales line, up 15% Y-o-Y in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Galvanized fabricated products
parts.what: Structural steel is fabricated and galvanized in-house for supply to Indian Railways, power utilities and discoms — previously the steel was bought from the market, so doing it captively is described as cost and value accretive; one of the few products whose realization held up in FY26.

parts.name: Ferro alloys (Hira Ferro Alloys / Alok Ferro Alloys)
parts.what: Subsidiary plants making ferro alloys used in steel making, progressively bought up as part of group simplification (Alok Ferro Alloys stake raised to 88.34% direct, 97.62% including holdings via Hira Ferro Alloys); one of the few lines with firm realizations in FY26.

parts.name: Captive power
parts.what: Self-generated electricity from waste-heat recovery (49 MW), biomass, a windmill and a large solar fleet being tripled from 165 MW to 540 MW, plus a 45 MWh battery storage unit — all consumed in-house to cut grid power cost and carbon, not sold.

parts.name: CRM complex (upcoming)
parts.what: A 0.7-million-ton cold rolling mill complex under construction with equipment ordered and bank funding secured, targeted for commissioning by March 2027.

parts.name: Integrated steel plant (upcoming)
parts.what: A board-approved 1-million-ton integrated plant for structural steel and wire rods, with land and environmental approval in place and construction expected to begin October 2026 — a scaled-down successor to the 2-million-ton plant discussed in earlier calls.

parts.name: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) manufacturing (new venture)
parts.what: A brand-new, non-steel business: a 20-gigawatt BESS manufacturing facility costing INR 1,025 crores, with LFP cell and balance-of-system supply agreements signed, targeted to commission from March 2027.

parts.name: Ardent Steel (divested)
parts.what: A merchant iron-ore pellet plant in which GPIL held 37.85%; the stake was sold for about INR 91 crores and completed in FY26 as part of simplifying the group structure.

overview.what_it_does: Gujarat Pipavav Port Limited runs a commercial seaport at Pipavav on India's Gujarat coast, where it loads, unloads, stores and moves other people's cargo for a fee. Its customers are global shipping lines such as Maersk and the OOCL-COSCO group, fertiliser and LPG importers buying on government or private tenders, car exporters, and since October 2025 ONGC, which uses the port as an offshore supply base for its Arabian Sea oil fields. It earns money on a per-unit tariff basis — roughly Rs. 9,000-10,500 per container (TEU) and Rs. 550-650 per metric tonne of bulk or liquid cargo, plus marine services charged across all cargo types — with tariffs raised about 5% in January 2026. The port is not owned outright: GPPL operates it under a concession from the Gujarat Maritime Board on which it pays a waterfront royalty (currently at a concessional rate offset against its investment), the concession runs out around 2028, and renewal talks were still unresolved as of May 2026. Volumes are heavy-fixed-cost and high-margin, with EBITDA margins of 58-65% and a near-100% dividend payout.

parts.name: Containers
parts.what: Handling import/export containers for shipping lines, running around 165,000-180,000 TEUs a quarter at Rs. 8,000-10,500 per TEU; it is the biggest and most-discussed cargo line but has been the weak spot, down roughly 4-5% a year through FY26 after the Red Sea crisis, a withdrawn Maersk service and US tariffs on textiles hit the services calling at Pipavav, with a new Maersk far-East service (FI2) starting July 2026 expected to add about 1,000 moves a week.

parts.name: Dry Bulk
parts.what: Handling loose dry cargo, mostly imported fertiliser (urea and others) bought on government tenders, at roughly 500,000+ tonnes a quarter and Rs. 550-650 per tonne; it grew about 35% in FY26 and was the standout volume story, though management calls it slightly margin-dilutive and lumpy because it depends on when the government opens tenders — coal is a smaller piece management was still deciding what to do with in late 2024.

parts.name: Liquid Bulk
parts.what: Handling liquid cargo including LPG at Rs. 550-600 per tonne, running at 1.6-1.65 million tonnes a year against a single jetty that can only hold about 1.7 million — so it is effectively capacity-capped, grew about 8-13% in FY26, and management expects strong growth for several years once the new liquid jetty (targeted for completion around Q3 FY27, weather permitting) opens up room.

parts.name: RoRo
parts.what: Roll-on/roll-off handling of cars driven on and off vessels, guided at 150,000-175,000 cars a year back in 2024 and hitting a record 62,000+ cars in a single quarter by Q3 FY26; it is the fastest-growing and most trouble-free line, up about 39-40% in FY26, with a dedicated RoRo staging area due to finish around June 2026.

parts.name: Offshore supply base (ONGC contract)
parts.what: A five-year contract effective 1 October 2025 to act as ONGC's second offshore supply base after Nhava, providing marine, storage and related services for its Arabian Sea oil fields; management refuses to disclose the revenue as it is confidential customer information, so the calls give no sense of its size.

parts.name: Marine services
parts.what: Charges for vessel-side services that apply across every cargo stream regardless of what is in the hold, and were included alongside containers in the roughly 5% January 2026 tariff increase that management expected to lift total revenue by about 3-4%.

parts.name: Concession and future expansion
parts.what: Not a revenue line but the frame around the whole business: GPPL operates under a Gujarat Maritime Board concession expiring around 2028, and has signed a non-binding MOU with GMB for roughly Rs. 17,000 crore of port infrastructure spending over 30 years — new liquid, bulk, container and RoRo jetties plus land development — all of which is explicitly contingent on the concession being extended.

overview.what_it_does: Granules India is a Hyderabad-based pharmaceutical manufacturer that makes generic medicines and the chemical ingredients that go into them — it describes itself as integrated "from molecule to the tablet," making the chemistry, converting it into the finished formulation, and supplying it into regulated markets. It sells three linked product forms — active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), pharmaceutical formulation intermediates (PFIs), and finished dosages (tablets/capsules) — historically built on large-volume molecules like paracetamol and metformin, and increasingly on complex generics, ADHD/controlled-substance products, and oncology. Its customers are mainly other pharma companies, distributors and retailers in the US (its largest market), Europe (about 15% of revenue in FY26) and the rest of the world, and it makes money by manufacturing at scale and low cost, filing regulatory dossiers (ANDAs, DMFs, EU/Canada filings) to win approvals, and then selling volume at a gross margin of roughly 65%. It manufactures both in India (Gagillapur, Vizag, Genome Valley) and in the US (its GPI plant in Virginia and Chantilly R&D site, plus a packaging site), and has recently added a Swiss/India peptide contract-manufacturing arm; Q1 FY27 revenue was about INR 1,477 crore.

parts.name: Finished Dosages (FD)
parts.what: Actual pills and capsules sold to customers — now the core of the company at 74% of FY26 revenue (up from 50% in FY23), and the stated growth engine, with complex generics rising from 39% to 50% of finished dosages in a year.

parts.name: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API)
parts.what: The bulk drug chemicals Granules makes and sells to other drug makers as well as feeding its own tablet plants — a legacy volume business (paracetamol, metformin) that has seen price erosion, with a new oncology API facility being built at Vizag.

parts.name: Pharmaceutical Formulation Intermediates (PFI)
parts.what: A half-way product between raw chemical and finished tablet supplied to customers who do their own final tableting; grouped with API as the older, lower-growth part of the mix, with volumes and prices declining as the company shifts toward finished dosages.

parts.name: Granules Pharmaceuticals Inc. (GPI) – US manufacturing, CNS/ADHD
parts.what: The company's own US manufacturing and R&D operation in Virginia and Chantilly, focused on central-nervous-system and ADHD controlled-substance products; management calls it a key US growth driver, ranked 27th among all US generic companies by sales value in FY26 (from 74th in FY21) and 4th in controlled substances.

parts.name: Granules Consumer Health (GCH)
parts.what: The US commercial arm selling over-the-counter private-label products (medicines sold under retailers' own brands), described as gaining traction and contributing to US growth; it also runs a Virginia site that passed inspection with zero observations.

parts.name: Peptide CDMO – Senn Chemicals / Ascelis Peptides
parts.what: An acquired Swiss (Zurich) contract development and manufacturing business making peptides for pharma and cosmetics customers, now called the "fourth revenue pillar" — INR 1,593 million of FY26 revenue, EBITDA-positive within three quarters of acquisition, growing over 100% year-on-year, with an India footprint being added at Vizag.

parts.name: Granules Life Sciences (GLS) – Genome Valley
parts.what: A new Hyderabad formulation plant that started operations in March 2024 with an initial 2 billion-unit capacity; management says scaling it adds roughly 40% to total formulation capacity.

parts.name: Oncology platform (Vizag)
parts.what: API and finished-dosage capability for cancer drugs at the Vizag site, with first-to-file and first-to-launch filings aimed at US, Europe and rest of world; launches were guided to begin from FY26.

parts.name: R&D and technology platforms (biocatalysis / enzymes, continuous manufacturing, CZRO green molecules)
parts.what: In-house research at Genome Valley and Chantilly aimed at cheaper, greener chemistry and complex products — R&D spend rose from about INR 32 crore a quarter in FY23 to INR 62 crore in Q1 FY25 — and it is the source of the complex-generic, 505(b)(2) and first-to-file pipeline management says will drive future value.

overview.what_it_does: Grasim Industries is a large Indian manufacturing group (part of the Aditya Birla group, incorporated in 1947) that makes and sells industrial and consumer products, and it also owns controlling stakes in listed companies in cement and financial services, so most of its reported revenue comes from those subsidiaries. Its own factories make man-made cellulosic fibre and yarn sold to textile makers, and chlor-alkali/specialty chemicals (caustic soda, chlorine derivatives, epoxy) sold to industrial customers; since 2021-22 it has added two new consumer- and trade-facing businesses, decorative paints under the Birla Opus brand and a B2B e-commerce platform called Birla Pivot. It makes money mainly by selling tonnes of fibre and chemicals at prevailing global prices (caustic soda and viscose prices, cotton prices and the rupee all swing its earnings), and increasingly by selling branded paint through dealers, contractors and institutional projects. It operates chiefly in India, with plants at sites such as Vilayat, Nagda and Kharagpur, while selling into and competing against global fibre and chemical markets (China, Indonesia, US, EU). Consolidated revenue reached a record INR 1,75,431 crore (over $18 billion) in FY26, versus INR 41,039 crore on a standalone (own-operations) basis.

parts.name: Cellulosic Fibre (VSF / CSF)
parts.what: Makes viscose staple fibre, a wood-pulp-based fibre used by textile mills as an alternative to cotton and polyester; it is one of the company's two traditional core businesses, with quarterly volumes around 200 kilotonnes and quarterly revenue of roughly INR 3,700 crore in the earlier calls.

parts.name: Cellulosic Fashion Yarn (VFY / CFY) and Insulators
