parts.what: A smaller sister business making filament yarn for fashion textiles plus electrical insulators, running at roughly INR 583 crore of revenue in a quarter (about a sixth the size of the fibre business).

parts.name: Chemicals (Chlor-Alkali and Specialty Chemicals)
parts.what: Produces caustic soda and chlorine plus value-added chlorine products, chloromethanes, water-treatment and sanitation chemicals, epoxy and ECH; earnings hinge on the 'ECU realization' per tonne, and the specialty chemicals piece had grown to about 30% of chemical business revenue by mid-2024.

parts.name: Paints – Birla Opus
parts.what: A decorative paints business launched commercially in April 2024 across six new plants, selling emulsions, enamels, waterproofing, wood finish, wallpaper and tools through 50,000+ dealers, ~1,000 exclusive galleries and institutional projects; it doubled revenue in FY26 and is the number three player in organized decorative paints, closing in on number two when combined with Birla White putty.

parts.name: B2B E-commerce – Birla Pivot
parts.what: An online marketplace selling building and construction materials to businesses, including its own private-label plywood, doors and tiles; described as high-growth and less capital-hungry, running at over INR 550 crore of revenue per quarter as of mid-2024.

parts.name: Building Materials – UltraTech Cement
parts.what: The group's cement arm, consolidated into Grasim's results, which crossed 150-155 million tonnes of annual capacity and has been buying stakes in rivals such as Kesoram and India Cements; it is the single largest contributor to consolidated revenue.

parts.name: Financial Services – Aditya Birla Capital
parts.what: The group's lending, insurance and financial-products arm, described as growing through an omnichannel distribution network with a focus on risk management and return on capital.

parts.name: Textiles / Birla White putty
parts.what: Legacy fabric and wall-putty lines mentioned alongside the newer businesses; textiles delivered a record quarterly EBITDA in Q1 FY23, and Birla White putty revenue is counted together with Birla Opus when management measures paints market share.

overview.what_it_does: Gravita India is a recycler: it buys scrap — mainly used lead-acid batteries, plus aluminium, plastic and copper scrap — melts and refines it, and sells the recovered metals and plastic granules to industrial buyers, including battery makers and global OEMs (its Mundra lead is now LME brand-listed under 'GRAVITA M' and its Chittoor, Mundra and Phagi plants are MCX-empanelled). It makes money on the spread between scrap cost and finished-metal price, quoted internally as EBITDA per tonne (Q1 FY27: about INR24,181/t lead, INR25,175/t aluminium, INR10,197/t plastic, INR55,151/t copper), and pushes margins up by selling more 'value-added products' (63% of revenue in Q1 FY27) and by hedging metal prices back-to-back. It runs plants in India (Jaipur/Phagi, Mundra, Chittoor, Kathua being merged into Jaipur) and overseas (Sri Lanka, Ghana, Togo, a Romanian rubber plant via its Netherlands arm), with 12-plus facilities globally and sales into 70-plus countries; overseas operations were 42% of revenue and 76% of profit in Q1 FY23. Scale: quarterly revenue grew from about INR630 crores (Q1 FY23) to INR1,475 crores (Q1 FY27), with installed capacity of 4.97 lakh tonnes a year targeted to exceed 8 lakh tonnes by FY29.

parts.name: Lead recycling
parts.what: Recycles used lead-acid batteries into lead metal and lead alloys — the company's original and by far largest business (42,151 tonnes in Q2 FY25 versus about 3,500 tonnes aluminium and 3,000 tonnes plastic), with management targeting non-lead to rise above 30% of the business.

parts.name: Aluminium recycling
parts.what: Turns aluminium scrap into alloys such as ADC12; a much smaller volume line than lead but one of the faster-growing ones, guided at 35%-40% growth, and earning per-tonne margins similar to or above lead.

parts.name: Plastic recycling
parts.what: Recovers plastic (largely from battery casings) into granules; the smallest of the older segments by volume and the lowest per-tonne margin, but grouped with aluminium as a high-growth vertical.

parts.name: Copper recycling
parts.what: Newest large vertical, entered by acquiring Rashtriya Metal Industries plus a 29,400 tonne-per-annum Gujarat plant costing about INR160 crores; already meaningful, contributing INR376 crores of revenue in Q1 FY27 at only 50% utilisation and the highest per-tonne margin of any segment.

parts.name: Rubber recycling
parts.what: A newer diversification, with a roughly 17,000 tonne-per-annum waste-rubber plant in Romania (Gravita's first European facility, about INR40 crores, 80% owned via its Netherlands subsidiary) and a first Indian rubber plant at Mundra.

parts.name: Lithium-ion battery recycling
parts.what: Still early-stage — a pilot project targeted to be operational around H1 FY26 — and one of the new verticals the company's INR1,680 crore capex plan through FY29 is meant to fund.

parts.name: Paper and steel recycling
parts.what: Planned future verticals mentioned in capex and Vision plans; no operating volumes or revenue disclosed in the calls.

parts.name: Overseas business
parts.what: Plants and sourcing operations outside India (Sri Lanka, Ghana, Togo, Romania, plus the Netherlands holding arm) that sit close to scrap supply and earn better margins — 42% of revenue but 76% of profit in Q1 FY23.

parts.name: Value-added products
parts.what: The higher-margin finished items (alloys and specialty grades) rather than plain refined metal; management tracks this as a share of revenue, up from 41% in Q1 FY23 to 63% in Q1 FY27 against an earlier goal of 50%.

overview.what_it_does: Greaves Cotton is an old Indian engineering company (it dates itself to 1859, incorporated 1922, registered in Maharashtra and headquartered in Mumbai) that designs and manufactures engines, generator sets, vehicle components and electric vehicles, and then makes money again servicing them. Its biggest traditional business is small diesel engines that go into three-wheeler auto-rickshaws sold to vehicle makers (OEMs), plus engines for non-automotive uses like gensets, marine, firefighting, defence, construction and agriculture; alongside this it sells control cables and other engineered components (Excel Controlinkage), spare parts and servicing through a franchise retail/workshop network, and builds its own electric scooters (Ampere brand) and electric three-wheelers (Eltra) through subsidiary Greaves Electric Mobility. So it earns revenue partly B2B from OEMs and industrial customers, and partly B2C from consumers buying electric two- and three-wheelers, spare parts and service. It is mainly an India business with a pan-India dealer and service network, and a growing export share — roughly 9% of revenue in FY25 rising to about 13% in FY26 — going to Europe, the US and the Middle East; consolidated quarterly revenue has run in the region of Rs 640-660 crore, and management has grouped everything under three segments called Energy Solutions, Mobility Solutions and Industrial Solutions.

parts.name: Energy Solutions
parts.what: Generator sets (gensets) and the engines behind them, plus the spares, service and annual maintenance contracts sold afterwards — management calls India's genset market a 10-12% annual growth market, and this segment grew about 20-21% year-on-year in FY26 with the aftermarket/spares part growing even faster at 35-40%; it recently launched a 650 kVA genset built on an in-house engine and won a single Rs 35 crore institutional order.

parts.name: Mobility Solutions
parts.what: The automotive side — diesel and other fuel engines for three-wheelers sold to OEMs, exports of Euro V+ engines to Europe (including to Ligier), the Excel Controlinkage components business making control cables and assemblies, and the aftermarket retail spares business; it grew about 15-16% in FY26 with the automotive piece up 48% year-on-year in the March quarter, and management describes it as deliberately 'fuel-agnostic', noting diesel still holds 18-20% of the three-wheeler market.

parts.name: Greaves Retail / Greaves Care (aftermarket retail, part of Mobility Solutions)
parts.what: Sells multi-brand spare parts and runs franchisee-owned Greaves Care service workshops (163 outlets as of mid-2024) for three-wheelers, small commercial vehicles and EVs — roughly Rs 148 crore of revenue in a quarter, described as asset-light, cash-generating and high-return, though by FY26 the company exited non-core lines like two-wheeler parts and construction equipment parts to focus on the core.

parts.name: Industrial Solutions
parts.what: Special-purpose engines for demanding applications such as firefighting, marine, defence and agriculture — the smallest and slowest-growing of the three segments (about 3% growth over nine months of FY26, 15% in the March quarter), but with wins like a direct defence supply order, FM/UL-certified engines for a European customer, and over 300 engines supplied to Assam Inland Waterways.

parts.name: Greaves Electric Mobility (GEMPL)
parts.what: The separately-run electric vehicle arm making Ampere electric scooters (roughly Rs 40,000 to Rs 1,10,000 price points, about 3.4% market share and a top-five position in e-two-wheelers in mid-2024) and Eltra electric three-wheelers for passengers and cargo; it was scaled up with a committed investment of up to about $220 million from partner Abdul Latif Jameel, and its products depend partly on government subsidy schemes.

parts.name: Greaves Finance
parts.what: Mentioned by management as a post-purchase/financing arm alongside Greaves Retail, helping customers fund vehicle purchases; the calls give no size for it.

overview.what_it_does: Groww (legal name Billionbrains Garage Ventures Limited, based in Bangalore and listed on the BSE and NSE since FY26) runs an app-based investing platform for retail savers and traders in India, which it describes as building 'India's largest investing and wealth platform.' Customers open an account and buy mutual funds, stocks, equity futures and options, ETFs, commodities and bonds, and the company also lends against their holdings; a US stocks offering via the GIFT City route is licensed and in testing. It earns money mainly from brokerage — a flat INR 20 per derivatives order plus charges on cash trades, with roughly 70% of that revenue from derivatives and 30% from cash — and from interest on loans such as margin funding priced at 14.95%. Management says about 80% of new customers arrive organically, with the rest largely from digital performance marketing, and the whole business is India-focused, aimed at a market of 70-80 million existing stock and mutual fund investors out of 500-600 million Indians already transacting online.

parts.name: Broking (cash / equity)
parts.what: Buying and selling of shares and mutual funds/ETFs for retail customers; it is about 30% of broking revenue, and management says its cash yield has improved roughly 5% year-on-year as margin funding spreads through the base.

parts.name: Broking (derivatives / F&O)
parts.what: Futures and options trading charged at a flat INR 20 per order; the largest revenue line at roughly 70% of broking revenue, with equity derivatives market share rising from 9.1% to 10.6% in Q4 FY26 and about 17 lakh customers trading in that quarter versus 14 lakh earlier.

parts.name: MTF (Margin Trading Facility)
parts.what: Lending customers money at 14.95% to buy shares on margin — an AUM-style book that management calls their best-scaling product, where they aim for a double-digit market share within about three years.

parts.name: LAS (Loan Against Securities)
parts.what: Loans against a customer's investments, so far only against mutual funds with loan against securities still to launch; early stage but growing fast, and by Q1 FY27 it made up 34% of disbursements.

parts.name: Commodities
parts.what: A newly launched commodities trading product that reached more than 28% retail market share by notional average daily turnover.

parts.name: Bonds
parts.what: Bond investing, launched first in the primary market and then extended to secondary; management says it is 'scaling really, really well.'

parts.name: Wealth management — Fisdom, W by Groww, Groww Prime
parts.what: Three advice-led offerings added via the Fisdom acquisition in late 2025 — Fisdom sold through bank partnerships, W for affluent and HNI customers, and Prime (launched January 2026) for mass-affluent customers — covering research-backed investment selection, rebalancing and tax planning; still small and early, with Fisdom expected to turn profitable by FY28.

parts.name: AMC (asset management)
parts.what: A planned fund-management business through a partnership with State Street Global (SSG), which had received SEBI and CCI approval as of the July 2026 call.

overview.what_it_does: GRSE is a Kolkata-based shipyard owned by the Government of India and run under the Ministry of Defence, and its core business — roughly 98% of its order book — is building warships and other vessels to order. Its main customer is the Indian Navy (frigates, anti-submarine craft, survey and patrol vessels), alongside the Indian Coast Guard, other government bodies such as the Ministry of Earth Sciences, DRDO and the Geological Survey of India, the Government of West Bengal, and export clients including Bangladesh, Guyana and a German buyer. It makes money from long-dated construction contracts booked as work progresses, with cash coming in as stage payments are earned at milestones like keel laying, launch and delivery — so revenue tracks how fast ships are physically built. Alongside shipbuilding it runs smaller engineering lines (portable steel bridges, deck machinery, naval guns, an engines unit at Ranchi) and a ship-repair business; FY26 revenue was ₹7,002 crore with profit after tax of ₹748 crore, against an order book of ₹15,324 crore as of March 2026.

parts.name: Shipbuilding (including commercial shipbuilding)
parts.what: Designs and builds warships and other vessels to order — P-17 Alpha frigates, Anti-Submarine Shallow Water Crafts, Survey Vessels Large, Next-Generation Offshore Patrol Vessels for the Navy and Coast Guard, plus research vessels for civilian ministries — and management repeatedly calls it the core business at about 98% of order book and revenue; the March 2026 book of ₹15,324 crore covers nine projects and 39 platforms.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: The same shipyard building for overseas buyers — a passenger-cum-cargo vessel for Guyana, patrol boats and a 1,000 m³ dredger for Bangladesh, and a 12-ship multipurpose vessel order for a German client that grew from 4 to 8 to 12 — contributing over ₹270 crore of revenue in FY26 and described as a focus area.

parts.name: Green shipping / hybrid and electric ferries
parts.what: Builds battery-electric and hybrid passenger ferries, starting with a 150-passenger fully electric ferry for the Government of West Bengal and now a 13-ferry hybrid order (seven 100-seat, six 200-seat); small in rupee terms but management calls it a foothold in a market with 'huge potential' for inland water transport.

parts.name: Ship repair
parts.what: Refits and repairs of vessels, mainly Coast Guard ships; started from scratch around 2022 at about 1% of revenue and had grown to roughly 5% of revenue by August 2024.

parts.name: Engineering Division — Portable Steel (Bailey) Bridges
parts.what: Makes prefabricated steel bridges sold to the Border Roads Organisation, the National Highways Infrastructure Development Corporation and state PWDs; GRSE calls itself the Indian market leader, and turnover rose from around ₹60 crore to ₹140 crore by 2024 and crossed ₹200 crore for the first time in FY26 on 110 bridges delivered, 30 of them exported.

parts.name: Engineering Division — Deck Machinery
parts.what: Supplies deck equipment for ships; grouped with the bridges business in a segment that carried only about ₹102 crore of order book in June 2022, so it is a minor contributor.

parts.name: Naval guns
parts.what: Builds and delivers naval surface guns — seven delivered in FY26, four of which cleared Sea Acceptance Trials — a small but distinct product line outside shipbuilding.

parts.name: Engines Division, Ranchi
parts.what: A separate engine-making unit that held ₹138 crore of order book in June 2022, a small share of the company total.

overview.what_it_does: Garware Hi-Tech Films is an Indian manufacturer of specialty plastic films — thin coated polyester films that are stuck onto glass and car bodies, plus industrial films sold to other manufacturers. Its main products are sun-control films (window films for cars and buildings that block ~99% of harmful UV rays), paint protection film (PPF, a clear protective wrap applied over car paint), and a range of industrial films such as shrinkable/PCR shrink films, low-oligomer films for electrical and electronic uses, release liners and some commodity items like thermal lamination, packaging and lidding films and metallized film. It makes money by selling these films at high margins through distributors, dealers, car OEMs and its own branded 'Garware Application Studio' outlets, under brands including 'Global'; it is fully vertically integrated, making its own PET resin, metallized, dyed and laminated components in-house at its plants in Aurangabad/Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. It is mainly an exporter — roughly 74–81% of revenue comes from outside India, shipping to 90-plus countries with North America, India, the rest of Asia, Europe and now the Middle East as key markets — and FY26 revenue was about ₹2,120 crore with ₹500 crore EBITDA and ₹338 crore PAT, debt-free with ₹774 crore of cash.

parts.name: Sun Control Films (SCF) / Solar Control Films — automotive and architectural
parts.what: Window films for car glass and building glass that cut heat and block 99% of UV rays, sold under brands like Spectra Pro and DecoVista; management calls this the largest business at roughly 50% of FY26 revenue, says Garware has the world's second-largest sun-control capacity and is the third-largest branded player in the US and Europe, with capacity expanded 75% to 1,800 lakh sq ft and a further ₹191 crore, 1,200 lakh sq ft line announced.

parts.name: Paint Protection Film (PPF)
parts.what: Clear (and now coloured, matte, white, black and Titanium series) film wrapped over car paint to protect it, sold to dealers, OEMs and consumers; about 25% of FY26 revenue, over 70% exported, with Garware described as the only PPF manufacturer in India and capacity doubled to 600 lakh sq ft in September 2025.

parts.name: Industrial Product Division (IPD)
parts.what: Business-to-business films — shrinkable and floatable/PCR (recycled-content) shrink films, low-oligomer films for electrical and electronic applications, release liners/PRU, plus commodity lines like thermal lamination, plain, packaging and lidding films and metallizers; about 25% of FY26 revenue, with management steering it toward the higher-margin specialty items.

parts.name: Garware Application Studios (GAS)
parts.what: A direct-to-consumer retail network of branded studios that fit premium PPF and glazing films onto customers' cars, plus training of applicators; it grew from around 65 studios in 2023 to over 250 by FY26 across Tier-1, 2 and 3 cities, targeting 300-plus, and management treats it as the main way it created and now feeds India's PPF market.

parts.name: Garware Home Solutions (GHS)
parts.what: A newly launched direct-to-consumer vertical selling architectural/home window films through studios run with local interior design firms, with the first studio in Chembur, Mumbai and 6 operational by FY26, targeted to reach 50 by end-FY27 — small today but positioned as a higher-margin domestic growth engine.

parts.name: UAE subsidiary / MENA trading arm
parts.what: A newly announced wholly owned subsidiary in the UAE to handle trading and export of films, ceramic coatings and paint protection films across the Middle East/North Africa and other international markets, alongside a flagship global application studio there; described as a step to expand the fast-growing Middle East architectural film business.

parts.name: Backward integration and new product lines (TPU, graphics, PDLC)
parts.what: In-house production of raw materials and components — PET resin from PTA and MEG, metallized film, dyed film and lamination — plus an upcoming TPU manufacturing line to be commissioned by October 2026 (25% of its capacity earmarked for new-generation products such as TPU-based UV-printable films, graphic solutions and PDLC privacy films); over ₹500 crore of capacity expansion in recent years, all funded from internal cash.

overview.what_it_does: GSFC (Gujarat State Fertilizers & Chemicals Limited) is a Gujarat, India-based manufacturer that makes and sells crop fertilizers and industrial chemicals, run out of two plant complexes — Fertilizernagar in Vadodara and Sikka near Jamnagar — and listed on the BSE and NSE with the Gujarat state government associated with it (a shareholder on one call called it "the Navaratna of the State Government of Gujarat"). On the fertilizer side it produces urea, DAP, Ammonium Sulphate (AS), Ammonium Phosphate Sulphate (APS) and other NPK/water-soluble grades, sells them through a dealer-retailer chain to farmers at a government-set MRP, and collects a large part of its revenue as subsidy paid by the Government of India when the farmer actually buys at the point-of-sale terminal; it also imports and trades DAP and urea to supplement its own output. On the industrial side it makes and sells chemicals such as Caprolactam, Nylon-6, Melamine, HX Crystal, technical-grade urea, methanol, ammonia and sulphuric acid to domestic and export industrial customers. Profits swing with the gap between selling prices/subsidy rates and bought-in input costs — phosphoric acid, sulphur, sulphuric acid, ammonia, natural gas and benzene — and in FY26 standalone sales were about Rs. 10,827 crore with profit after tax of about Rs. 652 crore, on a balance sheet management describes as having no long-term debt.

parts.name: Fertilizer segment
parts.what: The much larger of the two businesses — roughly Rs. 2,000-2,300 crore of sales in a single quarter versus about Rs. 600 crore for industrial products — it manufactures and sells urea, DAP, Ammonium Sulphate, Ammonium Phosphate Sulphate and other P&K/water-soluble grades to farmers, with FY26 volumes of 22.31 lakh metric tons sold and 17.59 lakh metric tons produced, and margins management pegs at only about 5%-6% EBITDA (roughly Rs. 2,500 per ton in an earlier quarter).

parts.name: Industrial Products (IP) segment / chemicals
parts.what: The smaller, non-farm arm selling Caprolactam, Nylon-6, Melamine, HX Crystal, technical-grade urea, methanol and traded ammonia into domestic and export markets, contributing about Rs. 596 crore of quarterly sales and Rs. 200 crore of annual profit in FY26, with earnings driven largely by the Caprolactam-Benzene price spread (quoted at $620-$1,000 per metric ton in various quarters, down to $495 in Q3 FY26).

parts.name: Trading / imported fertilizers
parts.what: Alongside its own factories, GSFC buys in and resells DAP and urea — for example finalizing import contracts of about 1.25 lakh metric tons for one quarter — to meet government pressure to supply more DAP; volumes here move up and down with policy and are tracked separately from manufactured volumes.

parts.name: Government subsidy receipts
parts.what: Not a product line but the mechanism behind most fertilizer revenue: the Government of India pays subsidy per ton (NBS rates for P&K, plus urea subsidy) when the farmer buys, so changes in subsidy rates swing reported revenue and profit sharply, and management repeatedly reports how current the subsidy collections are — for instance, dues received up to the third/fourth week of April 2026 as of the May 2026 call.

parts.name: Capex / captive input projects
parts.what: Ongoing investments — the Sulphuric Acid-V plant commissioned 7 January 2026, Urea-II revamp, the HX Crystal plant started October 2024 at 20 tons per day, and cheaper solar power sourced from GIPCL — aimed at making its own key inputs and cutting cost, with over Rs. 670 crore of projects capitalized in FY26.

overview.what_it_does: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) is an Indian state-owned ("CPSE", granted Maharatna status in October 2024) aerospace and defence manufacturer that designs, builds, repairs and overhauls military aircraft, helicopters and aero engines. Its main customers are India's armed forces — the Indian Air Force, Army, Navy and Coast Guard — with smaller amounts from ISRO (space hardware), civil operators such as Pawan Hans, foreign buyers like Guyana, and global engine makers like Safran. It makes money two ways: selling newly manufactured platforms and engines (₹9,227 crores of FY26 revenue) and, more heavily, repair-and-overhaul (ROH) work on aircraft already in service (₹20,524 crores of FY26 revenue), all executed against long-dated government contracts, with customers funding much of the working capital upfront. It operates entirely from plants in India — Bangalore/Bengaluru, Nashik, Tumakuru and other locations — with about 24,000 employees, FY26 revenue of ₹33,050 crores, profit before tax of ₹12,112 crores, roughly 30% operating EBITDA margin, and an order book of ₹2,54,538 crores that management says keeps its lines busy to 2032-33.

parts.name: Manufacturing
parts.what: Building and delivering new aircraft, helicopters and engines; ₹9,227 crores of FY26 revenue (up from ₹7,957 crores), the smaller of the two revenue lines but the one management expects to grow as LCA Mark-1A and HTT-40 deliveries begin.

parts.name: ROH (Repair and Overhaul)
parts.what: Servicing, repairing and overhauling platforms already flying with the customer; at ₹20,524 crores it was the majority of FY26 revenue, brought in ₹26,539 crores of fresh orders in FY26, and management is investing capex in new ROH facilities and expects roughly ₹20,000 crores more of such orders.

parts.name: Fighter aircraft (LCA Tejas / Sukhoi-30MKI)
parts.what: The flagship programme — indigenous LCA Tejas Mark-1A plus Su-30MKI supply and upgrades; the 97 LCA Mark-1A order was booked in FY26, a third production line at Nashik took capacity to 8 aircraft a year, and deliveries have been repeatedly delayed by GE engine supply.

parts.name: Helicopters
parts.what: Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH Dhruv and Dhruv NG), Light Combat Helicopter (LCH Prachand), Light Utility Helicopter (LUH) and the future Indian Multi Role Helicopter (IMRH); the 156 LCH Prachand contract alone was worth ₹62,777 crores, and helicopter deliveries were a main revenue prop in FY26.

parts.name: Trainer and transport aircraft
parts.what: The HTT-40 basic trainer and the Dornier / Hindustan-228 light transport aircraft, sold to the Air Force, Navy and Coast Guard and also exported (two aircraft to Guyana), with a 40-Dornier upgrade contract still awaited.

parts.name: Aero engines
parts.what: Manufacture and supply of AL-31FP engines for the Sukhoi-30 (a 240-engine, ₹25,500 crore contract) and RD-33 engines, plus the indigenously certified Shakti civil engine and planned GE F414 and IMRH engine manufacture; engine deliveries repeatedly rescued revenue when aircraft programmes slipped.

parts.name: Design and Development / R&D
parts.what: In-house design of indigenous platforms (LCA Mark 2, AMCA, IMRH, naval utility helicopter), funded partly by customers (₹3,180 crores of D&D orders in FY25) and partly internally — R&D spend was ₹2,794 crores, about 8.4% of FY26 revenue, with 15% of profit set aside annually as an R&D corpus.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Sales to foreign customers, still very small at ₹501 crores in FY26 versus ₹400 crores the year before, but described as an area management wants to pursue aggressively as capacity frees up.

parts.name: Space / ISRO work
parts.what: Supplying space-worthy hardware to ISRO — Gaganyaan crew module fairing, propellant tanks and machining for the LVM3 heavy rocket — and a technology-transfer licence signed in September 2025 to manufacture the SSLV small launch vehicle; presented as diversification rather than a large revenue line.

parts.name: Civil aerospace and global supply chain
parts.what: A newer diversification push: an agreement with Safran to produce rotating parts for LEAP engines used on the Airbus A320neo and Boeing 737 MAX, an MoU with Russia's UAC to build the SJ-100 civil commuter aircraft in India, civil-certified Dhruv helicopters for operators like Pawan Hans, and an IAI tie-up to convert passenger jets into tanker aircraft.

overview.what_it_does: Happiest Minds Technologies is an India-headquartered IT services company that builds and maintains software and technology for other companies — product and digital engineering, application modernization, cloud, data and analytics, cybersecurity, IT infrastructure management, and, more recently, AI/generative-AI work. Its customers are enterprises across banking and financial services and insurance (BFSI, its largest vertical at about 27% of revenue), healthcare and life sciences, edtech/education, retail and consumer goods, high-tech, industrial, and travel/media; management says it ended FY26 with 306 active customers, including many billion-dollar corporations, and grows by landing accounts and expanding them. It earns money mainly by billing for people-based project and managed-services work, increasingly supplemented by its own repeatable platforms (an enterprise AI platform, plus Arttha, Insurance in a Box, Multi-Omics and EduWeave) that it sells alongside services for less headcount-dependent growth. The United States/Americas is the biggest market at roughly 57% of revenue, with India, Europe, APAC and Africa making up the rest; FY26 revenue crossed ₹2,315 crore with EBITDA margins in a guided 20–22% band, and management targets $1 billion of revenue by 2031.

parts.name: Product & Digital Engineering Services (PDES)
parts.what: Formed in FY25 by merging the older Product Engineering Services (PES) and Digital Business Services (DBS) units, this is the company's main and largest business — building software products for technology firms and running digital transformation, modernization and application work for enterprises; the acquired businesses PureSoftware and Aureus were folded into it.

parts.name: Infrastructure Management and Security Services (IMSS)
parts.what: Runs and secures customers' IT infrastructure — cloud and infrastructure management plus cybersecurity and managed security services, such as a multi-year managed security engagement with a Middle Eastern retailer; it has been a standing business unit with its own CEO throughout the period.

parts.name: Generative AI Business Services (GBS)
parts.what: A newer business unit carved out and reported separately from FY25, selling AI and generative-AI services and the company's enterprise AI platform, AI agents and reusable accelerators; management calls it central to strategy and says the bulk of FY27's planned 1,050 hires goes into GBS and the analytics/AI centre of excellence.

parts.name: Industry groups / verticals
parts.what: From FY25 the company reorganized so industry groups (BFSI, Healthcare & Life Sciences, EdTech, Retail/CPG, High-Tech, Industrial, Travel/Media & Entertainment) act as profit centres selling domain-specific solutions; BFSI is the largest at ~27% of revenue, EdTech ~16%, and Healthcare & Life Sciences the fastest-growing at 22% year-on-year in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Proprietary platforms and repeatable solutions
parts.what: A smaller but strategically emphasized layer of owned products — the enterprise AI platform, Arttha, Insurance in a Box, Multi-Omics and EduWeave — that management says create differentiated entry points into accounts and 'non-linear' growth alongside the services business.

parts.name: Acquisitions (PureSoftware, Aureus)
parts.what: Two deals closed in May 2024 that management called transformational: PureSoftware added scale and opened the APAC and Africa markets, while Aureus brought reinsurance-domain capability and a Hyderabad presence; both were consolidated into PDES and contributed to that year's growth.

overview.what_it_does: Havells India Limited is an Indian company that makes and sells electrical goods and home appliances, selling under brand names including Havells, Lloyd, Crabtree and Standard. Its products run from building-electrical items like cables, wires, switches and switchgear and lighting, through household products like fans, air coolers, kitchen appliances, air conditioners and refrigerators, and more recently solar panels and inverters. It earns money by manufacturing these goods in its own plants and selling them mainly in India through a dealer/distributor trade channel plus an omni-channel retail presence, with a smaller export business (about 15% of switchgear sales), passing raw-material cost swings in copper, aluminium and electronics through to customers via calibrated price hikes. Demand splits between consumer/residential buyers — heavily seasonal, since roughly 65%-70% of air conditioner sales fall in the January-June cooling season — and industrial/infrastructure customers, and the company spends heavily and continuously on advertising and brand building (around Rs 600 crores in FY26) as a long-term investment.

parts.name: Cables and Wires
parts.what: Makes industrial cables and domestic house wires; called one of the largest revenue contributors, its margins swing with copper and aluminium prices and with dealers stocking or destocking, and lately industrial cables have grown much faster than domestic wires.

parts.name: Lloyd (consumer durables / home appliances)
parts.what: The air-conditioner-led appliance brand, being built into a 'full stack home appliances player' with a new refrigerator plant at Ghiloth; it is one of the biggest revenue contributors and a long-term investment case — it went from losses to only about 3%-3.5% EBIT margins by FY25, with management stressing small market shares in a very large industry.

parts.name: ECD (Electrical Consumer Durables)
parts.what: Fans, air coolers and kitchen appliances sold to households; another top-three revenue contributor, growing about 20% in one quarter with margins helped by premiumisation (higher-priced fans) and cost savings.

parts.name: Switchgears (switches and switchgear)
parts.what: Electrical switches and protection devices for buildings; about 10% of revenue but roughly one-third of margin contribution, with contribution margins consistently in the 38%-41% band, and roughly 15% of it exported.

parts.name: Lighting and Fixtures
parts.what: Lighting products where selling prices had been falling for years but have now stabilised, with contribution margins that management says average 30%-32% over the long run.

parts.name: Renewables
parts.what: A fast-growing solar business — panels, inverters and solar pumps — backed by a Rs 600 crore investment in Goldi Solar for module manufacturing (on which a Rs 283 crore fair-value gain was booked in Q4 FY26); it became a separately reported segment from Q1 FY27, with panels carrying lower margins than inverters.

parts.name: Industrial and infrastructure categories
parts.what: The project- and industry-facing side of the portfolio (as opposed to consumer/residential), repeatedly described as the stronger, more resilient demand pocket in recent quarters.

overview.what_it_does: HBL Engineering (formerly HBL Power Systems) is a roughly 40-year-old Indian manufacturer that develops its own technology for small, hard-to-enter markets rather than competing on volume — batteries, railway signalling and safety electronics, and electronic fuzes and other defence hardware. Its customers are mostly government bodies and state-owned buyers: Indian Railways (which is buying its Kavach train-collision-avoidance system), the Ministry of Defence and the armed forces (fuzes for ammunition, grenades, rockets, bombs; lithium-ion cells and torpedo motors for the Navy), plus industrial and export customers for nickel-cadmium batteries. It makes money by selling this equipment on contracts and tenders, deliberately choosing niches with few competitors so it can hold good margins; management stresses that products take 10–15 years of in-house R&D before they earn anything (Kavach R&D started in 2005 and only began paying off in 2025). Operations are almost entirely in India and made in India — the company says it manufactures every component of its fuzes in-house — with exports a small slice, notably nickel-cadmium batteries (Middle East was raised as a market) and negligible exposure to US tariffs. Sales were flat/slightly down in FY25 at roughly ₹2,000 crore; management is 'budgeting' about ₹3,000 crore for FY26 and has said ₹4,500 crore by FY30 still looks reasonable, run through nine largely independent divisions under what the chairman wants to become a holding-company structure.

parts.name: Kavach (railway signalling / train collision avoidance)
parts.what: A complex train-protection system supplied to Indian Railways in two forms — loco (on-train) sets and trackside sections — and it is 'the big story of the year': orders went from a drought to a flood, it drives the jump to ~₹3,000 crore of sales, and the company can't even finish its current order book this year, with track-section orders booked out roughly 24 months.

parts.name: Electronic fuzes for ammunition and other explosive devices
parts.what: In-house-developed electronic detonating devices for artillery shells, grenades, air-defence/anti-drone rounds (23mm, 30mm, 40mm), naval rockets, air-dropped bombs and avalanche-control shells, sold to the Indian armed forces; management calls this the next growth engine after Kavach — expected to ramp from FY28 and become the second-biggest business in three to five years — and notes the high-volume artillery ammunition fuzes are actually the least profitable part of it.

parts.name: Fuze batteries
parts.what: The specialist batteries that go inside fuzes — the adjacent product HBL entered first and the reason it could build the whole fuze; the company says it is the only Indian maker and one of only a handful of factories worldwide, and it declines to sell these to rivals like BEL.

parts.name: Nickel-cadmium batteries
parts.what: A mature, slow-growing industrial battery line where technology was developed fully in-house and suppliers worldwide are few; described as one of the company's big export earners.

parts.name: Lithium-ion cells for the Navy
parts.what: A deliberately narrow defence niche — instead of chasing mass-market lithium cells (which management says nobody outside China makes money on), HBL is putting in about ₹200 crore or less of capex and expects to be profitable from year one.

parts.name: TMS and CTC (railway traffic management / centralised traffic control)
parts.what: Additional railway control systems where the only competitors are foreign firms; HBL has now cleared the qualification hurdle, but management sizes the opportunity modestly at maybe ₹100–300 crore a year and warns it will not be another Kavach.

parts.name: Electric trucks
parts.what: An electric heavy-vehicle effort now focused on 55-tonne and 35-tonne trucks (smaller prototypes were dropped), built without importing kits on the bet that government indigenisation pressure will favour a domestic maker — still pre-commercial, with no orders reported.

parts.name: Torpedo motors and homing heads
parts.what: Naval defence components under development — motor prototypes in FY27 with sales possible from FY28, while the homing head needs at least three more years to qualify; neither is counted in the ₹4,500 crore FY30 target.

parts.name: Surplus cash / Mittelstand Technology Partners
parts.what: Not an operating business but a newly set-up trust through which HBL plans to invest its growing surplus cash into smaller high-tech Indian manufacturers that also widen its own market access — the alternative to mutual funds, big acquisitions or buybacks, alongside a second dividend planned for March.

overview.what_it_does: HCC (Hindustan Construction Company) is a roughly 100-year-old Indian construction contractor that builds large, technically difficult infrastructure — highways, road and rail tunnels, metro lines and stations, bridges, dams and hydropower plants, pumped-storage schemes, nuclear power facilities and water projects. Its customers are almost entirely government bodies and state-owned agencies (railways, metro corporations, NTPC, NHPC/THDC-type hydro developers, the Department of Atomic Energy), which award work by competitive bidding; HCC makes money by executing these contracts over several years and billing against milestones, earning an EBITDA margin that has run from about 10% to 18%. It works across India — Maharashtra, Uttarakhand, Delhi, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, J&K, Tamil Nadu and elsewhere — plus a hydro project in Bhutan and a property-development subsidiary in Switzerland. The calls describe a company whose sales run around ₹4,000 crore a year standalone on an order backlog of roughly ₹11,000–15,000 crore, and which spent these years paying down heavy debt (from a lender restructuring into an SPV, then a ₹1,000 crore rights issue, cutting debt to about ₹1,995 crore by March 2026) while chasing a large pipeline of new bids.

parts.name: Engineering & Construction (E&C) — the standalone business
parts.what: The core contracting arm that actually builds the projects and produces essentially all of the standalone revenue (₹3,937 crore in FY26); management describes the order book as diversified across sectors and geographies, around ₹13,000 crore at end-FY26.

parts.name: Transport
parts.what: Roads, highways, bridges and especially urban metro work (Delhi DC06, Mumbai Metro stations, Mumbai Coastal Road, Patna Metro PC05/PC06, Indore Metro, the Anji Khad cable-stayed bridge, the T-49 railway tunnel in J&K, Agardanda Creek bridge) — consistently the single largest slice of the order backlog, around half of it, and the company says it built India's first metro plus work in Delhi, Chennai and Mumbai.

parts.name: Hydropower and Pumped Storage (PSP)
parts.what: Dams, head-race tunnels and underground powerhouses — Vishnugad Pipalkoti, Tapovan Vishnugad, Tehri 1,000 MW pumped storage (all four units now commissioned), Bhivpuri PSP and Nikachhu in Bhutan; the second-biggest part of the backlog, and management claims HCC has built about 26–27% of India's installed hydro capacity and sees a ₹70,000 crore near-term bidding opportunity here.

parts.name: Nuclear and special projects
parts.what: Reactor buildings, containment domes, fuel-recycling and fuel-cycle facilities for the atomic energy programme (RAPP Units 7 & 8, BARC Tarapur, the Fast Reactor Fuel Cycle Facility at Kalpakkam); smaller in current backlog but repeatedly called HCC's most distinctive niche — it says it has built over 60–65% of India's installed nuclear capacity and expects a large order wave as the country targets 100 GW of nuclear by 2047, with real contracts only from about 2028.

parts.name: Water and buildings
parts.what: Water-sector and building works listed as the smaller remaining categories of the order backlog, mentioned only in passing alongside the four main sectors.

parts.name: Concessions / BOT assets (HCC Infrastructure)
parts.what: Toll-road assets the group owns and earns traffic-based revenue from, including BFHL, which grew 31% in the June 2022 quarter; the calls treat it as a portfolio being monetised — a stake sale in BFHL was 'on track' and management spoke of rebuilding the portfolio with new bids — and it fades out of the discussion in later calls.

parts.name: Steiner AG (Switzerland)
parts.what: A Zurich-based subsidiary founded in 1915 and bought by HCC in 2010, which sold off its low-margin construction business in 2023 and now does only real estate development, with 65+ active projects mainly in western Switzerland; HCC treats it as an asset to monetise and pull cash back from — ₹84 crore of a ₹89 crore receivable was recovered by Q3 FY26.

overview.what_it_does: Healthcare Global Enterprises (HCG) runs a chain of specialist cancer hospitals across India, describing itself as the only organized, pan-India cancer care chain, with centres in roughly 18-20 cities spanning metros and tier-2/tier-3 towns plus one overseas operation in Kenya. It makes money by charging patients (and their payors — insurance, government-sponsored schemes, and cash-paying and overseas patients) for cancer diagnosis and treatment: medical oncology including chemotherapy, immunotherapy and CAR-T, surgical oncology including robotic surgery, radiation therapy on machines such as CyberKnife and MR-LINAC, plus supporting diagnostics like PET-CT, digital pathology and genomic sequencing. Revenue comes from patient volumes multiplied by average revenue per patient, which was about INR 84,000 in Q3 FY26; full-year FY26 revenue was INR 2,545 crore, up 15%, with an adjusted EBITDA margin around 17-19%. Historically it also owned a fertility/IVF business (Milann) and a few multispecialty hospitals, but in FY26 the board approved selling Milann to focus purely on oncology.

parts.name: Oncology hospital network (the core business)
parts.what: Cancer hospitals and day-care centres offering medical, surgical and radiation oncology under one roof, tumour-board-led care and complex/high-acuity cases; this is essentially the whole company — about INR 618 crore of the INR 633 crore Q3 FY26 revenue came from it excluding fertility.

parts.name: South cluster
parts.what: Centres led by the Bangalore Centre of Excellence plus Vizag and other tier-2 sites; about 39% of FY26 revenue, growing ~13%, and home to the newly opened North Bangalore hospital (120+ beds, first MR-LINAC in the city).

parts.name: West cluster
parts.what: Hospitals across Gujarat and Maharashtra including Ahmedabad and Mumbai; the largest contributor at about 45% of FY26 revenue, growing ~14% on capacity expansion and new clinicians.

parts.name: East cluster
parts.what: Centres in Cuttack, Ranchi and Kolkata; about 11% of FY26 revenue growing ~11%, with Kolkata still ramping up after turning EBITDA-positive.

parts.name: International business (Kenya)
parts.what: An overseas oncology operation offering radiation oncology and PET services; management calls it a smaller part of the portfolio but it grew 71% in FY26.

parts.name: Medical value travel
parts.what: Treating international patients who travel to HCG's Indian hospitals, supported by overseas information centres; a growth initiative rather than a large segment, and it was noted as soft in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Milann — fertility business
parts.what: An IVF/infertility chain that was roughly 4% of revenue in FY23 (about INR 15 crore of INR 633 crore in Q3 FY26) and is being sold to Inviga Healthcare Fund at an enterprise value of INR 63 crore so HCG can focus on oncology.

parts.name: Digital patient acquisition
parts.what: Website, mobile app and marketing campaigns that bring patients in directly and reduce reliance on third-party aggregators; digital revenue grew 26% year-on-year in Q3 FY26, with the website contributing 67% and the app 13% of digital revenue.

parts.name: Research, genomics and clinical trials
parts.what: Genomic sequencing, molecular/precision-medicine capability, an in-house research committee and pharma-partnered clinical trials, presented mainly as a clinical differentiator rather than a separately sized revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: HCLTech is an India-headquartered technology services company that does IT and engineering work for large corporations around the world — running and modernising their computer systems, moving them to the cloud, writing and maintaining their software applications, handling back-office processes, and designing products and chips for technology manufacturers. It also sells its own software products under the HCL Software label. It earns money mostly from multi-year service contracts and staffed project work billed to clients (it books $9.3 billion of new contract value a year and reported $14.7 billion of revenue in FY26 at about a 17% operating margin), plus software licence and subscription fees. Clients are large global enterprises spread across the Americas, Europe and the rest of the world, served by roughly 224,000 employees working from India and local delivery centres, across verticals such as financial services, manufacturing, life sciences and healthcare, telecom and media, retail and consumer, and technology.

parts.name: IT and Business Services (ITBS)
parts.what: Runs and modernises clients' IT — cloud migration and hybrid cloud operations, digital application development, digital workplace, data platforms and outsourced business/process operations — and is the company's biggest business, growing 3.7% in FY26.

parts.name: Engineering and R&D Services (ERS)
parts.what: Helps product companies design and build their own products — chip design and verification, embedded/IoT software, product sustenance engineering and autonomous-robot navigation software — and was the fastest-growing service line in FY26 at 9.8%.

parts.name: HCL Software (products and platforms)
parts.what: Sells HCLTech's own software licences and subscriptions, notably a data-management product family (DataConnect, Informix, Ingres, Zen, VectorAI DB, Zeenea, Jaspersoft), worth about $1.4 billion of revenue with $1.05 billion of annual recurring revenue — under a tenth of the group, lumpy quarter to quarter, and roughly flat to slightly declining recently.

parts.name: Advanced AI / AI offerings
parts.what: A newer, cross-cutting revenue line built on in-house platforms (AI Force for service delivery, Enterprise AI Foundry, AI Labs, VisionX edge AI, AI Factory datacentre build-outs) that reached about $620 million annualised in FY26 and is the company's main growth engine, with management saying nearly all deals now include an AI component.

overview.what_it_does: HDB Financial Services (HDBFS) is an Indian non-banking finance company (NBFC) started in 2007, majority-owned by its parent HDFC Bank and listed on the NSE and BSE since mid-2025. It lends money to ordinary retail borrowers and small businesses — 23.9 million customers as of June 2026, with an average loan of only about ₹1.66 lakh per customer, so the book is 100% retail and very granular; roughly 74% of loans are backed by collateral such as property, gold or the vehicle/equipment financed. It earns mainly on the spread between what it pays to borrow (NCDs, bank loans, commercial paper, external commercial borrowings, sub-debt and perpetual debt) and what it charges borrowers: net interest income of ₹2,509 crores in the June 2026 quarter at a net interest margin of 8.35%, giving a gross loan book of ₹1,21,846 crores and quarterly profit of ₹785 crores. It operates only in India, through about 1,730 branches across 1,161 cities and towns (over 80% of them outside the 20 largest cities, serving what management calls 'aspirational India'), plus 1.6 lakh+ retail and dealer touchpoints, a 38,000-strong field sales force, tele-calling, DSAs and digital channels including its HDB OnTheGo app and a do-it-yourself online platform.

parts.name: Enterprise Lending
parts.what: Secured and unsecured loans to business customers (individuals and firms) and some salaried people for growth and working capital, sold mainly through branches; it is the largest vertical at about 39% of the loan book.

parts.name: LAP + EBL (the mortgage business, within Enterprise Lending)
parts.what: Loans against property and enterprise business loans backed by property, which management calls its mortgage book; it grew 13.2% year-on-year in the June 2026 quarter and is described as on a continuing upward trajectory.

parts.name: Gold loans (within Enterprise Lending)
parts.what: Small loans against gold delivered through roughly 500 enabled branches; still a small piece but the fastest-growing one, with the book doubling in FY26 and again over the following year.

parts.name: Unsecured business loans (within Enterprise Lending)
parts.what: Business loans given without collateral, mainly to MSME/SME-type customers; this was a trouble spot for asset quality that management says it is now 'over', with disbursements starting to accelerate again.

parts.name: Asset Finance
parts.what: Financing for income-generating assets — new and used commercial vehicles, construction equipment and tractors — sourced through OEM tie-ups, dealers and an in-house sales team; about 38% of the book, and the slowest-growing vertical recently (CV book +10% and CE +8% year-on-year in Q1 FY27) as management deliberately reworked its used-CV and new-CV product focus.

parts.name: Consumer Finance
parts.what: Loans to individuals to buy two-wheelers, cars, consumer durables (ACs, refrigerators and other 'compressor products'), digital products and other lifestyle items, sourced at the point of sale via OEM and dealer partnerships; about 23% of the book and the strongest grower, up 21% year-on-year with the consumer durables book up over 50%.

parts.name: Credit and collections
parts.what: An in-house function rather than a product — a 12,500+ person collections team plus tele-callers, scorecard-driven strategies and, more recently, AI bots for early-bucket customers; it is central to the model, with gross Stage 3 (bad loans) at 2.34% of book and credit cost running around 2.3% of the loan book.

parts.name: Treasury / borrowings
parts.what: An independent department that raises and manages the money HDBFS lends out, keeping funding diversified (around 39% NCDs and 39% bank loans, rest CPs, ECBs and perpetual/sub-debt) and capital adequacy strong at 21.29%.

parts.name: BPO services
parts.what: A small non-lending business providing back-office/outsourced services; it contributed just ₹14 crores, or 1.9% of total pre-tax profit, in the June 2025 quarter.

overview.what_it_does: HDFC Asset Management Company runs HDFC Mutual Fund in India: it pools money from investors and manages it in schemes across shares (equity), bonds (debt), very short-term cash funds (liquid), and low-cost index-tracking products (ETFs and index funds), plus a smaller set of non-mutual-fund products. Its customers are mainly Indian retail/individual savers — 17.1 million unique investors as of June 2026, roughly 28 of every 100 mutual fund investors in the country — reached through distributors, its own physical branch network including smaller 'B-30' towns, direct plans (about 31% of equity assets), and digital channels that now carry 97% of transactions; it also serves institutions such as the EPFO through mandates. It earns money as an annual fee charged on the assets it manages, so revenue rises and falls with asset size and mix: in the quarter to June 2026 blended yields were about 58 basis points on equity, 28 on debt and 13 on liquid, on quarterly average assets of INR9.35 trillion, producing FY26 operating revenue of INR41.2 billion and profit after tax of INR28.6 billion; it also earns 'other income' on its own money invested in its schemes. It operates out of Mumbai across India, with a wholly owned international subsidiary in GIFT City handling money coming into India and Indian money going abroad.

parts.name: Actively managed equity-oriented funds
parts.what: Stock-picking mutual fund schemes run by an in-house fund manager and analyst team — this is the core of the business at INR5.74 trillion of quarterly average AUM (June 2026), about 65.7% of the company's total versus 56.6% for the industry, and the highest-fee part at roughly 58 basis points.

parts.name: Debt / fixed income funds
parts.what: Bond and other fixed income schemes, INR1.66 trillion of quarterly average AUM with a 12.9% market share in June 2026, earning about 28 basis points; flows here are lumpy and management noted redemptions in mid-2026 driven by rupee and interest-rate volatility.

parts.name: Liquid funds
parts.what: Very short-term parking products for cash, INR851 billion of quarterly average AUM and a 10.7% market share, the lowest-fee category at about 13 basis points, with money moving in as investors exited longer-dated debt.

parts.name: Passive products — ETFs and index funds
parts.what: Low-cost funds that simply track an index (including equity, debt, MSCI Emerging Markets and, industry-wide, gold and silver ETFs); the company built out this range from 2022 onward and it is clearly a smaller share for them than for peers — market share is 11.2% including ETFs but 12.4% excluding them.

parts.name: Alternatives (AIF / private credit / private equity funds)
parts.what: Category-II Alternative Investment Funds sold to sophisticated investors — a fund-of-funds investing in early-stage VC through buyout funds, a private credit fund anchored by IFC closing in 2026, and an approved second venture capital/private equity fund seeded with a $50 million commitment from a global investor; still small but growing fast, with fees of 80–90 basis points, better than mutual funds.

parts.name: Portfolio Management Services (PMS)
parts.what: Managing money under separate mandates rather than pooled schemes — two marquee fixed income wins in FY26 from the EPFO and the Seaman's Provident Fund Organisation; discretionary mandates earn roughly equity-like fees while non-discretionary work runs on 'very, very tight economics.'

parts.name: Alternatives platform total (AIF commitments + PMS + advisory)
parts.what: Taken together, the non-mutual-fund book stood at INR148 billion in June 2026, up from INR60 billion a year earlier — management calls the revenue contribution 'still very small' relative to mutual funds but flags it as a multi-year growth priority.

parts.name: International business (GIFT City subsidiary)
parts.what: A wholly owned overseas-facing arm based in India's GIFT City, live with five funds after launching two inbound funds in FY26, aimed at both global investors putting money into India and Indian investors investing abroad; described as an early-stage opportunity being built out over time.

parts.name: Systematic investment book (SIP/STP) and distribution
parts.what: Not a product but the engine management repeatedly points to — monthly recurring contributions plus systematic transfers totalling INR48.1 billion in June 2026, up 20% year on year, feeding mostly equity funds and supported by a 'phygital' model of expanded branches plus a top-rated app and portal.

overview.what_it_does: HDFC Bank is an Indian bank that takes deposits from savers and lends the money out, operating across India through a branch network that has grown to about 9,700 branches serving roughly 100 million customers. It sells everyday banking to individuals — savings and current accounts, fixed deposits, credit cards, car and two-wheeler loans, gold loans, home loans and wealth management — and banking to businesses, from small shopkeepers and MSMEs up to large corporates, including cash management, trade finance for importers and exporters, and settlement services for capital-market clients. It makes money mainly on the gap between what it pays depositors and what it earns on loans (net interest income, with a margin around 3.4%-4%), plus fees and commissions from cards, merchant payments, and distributing third-party products like insurance and mutual funds, and some income from its bond and derivatives book. In FY26 it reported deposit growth of 14.4%, loan growth of 12%, gross bad loans of 1.15% and a return on assets of 1.9%; it merged with mortgage lender HDFC Limited around 2023 and also owns lending subsidiary HDB Financial Services.

parts.name: Retail liabilities / deposits (CASA and term deposits)
parts.what: Current, savings and fixed-deposit accounts gathered mostly through branches — the bank's core funding, described as 84% sourced from retail branches, with deposits of about Rs 16 lakh crore back in mid-2022 and management repeatedly calling this the 'granular and sustainable' franchise it prizes most.

parts.name: Retail advances (including mortgages and 'wheels')
parts.what: Loans to individuals — home loans, car, two-wheeler and transportation finance, personal and gold loans — where management says it is a top-2 mortgage bank and the top 'wheels' bank in India; retail loans were growing ~22% year-on-year in 2022.

parts.name: Payments business — credit cards and merchant acquiring
parts.what: Issuing credit cards and processing card payments for shops; in 2022 it had a 17.6 million card base and 3.2 million payment acceptance points, and by FY26 it accounted for roughly 21%-22% of card issuance, 26%-28% of card spends and 35%-36% of merchant acquiring in the country — a major fee generator.

parts.name: Commercial and rural banking (MSME / priority sector)
parts.what: Lending and banking services to small and medium businesses and rural borrowers, offered in 640 districts as of 2022 and growing ~29% year-on-year then; management says it is among the top 2 MSME banks in India.

parts.name: Wholesale / corporate banking
parts.what: Loans and services to large companies, plus trade finance handling 18%-20% of India's exports and 13%-15% of import flows; growth here is deliberately selective because corporate lending spreads are thin, and the book grew ~16% in 2022 even after letting go of Rs 40,000-50,000 crore of low-priced assets.

parts.name: Transaction banking — cash management and capital markets settlement
parts.what: Handling companies' collections and payments and settling capital-market and share-issue money, where the bank claims market leadership with 35%-40% of capital-market account settlements and 40%-50% of banker-to-issue escrow settlements.

parts.name: Wealth management and third-party product distribution
parts.what: Selling investment and insurance products of other providers to customers through a hub-and-spoke model — offered in 357 locations in 2022 with a plan to reach 900+ — and one of the fastest-growing fee lines, up 32% year-on-year in one 2024 quarter.

parts.name: Treasury / investments
parts.what: The bank's own portfolio of government securities, corporate bonds and derivatives, which produces trading gains or losses depending on interest rates — for example a Rs 1,312 crore mark-to-market loss in the June 2022 quarter when bond yields spiked.

parts.name: Digital banking and technology platforms
parts.what: Mobile and net banking, the PayZapp payments app, SmartHub Vyapar for merchants and the UPI-linked 'Zapp' wallet — now serving over 60 million registered mobile app users, with 97% of payment and service transactions and 92% of new customer acquisitions done digitally; tech spend has more than quadrupled to around $1 billion.

parts.name: HDB Financial Services (subsidiary)
parts.what: A separately RBI-licensed non-bank lender within the group that serves a different, more hands-on customer segment through its own branches, and which regulation required to be listed by September 2025.

overview.what_it_does: HDFC Life is an Indian life insurance company that sells long-term savings and protection policies — unit-linked (market-linked) plans, participating and non-participating guaranteed-return savings plans, pure term life cover, and annuity/pension products — to individual retail customers as well as to groups, including borrowers of partner lenders who are covered under credit-life policies. It earns money by collecting new-business and renewal premiums (renewals grew 15% in FY26 and 19% in Q1 FY27), investing and managing that money (assets under management crossed INR 4 trillion in Q1 FY27), and keeping the margin between what it charges and what it pays out; the calls measure this as value of new business (INR 4,034 crore in FY26) at a new-business margin of roughly 24-25%, with profit after tax of INR 1,910 crore in FY26 and embedded value of INR 65,860 crore by Q1 FY27. It reaches customers mainly through banks (HDFC Bank is both its largest distribution partner and, after the HDFC Ltd merger, its parent), its own agency and direct channels, and broker/online partners. Operations are overwhelmingly Indian — it is consistently among the top three life insurers with about 15-16% private-sector market share — with a small overseas/GIFT City arm serving NRIs and reinsurance, plus a pension fund management subsidiary.

parts.name: ULIP / unit-linked savings
parts.what: Market-linked savings-cum-insurance plans where returns follow investment markets; the single largest slice of retail sales at 44% of individual APE in FY26 and Q1 FY27, though management says it does not expect this share to rise further.

parts.name: Non-par savings
parts.what: Guaranteed-return savings policies where the payout is fixed upfront rather than market-linked; 18% of individual APE in FY26 (22% in Q1 FY27), it was 38% back in H1 FY25 and shrank because management held pricing discipline rather than chase volume, but is expected to recover as interest rates turn favourable.

parts.name: Participating (par) products
parts.what: Savings policies that share in the insurer's investment surplus via bonuses; a steady mid-sized block at 25% of individual APE in FY26 and 15% in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Retail protection / term
parts.what: Pure life cover with no savings element, sold one policy at a time; small in premium terms (7% of individual APE in FY26, 8% in Q1 FY27, near 11% including riders) but the fastest-growing and most profitable line, up 43% in FY26 and 42% in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Credit protect (group credit life)
parts.what: Loan-linked life cover sold through lending partners so a borrower's loan is repaid if they die; described as a leadership position for the company, it swung from 96% growth in Q1 FY23 to softness in FY25 and back to 19% growth in Q1 FY27 on microfinance recovery, tracking partners' loan disbursements.

parts.name: Annuity / retirement
parts.what: Products that pay a guaranteed income for life after retirement, around 5% of individual APE in FY26 rising to about 11% in Q1 FY27, boosted by a new variable annuity product (AGNI) that mixes lifelong guaranteed income with Nifty 50-linked growth.

parts.name: Group business
parts.what: Cover sold to organisations for their members rather than to individuals; reported alongside individual business in total APE and cited as a driver of the stronger 9% overall APE growth in Q1 FY27, with the company describing itself as a top-three insurer across both individual and group.

parts.name: Bancassurance / partnership distribution
parts.what: Selling policies through bank branches — HDFC Bank is the biggest (counter share around 65%) alongside Yes Bank, Bandhan Bank, IDFC and non-bank alliances; the largest source of business, and the channel whose volatility drove the weak fourth quarter of FY26.

parts.name: Agency channel
parts.what: The company's own network of individual financial consultants and branches (250+ branches added over 30 months); a multi-year investment that grew 21% in Q1 FY27, ahead of the company average, with a strong protection mix.

parts.name: HDFC Pension Fund Management
parts.what: A wholly owned subsidiary that manages retirement money under the national pension system; the market leader with roughly 43% share and about INR 1.75 lakh crore of assets under management, growing 33% year-on-year.

parts.name: HDFC International Re / GIFT City
parts.what: The overseas and GIFT City arm — a reinsurance subsidiary plus a branch offering US dollar-denominated life and health products to NRIs and resident Indians; small, described only as delivering steady performance with encouraging traction.

parts.name: Exide Life (acquired, since merged)
parts.what: A separately bought life insurer that was growing 34% when acquired and was folded into HDFC Life through an NCLT/IRDAI-approved merger completed around the second half of FY23.

overview.what_it_does: HEG Limited makes graphite electrodes — the large consumable carbon rods that electric arc furnaces need to melt scrap and make steel — from a single plant near Bhopal, India, with an installed capacity of 100,000 tonnes a year, which management says is by far the world's largest electrode plant at one location (the next two biggest are around 70,000 tonnes). Its customers are steel mills running electric arc furnaces, in both ultra-high-power (UHP) and non-UHP grades; management says about two-thirds of output is exported to 25–30 countries, and it does not sell electrodes directly to China. It makes money on the spread between electrode selling prices and its main raw material, needle coke, plus power and fuel costs, so profits swing with global steel output, electrode prices and needle coke prices — FY26 revenue was about Rs. 2,569 crores with EBITDA of Rs. 497 crores at more than 90% capacity utilisation. The company has no long-term debt, holds a treasury portfolio (about Rs. 792 crores at March 2026) plus an equity stake in GrafTech, and is building capacity out to 115,000 tonnes by early 2028 on the view that global decarbonisation is shifting steelmaking toward electric arc furnaces.

parts.name: Graphite electrodes
parts.what: The core and by far the dominant business — manufacturing UHP and non-UHP graphite electrodes at the 100,000-tonne Bhopal plant for electric arc furnace steel mills worldwide; it accounts for essentially all of the roughly Rs. 2,500-crore annual revenue discussed on the calls.

parts.name: HEG Greentech (later referred to as HEG Advanced Materials)
parts.what: A separate green-energy and materials arm holding hydro power assets, some wind assets, a battery-storage business and a planned graphite anode project for batteries; management put its consolidated EBITDA at roughly Rs. 125 crores in late 2024, small next to the electrode business, and it is being separated out and listed via a court-approved scheme of arrangement (NCLT order awaited as of July 2026).

parts.name: Treasury and investments
parts.what: A debt-free balance sheet with a treasury book of roughly Rs. 800–1,150 crores over the period, earning interest and mark-to-market gains or losses, plus a deliberate long-term equity investment in GrafTech; these swing 'other income' and quarterly reported profit sharply — a Rs. 189-crore quarterly loss in Q4 FY26 came mainly from fair-value and currency effects on that foreign investment, not from operations.

parts.name: Capacity expansion to 115,000 tonnes
parts.what: An ongoing electrode capacity addition of 15,000 tonnes targeted for early 2028, following the completed 80,000-to-100,000-tonne expansion, aimed at capturing demand from over 100 million tonnes of new electric arc furnace steel capacity management expects globally by 2030.

overview.what_it_does: Heritage Foods is an Indian dairy company, founded in 1992 and headquartered in Hyderabad, that buys raw milk directly from farmers and sells it to consumers as packaged liquid milk and as branded milk products such as curd, paneer, ghee, butter, buttermilk, lassi, ice cream and Indian sweets like gulab jamun and rasgulla. It makes money on the spread between what it pays farmers per litre (₹46.61/litre in Q1 FY27) and what it charges consumers (₹58.68/litre average milk selling price), with fatter margins on the value-added products; it describes this as an 'integrated farm-to-consumer model'. Selling is through consumer channels — its own distribution, general trade, and organized/national retail customers — rather than bulk institutional orders, which management says it does not do. Its milk and milk products are sold across Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Odisha, NCR Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand; consolidated quarterly revenue was about ₹1,338 crore in Q1 FY27, up 18% year-on-year, with EBITDA margin of 4.6% and PAT margin of 1.9%.

parts.name: Dairy — liquid milk
parts.what: The core business of procuring raw milk from farmers (18.10 lakh litres a day in Q1 FY27, up 2%) and selling packaged milk; it is the volume backbone and the largest single revenue line, though management says milk sales volume has been roughly flat lately and profitability swings with procurement costs.

parts.name: Value-Added Products (VAP)
parts.what: Curd, paneer, buttermilk, lassi, ice cream, sweets and similar branded products — the stated 'primary growth engine', at ₹5,636 million in Q1 FY27 (up 40%) and a record 44% of consolidated revenue, or 49% (₹6,322 million) if consumer-pack ghee and butter are included, versus about 35% back in Q1 FY23.

parts.name: Ice cream (Alpenvie and Get-A-Way)
parts.what: A fast-growing premium ice cream and nutrition-led frozen dessert business that crossed ₹550 million in Q1 FY27 (up 65%), made at a newly commissioned dedicated factory running at roughly 40% utilisation, with Get-A-Way revenue up 196% and near breakeven.

parts.name: Heritage Nutrivet Limited (cattle feed / animal nutrition)
parts.what: A wholly owned subsidiary selling cattle feed and animal nutrition products, largely to the farmer base that supplies milk; small relative to dairy at ₹728 million revenue in Q1 FY27 (up 37%) with ₹20 million profit before tax.

parts.name: Renewable energy
parts.what: 10.50 MW of solar and wind generation capacity used captively to power the company's own dairy factories rather than sold outside — described as a business division but essentially a cost-saving support activity, with no separate revenue discussed on the calls.

parts.name: Heritage Novandie Foods (Livo)
parts.what: A high-protein yogurt business under the Livo brand that became a wholly owned subsidiary in Q1 FY27; small and early-stage, described as performing well in organized retail.

parts.name: Peanut Butter and Jelly Limited
parts.what: A 'better-for-you' premium nutrition foods venture in which Heritage raised its stake to 71% in Q1 FY27; an early-stage growth platform, with no revenue figures given on the calls.

parts.name: New/premium brand launches
parts.what: Nourish+ (including a high-protein paneer), Sampurna A2 curd, chef's choice curd and organic milk — recently introduced premium lines management says are gaining acceptance, but which are not yet sized in the calls.

overview.what_it_does: Hero MotoCorp makes and sells two-wheelers — motorcycles and scooters — mainly to everyday retail buyers in India through a large dealer network, and the calls say it has been the world's largest motorcycle and scooter manufacturer for 25 straight years, dispatching 6.1 million vehicles in calendar 2025. Most of its money comes from selling petrol-engine (ICE) bikes and scooters, ranging from mass-market commuter models like Splendor, Passion and Glamour up to premium bikes in the 400-500cc range built under a partnership with Harley-Davidson; on top of that it earns a high-margin stream from selling spare parts, accessories and merchandise to the huge base of Hero vehicles already on Indian roads. Smaller but growing pieces are electric scooters under the VIDA brand and exports to overseas markets. In FY26 it reported revenue of about ₹46,830 crore, EBITDA of ₹6,871 crore and profit of ₹5,268 crore, with the ICE business running at roughly a 17% EBITDA margin and the EV business still absorbing investment.

parts.name: India Business Unit (ICE motorcycles and scooters)
parts.what: The core business — petrol-engine commuter motorcycles (Splendor, Passion, Glamour, Super Splendor, Xtreme 125) and scooters (Destini, Xoom) sold across India; it drives almost all revenue and profit, with ICE EBITDA margin at about 17% in FY26 and scooters growing 48% year-on-year in the March 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Premium segment
parts.what: Higher-priced, larger motorcycles including Karizma, Mavrick 440 and the Harley-Davidson 400-500cc range made and sold under partnership; management calls it a segment where Hero is under-represented and is investing heavily in launches, brand building and separate 'Premia' dealerships, with Harley-Davidson range volumes up 26% year-on-year in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Parts, Accessories & Merchandise (PAM)
parts.what: Sells replacement parts, accessories and branded merchandise to owners of the large installed base of Hero vehicles; it was ₹1,061 crore (12.6% of revenue) in one quarter of FY23, has roughly doubled in size over three to four years, keeps growing in double digits, and Hero is spending over ₹700 crore on a second global parts centre in south India to expand it.

parts.name: Emerging Mobility Business Unit / EV (VIDA)
parts.what: Electric scooters sold under the VIDA brand plus the dealer and charging infrastructure behind them (180+ dealers across 120+ cities as of FY24); still loss-making and a drag on group margin — ₹220 crore of investment in Q4 FY26 alone — but volumes grew 2.5x year-on-year and capacity is being doubled.

parts.name: Global business
parts.what: Exports of two-wheelers to overseas markets; management describes it as a growth pillar where Hero is under-represented, citing a 7.2% market share (up 230 bps) in Q4 FY24 and 41% year-on-year dispatch growth in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Associate company investments
parts.what: Minority stakes in other mobility companies — Ather (electric two-wheelers) and Euler Motors — described by the CEO as bold strategic moves rather than a day-to-day operating business.

overview.what_it_does: Hexaware Technologies (HEXT) is an India-headquartered IT services and outsourcing company, listed in Mumbai since February 2025, that runs and rebuilds the technology of large corporations for a fee. Clients hand it work such as day-to-day IT operations, application maintenance, software engineering, data engineering, modernizing decades-old legacy code, cybersecurity and back-office business process services, and Hexaware delivers it with roughly 34,000 employees, so revenue is essentially billings for people and platform-based services under multi-year outsourcing, consolidation and transformation contracts (quarterly revenue was $389 million in Q1 CY26). Customers are big global firms in financial services, banking, insurance, manufacturing and consumer, high tech and professional services, plus named examples in airlines, pharma/clinical research, casual dining, data centres and asset management; the top 10 clients are about 36% of revenue and it now has two clients above $100 million a year. Its largest market by far is the U.S., followed by Europe/UK and Asia Pacific (including India and a build-out in the Middle East), and it reports on a calendar-year fiscal.

parts.name: IT Services
parts.what: The core business — application, infrastructure, engineering and data work for clients — and the larger, faster-growing part of the company: management said IT grew close to 9% year-on-year versus 4.7% for BPS, and IT headcount has risen for 11 straight quarters.

parts.name: BPS (Business Process Services)
parts.what: Outsourced back-office/process work, reported separately from IT; it is the smaller, slower-growing piece and was where headcount actually shrank in Q1 CY26.

parts.name: Financial Services (FS)
