parts.what: Serving asset managers, insurers and similar firms; called out as one of the strongest growth verticals after a 'smart recovery', at ~19% growth in CY24, though one large client's spending cuts made a quarter or two lumpy.

parts.name: Banking
parts.what: Work for banks, including large consolidation deals where a bank cuts its vendor list and Hexaware wins a bigger share; it was the weak spot in CY24 at 7.6% growth but rebounded 13.5% sequentially in Q2 CY25 and is described as a growth driver into CY26.

parts.name: High Tech and Professional Services (HTPS)
parts.what: Technology companies and professional-services firms; the fastest-growing vertical at about 22% in CY24, and management hired a dedicated head to attack what it calls a large untapped segment.

parts.name: Technology, Products and Platforms (TPP)
parts.what: A new vertical being carved out of HTPS and reported separately from Q1 CY26 — management's bet on selling to software and technology product companies as a distinct growth engine.

parts.name: Manufacturing and Consumer (M&C)
parts.what: Factory and consumer-goods clients; the problem area — the only vertical with negative growth, hurt by tariffs, trade uncertainty and two clients that went through Chapter 11 bankruptcy.

parts.name: RapidX (legacy modernization / software engineering)
parts.what: An in-house AI platform that reverse-engineers very old code and the business logic buried in it (one U.S. airline's code was over 50 years old) and rebuilds it; billed as a 'growth accelerator', with two or three large modernizations due to complete in CY26 and a 'zero-license' offering built on it to move clients off paid SaaS software.

parts.name: Tensai (IT operations platform)
parts.what: The platform behind its IT outsourcing work, being rebuilt around AI agents — roughly 80 supervisory and 400 atomic agents — which management says let it renew one large outsourcing contract at 50% more volume for about 10% more revenue.

parts.name: AI for business services
parts.what: Building AI agents into clients' own operations (clinical research steps for a global CRO, aircraft-repair guidance for an airline, factory yield models for a chip maker); management says this pool of opportunity is bigger in total than all its AI-for-IT work.

parts.name: GCC setup (SMC acquisition)
parts.what: Helping multinationals set up and then run their own captive offshore centres in India and elsewhere; acquired in mid-2025 with about $22 million of prior-year revenue, EPS accretive from day one, aimed at a market growing from roughly 1,700 to 2,700 GCCs in India.

parts.name: Cybersolve (cybersecurity)
parts.what: An acquired identity-led cybersecurity capability, credited with winning a deal at a data centre company in Q1 CY26.

parts.name: Private equity / private markets practice
parts.what: A new sales push at PE firms and the companies they own, launched in 2025 with a dedicated Chief Private Markets Officer hired in early 2026; pipeline is building, with revenue expected to follow.

overview.what_it_does: HFCL Limited is an Indian manufacturer of telecom and networking hardware, headquartered in New Delhi with its registered works at Solan, Himachal Pradesh. Its core business is making optical fibre and optical fibre cable, plus the connectivity products that go with them, and selling these to telecom operators (private telcos and BSNL), enterprises like banks, hotels and schools, government-funded network programmes such as BharatNet, and increasingly to hyperscale data-centre customers overseas. Alongside cable it designs and sells its own telecom equipment (backhaul radios, 5G fixed-wireless devices, routers, switches, Wi-Fi access points) and a growing range of defence electronics, and it also earns fees from turnkey network-building (EPC) work billed against project milestones. It makes money by manufacturing and shipping products at a margin, and it has shifted heavily toward exports — over 70% of cable output was exported by FY26, with exports at 41.36% of revenue versus 12.23% the prior year — selling into 30-plus countries; the order book stood at about Rs 26,665 crore in Q1 FY27, roughly five times FY26 revenue.

parts.name: Optical Fibre and Optical Fibre Cable (Optical Connectivity)
parts.what: The traditional core: HFCL draws optical fibre and manufactures it into cables, including very high fibre-count cables of up to 6,912 fibres designed in-house, with capacity being expanded from 28 to 34 million fibre-km of fibre and 34 to 43 million fibre-km of cable, and it won a single long-term global supply contract worth about USD 1.1 billion (Rs 10,159 crore) — management calls it the largest such contract ever secured by an Indian telecom company.

parts.name: Data Centre Interconnect / connectivity solutions
parts.what: A fast-growing newer line making pre-connectorised cable assemblies and high-density fibre termination products for AI and hyperscale data centres, produced partly through subsidiary HTL Limited, with capacity being raised five-fold and expected revenue of more than Rs 700 crore in its first year of production (FY27) and multiples of that later.

parts.name: Telecom and Networking Products (Telecom Equipment segment)
parts.what: HFCL's own-designed equipment — unlicensed-band backhaul radios (where it says it holds over 70% of the Indian market and has shipped 500,000+ units globally), 5G fixed wireless access customer devices, IP/MPLS routers, switches and Wi-Fi access points — sold to telcos and enterprises; management guided this segment from Rs 143 crore in FY24 to roughly Rs 2,000 crore in FY25, with Rs 401 crore booked in the first quarter alone.

parts.name: Defence and Aerospace
parts.what: Indigenously developed defence electronics — electronic fuzes for artillery ammunition, thermal weapon sights and their titanium cores, ground and coastal surveillance radars, high-capacity radio relay, with multimode hand grenades and trans-horizon communications in the pipeline — now being consolidated under subsidiary HFCL Advance Systems along with an acquired aerospace business that brings an export order book of about Rs 1,930 crore; management sizes the domestic market for its current products at over USD 35 billion over six to seven years.

parts.name: EPC / turnkey network services and Digital Infrastructure
parts.what: Project work laying and building networks (for example under BharatNet and highway projects), billed on completed milestones so revenue can slip when the customer's site infrastructure isn't ready; management names EPC as one of the segments driving FY26's record results, though it is described as more working-capital hungry than product sales, which is why HFCL has deliberately tilted the mix toward products (product revenue rose to 59% of sales in Q1 FY23 from 43% in FY22).

parts.name: Preform manufacturing (backward integration, under construction)
parts.what: A new greenfield plant of 300 tonnes a year costing about Rs 580 crore to make the glass preforms from which optical fibre is drawn — not a selling business itself but described by management as a key margin-expansion lever and supply-chain safeguard for the fibre business.

parts.name: R&D and technology development
parts.what: In-house design centres near Bengaluru, Gurgaon, Hyderabad and the United States, plus engineering tie-ups with firms such as Wipro and Capgemini, that create the telecom, cable and defence products the company sells — presented across the calls as the engine behind the shift from commodity cable to higher-margin technology-led products.

overview.what_it_does: H.G. Infra Engineering Limited (HGIEL / HGINFRA) is an Indian construction and infrastructure company, in business for over 23 years, that builds highways, expressways, railway lines and stations, metro works, and more recently solar plants, battery storage and power transmission lines. Its customers are mainly government bodies — NHAI, the Ministry of Road Transport, Indian Railways, DMRC, MSRDC, state DISCOMs, GUVNL/NVVN — plus large private developers such as the Adani Group, IRB, Welspun and DLF. It makes money in two ways: as a contractor paid a fixed price to build a project (EPC), and by putting in its own equity to build and hold projects for a period under HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) or as power/storage assets, later selling those completed assets to infrastructure funds to recycle capital. Work is spread across many Indian states — Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Haryana, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand and Delhi — and the size of the business is tracked by an order book that ran from about ₹11,508 crore (June 2022) to a peak of ₹15,642 crore (June 2024) and ₹10,147 crore (March 2026), with annual revenue guided at around ₹5,000 crore in FY23 and quarterly revenue of roughly ₹1,500 crore by FY25.

parts.name: Roads & Highways — EPC
parts.what: Builds highways and access-controlled expressways for a fixed contract price, with no ownership stake — examples include the Ganga Expressway for Adani (a single ₹4,971 crore order, now 100% complete and handed over), Delhi UER-2, Delhi-Vadodara packages, Nelamangala-Tumkur and the ₹3,940 crore Pune-Shirur job from Welspun; this is the company's oldest and biggest activity, and together with HAM roads it made up 53%-64% of the order book in FY26 and virtually all of it in FY23.

parts.name: Roads & Highways — HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model)
parts.what: Builds road projects through wholly-owned project companies (SPVs) into which HGIEL invests its own equity and takes bank project loans, then gets paid over time by the government — projects include Raipur-Visakhapatnam OD-5/OD-6/AP-1, Khammam-Devarapalle 1 and 2, Karnal Ring Road, Chennai-Tirupati, Varanasi-Kolkata and Narol-Sarkhej; management said HAM was 36% of the order book in FY23 and 28% in FY25, with total equity commitments of about ₹1,137 crore (FY23 estimate) rising to ₹1,461 crore across 10 HAM projects by FY25.

parts.name: HAM asset monetization
parts.what: Sells completed road SPVs to infrastructure funds to get its invested equity back and fund new work — three projects (Gurgaon-Sohna, Rewari-Ateli, Ateli-Narnaul) were sold to Highway Infrastructure Trust in November 2023 for about ₹315 crore received plus ₹60 crore pending, Rewari Bypass was expected to bring roughly ₹130 crore against ₹75.7 crore of equity invested, and a further five HAM subsidiaries were being sold to Neo Infra Income Opportunities Fund under agreements signed in 2025.

parts.name: Railways & Metro
parts.what: Builds railway lines, station redevelopment and metro civil works — the DMRC metro project, Bilaspur (Himachal Pradesh) railway, Kanpur and New Delhi railway stations, Dhule-Nardana, Karanjaon, Gaya-Son Nagar, Thane Metro and two Adani thermal-plant rail projects at Anuppur (₹340 crore) and Mirzapur (₹440 crore); this segment was started as a diversification, grew to about ₹2,498 crore of order book in FY25 and ₹2,825 crore (27% of the total) by March 2026 across around 10 ongoing projects.

parts.name: Solar energy
parts.what: Builds and owns solar power plants — around 700 MW DC of KUSUM-C scheme projects worth about ₹1,763 crore of EPC value, of which 350+ MW was executed by December 2025 and physical progress was 96.3% by March 2026, delayed by heavy Rajasthan monsoons and transmission-line land problems; HGIEL had put in ₹731 crore of its own equity by December 2025 and sells the power to state DISCOMs, though only ₹72.88 crore had been billed and ₹56.33 crore collected at that point.

parts.name: BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems)
parts.what: Develops and will own large battery storage projects under binding agreements with GUVNL and NVVN — three projects totalling 735 MW / 1,470 MWh at sites including Banaskantha and Dholera, worth about ₹1,620 crore of order book in December 2025 and ₹1,527 crore in March 2026, which management expects to generate roughly ₹225 crore of annual revenue once all are commissioned.

parts.name: Power transmission
parts.what: A newly entered line building transmission infrastructure, with two projects backed in Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand worth roughly ₹1,200 crore combined; it is still small, showing about ₹318 crore in the March 2026 order book with SPVs formed and long-lead equipment ordered.

parts.name: New areas being evaluated
parts.what: Management said it is actively looking at tunnels, water infrastructure, buildings and other specialised EPC work for future diversification, but the calls report no order book or revenue from these yet.

overview.what_it_does: Hindalco is an Indian metals manufacturer that digs up bauxite, refines it into alumina, smelts that into primary aluminium, and also runs one of Asia's largest copper smelters, selling metal in bulk (ingots, rods, sheets, foils) to industrial customers in packaging, electrical, machinery, construction, transport and autos. Through its wholly-owned overseas arm Novelis it is also the world's largest maker and recycler of aluminium flat rolled products, supplying beverage-can makers, automakers, aerospace and specialty customers. It makes money on the spread between metal prices (aluminium and copper on global exchanges, plus premiums and conversion/treatment charges) and its input costs of bauxite, coal, power and scrap, so earnings swing with commodity prices, and it hedges part of its metal and currency exposure. It reported roughly USD 28 billion of revenue and USD 3.2 billion of EBITDA (trailing twelve months to December 2022), with operations in about 10 countries and around 40,000 employees; the India business runs on net cash while most of the group's debt sits at Novelis.

parts.name: Novelis
parts.what: The overseas rolled-products and recycling business — aluminium sheet for beverage cans, autos, specialties and aerospace, with about 4.1 million tonnes of rolling capacity and 2.2 million tonnes of scrap recycled a year (including 82 billion used beverage cans); it is the single biggest piece of the group, shipping around 945 kt in a quarter and earning about USD 462 million of EBITDA in Q2 FY25 (roughly USD 489 per tonne).

parts.name: India Aluminium – upstream
parts.what: Bauxite mining, alumina refining (3.6 MT capacity, including the low-cost Utkal refinery) and primary aluminium smelting (1.3 MT capacity) in India, backed by captive coal and power — the most profitable India segment, with INR 3,709 crores of EBITDA in Q2 FY25 at about 41% margin, which management calls the best in the global industry.

parts.name: India Aluminium – downstream
parts.what: Value-added aluminium products in India (about 400 kt capacity of rolled sheet, foil, extrusions and similar), a smaller, thin-margin conversion business shipping roughly 103 kt a quarter for around INR 154 crores of EBITDA (about USD 179 per tonne).

parts.name: Copper
parts.what: One of Asia's largest single-location custom copper smelters, producing cathodes (421 kt capacity) and continuous cast copper rods (540 kt capacity), with extra income from by-products like sulphuric acid and precious metals — around 117 kt of metal shipped and a record INR 829 crores of EBITDA in Q2 FY25.

overview.what_it_does: Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL) is an Indian copper mining company that digs copper ore out of its own underground mines, processes it at its concentrator plants, and sells the output as copper concentrate — measured as "MIC" (metal in concentrate) — with roughly 30,000 tonnes of MIC expected this year. Its customers are domestic copper smelters and vendors in India (management names Adani, Hindalco, and the shut Vedanta Tuticorin plant as the smelting capacity in the market), and it currently does not export because Indian buyers are short of concentrate and pay faster, via LC or advance. Revenue is priced by a simple formula — the LME copper price minus TCRC (treatment/refining charges) — so earnings swing with global copper prices; cost of production is about $5,000 per tonne of MIC at Malanjkhand and about $6,000 at Khetri and the Jharkhand mines, all-in including mining, beneficiation and overheads. It operates three mining areas under leases valid to about 2040-42 — Khetri/Kolihan in Rajasthan, Malanjkhand in Madhya Pradesh, and the Ghatsila cluster (Surda, Kendadih, Rakha) in Jharkhand — and is a government-linked company that answers to the Ministry of Mines, targeting 12 million tonnes of ore a year by 2030-31 (roughly 80,000-90,000 tonnes of MIC) on about Rs 2,000 crore of its own capex.

parts.name: Khetri (Rajasthan) — Khetri, Kolihan and Chandmari mines
parts.what: The company's original operation (HCL was formed out of Khetri in 1967): two producing underground mines currently doing about 1-1.2 million tonnes of ore, targeted to reach 2.9 million tonnes by 2030-31 (1.5 from Khetri, 1.4 from Kolihan), with Kolihan restarted in April after an accident and prized for its high 0.9 grade, while the third mine Chandmari stays shut since 2001 pending clearance of environmental violations.

parts.name: Malanjkhand (Madhya Pradesh)
parts.what: The biggest and cheapest mine — 2.73 million tonnes of ore last year, 2.90 targeted this year and 5 million tonnes by 2030-31 — converted from opencast to underground, with a production cost near $5,000 per tonne of MIC and the bulk of capex (about Rs 900 crore of the Rs 1,300 crore near-term spend) going here for shaft equipping, a new concentrator plant, crusher, fans and power infrastructure.

parts.name: ICC / Ghatsila (Jharkhand) — Surda, Kendadih and Rakha
parts.what: Three underground mines around 40 km from Jamshedpur that were shut on statutory clearances and are now reopening — Surda restarted last October and should do about 0.3 million tonnes this year, Kendadih is dewatered and ready once its lease is signed, and together with Rakha the cluster is targeted at 4.3 million tonnes by 2030-31 at roughly $6,000 per tonne cost.

parts.name: Rakha under MDO (mine developer cum operator) mode
parts.what: The Rakha mine is contracted out for 30 years (extendable by 10) to Southwest Mining Limited, a JSW company, which invests the whole Rs 2,600-2,700 crore itself over 6-7 years and pays HCL 12.5% of revenue plus statutory dues, with production of up to 3 million tonnes targeted by 2030-31 but nothing expected for roughly 16-24 months from lease signing.

parts.name: Concentrator (beneficiation) plants
parts.what: Each mining area has a washing/concentrator plant designed around the ore grade of its own mines, so throughput and MIC output depend on the right mines feeding them — new concentrators are planned at both Malanjkhand and Khetri as part of the expansion.

parts.name: KABIL / Khanij Bidesh (overseas critical minerals) and exploration
parts.what: A small, early-stage side interest outside copper: non-invasive exploration is done on five lithium brine blocks in Argentina with a draft geological report pending, and HCL has recently won an exploration licence in India, though management stresses KABIL's mandate is non-copper minerals (lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths) and that the company's focus remains reaching 12 million tonnes of copper ore.

overview.what_it_does: HPCL is an Indian state-linked oil refining and marketing company: it buys crude oil, refines it into fuels like petrol (MS), diesel, LPG cooking gas, bitumen and lubricants, and sells them across India to motorists, households and industrial customers. It earns money on two legs — the refining margin between crude cost and product prices, and the marketing margin on selling through its own network of roughly 22,000 retail fuel outlets and to about 9.3 crore LPG customers. It runs refineries at Mumbai (expanded to 9.5 million tonnes) and Visakhapatnam (expanded from 8.3 to 15 million tonnes), plus a new refinery-cum-petrochemical complex in Barmer, Rajasthan, and moves product through its own pipeline and terminal network. Scale is large and volatile: it sold over 13 million tonnes in a single quarter, posted quarterly revenue of about INR 123,000 crores and a record FY26 standalone profit of INR 17,175 crores, but swung to a loss the very next quarter when crude prices and supply chains turned against it.

parts.name: Refining
parts.what: Turns crude into fuels at its Mumbai, Visakhapatnam and now Rajasthan (HRRL) refineries — roughly 6.6 million tonnes processed in a quarter at over 100% capacity utilisation, and management treats widening the crude basket and lifting throughput as a core profit lever.

parts.name: Marketing (retail and direct sales)
parts.what: Sells petrol, diesel and other fuels through about 22,000 retail outlets nationwide plus direct supply to industrial customers; management runs programmes like 'Abhyuday' to push more volume through 4,500 selected pumps and says it has been gaining market share against private competitors.

parts.name: LPG (cooking gas)
parts.what: Supplies bottled cooking gas to roughly 9.3 crore customers — described as a mass-market, home-delivery business, with a new premium on-demand variant 'HP Navya' being piloted in cities through partners like Swiggy.

parts.name: Pipelines and logistics
parts.what: Owns pipelines and import terminals (Hassan–Cherlapally, Vijayawada–Dharmapuri, Mangalore import terminal and LPG cavern) used to move crude and products cheaply — framed as a way to cut logistics cost rather than a separate revenue engine.

parts.name: Petrochemicals
parts.what: Sells petrochemical products under its own brand; a small presence today that management expects to become substantial once the Rajasthan refinery's petchem section (73% complete in Aug 2025) ramps up by end-FY27.

parts.name: Natural gas
parts.what: Covers the gas chain end to end — a 5 million tonne LNG storage and regasification terminal at Chhara, a share in gas transmission pipelines, city gas distribution in 23 geographies, and direct gas sales to industry, backed by long-term supply deals such as a 10-year contract with ADNOC from 2028.

parts.name: Biofuels / green business
parts.what: Described as the country's largest blender of ethanol into petrol (about 12% blending), with two sugar mills in Bihar, compressed biogas (CBG) plants starting in Uttar Pradesh, and green hydrogen at Vizag — being housed in a wholly owned green-business subsidiary.

parts.name: Lubricants
parts.what: A lubricants business that management said was being carved out into a separate company, pending Government of India approvals as a PSU.

parts.name: Refinery investments (HMEL, MRPL)
parts.what: Stakes in two other refining companies that feed into consolidated profit — they lifted FY26 consolidated PAT to INR 18,047 crores versus INR 17,175 crores standalone.

overview.what_it_does: Hindustan Unilever Limited (HUL) is an Indian consumer-goods company that makes and sells everyday branded household and personal products — soaps and skin cleansing, shampoo and hair care, skin care, toothpaste, laundry and dishwashing products, tea, and packaged foods — under brands such as Dove, Vaseline, TRESemmé, Clinic Plus, Closeup, Vim, Kissan, Bru, Minimalist and OZiva. It sells to ordinary Indian households, reaching them through millions of small general-trade shops (direct coverage was expanded by about 2 lakh outlets in FY26), modern-trade supermarkets, specialty retail such as chemists and cosmetic stores, fast-growing quick-commerce apps (about 3% of business and doubling every quarter), and its own direct-to-consumer online brands. It makes money on the volume and price of goods sold, with results driven by underlying volume growth, price changes it passes on as commodity costs (palm oil, tea, crude derivatives, soda ash) move, and cost savings; FY26 turnover was Rs. 63,763 crores with EBITDA margin around 23-24% and profit after tax before exceptional items of Rs. 2,711 crores in the March 2026 quarter alone. It operates essentially entirely in India, is majority-linked to the global Unilever group, is listed on the BSE and NSE, and pays large dividends (a Rs. 19 interim plus Rs. 10 special dividend in October 2024 totalled Rs. 6,814 crores).

parts.name: Beauty & Wellbeing
parts.what: Hair care, skin care and premium beauty brands such as Dove, TRESemmé (Lamellar Gloss, Hydramatrix ranges) and Clinic Plus, which management calls out as a reported segment and a focus of premiumisation — HUL has committed Rs. 2,000 crores of capex to premium formats in Beauty and Home Care.

parts.name: Personal Care
parts.what: Everyday personal products including skin cleansing (soaps), bodywash — described as "a core strategic priority" — Vaseline (which crossed Rs. 1,000 crores in FY26 with double-digit growth) and Closeup; the segment is important enough to have its own finance head.

parts.name: Home Care
parts.what: Laundry and household cleaning plus dishwashing, led by Vim (over 30 years old, with Vim Liquid delivering double-digit growth on its RhamnoTech bio-surfactant technology); it is the portfolio most exposed to chemical input costs like soda ash and sulfuric acid, where HUL has repeatedly taken price increases.

parts.name: Foods (and Refreshment)
parts.what: Packaged food and beverages including Kissan (being extended from ketchup into chutneys, a space management says has roughly four times the consumption occasions), tea brands and Bru coffee; tea prices are a recurring cost swing factor discussed on the calls.

parts.name: Masstige / D2C (Minimalist and OZiva)
parts.what: Acquired and incubated digital-first premium brands sold mainly online and now being pushed into offline stores, described as a "fewer, bigger bets" priority and together running at about Rs. 1,100 crores of annual revenue.

parts.name: Premium Beauty Business Unit / Agile Innovation Hub
parts.what: An in-house incubator that launches digital-native brands (for example Acne Squad and Find Your Happy Place) using small "nano factories", 14 bespoke D2C websites and influencer marketing; it is small in revenue terms but positioned as the innovation engine for new products.

parts.name: Ice Cream (demerged)
parts.what: A former business line that was separated out of HUL in the December 2025 quarter, so recent reported numbers exclude it; the demerger produced large one-off accounting gains and was framed as improving the growth quality of the remaining portfolio.

parts.name: Water business (sold)
parts.what: A business HUL exited by sale in December 2024, referenced only as a one-off gain in the prior-year comparison base.

overview.what_it_does: Hindustan Zinc digs zinc, lead and silver out of its own underground mines in Rajasthan, India, and then smelts that ore into finished metal at its own smelters — so it earns money across the whole chain from rock to saleable metal rather than just one step. It sells refined zinc (largely for galvanizing steel and for infrastructure and battery uses), refined lead, and silver, plus some by-products and unprocessed lead concentrate, into both the Indian domestic market and export markets, with prices set by global London Metal Exchange benchmarks in US dollars. Because prices are set by the market, profit comes down to volume and cost: management runs roughly 1.1 million tonnes a year of mined metal and about 1.0-1.1 million tonnes of refined metal, at a zinc cost of production of about $959 per tonne for FY26 (a five-year low, and $851/t in the June 2026 quarter), which they say places them at the low end of the global cost curve. It is part of the Vedanta group, listed in India (BSE 500188 / NSE HINDZINC), with all mining and smelting concentrated in Rajasthan, and it is now branching into fertilizer and critical minerals such as potash, tungsten and rare earths.

parts.name: Mining / mined metal
parts.what: The underground mines — Rampura Agucha, Sindesar Khurd, Zawar, Rajpura Dariba — that produce zinc-lead ore; output crossed 1.1 million tonnes of mined metal in FY26 with reserves and resources of 468.6 million tonnes and 25-plus years of mine life, and management guides to 1,150 KT for FY27.

parts.name: Smelting / refined metal (zinc and lead)
parts.what: Smelters at Chanderiya, Dariba and Debari that turn the mined concentrate into saleable refined zinc and lead; refined output was 1,048 KT in FY26 (over 1 million tonnes for four straight years) and this is the core revenue engine, helped by debottlenecking and the new 160,000 tonne-per-annum roaster at Debari.

parts.name: Silver / precious metals
parts.what: Silver recovered alongside lead production and sold as refined silver — 627 tonnes in FY26 with FY27 guidance of 680 tonnes — and although it is a by-product by volume, management says the silver portfolio contributes about 45-46% of total profitability, driven by solar, electronics and investor demand.

parts.name: Lead concentrate sales
parts.what: Opportunistic direct sales of unprocessed lead concentrate to cash in on high silver prices and clear inventory — 12,000 tonnes sold in the March 2026 quarter and 10,000 tonnes in the June 2026 quarter, described as adding roughly 37 tonnes of silver-equivalent sales.

parts.name: Growth and expansion projects
parts.what: A pipeline of capital projects including a 250,000 tonne-per-annum integrated zinc smelter at Debari, a tailings reprocessing plant at Rampura Agucha, and a hot acid leaching plant at Dariba to pull extra lead and silver out of smelter waste (commissioning pushed to Q2 FY27).

parts.name: Fertilizer business (Hindustan Zinc Fertilizer Pvt Ltd)
parts.what: A 510,000-tonne fertilizer plant at Chanderiya built to use a by-product of the smelting process, described as a synergistic project along the value chain, with commissioning expected in early Q2 FY27.

parts.name: Critical minerals / multi-metal diversification
parts.what: A newer, still pre-production push to become a diversified multi-metal miner — three secured critical mineral blocks in potash, tungsten and rare earths, plus a rare earth and yttrium mining lease at Gundlupet, Karnataka won in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Zinc-based batteries (early stage)
parts.what: A small exploratory effort to create new demand for its own metal, via a supply tie-up with US-based AEsir Technologies for nickel-zinc batteries and a research collaboration with the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research.

parts.name: Power and cost management
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a major profit lever the calls keep returning to — long-term 25-year renewable power deals with Serentica (530 MW capacity contracted) that lock in flat power rates, with renewable consumption at 22% by mid-2026 and power being the company's largest single cost bucket.

overview.what_it_does: Home First Finance is an Indian housing finance company that lends money to people buying or building homes, mostly in the affordable-housing segment, and takes the property as security. It makes loans at an origination yield of about 13% while borrowing at roughly 8% from banks, the National Housing Bank, and other sources, and earns the difference — a spread of about 5.3% and a net interest margin near 5.7%–6% — plus fees; profit after tax was Rs 540 crore in FY26 on assets under management of Rs 15,878 crore, up from Rs 5,832 crore in mid-2022. It runs a branch-and-touchpoint network (171 branches and 373 touchpoints as of March 2026) concentrated in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. The business is deliberately technology-heavy — app-based customer service, account-aggregator-based approvals, e-agreements and e-NACH mandates, and now AI tools in underwriting — which management says keeps operating costs at about 2.7% of assets.

parts.name: Individual housing loans (home loans)
parts.what: The core product — home loans to individual buyers, making up about 83% of new disbursements, priced at roughly 13% and all on a floating rate so they can be repriced when funding costs move.

parts.name: Loan against property (LAP)
parts.what: Loans given against a property the customer already owns; management says this runs steadily at about 15%–20% of disbursements, a small but consistent slice alongside home loans.

parts.name: Co-lending with banks
parts.what: Loans originated jointly with banks (starting with a Union Bank of India tie-up in 2022), which lets Home First serve larger-ticket customers without using its own balance sheet; the co-lending book was Rs 585 crore, or 3.9% of AUM, in Dec 2025, and management wants it at 10% of AUM.

parts.name: Direct assignment (portfolio sell-down)
parts.what: Selling pools of already-made loans to banks and other buyers to raise cash — described as a liquidity strategy, done in chunks like Rs 152 crore in Q1 FY25 and Rs 215 crore in Q3 FY26; assignment plus co-lending together funded about 20% of the balance sheet.

parts.name: Borrowings / treasury
parts.what: The funding engine rather than a sales line: about 57% from public and private sector banks, 16% NHB refinance, the rest from assignment, co-lending, NCDs and external commercial borrowings, with no commercial paper at all, at a cost of borrowing of about 7.9%.

parts.name: Distribution network (branches and touchpoints)
parts.what: The physical footprint that sources the loans, expanded steadily from 93 branches and 224 distribution points in 2022 to 171 branches and 373 touchpoints by March 2026, with state-by-state performance discussed as the main growth driver.

parts.name: Technology and digital platform
parts.what: Not sold separately, but management calls it central to how they source, underwrite, service and scale — 96% of customers on the mobile app, 81% of approvals via account aggregator, 80%+ of loans digitally fulfilled, and proprietary AI agents now live for income assessment and bank-statement analysis.

parts.name: PMAY 2.0 government subsidy facilitation
parts.what: Helping customers claim government housing subsidies — around 4,500 applications received as of January 2026, with 103 customers having received a first tranche; small today but expected to gain traction.

parts.name: Green homes certification
parts.what: A sustainability initiative in which financed homes are certified as green — 450 cumulative certifications by March 2026, mentioned as a side initiative rather than a revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: Honasa Consumer is an Indian beauty and personal care (BPC) company that sells everyday skin care, hair care and personal care products — face washes, sunscreens, serums, moisturizers, hair colour and similar items — to Indian consumers under a family of its own consumer brands, the best known being Mamaearth. Management describes it as "India's largest digital-first beauty and personal care company": it started life selling mostly online (over 60% of sales came from online/digital channels as of FY24) and has since pushed hard into physical retail, appointing its own distributors and selling through chemists, modern trade, general trade and fast-growing quick-commerce apps. It makes money the way a normal consumer-goods company does — buying/making product cheaply and selling it at a much higher price, running gross margins of about 70-71%, and spending a large slice of that on advertising and brand building; as marketing and overheads grow slower than sales, the leftover profit margin rises (EBITDA went from roughly 1.9% in H1 FY23 to 9.3% for full-year FY26, with PAT of about ₹200 crore in FY26 on quarterly revenue of ₹682 crore in Q4 FY26). It operates in India, run from a Gurugram head office with a New Delhi registered office, and has repeatedly bought small brands to fill gaps in its range; it runs on negative working capital, generates cash, and paid its first dividend (₹3 per share) for FY26.

parts.name: Mamaearth
parts.what: The founding brand, launched in 2016, selling "clean-label, toxin-free, natural" personal care built around India-specific ingredients like onion, ubtan and multani mitti; it is the company's core and largest brand — the fastest brand in India to reach ₹1,000 crore and a "Top 15 BPC" brand — which stumbled during a distribution overhaul in FY25 and was back to mid-teens growth by FY26.

parts.name: The Derma Co
parts.what: Launched in 2020 as a science-led, active-ingredients skincare brand (serums, sunscreens, face cleansers, and newer peptide/stem-cell hair care); management repeatedly calls it the "star" of the portfolio — strong growth, a face-cleanser business that nearly doubled, and the only brand they specifically flag as having reached double-digit EBITDA margins on its own.

parts.name: Aqualogica
parts.what: A hydration-focused skincare brand aimed at Gen Z, launched in-house, now being extended into moisturizers; counted among the "young brands" that drive above-average growth.

parts.name: Dr. Sheth's
parts.what: An acquired brand (bought in 2022) positioned at the premium end, especially premium serums, used to show the company can grow brands it buys, not just ones it creates.

parts.name: BBLUNT
parts.what: The other 2022 acquisition, a hair brand; the calls flag hair colour as one of the categories the young brands are winning in, but give little separate detail on its size.

parts.name: Ayuga
parts.what: An Ayurveda and natural-ingredients "masstige" brand targeted at Indian millennials; mentioned as part of the six-brand portfolio in FY24 but barely discussed in later calls.

parts.name: Staze
parts.what: A newer brand within the young-brand group that had crossed roughly ₹50 crore annualised revenue (ARR) as of Q3 FY26 and was still growing well.

parts.name: Reginald Men
parts.what: A men's skincare brand acquired around FY26 to play the men's grooming trend — described as the most-searched men's sunscreen brand — which doubled revenue year-on-year, crossed ₹100 crore ARR to become the sixth brand in the group at that scale, and also brought the company a Hyderabad-based team to strengthen it in South India.

parts.name: BTM Ventures
parts.what: A recent acquisition whose numbers are included in the Q4 FY26 results; the calls mention it only as part of reported growth and give no description of what it sells.

parts.name: "Young brands" (the non-Mamaearth portfolio as a group)
parts.what: Management tracks everything other than Mamaearth as one growth engine: it was over 40% of company revenue by Q3 FY25 and grew 25-40% year-on-year through FY26, versus Mamaearth's slower mid-teens pace.

parts.name: Online channels (e-commerce and quick commerce)
parts.what: The company's original and still largest route to market — more than 60% of sales in FY24, growing 20%+ in FY26 — within which quick commerce was the fastest-growing piece, rising from 4-5% to 7-8% of sales within a single quarter of FY25.

parts.name: Offline distribution (general trade and modern trade)
parts.what: Physical retail — chemists, modern trade, and under 500 beauty-advisor counters (less than 20% of general-trade sales) — which the company rebuilt from FY25 by appointing 150+ new distributors across the top 50 cities; by FY26 direct distribution was about 80% of revenue, stock levels were normalised at 25-30 days, and general/modern trade were growing 25%+.

parts.name: Services business (discontinued)
parts.what: A small non-core services line the company was deliberately scaling down in FY24, mentioned only as the reason reported growth looked lower than "like-for-like" growth.

overview.what_it_does: Honeywell Automation India Limited (HAIL) is the Indian listed arm of the global Honeywell group, and it sells industrial and building automation — the control systems, software and equipment that run and monitor large facilities. Its customers are industrial and infrastructure owners: refineries and petrochemical complexes, thermal power plants, pulp and paper mills, airports, metro stations, commercial buildings, data centres, pharma/life-sciences plants and newer areas like green hydrogen and lithium-ion battery gigafactories, plus other Honeywell companies abroad that buy its manufacturing and engineering work. It makes money by integrating and installing these systems as projects (often large, multi-year domestic contracts that tie up working capital), by distributing specific Honeywell building-management and sensing products, and then by earning steady lifecycle service and annuity revenue off the installed base — management's stated strategy is to build install base in an asset class and harvest that annuity. It operates in India as its home geography plus exports to Honeywell subsidiaries worldwide; FY2023-24 revenue was ₹4,582 crore, up 18% (FY2022-23 was ₹3,448 crore), with exports growing 16% and domestic 10%, and the company aims to grow at 2x India's GDP versus a historical ~11.5%, or 1.5x GDP.

parts.name: System Integration – Process Solutions
parts.what: Designs, installs and upgrades control and safety systems for heavy process industries such as refineries, petrochemical complexes, pulp and paper machines and thermal power plants (a named FY24 win was upgrading the distributed control system at a thermal plant); the calls describe Oil & Gas as historically a major end market and this as a 'core business platform and offering.'

parts.name: System Integration – Building Solutions
parts.what: Supplies integrated building management, safety, security and access-control systems for infrastructure and commercial sites — airports (including an advanced visual guidance docking system), metro stations, commercial buildings, data centres, a lithium-ion battery gigafactory and a leading life-sciences/pharma manufacturer; the calls list several of these as FY24 key wins but give no separate revenue figure.

parts.name: Distribution of Building Management Systems and Sensing Solutions
parts.what: Sells specified Honeywell building-management and sensing product lines into the Indian market as a distributor; management names it as one of the three legs of the HAIL portfolio but does not size it in the calls.

parts.name: Global manufacturing and Engineering Services (exports)
parts.what: Manufactures and does engineering work in India for Honeywell subsidiaries worldwide; the calls say exports grew 16% year-on-year versus 10% domestic, so it is a meaningfully faster-growing part of the mix, though the exact share is not disclosed.

parts.name: Services / lifecycle annuity on installed base
parts.what: Ongoing service, digital and performance-management work (process control, cyber security, remote visibility, managed performance) on systems already installed — management calls this the point of building install base and notes service growth is 'linear', i.e. steadier than lumpy project revenue.

parts.name: Energy transition and sustainability projects (within automation)
parts.what: Automation for newer energy-related assets — an indigenously built green hydrogen plant and a battery energy storage/load management project in Lakshadweep — described as an emerging-industry pivot rather than a separately reported segment; note management explicitly says Honeywell's Aerospace and Energy & Sustainability Solutions businesses sit with Honeywell Inc, not with HAIL.

overview.what_it_does: Himadri Speciality Chemical is an Indian company that started in 1990 as a small coal tar distillation unit and now turns coal tar and related feedstock into a range of industrial chemicals and advanced materials. Its core money-makers are coal tar pitch (sold mainly to aluminium and graphite makers), speciality carbon black (a black pigment/filler used in plastics, inks, paints, coatings, wires and cables, fibres, rubber and tyres) plus speciality oils and naphthalene-based products; it earns revenue by making these at low cost from an integrated, backward-linked plant base and selling to industrial customers in roughly 56 countries. Manufacturing is in India, including a large integrated carbon complex, a speciality carbon black site at Singur and an anode plant at Mahistikry in West Bengal, with liquid coal tar pitch exported through dedicated terminals at Haldia and Mangalore. On top of this base it has added a tyre business (Birla Tyres) and is investing heavily in lithium-ion battery materials; in the quarter ended June 2026 the group reported consolidated revenue of INR 1,432 crore, EBITDA of INR 313 crore (22% margin) and PAT of INR 228 crore.

parts.name: Coal Tar Pitch
parts.what: Distills coal tar into pitch for aluminium and graphite customers and is described as the business that 'anchors the company', with 600,000 MTPA of coal tar distillation capacity, over 65% domestic market share, and the world's largest single-location fully integrated carbon complex, now also exporting liquid pitch via the Haldia and Mangalore terminals.

parts.name: Speciality Carbon Black
parts.what: Makes high-value carbon black grades (over 70 grades) for plastics, inks, high-performance coatings, paints, batteries, wires and cables, fibres, rubber and EV tyres; total carbon black capacity is 250,000 MTPA including 130,000 MTPA of speciality carbon black after the Singur expansion, which management calls the world's largest single-site speciality carbon black plant.

parts.name: Super Speciality Carbon Black
parts.what: A newly announced higher-purity, premium-priced version of the above for lithium-ion batteries, engineered plastics, fabrics, fibres, coatings and conductive black, being created by converting 6,000 MTPA of existing capacity at a capex of about INR 170 crore.

parts.name: Speciality Oils and Naphthalene (including derivatives SNF and PCE)
parts.what: Sells oils and naphthalene-based chemicals derived from the same coal tar stream, described as part of the core along with pitch and carbon black, and now including a consumer-facing branded naphthalene ball, 'Durofresh', which management says has had an encouraging response in retail.

parts.name: Anthraquinone and Carbazole (forward integration)
parts.what: A new plant making ingredients for dyes, pigments, pharmaceuticals and electronics from Himadri's own oils, billed as India's first commercial facility of its kind and an import substitute, with total capacity of 5,300 MTPA — an initial 2,600 MTPA phase from Q2 FY27 and full commissioning targeted by FY28.

parts.name: New Energy / Lithium-ion Battery Materials — Anode
parts.what: Commissioned its first anode material plant at Mahistikry, West Bengal in April 2026 with an initial 200 MTPA, using technology developed fully in-house and fed by specially engineered high-purity coal tar pitch made by Himadri itself; still small in volume but described as the most transformational part of the company's future, with samples going to cell makers (OEMs) for approval.

parts.name: New Energy / Lithium-ion Battery Materials — LFP Cathode Active Material
parts.what: A planned lithium iron phosphate cathode business where a first 2,000 MTPA milestone is due in Q3 FY27, building to 40,000 MTPA under Phase 1 by around FY29 and a long-term ambition of 200,000 MTPA (enough for roughly 100 GWh of batteries), which management says would make Himadri the first commercial-scale LFP cathode plant outside China.

parts.name: Carbon Nanotube (CNT)
parts.what: A newly developed in-house technology with a 200 MTPA plant planned for Q4 FY27 at about INR 70 crore capex, aimed at lithium-ion batteries, semiconductors, electronics, sensors, polymers, coatings and aerospace; small in size today but positioned as a long-term growth option.

parts.name: Birla Tyres (tyre manufacturing)
parts.what: A tyre business Himadri entered as a strategic partner alongside resolution applicant Dalmia Bharat Refractories, which restarted commercial operations on 29 May 2025 and now sells over 80 products through 49 distributors and more than 1,000 dealers in India, Asia, the Middle East and Africa, with capacity being shifted from truck-and-bus bias to off-the-road tyres and a passenger car radial plant for EV/SUV tyres targeted by FY28; notably, Himadri says it does not sell carbon black to Birla Tyres.

parts.name: Strategic investments and partnerships (Sicona, International Battery Company, Invati Creations)
parts.what: Minority stakes and licensing tie-ups rather than operating businesses — an exclusive licence to Sicona's silicon-carbon anode technology, a stake in US-headquartered cell maker IBC (used to validate and deploy Himadri's materials via IBC's South Korea plant), and joint research with Invati on advanced electrode materials.

parts.name: Research & Development
parts.what: Not a revenue line but repeatedly presented as the engine of the business, with over 180 scientists and technologists including 28 PhDs drawn from Japan, South Korea, Australia, the US, Europe and China, and INR 120 crore spent in FY26.

overview.what_it_does: HUDCO is an Indian government-linked lender (an NBFC that RBI has since mandated to become an infrastructure finance company), sitting under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, that makes long-term loans for housing and urban infrastructure projects. Its customers are mainly state government entities, state-owned corporations and urban local bodies building things like metros, roads, water systems and housing — HUDCO itself does no capex, it only lends to those who do. It earns money on the gap between what it pays for funds (bank loans, repo-linked loans, domestic bonds, external commercial borrowings including Japanese-yen loans, FCNR deposits and an RBI forex window) and what it charges borrowers, running a spread of about 2% and a net interest margin of about 3%. It operates across India in every state and calls itself 'sector agnostic' — free to fund anything on the government's harmonized infrastructure list — with the loan book growing from roughly INR80,000 crore in FY23 to about INR1.34 lakh crore by Q1 FY26 and a stated target of INR3 lakh crore by 2030.

parts.name: Infrastructure project finance (lending to state government entities)
parts.what: The core business: sanctioning and then disbursing long-term loans to state entities for capital-intensive projects, and by far the biggest driver — sanctions went from about INR25,000 crore in FY23 to INR83,000 crore in FY24 to roughly INR1.24–1.27 lakh crore in FY25, with disbursements rising from INR8,400 crore to about INR40,000 crore over the same period.

parts.name: Mobility / transport financing
parts.what: Funding metros, rapid rail (RRTS), state road transport corporations, e-mobility, ring roads and multi-modal corridors, plus refinancing metros' existing foreign-currency loans with cheaper domestic loans — described as a newer, fast-expanding segment rather than a separately sized one.

parts.name: Water and sanitation / basic urban services
parts.what: Loans for water supply and water-body rejuvenation projects tied to central government programmes like AMRUT 2.0 and Swachh Bharat Mission, which management says is drawing heavy demand from states.

parts.name: Roads
parts.what: Financing state-level HAM (hybrid annuity) and state-owned EPC road projects, cited as one of the capital-intensive areas the company moved into as it diversified beyond housing.

parts.name: Housing
parts.what: The company's founding purpose and still in the name — lending for housing projects including PMAY-linked work, though on recent calls management talks about it far less than urban infrastructure.

parts.name: Consultancy / advisory to states and urban local bodies
parts.what: Advising state counterparts on structuring and understanding projects (for example under AMRUT 2.0) alongside the lending — presented as a support activity, with no revenue figure given on the calls.

parts.name: Urban Invest window / Urban Challenge Fund role
parts.what: A recently launched platform meant to be a one-stop shop taking a city project from concept to bankability, financial closure, investors, a HUDCO loan and central-scheme funding — positioned as the vehicle to capture the government's INR1 lakh crore Urban Challenge Fund subsidy plus roughly INR2 lakh crore of institutional finance, and still awaiting final guidelines as of the Feb 2026 and Jul 2026 calls.

parts.name: Borrowing / treasury
parts.what: Not a revenue line but central to how it makes money: raising funds cheaply across banks, bonds, ECBs and FCNR (borrowing about INR20,000 crore at ~6.32% in one quarter) — and the source of a one-off INR470 crore fair-value loss on FCNR borrowings in 9M FY26 that the company says has now been exited.

overview.what_it_does: Hyundai Motor India Limited (HMIL) makes and sells passenger cars and SUVs in India under the Hyundai brand, with models like Creta, Venue, Exter, Alcazar, Verna and Grand i10 Nios sold to retail buyers through a dealer network that it keeps expanding, including into rural markets (rural penetration reached about 24% of sales). It earns money by manufacturing vehicles at its own plants in Chennai and at a newer Pune/Talegaon facility (engine production from mid-2025, vehicle production from 1 October 2025) and selling them for a profit, with revenue of roughly ₹172-175 billion per quarter and EBITDA margins of about 12-14%. Roughly three-quarters of its volumes go to Indian customers and the rest is exported — management calls this a 'two-pronged' or 'dual engine' strategy, and describes India as parent Hyundai Motor Company's manufacturing hub for emerging markets ('Make in India, Made for the World'). Profitability is driven by selling a richer mix (more SUVs, higher trims with sunroof and ADAS), cost control, localisation of parts, and calibrated price increases.

parts.name: Domestic vehicle sales (India)
parts.what: Selling cars and SUVs to Indian retail customers — about 132,000-149,000 units a quarter, the larger share of total volumes; demand was weak through FY25 and H1 FY26 and then recovered strongly after the September 2025 GST rate cuts, with Q4 FY26 the highest-ever quarterly domestic sales.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Shipping India-built vehicles to emerging markets such as the Middle East, Africa, Mexico and South Africa; exports rose to about 27% of the sales mix, grew 16.4% for full-year FY26, and management guides to 8-10% growth in FY27 — it is repeatedly described as the cushion that offsets weak domestic demand.

parts.name: SUV portfolio
parts.what: By far the most important product group, at roughly 68-71% of volumes, led by Creta (the mid-size segment leader for ten years running), plus Venue and Exter in the compact/entry SUV space and Alcazar higher up; the all-new Venue launched November 2025 is called a key growth driver.

parts.name: Hatchbacks
parts.what: Smaller cars such as Grand i10 Nios; a declining part of the mix (about 30,000 units in Q2 FY25) as customers shift to SUVs, though brand i10 has cumulatively sold over 3 million units in India and export markets.

parts.name: Sedans
parts.what: Cars like Verna, contributing roughly 12% of volumes and broadly flat — the smallest of the three body-type groups.

parts.name: Powertrain / fuel mix
parts.what: A deliberately 'technology-agnostic' spread across petrol, diesel (about 23% of volumes), CNG including its dual-cylinder technology (a record ~15-16%) and electric (only about 1.4%), with a first locally built dedicated compact-SUV EV planned for FY27 and a hydrogen R&D centre (HTWO) set up with IIT Madras.

parts.name: Manufacturing operations
parts.what: Two manufacturing bases — the long-standing Chennai plant and the new Pune/Talegaon plant — which together add capacity for the planned 26 product launches by FY2030 and are backed by record capex of about ₹7,500 crore in FY27; the new plant's start-up costs weigh on near-term margins.

overview.what_it_does: ICICI Prudential Asset Management Company manages other people's money for a fee: it runs mutual fund schemes and other investment products in India under the ICICI Prudential brand, and is majority-owned by ICICI Bank (its holding company), whose shares are listed on the BSE and NSE. Its customers are mainly Indian retail savers — 1.73 crore (17.3 million) unique customers as of June 2026 — reached largely through mutual fund distributors, national distributors, banks including ICICI Bank, and direct/digital channels, plus institutional and wealthy investors for its higher-end products and NRIs/overseas investors through GIFT City and Dubai. It earns money almost entirely as an annual management fee charged as a small percentage of the assets it manages: roughly 67 basis points on equity money, 32 on debt, 12 on liquid, 10-12 on passives and 30 on arbitrage, giving an overall gross yield of about 52 basis points on total assets. It is India's second-largest AMC with mutual fund quarterly average assets of INR 11.17 lakh crore (13.4% market share) as of June 2026, operating mainly in India with new offices in GIFT City (IFSC) and DIFC Dubai.

parts.name: Mutual fund business
parts.what: The core business of running open pooled investment schemes for the public; it is by far the biggest part, at about 90% of operating net revenue and INR 11.17 lakh crore of quarterly average AUM in the June 2026 quarter, making it the second-largest fund house in India.

parts.name: Equity and equity-oriented schemes
parts.what: Share-investing funds that are the largest and highest-fee slice of the mutual fund book — INR 6.31 lakh crore quarterly average AUM and the industry's largest market share at about 14%, earning roughly 66-67 basis points a year.

parts.name: Equity-oriented hybrid schemes
parts.what: Funds that mix shares with other assets; management calls out its clear leadership here with the largest market share of about 26.6% and INR 2.22 lakh crore of quarterly average AUM.

parts.name: Debt schemes (including liquid)
parts.what: Bond and short-term money funds used heavily by institutions, around INR 1.99 lakh crore of quarterly average AUM at lower fees (32 basis points for debt, 12 for liquid), and prone to sequential dips when institutions redeem in tight liquidity.

parts.name: Passive schemes (index funds and ETFs)
parts.what: Low-cost funds that simply track indices or commodities like gold and silver; growing fastest of all (INR 1.84 lakh crore quarterly average AUM in March 2026, up 48% year-on-year) but earning only about 10-12 basis points.

parts.name: Systematic transactions (SIPs and STPs)
parts.what: Not a product but the retail engine management emphasises most — regular monthly investments totalling about INR 4,872 crore in June 2026, described as sticky and resilient even in falling markets.

parts.name: Alternates (PMS and AIF)
parts.what: Higher-end products for wealthy and institutional clients — listed-equity portfolio management services (INR 28,996 crore) and alternative investment funds (INR 22,737 crore) spanning private credit, real estate, private equity and early-stage private equity, together INR 79,446 crore of quarterly average AUM and about 8.5% of net revenue, at a gross yield of roughly 1.9-2.0% (about 0.95% net of distribution costs); it was expanded by taking over investment management of certain ICICI Venture AIFs from 1 April 2026.

parts.name: Specialized Investment Funds (iSIF)
parts.what: A new SEBI-created category sitting between ordinary mutual funds and alternatives, launched from January 2026 under the iSIF brand with four strategies live; still small at INR 2,678 crore quarterly average AUM and described as an early-stage, long-term opportunity.

parts.name: Advisory / offshore advisory business
parts.what: Advising other investors' portfolios rather than managing funds directly; the smallest piece at roughly 1.4-1.8% of net revenue and a yield of only about 30-33 basis points.

parts.name: International presence (GIFT City and DIFC Dubai)
parts.what: New offshore platforms — a retail FME branch in GIFT City with its first fund, the ICICI Prudential Smart Navigator Fund, launched February 2026, and an approved office in DIFC Dubai to serve NRIs and Middle East investors; both are early-stage additions, not yet material to revenue.

parts.name: Distribution mix
parts.what: How the equity money is gathered: mutual fund distributors 36.2%, direct 29.5%, national distributors 15.9%, other banks 10.7% and parent ICICI Bank only 7.7%, with management noting its share of new equity inflows runs ahead of its share of existing assets.

parts.name: Digital and AI operations
parts.what: A support function management highlights: about 95.7% of purchase transactions come through digital platforms, and AI now handles 60% of email customer queries, powers a natural-language search engine with 5 million-plus queries, and assists fund managers with report summarisation.

overview.what_it_does: ICICI Bank is an Indian bank that takes deposits from customers and lends the money out, earning most of its income from the gap between what it pays on deposits and what it charges on loans (net interest income, at a net interest margin of roughly 4.3%), plus fees on services (about ₹6,779 crore of fee income in the March 2026 quarter). It serves individuals, farmers and rural households, small shopkeepers and SMEs, and large Indian companies, offering home loans, auto loans, personal loans, credit cards, farm credit, working-capital and business loans, current and savings accounts, term deposits and money transfers. It operates mainly across India through a large branch network — 7,511 branches and 12,087 ATMs and cash recycling machines at March 31, 2026 — plus mobile and internet platforms such as iMobile for individuals and InstaBIZ for businesses, and a small set of international branches serving mostly Indian companies and non-resident Indians (about 2.4% of loans). Management runs it for what it calls 'risk-calibrated profitable growth', reporting profit after tax above ₹50,000 crore for FY2026 and a consolidated profit of ₹54,208 crore including subsidiaries.

parts.name: Deposits (current, savings and term accounts)
parts.what: The bank's funding base — money customers park in current accounts, savings accounts and fixed-term deposits — which grew 11.4% year-on-year at March 31, 2026 and which management repeatedly calls its key franchise strength, with among the lowest cost of deposits in the system.

parts.name: Retail loans
parts.what: Loans to individuals — home loans (mortgages), auto loans, commercial vehicle and equipment loans, personal loans and credit cards — the single largest chunk of lending at about 41.7% of the total portfolio including non-fund exposures at March 2026.

parts.name: Mortgage portfolio
parts.what: Home loans, the biggest single retail product, growing 13.2% year-on-year in FY2026 and consistently cited as a core growth driver.

parts.name: Personal loans and credit cards
parts.what: Unsecured lending to individuals, which was about 9.7% and 4.4% of the total loan book respectively in mid-2024 after very fast growth, but had slowed sharply by end-2025 (personal loans up 2.4%, cards down 3.5% year-on-year).

parts.name: Rural portfolio (including kisan credit card)
parts.what: Farm and rural lending, notably the kisan credit card given to farmers, which the calls flag as seasonally lumpy — it reliably produces higher bad-loan additions in the first and third quarters of each year (about ₹7.4 billion in the December 2025 quarter).

parts.name: Business banking
parts.what: Lending and banking services to small businesses and merchants, sourced through branches, cross-sell to current-account holders and digital tools; consistently the fastest-growing segment (up 44.7% year-on-year in mid-2022, 35.6% in mid-2024, 24.4% in FY2026).

parts.name: SME portfolio
parts.what: Loans to small and medium enterprises, grown through the branch network and digital platforms, expanding at 23-32% year-on-year in the earlier calls.

parts.name: Domestic corporate banking
parts.what: Lending and working-capital services to large Indian companies, growing around 5-14% year-on-year across the period, with 71.9% of the book rated 'A- and above' at March 2026; includes ₹791 billion of exposure to non-bank finance and housing finance companies (4.3% of advances) and a ₹681 billion builder/real-estate book (another 4.3%).

parts.name: International / overseas branches
parts.what: A small offshore book, down to about 2.4% of total loans by end-2025, made up almost entirely of Indian corporates and India-linked trade finance rather than genuinely foreign lending (about 92% Indian corporates in 2024).

parts.name: Digital platforms (iMobile, InstaBIZ, OneSCF, Money2India)
parts.what: The bank's apps and online channels — iMobile for individuals, InstaBIZ for businesses (including instant digital current accounts and overdrafts open to non-customers), OneSCF for corporate supply-chain finance and Money2India/iMobile Global for non-resident Indians — used to onboard customers, cross-sell and cut cost of service rather than reported as a separate profit line.

parts.name: Subsidiaries
parts.what: Separately managed group companies whose results are discussed on each call and which lift group profit above the bank's own — consolidated FY2026 profit of ₹54,208 crore versus above ₹50,000 crore standalone — and which also pay dividends up to the bank.

parts.name: Treasury
parts.what: The bank's own investment and markets activity, explicitly carved out of the profit measure management steers by ('profit before tax excluding treasury', ₹65,021 crore in FY2026) because it is seen as lumpy rather than core.

overview.what_it_does: ICICI Lombard is an Indian general (non-life) insurance company — it sells policies that pay out when something goes wrong with your vehicle, your health, your property, your cargo or your business, rather than life insurance (management explicitly says term/life insurance is 'not the business we are in'). Its customers span individuals (car, two-wheeler and retail health cover), companies and SMEs (fire, marine, liability, group health), and government schemes, all within India, and it describes itself as the largest private-sector general insurer in the country. It makes money two ways: underwriting profit — collecting Gross Direct Premium Income (₹247.76 billion in FY2024) and paying out less in claims and expenses than it takes in, measured by a combined ratio of 103.4% in FY2026 versus 117.8% for the industry — and investment income earned on the float, with an overall portfolio return of about 7.98% in FY2024 on a book that is mostly fixed income with roughly 11% in equities. It reaches customers through agents, its own website and app ('IL TakeCare'), digital ecosystem partners, and bancassurance tie-ups including ICICI Bank.

parts.name: Motor
parts.what: Insurance on cars, two-wheelers and commercial vehicles, split between Own Damage (damage to your own vehicle) and Third Party (legally mandated cover for injury or damage caused to others); it is a core retail line where the company holds market leadership, with FY2026 mix of 52.8% private car, 25.4% two-wheeler and 21.8% commercial vehicle, and a motor combined ratio of 106.6% versus 128.0% for the industry.

parts.name: Health (Retail Health)
parts.what: Individual and family medical/indemnity policies sold largely through an agency force the company has been deliberately building out (1,101 agency managers as of Q1 FY2023); it is the fastest-growing part of the book, up 51.1% in FY2026 with market share rising from 3.3% to 4.1%, and 42.1% of new retail health premium now coming from long-term policies.

parts.name: Health (Group Health)
parts.what: Medical cover sold to employers and other groups for their members; management runs it 'with a disciplined approach' focused on managing the book rather than chasing volume, and it grew 12.8% for the industry in FY2026 versus the much faster retail line.

parts.name: Mass Health
parts.what: Government-sponsored/mass health schemes, treated as a lumpy, low-margin line that management routinely strips out (alongside Crop) when quoting 'underlying' growth — for example FY2026 growth of 7.0% overall versus 10.2% excluding Crop and Mass Health.

parts.name: Commercial lines / Property & Casualty
parts.what: Corporate and SME cover for factories, offices, goods and business risks — the P&C segment was ₹19.54 billion of premium in Q1 FY2023, and the company says it holds leadership in the Liability and Marine Cargo lines, though FY2026 growth of 5.4% lagged the industry's 12.2% because management refused to match competitors' price cuts.

parts.name: Fire
parts.what: Property/fire cover for commercial premises, the largest single piece of the commercial book (₹11.43 billion in Q1 FY2023); it has recently been the most price-competitive line in the market, with the industry seeing 27.8% de-growth in Q1 FY2027 as rates collapsed at the April renewal cycle.

parts.name: Crop
parts.what: Agricultural/crop insurance, another lumpy government-linked line that management excludes from its 'like-for-like' growth comparisons rather than treating as a core growth driver.

parts.name: Investment book
parts.what: The pool of premium money held before claims are paid, invested mainly in fixed income (yield to maturity ~7.4%) with about 11% in equities, producing a realised return of 7.98% in FY2024 plus capital gains of ₹5.51 billion — a large and reliable second profit engine alongside underwriting.

parts.name: Distribution — agency, bancassurance and digital
parts.what: Not a product but how the company sells: an agency force for retail health, bancassurance and Key Relationship Groups including ICICI Bank (up 49.4% in Q1 FY2023), and a 'Digital One' team covering its own website, the IL TakeCare app (~1.7 million downloads by mid-2022) and ecosystem partners, contributing ₹2.10 billion or 3.9% of GDPI in that quarter.

parts.name: Reinsurance and CAT exposure
parts.what: The company cedes part of its risk to reinsurers and absorbs catastrophe losses when they hit — CAT losses cost ₹1.37 billion in FY2024 (worth 0.8 percentage points of combined ratio) — and softer FY2027 reinsurance renewal rates are flagged as a cost tailwind.

overview.what_it_does: ICICI Prudential Life Insurance is an Indian life insurance company, listed on the BSE and NSE and associated with the ICICI group, that sells life insurance and long-term savings products to individual retail customers in India (including NRIs through GIFT City) and to corporate/institutional groups. Management describes the business as resting on two pillars: protection, where the company collects premiums for providing death and disability risk cover, and savings, where it takes in customer money and earns from managing those funds over long periods — as of June 30, 2026 it managed assets of about ₹3.34 trillion and had ₹48.06 trillion of in-force sum assured covering its policyholders. Money is made from new business premium and renewals (new business premium of ₹248.10 billion in FY2026), from the spread between what it charges and what claims and expenses cost, and from scale and cost efficiency in the savings book (savings cost-to-premium of 13.6% in Q1-FY2027); profitability is tracked as Value of New Business (₹26.29 billion in FY2026, margin 24.7%) and profit after tax (₹16 billion in FY2026). It sells almost entirely in India through banks, its own agents, direct channels and non-bank partners, and pays claims with a settlement ratio of about 99.3%.

parts.name: Retail protection
parts.what: Pure life-cover (term) policies sold to individuals, described as the company's core focus area — it was about 10.5% of APE in Q1-FY2027 and grew 60%+ year-on-year for three straight quarters after the September 2025 GST exemption, with management saying only ~13% of the addressable population is covered, making it a multi-decade growth opportunity.

parts.name: Group protection (credit life and group term)
parts.what: Life cover sold to institutions — credit life bundled with loans from lending partners (including microfinance/MFI borrowers) and yearly-renewable group term cover for employee/member pools; it grew 7.1% in FY2026 and 37.8% year-on-year in Q1-FY2027, and management underwrites it only when the risk-reward fits.

parts.name: Linked savings (ULIPs)
parts.what: Unit-linked policies where the customer's savings are invested in market-linked funds and returns move with equity markets; it is the single largest savings line — 51.4% of APE in Q1-FY2025 — and its sales swing with market volatility, so the company is pushing higher sum-assured ULIPs for stability.

parts.name: Non-linked savings (participating and non-participating)
parts.what: Traditional guaranteed or bonus-bearing savings policies, including the flagship par product 'Gold' aimed at customers wanting early income/liquidity; contribution has moved around with rates and competing fixed-return products, sitting at roughly ₹4.94 billion of APE (with annuity) in Q1-FY2027.

parts.name: Annuity
parts.what: Retirement-income products that pay a regular pension to the customer, growing at roughly a 20% four-year CAGR and stabilised at about 7% of the retail mix, with demand tilting toward regular-premium over single-premium annuities.

parts.name: Group funds / group savings business
parts.what: Fund-management-style savings products for corporate schemes (e.g. employee benefit funds), a smaller line that grew 26% in FY2026 and 42.2% year-on-year in Q1-FY2027.

parts.name: Bancassurance
parts.what: Selling through bank branches — ICICI Bank plus other banks — with 53 bank tie-ups and access to over 26,400 branches; it contributed 29.8% of APE in FY2026.

parts.name: Agency channel
parts.what: The company's own advisers/agents, over 2.42 lakh of them, contributing ₹26.86 billion of APE in FY2026 — a proprietary channel management is deliberately investing in via a micro-market branch strategy and analytics-driven agent productivity.

parts.name: Direct channel
parts.what: Sales made straight to customers online and through company staff, ₹14.30 billion of APE in FY2026, with focus areas being the NRI segment through GIFT City and scaling the online channel.

parts.name: Partnership distribution
parts.what: Sales through non-bank partners such as brokers, fintechs and lenders — over 1,500 partnerships — contributing 13.2% of APE in FY2026 and growing 23.4% that year.

parts.name: Investments / shareholder and policyholder funds
parts.what: The in-house investment operation run by a Chief Investment Officer that manages the ₹3.34 trillion of assets backing policies, with a stated record of no non-performing asset since inception and a solvency ratio of 225.4% against a 150% requirement.

overview.what_it_does: Indo Count Industries (ICIL) is an Indian textile manufacturer that makes home textiles — mainly cotton bed linen and bed sheets, plus fashion, utility and institutional bedding, and more recently curtains, towels, bath rugs and blankets. It sells overwhelmingly business-to-business to large global retailers (big box chains and omni-channel/e-commerce platforms) in over 50 countries, with the United States as its biggest market and roughly 30% of core revenue now from non-US markets; a small domestic India business sells under its own brands. It earns money by converting cotton into finished made-ups at its plants in Maharashtra and Gujarat (India) and, since FY26, at three pillow/quilt factories in the United States, and by selling under owned and licensed consumer brands. Volumes are measured in metres of fabric — 94 million metres in FY26 — and revenue was roughly flat in FY26 (management guides to about INR 5,500 crore in FY27 at around 13% EBITDA margin), with US import tariffs the main swing factor.

parts.name: Core business (home textile / bed linen exports)
parts.what: The original and still dominant business — manufacturing and exporting bed sheets and bed linen from India to global retailers; it has won India's TEXPROCIL gold trophy for the highest cotton made-ups exports six years running, and management expects it to bring in about INR 4,000 crore of the INR 5,500 crore targeted for FY27, though it declined by a low-teens percentage in FY26 because of US tariffs.

parts.name: Fashion, utility and institutional bedding
parts.what: Higher-value bedding categories the company pushed into from around FY19 onwards to move beyond plain sheets and lift margins; management describes them as central to growth and to winning a bigger share of each retailer's spend.

parts.name: New business — US utility bedding manufacturing
parts.what: Three factories in the United States making pillows and quilts, started only about 16-17 months before Feb 2026, with capacity raised from 13 million to 31 million pillows and 1.5 million quilts a year after a new greenfield plant in Kernersville, North Carolina; existing units run at about 65% utilisation and management expects roughly USD 175 million of revenue from this over the next few years.

parts.name: New business — brands (owned and licensed)
parts.what: Selling under consumer brand names rather than as an anonymous supplier: the 180-year-old US brand Wamsutta, bought outright for INR 85 crore in 2024 and relaunched, plus six licensed brands including Fieldcrest, Waverly, GAIAM, Jasper Conran and Tommy Hilfiger; together with US utility bedding this 'new business' was 20% of Q3 FY26 sales, INR 792 crore in FY26, and is targeted to roughly double in FY27.

parts.name: Domestic India / B2C and D2C business
parts.what: Own-brand sales inside India under Boutique Living (also called Boutique Clothing) and Layers through about 2,000 retail touch points and digital marketplaces; small at roughly 2.25% of FY26 revenue but an area management wants to build.

parts.name: Acquired GHCL home textile unit
parts.what: The home textile business bought from GHCL Limited in 2022, which management said made Indo Count the largest global bed linen company and which it now runs as a single combined manufacturing operation rather than reporting separately.

parts.name: Spinning division
parts.what: A yarn spinning unit at Gokul Shirgaon, Kolhapur listed among the company's facilities, feeding into the home textile operation; the calls give no separate size for it.

overview.what_it_does: IDBI Bank Limited is an Indian bank, headquartered in Mumbai and listed on the BSE and NSE, that takes deposits from customers and lends the money out as loans. It serves both retail (individual) customers and corporate borrowers — management says the loan book is run to a target mix of roughly 62%–68% retail with the balance corporate — and as of the September 2022 quarter it held about Rs. 2,30,000 crores of deposits against net advances of about Rs. 1,46,752 crores, on a balance sheet of roughly Rs. 3,09,000 crores. It earns mainly from the spread between interest on loans and investments and what it pays on deposits (net interest income of Rs. 2,738 crores in Q2 FY23 at a net interest margin of about 4.37%), plus fee-type 'other income' such as commission, exchange and brokerage, forex income, dividends from its three subsidiaries, and recoveries on previously written-off loans. It operates in India, is majority-owned by the Government of India (about 45%) and LIC (about 49%) — who are running a disinvestment process — and it came out of the RBI's Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) restrictions in March 2021, after which it resumed growing both retail and corporate lending.

parts.name: Retail advances
