parts.what: Loans to individual/small customers, which management calls its priority — a 'differentiated granular approach to build up more retail business' — and the main driver of loan growth, adding about Rs. 4,800 crores in the September 2022 quarter; retail is targeted at roughly 62%–68% of total advances.

parts.name: Corporate advances
parts.what: Loans to companies, pursued on a 'calibrated approach' with emphasis on mid-corporate relationships (including rebuilding ties with mid-corporates it had to exit during the PCA period) and 'lesser emphasis' on large corporates; corporate makes up the remaining roughly one-third of the loan book.

parts.name: Deposits (CASA, retail and bulk)
parts.what: The bank's funding base of about Rs. 2,30,000 crores, unusually skewed to cheap current and savings accounts with a CASA ratio of about 56%, alongside retail term deposits and a small bulk-deposit book (about 5.5%) that management plans to grow toward 8%–10%.

parts.name: Treasury / investments
parts.what: The bank's portfolio of securities, largely government bonds, split into AFS (available-for-sale, modified duration about 1.27) and HTM buckets; it earns interest on investments (up about 15% year-on-year) and occasionally books trading gains, such as the G-sec sale gains in the June 2022 quarter.

parts.name: Priority sector lending
parts.what: Regulator-mandated lending to designated sectors, where management says the bank has 'achieved all the targets' with no shortfall, so its associated RIDF/PSL deposits are simply running off on maturity.

parts.name: Fee and other income
parts.what: Non-interest earnings including commission, exchange and brokerage (up about 10% year-on-year), forex income, dividends from the three subsidiaries, and recoveries from written-off accounts (Rs. 26 crores in the September 2022 quarter); total other income grew about 11% year-on-year.

parts.name: Stressed-asset recovery and resolution
parts.what: A significant, actively managed activity of recovering money from bad loans through settlements, upgrades, NCLT/insolvency cases and write-offs — the bank guided to about Rs. 4,000 crores of recoveries and upgrades for FY23, had recovered Rs. 1,136 crores by the June quarter, and wrote off about Rs. 5,200 crores in the September quarter, bringing net NPA down to 1.15% with a provision coverage ratio of 97.86%.

parts.name: Digital banking channels
parts.what: ATMs, internet banking, a mobile app and other alternate channels through which over 95% of customer-initiated transactions now flow, with UPI taking 'the lion's share' (about 75%); the bank says it keeps investing in IT to expand this footprint and plans to set up digital banking units eventually.

parts.name: Subsidiaries and joint ventures
parts.what: Three subsidiaries that pay dividends into other income; the bank also fully exited its life insurance joint venture with Ageas (Ageas Federal), booking a gain of Rs. 380 crores in the September 2022 quarter on top of an earlier Rs. 140–141 crore stake-sale gain in the June quarter.

overview.what_it_does: Vodafone Idea Limited (brand name "Vi") is an Indian mobile phone network operator — it sells wireless voice, SMS and mobile internet connectivity to consumers and businesses across India, using radio spectrum it buys at government auctions and a network of 4G and 5G sites it builds and runs. Most of its money comes from monthly recharges and plans bought by individual mobile subscribers, measured on the calls as ARPU (average revenue per user), which rose from Rs. 128 in the June 2022 quarter to Rs. 190 in the March 2026 quarter, across a subscriber base that fell from about 240 million in 2022 to 192.8 million by March 2026. It operates only in India, and concentrates its spending on 17 "priority circles" (licence regions) that management says generate about 98–99% of revenue. Full-year FY26 revenue was Rs. 44,873 crore with cash EBITDA of Rs. 9,217 crore; alongside the operating business, the calls devote heavy attention to raising equity and debt and to settling large government AGR dues, finalised at Rs. 64,046 crore.

parts.name: Consumer mobile — prepaid
parts.what: Pay-as-you-go mobile plans sold to individuals (e.g. the "Non-Stop Hero" unlimited-data plan and the "Vi Guarantee" extra-validity offer), which the calls describe as the main engine of new customer acquisition, renewals and upgrades and therefore the bulk of the business.

parts.name: Consumer mobile — postpaid
parts.what: Monthly-billed plans for higher-spending customers, such as Vi Max and the REDX / REDX Family plans bundling unlimited 4G/5G data, international roaming and lifestyle perks; smaller than prepaid but growing, with eight straight quarters of positive net additions by Q4 FY26.

parts.name: 4G / 5G network and spectrum
parts.what: The underlying asset base the company keeps buying and building — spectrum bought in auctions (Rs. 188 billion committed in 2022, Rs. 35.1 billion in 2024), around 527,000 broadband sites by September 2025, 5G live in 80+ cities across all 17 5G circles by May 2026, funded by capex of roughly Rs. 16,000 crore over six quarters against a stated three-year plan of Rs. 500–550 billion.

parts.name: Enterprise / business services ("Vi Business")
parts.what: Selling connectivity plus IoT, cloud, mobility, business communications, cybersecurity and fixed-line services to companies in banking, manufacturing, utilities, logistics and government; management repeatedly calls it a long-standing "strength area" and is adding a "Dedicated Enterprise Corridor" with ~1.3 Tbps of capacity across data centres, though no revenue figure is given.

parts.name: Digital services and advertising
parts.what: Apps and platforms layered on top of the phone business — the Vi app (now with an AI recharge assistant), Vi Movies & TV, music/gaming/jobs/education tie-ups, and the "Vi Ads" ad-tech platform that lets marketers reach its subscriber base — positioned as extra monetisation and customer stickiness rather than a large revenue line.

parts.name: International roaming
parts.what: Packs letting Indian travellers use their phone abroad, expanded from 98 to 151 countries, with truly unlimited data and calls in 40+ countries; management flags it as a key differentiator and focus area but gives no size.

overview.what_it_does: IDFC FIRST Bank is an Indian bank, formed by the merger of IDFC Bank and Capital First, that takes deposits from the public and lends the money out. It sells savings and current accounts, fixed deposits, and a wide range of loans — home/mortgage, vehicle, consumer, small-business (MSME), rural/agri, microfinance and credit cards to individual and small-business borrowers, plus corporate and commercial loans to companies. It earns most of its money from the spread between the interest it charges on loans (net interest margin around 5.9-6.2% on assets) and its cost of deposits (about 6%), topped up by fee income from lending, credit-card spends, wealth management, trade and foreign exchange, and occasional treasury/trading gains. It operates only in India, is listed on the NSE and BSE, and by the June 2026 quarter had a loan book of about INR3.05 lakh crore, customer deposits of just under INR3 lakh crore, and quarterly profit of INR1,075 crore.

parts.name: Deposits (CASA and retail deposits)
parts.what: The bank's funding engine — savings, current and fixed-deposit accounts gathered mainly from retail customers; customer deposits were close to INR3 lakh crore with CASA (low-cost current and savings money) at INR1.58 lakh crore, a CASA ratio above 50%, and management repeatedly calls this the foundation that gives it 'license to grow the loans'.

parts.name: Retail, Rural and MSME loans
parts.what: The core lending business — mortgages, vehicle loans, consumer loans, rural/agri and small-business loans — at about INR2.4 lakh crore (roughly four-fifths of the loan book), growing ~18% a year with gross NPAs of 1.40% and collection efficiency of 99.5%.

parts.name: Wholesale / corporate loans
parts.what: Loans to companies (non-infrastructure corporate and commercial banking, including trade and FX services that generate fees); about INR64,000 crore and the fastest-growing part at ~30% year-on-year, after the bank deliberately went slow here for years following its legacy problems.

parts.name: Microfinance (MFI)
parts.what: Small loans to low-income borrowers, a INR6,700 crore book that caused a stretch of heavy provisions and losses from about 2024 through 2025 but has since 'largely got restored' on asset quality, with 93% of it now covered by the government CGFMU guarantee scheme.

parts.name: Credit cards
parts.what: A consumer card business with 4.8 million cards in force and a INR9,600 crore outstanding book growing ~19%, with card spends up 22% year-on-year — a source of both interest and fee income.

parts.name: Wealth management
parts.what: Managing and distributing investments for customers, with assets under management of about INR64,000 crore growing 24% a year; a fee-income business rather than a lending one.

parts.name: Legacy infrastructure book
parts.what: Old infrastructure project loans (roughly INR12,000-13,000 crore of accounts at merger, including toll roads) inherited from the pre-merger IDFC Bank, which management has been running down and provisioning away — a shrinking drag rather than a business they are growing.

parts.name: Treasury
parts.what: The bank's own investment/trading book in government securities, which produced a INR181 crore gain in the June 2026 quarter; management treats it as volatile and reports 'core operating profit' excluding it.

overview.what_it_does: IEX runs an online marketplace in India where electricity is bought and sold — sellers (power generators, and more recently battery-storage operators) post offers, buyers (state distribution companies and large industrial/commercial users) post bids, and the exchange's auction matches them and sets a clearing price, such as the Rs 7.7 per unit average in the day-ahead market in the June 2022 quarter. It is a platform, not a power producer: it does not own generation, and its business is measured almost entirely by the volume of electricity traded across it, quoted in billion units (BU) — 23.4 BU in the quarter to June 2022, growing about 21% year-on-year in the June 2024 quarter. Alongside actual electricity it also runs a market in renewable energy certificates (RECs), tradable green credits, and management says trading of carbon credit certificates on power exchanges is being set up. It operates only in India, under rules set by the central regulator CERC and the Ministry of Power, and has been in business about 18 years as of 2026; its main stated risk is 'market coupling', a regulator-driven change that would pool day-ahead bids across exchanges via Grid India.

parts.name: Day-Ahead Market (DAM)
parts.what: A once-a-day auction for electricity to be delivered the following day — historically the core of the business (about 95% of total volume six to seven years before 2026, and 11.3 BU of 23.4 BU in the June 2022 quarter), and the one segment the regulator intends to 'couple' across exchanges.

parts.name: Real-Time Market (RTM)
parts.what: Auctions held through the day for near-immediate delivery, used to balance last-minute shortfalls; 6.2 BU in the June 2022 quarter and growing fast (up 34.5% year-on-year), with CERC proposing to cut the bidding window from 15 minutes to 5 to help manage renewables.

parts.name: Term-Ahead Market (TAM) / longer-duration contracts
parts.what: Contracts for delivery further out — daily and monthly contracts up to 90 days, launched June 2022 after CERC approval — letting distribution companies lock in supply for longer; 3.1 BU in the June 2022 quarter, more than double a year earlier, and the fastest-growing conventional segment at the time.

parts.name: Green Market (green day-ahead and term-ahead)
parts.what: The same kind of trading but specifically for renewable power, serving open-access consumers going green and renewable generators; a small piece at 1.5 BU in the June 2022 quarter, but management ties its growth to open-access rules, virtual PPAs and renewable consumption obligations.

parts.name: Renewable Energy Certificates (REC) market
parts.what: Trading of certificates that prove renewable generation, bought by companies who must meet green-power obligations; 11.97 lakh certificates in the June 2022 quarter, which management equates to roughly 1.2 BU of electricity.

parts.name: Carbon credit certificates (in development)
parts.what: A planned market in carbon credits for heavy-emitting sectors such as cement, steel and petrochemicals, with trading procedures still being drafted by BEE and Grid India as of April 2026 — described as a foundation laid, not yet a revenue line.

parts.name: Technology and customer platform
parts.what: Not a separate revenue segment but repeatedly flagged as what keeps customers loyal — web-based bidding, online financial reconciliation, API links for automated bidding and back-office, and data analytics, which management argues will preserve its market share even if market coupling arrives.

parts.name: Indian Gas Exchange (IGX)
parts.what: A gas trading exchange whose Chief Business Officer presents alongside IEX management at the analyst meet; the excerpts show it as part of the group's line-up but give no volume or financial detail.

overview.what_it_does: IFB Industries is an Indian manufacturer and seller of household appliances — mainly washing machines (front-load and top-load), air conditioners, and microwave ovens — sold under its own IFB brand to consumers in India through dealers/retail outlets and e-commerce (e-commerce was roughly 13%-17% of appliance sales in FY23), plus a smaller volume made for other companies as OEM/third-party supply. Alongside the consumer business it runs a separate Engineering Division (with its own Managing Director, CFO and plant) and, in the earlier calls, a Motor Division, which sell industrial/engineering products rather than to households. It makes money by manufacturing the products in its own plants and selling them at a mark-up, so profits swing with raw-material costs (copper, steel/GP sheet), the rupee-dollar rate on imported inputs, and how much it can raise prices against aggressive competitors like Samsung. Revenue grew from about INR4,344 crores in FY24 to INR5,476 crores in FY26, but margins are thin — PBDIT around 5%-6.5% of revenue and net profit only about 2%-2.5%.

parts.name: Home Appliances Division
parts.what: The main consumer business — front-load and top-load washing machines, air conditioners and microwave ovens sold under the IFB brand through dealers and online; it is the division management spends nearly all call time on and has its own MD/CEO, manufacturing head, CFO and national sales head.

parts.name: Air conditioners (within Home Appliances)
parts.what: A newer, fast-scaling but loss-making category — targeted at 350,000-400,000 units in FY23 at roughly INR30,000 average selling price and raised to 500,000 units for FY25; growth is meant to come from IFB-branded sales rather than OEM supply (AC OEM was only about INR8.5 crores of the ~INR200 crores of Q4 FY24 AC revenue), and its losses were the main drag holding group PBDIT down.

parts.name: Washing machines (within Home Appliances)
parts.what: The core, long-standing category where IFB competes in both front-load and top-load; management reported good double-digit volume growth and market-share gains in Q4 FY26, with front-load volumes up 7% for the full year FY26 and revenue up 11%.

parts.name: Engineering Division
parts.what: A separate non-consumer business with its own Managing Director (P.H. Narayanan), CFO (Jayanta Chanda) and plant head, present on every call but discussed far less than appliances, so the excerpts give no size for it.

parts.name: Motor Division
parts.what: A third unit with its own CEO (Anand Reddy) present on the FY23 call; it is not mentioned in the later calls, and the excerpts give no revenue or size for it.

parts.name: IFB Refrigeration (associate company)
parts.what: A 41.40%-owned associate that IFB does not consolidate but takes a share of losses from — it lost over INR59 crores on revenue of INR161 crores in FY24, of which IFB's share was INR24.16 crores, and it was still not at breakeven.

overview.what_it_does: IGI is an independent testing-and-grading lab for diamonds, jewellery and coloured stones: customers send in stones and finished jewellery, IGI's gemologists examine them and issue a certificate (a "report") stating the 4Cs — cut, colour, clarity, carat — plus, increasingly, origin and traceability. Its customers are the trade rather than the public: diamond manufacturers, wholesalers, jewellery brands and retail chains (management says it serves nine of India's ten largest jewellery chains and over 7,500 customers globally), who need a trusted third-party stamp so buyers and sellers can price and transact with confidence. It makes money on a per-report fee, so revenue is essentially report volume times average selling price — about 3.56 million reports at roughly INR 1,010 per report in the June 2026 quarter — a very high-margin model (EBITDA margin around 60%, PAT margin around 45%, and the company is debt-free). It is headquartered in India but operates globally, with 31 laboratories, 12 in-factory labs and 18 gemology schools across 10 countries; the Indian listed entity bought the IGI Belgium and Netherlands businesses in December 2024 for Rs 1,345 crore and added US-based American Gemological Laboratories in January 2026, and it claims over 50% share in India, ~33% of global diamond certification and ~65% of lab-grown diamond certification.

parts.name: Lab-Grown Diamonds (LGD) - loose stones
parts.what: Grading and certifying man-made diamonds, described as the company's volume engine and the segment where it claims roughly 65% global share; it grew 24-35% year-on-year across the quarters discussed and management expects the growing supply and retail acceptance of lab-growns to keep widening the market for certification.

parts.name: LGD Jewellery
parts.what: Certifying finished jewellery set with lab-grown diamonds — one of the fastest-growing lines, up 26% in Q3 CY25, 29% in the March 2026 quarter and 44% in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Natural Diamonds - loose stones
parts.what: The original business of grading mined diamonds, which management calls a "key strategic pillar" where it is pushing to win share through new customers and more wallet share; growth has cooled from 29% in Q3 CY25 and 18% over the 15-month period to 6% in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Natural Diamond Jewellery
parts.what: Certification of finished jewellery containing natural diamonds; the softest line recently (about 2% growth in the June 2026 quarter), which management attributes to volatile gold and silver prices.

parts.name: Coloured Stones / Gemstones and other certification
parts.what: Certification of coloured gemstones, a newer and still small but rapidly expanding avenue that grew over 200% in the June 2026 quarter, driven mainly by the AGL acquisition; management frames it as a way to widen the addressable market beyond diamonds.

parts.name: American Gemological Laboratories (AGL)
parts.what: A US coloured-stone certification business acquired in January 2026 that gives IGI direct access to the US market; it added about 3% to revenue growth and 2% to EBITDA growth in the June 2026 quarter, with plans to extend it into other geographies.

parts.name: Overseas subsidiaries (Belgium / Netherlands holding structure)
parts.what: The international lab network bought into the Indian listed entity in December 2024 for Rs 1,345 crore; management says these subsidiaries grew in line with India in the June 2026 quarter and were used to open operations in Italy.

parts.name: Delivery formats - IGI labs, in-factory labs and mobile labs
parts.what: Rather than a separate revenue line, this is how the certification service reaches customers — 31 own laboratories plus 12 labs placed inside customers' factories and mobile units, which management says tighten customer relationships and are a competitive advantage.

parts.name: IGI School of Gemology
parts.what: 18 gemology schools that train people in the trade; management presents them not as a meaningful profit source but as a way to build the brand, open markets and bring in new customers.

overview.what_it_does: Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) is one of India's leading city gas distribution (CGD) companies: it buys natural gas, pipes it through its own network, and sells it in two forms — CNG as vehicle fuel sold through its own filling stations, and PNG (piped natural gas) delivered to homes, shops/restaurants and factories. Its customers are motorists (about 20 lakh vehicles as of 2024), roughly 32.75 lakh households, ~5,400 industrial and ~7,400 commercial customers, plus bus fleets such as Delhi's DTC and DIMTS. It makes money on the spread between the cost of the gas it procures and the price it charges, which management tracks as EBITDA per standard cubic metre (guided at Rs. 7–8 per SCM; Rs. 5.4 in Q3 FY26), on volumes of about 9.4 million standard cubic metres a day and quarterly revenue of roughly Rs. 4,465 crores. It operates 12 licensed 'geographical areas' across 4 states — Delhi (still ~70% of volumes but shrinking as a share), Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan — running over 2,500 km of steel pipeline, ~29,200 km of MDPE distribution pipe and 955 CNG stations.

parts.name: CNG (compressed natural gas for vehicles)
parts.what: Sells compressed gas as motor fuel at its own stations to cars, autos, taxis, commercial vehicles and city buses; it is the biggest part of the business at roughly 6.9–7.0 million SCM a day (over 50 lakh kg/day) out of ~9.4 million total, growing ~3% headline but ~10% once the shrinking DTC bus volumes are excluded.

parts.name: PNG – domestic (household piped gas)
parts.what: Piped gas supplied to more than 32.75 lakh homes for cooking and heating, growing around 8% year-on-year and part of the ~2.5 million SCM/day total PNG segment.

parts.name: PNG – industrial and commercial
parts.what: Piped gas sold to about 5,400 factories and 7,400 shops, hotels and other commercial establishments as a substitute for liquid fuels; commercial demand grew ~8% recently while industrial demand was described as subdued.

parts.name: LNG stations / green logistics
parts.what: A newer, small business of LNG refuelling stations for long-haul trucking — one station was doing 4,000–5,000 kg/day in 2024 with 5–6 more planned and a Board-approved target of around 100 stations over 5–6 years; management calls the sector 'at the nascent stage' but expects it to contribute meaningfully.

parts.name: Joint ventures / associate gas companies (CUGL, MNGL)
parts.what: Minority stakes in other city gas distributors whose profits add to IGL's earnings — MNGL was selling about 1.1 million SCM/day and growing ~9%, while CUGL was around 0.33 million SCM/day with flat volumes and lower profits (as of the Jan 2023 call).

parts.name: Saudi Arabia joint venture (new)
parts.what: A planned 40%-equity JV with a local partner to build gas distribution in Saudi industrial cities that currently run on liquid fuels — IGL contributes technical, operational and safety expertise, with each industrial city said to hold potential of 1–1.5 million SCM of gas; it is an early-stage investment, not yet contributing revenue.

overview.what_it_does: IIFL Finance is an Indian non-bank lender (an NBFC listed on the BSE and NSE, headquartered in Mumbai) that makes small-ticket retail loans to ordinary households, small shopkeepers and micro-businesses across India through a large branch network — over 30,000 employees and more than 1,000 branches added in a single 15-month stretch — supported by WhatsApp, app-based do-it-yourself borrowing and door-step 'gold loan at home' service. Its main products are loans against household gold jewellery, affordable home loans and loans against property, microfinance loans to low-income women, and MSME/business loans, with roughly 95%+ of its book classified by management as 'core' retail products and nearly 90% of it secured. It earns money on the spread between what it charges borrowers and its cost of borrowing (average cost of funds around 9.1% in FY27's first quarter, funded by bank term loans, bonds, commercial paper and a $500 million social bond), plus fee income; it deliberately keeps a large share of loans off its own balance sheet by co-lending with banks and by selling loans down through direct assignment and securitisation, which lets it grow without using much capital. It operates only in India; the loan book crossed ₹1,15,523 crore by June 2026, with return on equity around 19.5% and gross NPAs at 1.6%.

parts.name: Gold loans
parts.what: Short-term loans against customers' gold jewellery, described by management as the 'primary growth engine' — about ₹58,406 crore of the ₹1.15 lakh crore book (roughly half) by June 2026, backed by 62 tonnes of gold; the RBI barred new gold lending in March 2024 over assaying, cash-disbursal and auction lapses, which more than halved the book before the business was allowed to resume and rebuild.

parts.name: Home loans / mortgages (IIFL Home Finance Limited)
parts.what: A separately run housing finance subsidiary doing affordable home loans and mid-sized loans against property; management said it was almost half the group's business back in 2022, has grown slowly and flat more recently with stress in a legacy 'micro LAP' portfolio, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority put in ₹2,200 crore for a 20% stake in it.

parts.name: Microfinance (IIFL Samasta Finance Limited)
parts.what: Tiny unsecured loans to low-income, largely rural and semi-urban women borrowers through a separate subsidiary; it has been the group's most volatile part — repeated restructuring, high provisions and election-period stress — but management describes it as recovering, and they are considering a stake sale or listing of it to raise capital.

parts.name: MSME / business loans and digital finance
parts.what: Loans to small and medium businesses, increasingly sold through the existing branch network and digital channels (including a joint venture with SME neo-banking platform Open Financial Technologies); one of the four 'core products' but a smaller, faster-growing base on which management stays cautious because much of it is unsecured.

parts.name: Co-lending and assigned loan book (capital-efficient / off-book model)
parts.what: Rather than holding every loan itself, IIFL originates loans jointly with banks or sells them on — ₹26,118 crore of assigned loans and ₹14,647 crore of co-lending assets as of June 2026, across 15 active bank partners — which management calls one of its three strategic pillars and the reason it can grow while capital adequacy in the parent NBFC sits near the regulatory edge.

parts.name: AI-led operating model
parts.what: Not a lending product but a stated third pillar: using AI across lead generation, underwriting, collections, fraud detection and cross-selling, which management says is moving from pilot to measurable gains in productivity and credit cost.

overview.what_it_does: IIFL Capital Services (formerly IIFL Securities) is an Indian capital-markets firm that lets people and institutions buy and sell shares and derivatives on the Indian exchanges, and sells them investment products alongside that. It earns brokerage commissions from retail customers and from institutional investors, fees from investment banking deals such as IPOs and NCD issues, commissions for distributing financial products like mutual funds, AIFs, PMS, insurance and fixed income, and interest income from lending money to clients to buy shares (the margin trading or MTF book). Management describes it as a focused Indian capital market and wealth management player, run out of India across a branch and partner network, and says the legacy retail broking business is being transformed into a wealth practice built on accumulating client assets rather than one-off transaction income. FY26 operational revenue was about INR2,439 crore; Fairfax India has proposed to invest INR2,000 crore and take at least 51%, subject to regulatory approval.

parts.name: Retail broking (retail equity)
parts.what: Share and derivatives trading accounts for individual investors, largely opened and traded digitally on discount/flat brokerage plans, contributing roughly INR1,121 crore of revenue in FY26 and making it the single largest revenue line; SEBI's tightening of index derivative expiry rules cut into it.

parts.name: Institutional equities (institutional broking)
parts.what: Broking and research services sold to large investing institutions, worth roughly INR450 crore of the combined INR712 crore institutional and investment banking revenue in FY26.

parts.name: Investment banking
parts.what: Raising capital for companies through share and bond issues, a lumpy but high-margin business worth roughly INR250 crore in FY26 that swings sharply with primary market conditions.

parts.name: Financial product distribution (FPD)
parts.what: Selling third-party investment and insurance products — mutual funds, AIFs, PMS, fixed income and insurance — for commission; income grew 16% to about INR590 crore in FY26 and assets under distribution rose from roughly INR31,000 crore to INR52,000 crore, making it the fastest-growing part of the company.

parts.name: Wealth management / affluent business
parts.what: Relationship-manager-led advice for well-off clients, the declared strategic priority under joint CEOs hired from ASK, staffed by about 50 wealth RMs plus around 300 affluent/PCG broking RMs.

parts.name: Margin trading facility (MTF) / lending book
parts.what: Lending clients money against securities so they can trade larger positions, generating interest income of about INR419 crore in FY25 and driving the company's borrowing and finance costs.

parts.name: Manufacturing (own funds - AIF, PMS, credit and late-stage funds)
parts.what: A newer effort to run its own investment products rather than only distribute others', including a roughly INR500 crore credit opportunities fund and about INR4,400 crore of AIF and PMS AUM, with the income currently reported inside financial product distribution.

overview.what_it_does: IKS Health (Inventurus Knowledge Solutions) sells what management calls a "care enablement platform" — a tech-plus-people service that takes over roughly 16 administrative and back-office "chore" tasks that US doctors and their staff would otherwise do themselves, such as clinical documentation, medical coding, billing and revenue-cycle work, patient financial clearance, scheduling and physician inbox management. Its customers are large US physician enterprises and health systems — some owned by hospital systems, some independent, private-equity-owned or listed — numbering a little over 600 client organizations as of March 2026, down from ~900 after the AQuity deal as IKS deliberately dropped small accounts. It earns money on long-running, largely outcome-based contracts that produce annuity-like revenue: about 90% of revenue comes from repeat customers, and the top 5 and top 10 clients average over five years of tenure. The work is sold into the United States but delivered by a global workforce of 13,331 people (as of March 2026), mainly split between the US and India, including 1,981 clinically trained staff and 550 technologists building its own software; management sizes the addressable market at over $260 billion of US provider spend on such tasks, of which ~$35 billion is currently outsourced and growing ~12% a year.

parts.name: Care Enablement Platform / "platform system of action"
parts.what: The core business: one bundled platform covering all ~16 delegable tasks at once instead of individual point solutions, which management calls its main competitive moat and the source of essentially all current revenue.

parts.name: Revenue cycle features (RCM, coding, patient financial clearance, denial prevention, optimized scheduling)
parts.what: The money side of the platform — getting the provider paid — and the area where management says AI is being applied hardest, including denial prediction and prevention.

parts.name: Clinical documentation and care-team productivity features
parts.what: The care side — an autonomous ambient clinical documentation ("scribe") product plus physician inbox and clinical data management, now stitched to the billing features into what IKS calls the industry's first "encounter-to-reimbursement" platform.

parts.name: AQuity (acquired ~Nov 2023)
parts.what: An acquisition that took the client base from ~50 large enterprise accounts to 850+ (since pruned toward 500–600) and brought a big health-system install base; management says integration is done and the margin turnaround from the 24% pro-forma level is essentially complete, and it is a main driver of recent margin expansion, while cross-selling into that base is still early ("first innings").

parts.name: TruBridge (definitive merger agreement signed April 2026, announced separately from quarterly results)
parts.what: A pending acquisition of the leading electronic-health-record "system of record" for small rural US hospitals — about 700 hospitals, roughly 40%+ share of the 0–50 bed segment and ~30% of all 2,200 rural hospitals in a $164 billion market — intended to let IKS own both the record system and the task platform in a niche where it won't compete with big EHR vendors like Epic.

overview.what_it_does: Indian Metals & Ferro Alloys Limited (IMFA) is an Odisha-based metals and mining company that makes ferrochrome, an alloy that stainless steel mills melt into their furnaces, and it describes itself as India's leading fully integrated ferrochrome producer. "Fully integrated" means it does the whole chain itself: it digs chrome ore out of its own mines (Sukinda and Mahagiri, with leases running to 2049 and 2055), burns coal in its own captive power plants to make the large amounts of electricity smelting requires, and smelts the ore into ferrochrome at its plants at Therubali and Choudwar, with 190 MVA of furnace capacity and about 204.55 MW of captive power before recent expansion. It earns money by selling roughly 60,000–68,000 tonnes of ferrochrome per quarter, mostly on long-term offtake contracts with prices reset monthly or quarterly rather than spot deals, at realizations that ranged from about INR 87,000 to INR 1,21,000 per tonne over the period discussed; profit is essentially the gap between that price and its cost of ore, coke and power. Around 90% of sales are exports with about 10% domestic (management says it is now pivoting toward more domestic sales), and it is growing through a new Kalinganagar plant plus the INR 610 crore purchase of Tata Steel's Kalinganagar ferrochrome plant, which management says makes it India's largest ferrochrome maker and sixth largest globally with capacity above 0.5 million tonnes.

parts.name: Ferro Alloys Business Unit
parts.what: The core money-maker: smelts chrome ore into ferrochrome and sells it, mainly exported to stainless steel producers under long-term contracts, running at roughly 63,000–68,500 tonnes of production a quarter and driving essentially all of the reported revenue and profit.

parts.name: Mines Business Unit
parts.what: Runs the company's own chrome ore mines (Sukinda and Mahagiri), raising roughly 1.58 lakh to 2.65 lakh tonnes of chrome ore per quarter to feed the smelters — it is a cost-control and security-of-supply arm rather than a separate sales business, and management says the reserves last as long as the leases, to 2049 and 2055.

parts.name: Power Business Unit
parts.what: Generates about 256–260 million units of captive electricity a quarter from coal-fired plants (plus 4.55 MWp of solar) to run the furnaces; since smelting consumes roughly 4,000 units of power per tonne of ferrochrome, coal and power cost swings are one of the biggest levers on profitability.

parts.name: Kalinganagar greenfield project ("KNR 1")
parts.what: A newly built smelting plant with furnaces being switched on around July 2026 — an expansion of ferrochrome capacity, not yet contributing to results in the period covered.

parts.name: Kalinganagar acquisition from Tata Steel ("KNR 2")
parts.what: The purchase of Tata Steel's Kalinganagar ferrochrome plant for a base INR 610 crores, adding 99 MVA of furnace capacity; the deal closed 27 February 2026 and it contributed about 2,200 tonnes in Q4 FY26 and is running at roughly 6,000 tonnes a month thereafter.

parts.name: Ethanol project
parts.what: A small diversification outside metals, delayed several times and now expected to commission in Q2 FY27, with management saying it will start adding to the top line only from FY27.

parts.name: Renewable power tie-ups
parts.what: Contracted hybrid renewable supply of 70 MW from JSW Energy and 65 MW from Enfinity Global, totalling 135 MW, intended to cut carbon emissions and lock in stable power prices rather than to be sold as a business.

overview.what_it_does: Indegene is a Bengaluru-headquartered services company that calls itself a "digital-first commercialization partner" to the global life sciences industry — large and mid-size pharmaceutical companies, biotech firms and medical device makers. It does not discover drugs; it runs the work that comes after the lab: sales and marketing content and campaigns, medical affairs, regulatory, drug safety/pharmacovigilance, and omnichannel operations, increasingly delivered through its own AI platforms (Invisage, Content Super App, NEXT Medical Writing, NAEM, plus Tandem data from its BioPharm acquisition in October 2025). It earns money from multi-year client engagements and project work — mostly an outcome-based managed-services pricing model rather than pure hourly billing — sold to business owners such as brand and commercial teams, chief medical officers and heads of regulatory and safety, not to client IT departments. Work is delivered from India plus 17 offices worldwide by roughly 5,000 staff mixing doctors, PhDs and pharmacologists with data scientists and creative/omnichannel specialists; about 65% of revenue comes from the United States and 32% from Europe, and it serves all of the top 20 global pharma companies, with revenue growing from INR 2,589 crore in FY24 to INR 3,510 crore in FY26.

parts.name: Enterprise Commercial Solutions (ECS)
parts.what: The largest segment — enterprise-wide sales and marketing work (content, campaigns, commercial operations) contracted across a client's whole brand portfolio and many countries at once, rather than brand by brand; together with EMS it made up 86.6% of revenue in Q1 FY26.

parts.name: Enterprise Medical Solutions (EMS)
parts.what: The medical side of the business — medical affairs, regulatory and drug-safety/pharmacovigilance processes run for clients globally; management put it at roughly 23% of revenue in FY24, with ECS + EMS then at about 82%.

parts.name: Brand Activation (renamed from Omnichannel Activation in FY26)
parts.what: Smaller, more project-like marketing work done for a single brand or therapeutic area in one country, focused mainly on the US and a few Western European markets; it is lumpier — it fell 21.6% quarter-on-quarter in Q1 FY26 when one project went on hold and another finished.

parts.name: Others
parts.what: A residual catch-all segment that contributed only about 3.5% of revenue in Q1 FY26 and is too small to move consolidated results.

parts.name: Tectonic (reported inside ECS)
parts.what: A newer push to move upstream into creative/agency-of-record marketing work traditionally done by specialist healthcare agencies, using Indegene's AI and global operations; it started with over $1 million of revenue across two top-20 clients in Q1 FY26 and won a significant engagement with the largest customer starting in Germany at the end of FY26.

overview.what_it_does: IHCL (The Indian Hotels Company Limited) is a Tata-group hospitality company that runs and franchises hotels, resorts, homestays and restaurants, mostly in India, under a family of brands led by the luxury Taj brand plus Vivanta, SeleQtions, Gateway, the budget/mid-scale Ginger, Tree of Life, Claridges (licensed) and the ama homestay brand. It makes money two ways: from hotels it owns or leases, where it books the full room, food and banquet revenue (weddings, conferences, leisure and business travellers, and increasingly foreign tourists), and from hotels owned by third parties that it merely operates under management contracts, where it collects a management fee with very little capital of its own — fees reached INR 168 crores in the June 2026 quarter, up 26%. Management calls this the 'capital-light' strategy: 68% of its operating portfolio and 93% of its pipeline are managed or asset-light. Consolidated revenue was INR 9,971 crores in FY 2025-26 with a 34.9% EBITDA margin and over INR 2,000 crores of profit, from a portfolio approaching 650 hotels (about 382 operational, 265 in pipeline, 64,000-plus rooms) concentrated in India but also including Dubai, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Nepal and Frankfurt.

parts.name: Hotel segment (owned, leased and managed hotels)
parts.what: The core business of running full-service hotels and resorts across luxury to mid-scale — described on the Q1 FY27 call as roughly 87-90% of the company's revenue, with domestic RevPAR up 14% and segment margins of 32.6%.

parts.name: Taj (flagship luxury brand)
parts.what: The company's crown-jewel luxury brand — grew from 31 hotels five years before the Feb 2023 call to 75 then, takes more than three-quarters of enterprise EBITDA, and was named India's strongest brand across all sectors for the fifth straight year with brand value near $900 million.

parts.name: Management contracts / capital-light growth (management fee income)
parts.what: Operating hotels for third-party owners in exchange for fees — a high-flow-through, margin-boosting income stream that crossed INR 100 crores in a quarter for the first time in Q2 FY25 and reached INR 168 crores in Q1 FY27, with management guiding to high-teens CAGR growth.

parts.name: Gateway
parts.what: The relaunched full-service upscale brand aimed at metros and Tier 2/3 cities with large banqueting facilities — 22 hotels when relaunched in late 2024, targeted to reach 100 hotels by 2030.

parts.name: Ginger (part of 'new'/'growth' businesses)
parts.what: The lean-luxe budget and mid-scale hotel chain, the largest of the growth brands — consolidated revenue of INR 183 crores in Q1 FY27 (up 20%) at a 39% EBITDA margin, having crossed a 100-hotel portfolio in 2024.

parts.name: Qmin
parts.what: The food-and-beverage brand — all-day dining inside Ginger hotels plus quick-service outlets, shop-in-shop counters in Westside stores and airport locations — which grew from 25 outlets in early 2023 to over 100 by mid-2026.

parts.name: ama Stays & Trails
parts.what: The homestay/bungalow business offering boutique stays outside conventional hotels — over 380 bungalows in the portfolio with 196 in operation as of Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Tree of Life
parts.what: A boutique experiential resort brand acquired via a 55% stake in Rajscape Hotels for INR 18 crores in 2024, now over 40 resorts with 23 in operation.

parts.name: TajSATS (airline and institutional catering)
parts.what: The inflight-catering arm, fully consolidated into IHCL in 2024, which leads the market with a 59% share of meals served in the skies and posted INR 254 crores of revenue at a 24% EBITDA margin in the quarter it was consolidated.

parts.name: Recent acquisitions — Brij and Atmantan
parts.what: Small bolt-on businesses adding boutique hotels (Brij: 11 operational hotels, INR 11 crores of quarterly revenue) and premium integrated wellness resorts (Atmantan: INR 19 crores of quarterly revenue), part of over INR 500 crores deployed across four strategic acquisitions.

parts.name: Asset management (upgrading owned hotels)
parts.what: Renovating and expanding its own marquee properties — over INR 2,500 crores spent in three years with INR 1,000-1,200 crores planned annually — to lift room rates and returns, as with the new 100-room wing at Taj Ganges that turned profitable in its first quarter.

parts.name: Loyalty and distribution (Tata Neu)
parts.what: The group loyalty program, with about seven million members by late 2024, that drove roughly 42% of enterprise revenue and is presented as a key customer-acquisition enabler rather than a separate profit line.

parts.name: New / growth businesses vertical (combined)
parts.what: Ginger, Qmin, ama and Tree of Life reported together as one vertical — INR 753 crores of consolidated revenue in FY26, up 25% (31% CAGR over four years) and about 10% of enterprise revenue, which management expects to rise.

overview.what_it_does: India Cements Limited is an Indian cement maker, run out of Chennai, that manufactures and sells bagged grey cement to builders, dealers and government/institutional buyers, mostly in southern India (its Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh belt, with a smaller share sold outside the south). It makes money by burning coal and petcoke to produce clinker at a collection of plants of different vintages — some built by the company, some acquired, such as the Raasi group, Sankarnagar/Sankari, Chilamakuru and Dalavoi — grinding that clinker with fly ash into cement, and selling it as close to the factory as possible so freight stays low; profitability swings mainly on cement prices, fuel cost per kilocalorie and how much of the plants' capacity it can actually run. Roughly 57% of volumes went through the 'trade' (dealer/retail) channel in Q4 FY24, the rest non-trade (bulk/institutional). By 2026 the company had become a subsidiary of UltraTech Cement: it now manufactures and sells cement under the UltraTech brand under a tolling-style arrangement, with marketing and distribution costs sitting at the parent and UltraTech charging it a markup per bag, and it reported EBITDA of ₹497 per tonne and a quarterly profit of ₹60 crore in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Cement
parts.what: The core and overwhelmingly dominant business — making clinker and grinding it into grey cement across several southern plants and selling it through trade and non-trade channels; everything management discusses on the calls (fuel cost per kilocalorie, prices, capacity utilisation, lead distance, efficiency capex) is about this business.

parts.name: Ready Mix Concrete (RMC) division
parts.what: A small side business supplying ready-mixed concrete, doing about ₹27 crore of revenue and ₹2.2 crore of EBITDA in the March 2024 quarter — a rounding error next to cement.

parts.name: Shipping
parts.what: A small shipping operation that management reports separately as a 'housekeeping' number, with about ₹7.4 crore turnover and ₹1.7 crore EBITDA in the March 2024 quarter.

parts.name: Wind power (windmills)
parts.what: A tiny captive/wind-generation arm described by management as 'very marginal' — about ₹0.5 crore of revenue and negative ₹1 crore EBITDA in the March 2024 quarter, i.e. it loses money.

parts.name: Non-core asset and land monetisation
parts.what: Not a trading business but a stated source of cash used to cut debt — selling surplus land parcels when the price and buyer are right, and disposing of units such as the Parli grinding unit, sold for ₹315 crore, with management saying it will sell only to the extent necessary.

parts.name: Efficiency / modernisation capex programme
parts.what: An ongoing spending plan of roughly ₹700 crore over two years (about ₹500 crore on efficiency projects such as waste heat recovery at Chilamakuru, a vertical roller mill at Sankari, cooler upgrades and a crusher at Sankarnagar, plus ~₹100 crore a year of routine capex) aimed at lowering power and grinding costs and lifting output — continued after the UltraTech acquisition as an 'investment phase'.

overview.what_it_does: India Glycols is an Indian manufacturer that turns alcohol (ethanol) made from crops — grain, rice, corn and molasses — into three main kinds of products: industrial chemicals, drinking liquor, and fuel-grade ethanol that oil companies blend into petrol. It sells bulk and specialty chemicals to industrial customers in India and abroad (including surfactant ingredients used by companies like Unilever and oilfield chemicals shipped to the Middle East), bottled Indian-made foreign liquor to consumers through state markets and the army canteen (CSD) channel, ethanol to the government's fuel-blending programme, and plant-based extracts and nutraceutical ingredients to pharma customers. Money comes mostly from selling these products at a margin over its main input costs — ethanol/grain, coal and energy — helped by making its own ethanol in-house instead of importing it, plus a steady stream of profit-share income from a chemicals joint venture with Clariant to which it supplies ethylene oxide. It is headquartered near Delhi (Noida) with plants at Kashipur in Uttarakhand and Gorakhpur, and reported FY26 gross revenue of about ₹9,827 crore, net revenue of ₹4,211 crore, EBITDA of ₹654 crore (15.5% margin) and profit of ₹293 crore.

parts.name: Bio-based Specialties and Performance Chemicals (BSPC / Chemicals)
parts.what: Makes ethanol-derived industrial and specialty chemicals — including green/bio-based surfactant ingredients, oilfield chemicals, specialty amines, plasticizers and green solvents — and at ₹1,203 crore of FY26 net revenue with ₹141 crore EBIT it is one of the three big segments; sales dipped about 10% in FY26 as management deliberately dropped low-margin business, but margins rose to 11.7%.

parts.name: Potable Spirits (Liquor / IMFL)
parts.what: Makes and sells Indian-made foreign liquor, including its own brands (Bunty Bubbly is described as the largest selling brand in the country) plus tie-ups with Bacardi and Amrut; at ₹1,331 crore FY26 revenue, 14.4% growth, ₹285 crore EBIT and roughly 23.7 million cases sold in nine months, it is the most profitable of the main segments and a key growth driver.

parts.name: Bio-Fuels
parts.what: Produces grain-based ethanol sold into India's petrol-blending programme; carved out as its own reported segment only from mid-2024 because it had grown too big to sit inside Chemicals, it was the fastest grower in FY26 at ₹1,470 crore revenue (up 40.9%) with EBIT nearly doubling to ₹115 crore as national blending reached 20%.

parts.name: Ennature Biopharma
parts.what: Sells plant-derived pharma and nutraceutical ingredients — management highlights leadership in thiocolchicoside plus a growing nicotine business and newly launched branded nutraceuticals — and is the smallest of the four segments, with FY26 revenue roughly flat and margins under pressure.

parts.name: Clariant joint venture (ethylene oxide derivatives, the former EOD business)
parts.what: The ethylene oxide derivatives business was transferred into a joint venture with Clariant, so instead of showing up as sales it appears mainly as 'other income'; India Glycols supplies EO to the JV, and management says this income is large enough that including it lifts the reported quarterly EBITDA margin from about 17.1% to roughly 20.8%.

parts.name: New value-added / performance chemicals pipeline
parts.what: A newer effort built from scratch through R&D, a pilot plant and a dedicated new plant, targeting around 20 products across six segments (specialty amines, oilfield products, plasticizers, green solvents and more); still a small part of Chemicals revenue but management calls the pipeline strong and expects it to drive future growth.

overview.what_it_does: IndiaMART InterMESH runs India's large online business-to-business marketplace, a website and app where buyers looking for products post enquiries and suppliers (mostly small and mid-sized Indian businesses) list their catalogues, so the platform's core job is matchmaking and discovery rather than trading goods itself. It makes money almost entirely by selling paid annual or monthly subscription packages to suppliers — tiered as Silver, Gold and Platinum — who pay to be listed and to receive buyer enquiries; buyers use the platform free, and management describes buyer-side income as indirect (via seller enquiries/RFQs and some advertising-style audience monetisation). Cash is collected upfront and recognised as revenue over the subscription period, which is why the calls track 'collections from customers' and a large 'deferred revenue' pool separately from reported revenue. The business is India-focused, and alongside the marketplace it owns BUSY Infotech, an accounting-software business that sells licences to small businesses; consolidated revenue was about Rs. 1,569 crores in FY26 (year to March 2026) with roughly 2.2 lakh paying suppliers.

parts.name: IndiaMART standalone (the B2B marketplace / web services business)
parts.what: The core online marketplace matching buyers' enquiries with suppliers, monetised through Silver/Gold/Platinum supplier subscriptions — it is the overwhelming bulk of the group, contributing Rs. 402 crores of the Rs. 463 crores of consolidated collections in the June 2026 quarter, with about 26–27 million unique business enquiries a quarter.

parts.name: Platinum and Gold subscribers
parts.what: The premium, higher-priced supplier tiers that management repeatedly calls the profit engine — roughly 50% of the paying customer base but more than 75% of revenue, with very low monthly churn (under 1% for Platinum, 1–1.5% for Gold).

parts.name: Silver subscribers (monthly and annual)
parts.what: The entry-level, cheaper supplier packages that bring in volume but churn heavily (about 4% a month for Silver annual and 7% for Silver monthly), and are the main reason the total paying-supplier count has stalled and even declined in recent quarters.

parts.name: BUSY Infotech (accounting software segment)
parts.what: A wholly-owned accounting-software subsidiary acquired in April 2022 that sells licences to small businesses — about 4.54 lakh cumulative licences sold by June 2026, with FY26 revenue of Rs. 119 crores and billing of Rs. 170 crores, so a small but fast-growing slice (well under a tenth) of group revenue.

parts.name: Trust, verification and platform-quality services
parts.what: Features layered onto the marketplace to make matching safer — multi-layer seller KYC, TrustSEAL verification, supplier ratings and reviews, newer buyer-side verification and a Buyer Payment Protection Programme — described as central to retention rather than as a separate revenue line.

parts.name: AI and automation on the platform
parts.what: AI embedded across discovery — standardised cataloguing, intelligent matchmaking, content moderation, and an agentic call-handling system said to handle over 1 lakh calls a day — presented as a cost and quality lever, not a standalone business.

parts.name: IndiaMART Finance Limited (new subsidiary)
parts.what: A wholly-owned finance arm approved in the June 2026 quarter to facilitate short-term transaction credit for MSMEs, explicitly working with partner lenders rather than lending large amounts off IndiaMART's own balance sheet; still at the starting line with no revenue disclosed.

parts.name: Minority investments (Finlite Technologies, IDfy/Baldor Technologies and similar)
parts.what: Stakes in adjacent digital businesses — 51% of Finlite Technologies alongside the BUSY deal, and a 10% stake in Baldor Technologies which runs IDfy, an identity/KYC and verification platform — small bets aligned with 'empowering businesses digitally' rather than material revenue contributors.

parts.name: Treasury / cash portfolio
parts.what: A large investment book built from the subscription cash collected upfront — Rs. 3,553 crores of cash and treasury as of June 2026 — whose mark-to-market swings move 'other income' and reported net profit sharply from quarter to quarter, in both directions.

parts.name: Buyer monetisation experiments
parts.what: Early-stage attempts to earn from the buyer side, including a paid buyer programme with value-added services being tested on the website and monetising buyer audience data through third-party advertising retargeting — management stresses these are experiments and it does not charge buyers per transaction.

overview.what_it_does: Indian Bank is an Indian commercial bank, run out of a corporate office in Chennai and listed on the NSE and BSE, that takes deposits from the public and lends the money back out. On the deposit side it gathers current and savings accounts (CASA, about 40% of deposits) plus fixed/term deposits; on the lending side it makes loans to individuals, farmers, small businesses and large companies, with total advances of roughly Rs 6.85 lakh crore as of Q1 FY27. It earns mainly the spread between what it pays depositors (cost of deposits) and what it charges borrowers (yield on advances) — the resulting net interest income was about Rs 26,915 crore in FY26 — topped up by fee income, foreign-exchange income, sale of priority-sector lending certificates, recoveries of previously written-off bad loans, and profits on its bond/treasury portfolio. It operates through a branch network and increasingly through digital channels (about 90% of transactions are digital), is mostly domestic but has some overseas/global business, and management steers the bank against public guidance on deposit growth, loan growth, margins, bad loans and recoveries.

parts.name: RAM — Retail, Agri and MSME
parts.what: The bank's core lending engine to individuals, farmers and small businesses, which management repeatedly calls out as its growth driver at about 61% of the loan book in 2022 rising to 66% by Q1 FY27, growing 14-15% a year.

parts.name: Retail loans
parts.what: Home loans, car/auto loans, personal loans and jewel (gold-backed) loans to individual customers; the fastest-growing piece within RAM at roughly 18-19% growth in FY26 and Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Jewel / gold loans
parts.what: Loans against gold jewellery, made to both retail and farm customers, which management calls a 'strength area' — it grew about 28% to Rs 1.27 trillion by FY26 and makes up around 78% of the farm credit book.

parts.name: Agriculture lending
parts.what: Crop/farm credit, investment credit, allied agri, farm infrastructure and self-help-group lending to rural borrowers; growing in the high teens in most years, though it slowed to about 10% in Q1 FY27 on jewel-loan system issues.

parts.name: MSME lending
parts.what: Loans to micro, small and medium businesses — roughly 6 lakh loans and Rs 48,000 crore sanctioned in FY26, growing 16-17% — and historically the segment where the bank sees the most repayment stress; it also carries government-guaranteed ECLGS credit of about Rs 11,000 crore eligible, Rs 5,000 crore disbursed.

parts.name: Corporate lending
parts.what: Large-company loans, which shrank or barely grew in some years (down 2% in FY23, up 3% in FY25) but picked up to about 9-11% growth in FY26 and Q1 FY27, with Rs 1.31 trillion sanctioned in FY26 and NBFC exposure that is 99% rated A or better.

parts.name: Deposits — CASA and term
parts.what: The bank's funding base: low-cost current and savings accounts, which management calls its main challenge and holds at roughly 40% of deposits, plus higher-cost term and bulk deposits it says it raises cautiously; total deposits grew 12-13% in the latest years.

parts.name: Treasury / investments
parts.what: A large bond and securities portfolio (about Rs 1.85 lakh crore in 2022, split across HTM, AFS and FVTPL) that earns interest — yield of about 7.15% in FY25 — and generates trading profits or mark-to-market losses depending on interest rates; management flags it as a swing factor in earnings.

parts.name: Non-interest income (fees, forex, PSLC, recoveries)
parts.what: Fee income from customers, foreign exchange, penal charges, sale of priority-sector lending certificates (Rs 627 crore earned in one year, amortised over four quarters) and cash recovered from bad debts already written off — recoveries alone were Rs 6,651 crore in FY26.

parts.name: Digital banking
parts.what: Mobile, internet and UPI banking, debit and credit cards, POS terminals and QR codes, plus digital lending 'journeys' — 90% of transactions are now digital, with 175 lakh mobile banking users and Rs 81,250 crore of digital business in one year.

overview.what_it_does: India Shelter Finance is a housing finance company that lends money to people in smaller Indian towns to buy, build or improve a home, or to borrow against property they already own; every loan is backed by property as security. Its typical customer is a low- or middle-income, largely self-employed family taking a first home loan of about Rs. 10 lakhs, with a woman as a borrower in almost all cases, and the company lends conservatively at roughly half the property's value. It makes money on the gap between what it charges borrowers (portfolio yield around 14.8%-14.9%) and what it pays to borrow from banks, the National Housing Bank and other lenders (cost of funds around 8.2%-8.8%), holding that spread above 6%, plus some fee income; profits come to about Rs. 500 crores a year on assets of Rs. 11,044 crores as of March 2026. It operates through its own branch network in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities (about 90% of the loan book), which grew from 215 branches across 15 states in early 2024 to over 300 branches by FY26, with nearly all loans sourced by its own staff rather than through agents.

parts.name: Home loans (HL)
parts.what: Loans to low- and middle-income customers building or buying their first home in Tier-2/Tier-3 towns; management describes this as about 50% of the loan book and the core focus, supported by government schemes like PMAY 2.0 under which over 2,000 of its customers had received subsidy by December 2025.

parts.name: Loan against property (LAP)
parts.what: Loans given against a customer's existing property, described as about 42% of the book, and management repeatedly says its repayment behaviour and bad-loan levels run essentially in line with home loans (a gap of only 1-2 basis points).

parts.name: In-house sourcing and branch network
parts.what: The company finds, underwrites, values, and collects on its own loans through its branches rather than buying business from outsiders — 97%-98% of sourcing is in-house — and it adds 40-45 branches a year, which management calls the main engine of both growth and its improving cost ratios (opex to assets down to about 4%).

parts.name: Digital sourcing channel
parts.what: A newly introduced online lead channel, described in the Q3FY26 call as contributing about 4%-5% of disbursements today with a plan to take it to 10%; small but flagged as the next step in its technology journey.

parts.name: Borrowing / funding operations
parts.what: Not a customer-facing product but central to earnings: it raises long-term money from more than 30 lenders, including refinance from the National Housing Bank (about 15%-16% of borrowings, and roughly 60 basis points cheaper than bank funding), with average borrowing tenure over eight years and positive asset-liability matching.

overview.what_it_does: IndiGo (InterGlobe Aviation Ltd.) is an Indian low-cost airline that sells seats on scheduled passenger flights, mainly to ordinary Indian travellers flying within India plus a growing number flying abroad. It earns money by filling a large fleet of single-aisle Airbus A320/A321 aircraft at low fares and high load factors — revenue is described in terms of yield (fare per passenger-kilometre) and unit revenue per seat-kilometre, against a cost base dominated by jet fuel and dollar-linked lease and maintenance costs, which is why fuel prices and the rupee-dollar rate swing its profits so much. Its home market is India, where it flew to 88 domestic destinations over 400+ direct routes (FY24) and served more than 123 million passengers in FY26, alongside about 100 international routes to 33 overseas destinations across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Europe. Total income was around 895 billion rupees in FY26 (versus about 712 billion in FY24), and results have swung from large post-Covid losses to an 82 billion rupee profit in FY24 and back to a 23.9 billion rupee loss in FY26 after currency depreciation and a December operational disruption.

parts.name: Domestic and short-haul passenger flying (the core airline)
parts.what: Scheduled low-fare flights connecting Indian cities — management calls it "the heart of IndiGo," anchored by the Airbus A320/A321 single-aisle programme, with the stated intent to fly to every Indian airport of a certain size (over 10 million domestic passengers carried in May 2026 alone, its best-ever month).

parts.name: International network / "internationalization"
parts.what: Flights from Indian cities to overseas destinations across Asia, Africa, the Middle East, the UK and Europe, expanding via new routes and larger aircraft (A321XLR and 30 ordered A350-900 widebodies); the Middle East and Europe together were said to be roughly 18% of total capacity and about 160 daily flights in FY26.

parts.name: Codeshare partnerships
parts.what: Tie-ups with foreign carriers such as British Airways, Qantas and Malaysia Airlines that let IndiGo sell onward connections beyond its own network — passengers flown through codeshares grew about 45% in FY24, though it is small relative to the main flying business.

parts.name: Premium / business product
parts.what: A tailor-made business-class-style cabin launched on the busiest business routes from late 2024 to capture growing demand for premium travel in India — an add-on to the low-cost core rather than a separate business.

parts.name: CarGo (air cargo / freighters)
parts.what: A freight operation that started commercial flying with its first two dedicated freighter aircraft in October 2022 — described as an exciting opportunity but a small side business next to passenger flying.

parts.name: Engine MRO and material services
parts.what: A newer, forward-looking effort to build in-house engine maintenance, repair and overhaul plus long-term parts supply, supported by a 2026 memorandum with CFM International for over 1,000 LEAP-1A engines; presented as investment ahead of growth rather than a current earner.

parts.name: Fleet and aircraft order book
parts.what: Not a revenue line but central to the story: a pending order book of close to 1,000 aircraft for delivery out to 2035 (including a record 500-aircraft A320neo family order), giving at least one new plane a week and a target of a 600-plus aircraft fleet by the end of the decade.

overview.what_it_does: Indigo Paints is an Indian paint company that makes and sells decorative paints and related coatings for buildings — emulsions (interior and exterior wall paints), enamels and wood coatings, primers and distempers, and cement-based putty and cement paints — plus a growing range of waterproofing and construction-chemical products. It sells through a dealer network across India (over 19,100 active dealers, close to 11,900 tinting machines placed at dealer counters and 55 depots as of December 2025), rather than directly to end customers; dealers stock and resell to painters, contractors and households, and the company pushes demand by advertising heavily (MS Dhoni nationally, Mohanlal for Kerala), running influencer/painter engagement programs, and opening branded 'Indigo Color Canvas' display stores at select dealer counters. It earns money on the manufacturing spread — management repeatedly points to industry-leading gross margins (45–49%) driven by a basket of 'differentiated' products that face less competition — with revenue of about Rs. 1,306 crores in FY24 and roughly Rs. 980 crores over the first nine months of FY26 on a consolidated basis. Operations are India-only (Kerala is called its strongest state, with plants in Tamil Nadu, Jodhpur, Cochin and a head office in Pune), with exports only just being explored for its subsidiary.

parts.name: Emulsions
parts.what: Water-based interior and exterior wall paints — described as the largest category by value, contributing almost half of value sales for any paint company, and where the premium end has recently grown faster than the mass end.

parts.name: Enamels and wood coatings
parts.what: Solvent-based glossy paints for metal and wood surfaces; a meaningful category that grew fastest in Q3 FY26 (18.9% value, 20.2% volume) and is now served by a new solvent-based plant at Jodhpur.

parts.name: Primers, distempers and others
parts.what: Cheaper base and budget wall coatings applied before or instead of emulsions; a smaller category that management has at times flagged as a weak spot and pushed with extra promotions.

parts.name: Putty and cement paints (powder paints)
parts.what: Powder products, mainly wall putty used to smooth surfaces before painting, made at Jodhpur where capacity was recently doubled through a brownfield expansion; growth here has been slower in recent quarters.

parts.name: Waterproofing and construction chemicals (Indigo Protect Plus)
parts.what: A newer product line sold through the same dealer network, growing 'at a phenomenal pace' from a mid-single-digit share of revenue in FY24 to close to 7% of the top line by Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Apple Chemie (subsidiary)
parts.what: A separately branded construction-chemicals business, strongest in Maharashtra and expanding into southern and eastern India, with quarterly revenue of about Rs. 20 crores in Q3 FY26 (up 31.5% year on year), a new sealant plant at Nagpur, and exports being explored — small next to the parent but the fastest-growing piece.

parts.name: Differentiated products
parts.what: Not a separate segment but how management describes its niche, low-competition offerings spread across the categories; these are credited with the company's best-in-industry gross margins and with the Q4 margin peak each year.

overview.what_it_does: IndusInd Bank is an Indian private-sector bank that takes deposits from the public and lends the money out, earning most of its income from the spread between what it pays savers and what it charges borrowers (net interest margin, run at roughly 4.2% in the earlier years), plus fees from things like credit-card spends, transaction banking and wealth products. It lends to a wide mix of customers: truck, car and tractor buyers through a large vehicle-finance arm; very small rural borrowers and village shopkeepers through its Bharat Financial Inclusion (BFIL) unit; homeowners, credit-card and personal-loan customers in cities; small and mid-sized businesses; and large companies including the global diamond and jewellery trade. On the funding side it gathers current, savings and term deposits through a branch network that crossed 3,000 branches in 2024, plus dedicated affluent and non-resident-Indian (NRI) franchises and a digital app called INDIE. It operates essentially across India, from metros to deep rural 'Bharat' locations, with the diamond business serving international trade hubs.

parts.name: Vehicle Finance
parts.what: Loans to buy commercial vehicles, cars, utility vehicles, tractors, two- and three-wheelers and construction equipment, at fixed rates; it is described as one of the key pillars of the bank, with a loan book of about Rs.99,876 crores and quarterly disbursements of roughly Rs.11,000–13,000 crores.

parts.name: Rural and Priority Sector Banking / Bharat Financial Inclusion Limited (BFIL)
parts.what: Tiny group loans to rural, mostly women borrowers plus other rural products, delivered at the customer's doorstep; the micro-loan book peaked far higher but shrank to about Rs.16,782 crores after a bad-loan cycle, with roughly 57% now covered by a government CGFMU credit guarantee, and it also helps the bank meet mandatory priority-sector lending targets.

parts.name: Bharat Super Shop (merchant acquiring / merchant loans)
parts.what: Business loans to small shopkeepers and merchants sourced through the BFIL network, grown from about Rs.2,237 crores in 2022 to roughly Rs.8,042 crores across some 570,000 merchant borrowers.

parts.name: Bharat Money Stores
parts.what: A network of roughly 88,000 kirana (corner-shop) outlets acting as banking points in remote villages, which had signed up about 2.6 million savings accounts.

parts.name: Consumer Banking Assets (other retail assets)
parts.what: Traditional city retail lending — home loans (about Rs.6,510 crores, growing fast off a small base), personal loans (~Rs.10,358 crores), credit cards (~Rs.9,751 crores of loans and about Rs.15,000 crores of quarterly card spends) and a new gold-loan product past Rs.1,000 crores — totalling about Rs.31,075 crores, with management deliberately shrinking the unsecured pieces.

parts.name: SME Banking (earlier called business banking / MSME)
parts.what: Working-capital and property-backed loans to small and mid-sized firms, about Rs.44,347 crores, repeatedly flagged by management as a relatively small presence and the bank's next big growth opportunity.

parts.name: Wholesale Banking (earlier Corporate Bank)
parts.what: Lending and transaction banking to large, mid and small companies; once a fast-growing book led by mid and small corporates, it is now being deliberately shrunk where returns are poor (down ~5-6% quarter on quarter), with 83% of clients rated A or better and transaction-banking fees making up 66% of wholesale and SME fee income.

parts.name: Global Diamond & Jewellery / Gems & Jewellery business
parts.what: Financing for the international rough- and polished-diamond trade, about 4.2% of the total loan book in 2022, and consistently described as having pristine asset quality with no stressed borrowers.

parts.name: Liabilities / Deposits franchise
parts.what: The deposit-gathering side — current and savings accounts (CASA ratio was around 43% in 2022), retail term deposits (now about 47.9% of deposits), affluent banking including Pioneer Private for clients above Rs.3 crores of relationship value, and NRI deposits which crossed Rs.50,000 crores; management calls deposit quantity and quality its foremost priority.

parts.name: INDIE (digital banking)
parts.what: The bank's mobile-app banking offering, which had passed 1.3 million customers by mid-2024.

overview.what_it_does: Indus Towers owns and operates passive telecom infrastructure in India — the towers, power systems and site equipment that mobile networks physically sit on — and rents space on those towers to telecom operators, who mount their own antennas and radios on them. Its customers are a small number of large mobile operators; the calls repeatedly name Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea as its two major customers (and past promoters), so revenue is highly concentrated. It makes money from long-term contracts (Master Service Agreements, renewed in 2022 on a roughly 10-year framework) that charge rent per tenant per site, plus extra 'loading' charges when a customer hangs more equipment on an existing tower — such as 5G radios — and it also recovers the cost of running the sites, where diesel, electricity and rent are its main expenses. It operates pan-India, from metros to remote areas like Lakshadweep, hill regions of Kerala and defence establishments, and by March 2026 ran about 264,500 macro towers carrying about 428,000 co-locations.

parts.name: Macro towers (tower rentals / co-locations)
parts.what: The core business: large ground- and rooftop-based towers rented out to operators, where the same tower can carry more than one customer ('co-locations') — about 264,500 macro towers and 428,000 co-locations as of March 2026, with an 'industry-leading' tenancy ratio of 1.62 tenants per tower, making this overwhelmingly the main source of revenue.

parts.name: Loading (additional equipment on existing towers)
parts.what: Incremental charges when a customer adds more radios or antennas to a tower it already occupies — driven by 5G rollout and network densification (industry 5G base stations rose from ~450,000 in 2024 to ~531,000 by early 2026), and repeatedly described as a growing 'fillip' to revenue that needs little new capital.

parts.name: Lean / leaner towers
parts.what: Slimmer, lower-cost tower structures used where a full macro tower doesn't fit or isn't needed, reported separately from macro towers — over 14,000 lean towers by March 2026, taking the total portfolio including their co-locations to roughly 442,000, so a small but steadily growing add-on.

parts.name: Non-tower segment — IBS, small cells and DAS
parts.what: In-Building Solutions and Distributed Antenna Systems that provide coverage inside buildings and in dense or enclosed spaces such as metros (e.g. DMRC), tunnels and highways, plus small cells for urban decongestion — management says it reached a leadership position in IBS in Q4 FY26 and expects growth, but gives no revenue figures, so it is presented as a smaller emerging business.

parts.name: Site energy and operations (uptime, solar, diesel reduction)
parts.what: Running and powering the sites so networks stay up — a cost centre and service promise rather than a separate product, with uptime around 99.97-99.98%, about 42,400 sites given solar access by March 2026, and diesel use falling roughly 4-7% year-on-year even as tenancy grew; management treats energy cost reduction as one of its four strategic pillars.

overview.what_it_does: Infosys is an India-headquartered IT services company (offices at Electronics City, Bengaluru; shares listed on the BSE, NSE and the New York Stock Exchange) that does technology work for large corporate clients under contracts — building, modernising and running their software, data and IT systems, and more recently putting AI into their businesses. It makes money by billing clients for the work of its very large employee base (it hired 21,000 people in a single quarter in 2022 and 15,000–20,000 freshers a year by 2024), so revenue depends on winning deals and profit depends on pricing, utilisation of staff, and the mix of junior-to-senior people (its 'pyramid'); management guides investors each year on revenue growth in constant currency and on operating margin, which has run around 20%–22%. Growth comes largely from 'large deals' — contracts typically above $50mn each, running $1.69bn of total contract value in one quarter of FY23 and $3.6bn–$4.1bn per quarter more recently — often consolidation, cost-takeout and efficiency work where a client hands Infosys more of its IT. Its main markets are the US/North America and Europe, and the company had grown to roughly $20bn of annual revenue by 2026, up from about $10bn a decade earlier.

parts.name: Financial services / Banking & Financial Services (BFSI)
parts.what: IT work for banks, cards, payments and capital-markets clients; repeatedly singled out as the swing factor for the whole company — weak spots like mortgages in 2022, then a 7.9% sequential jump in Q1 FY25 that management credited for its guidance upgrade.

parts.name: Manufacturing
parts.what: Technology and engineering services for manufacturers; described in 2024 as a consistently strong sector after a very strong prior year, and reinforced by the acquisition of in-tech (engineering services, about €170mn annual revenue), which was large enough to help lift full-year guidance.

parts.name: Retail and CPG / Logistics
