parts.what: IT services for consumer goods, retail and logistics clients; run as its own industry group with a dedicated industry head, and described in 2024 as steady but not a standout.

parts.name: Energy, Utilities, Resources & Services (EURS)
parts.what: IT services for energy, utility and resources companies plus other services industries; a named segment with its own segment head, characterised in 2024 as tracking in line with earlier commentary.

parts.name: Communication, Media and Technology (including hi-tech)
parts.what: Work for telecom, media and technology clients under a dedicated segment head; hi-tech was called out as the softer end of demand in 2024.

parts.name: Digital services (Cobalt cloud)
parts.what: The 'new technology' half of the business — cloud migration and digital transformation sold under the Cobalt brand; in Q1 FY23 digital was 61% of total revenue and growing 37.5% a year, with cloud growing faster still, and management called it the main reason it was gaining market share.

parts.name: AI services (Topaz, Topaz Fabric, 'Hexagon for AI')
parts.what: Generative and agentic AI work — building agents for business processes, data work, legacy modernisation and AI-assisted coding — delivered through the Topaz brand and a Topaz Fabric platform that lets clients use any foundation model while keeping their own data; it reached 8.2% of total revenue by Q1 FY27, growing double digits quarter-on-quarter, with over 80,000 employees using coding tools and a plan to build 6,000 'frontier engineers'.

parts.name: Large deals
parts.what: Not an industry but how management frames the order book — individual contracts typically over $50mn (a few near $500mn), reported every quarter with the share that is 'net new'; these are the company's stated proxy for future revenue, e.g. 34 deals worth $4.1bn in Q1 FY25 and $3.6bn at 61% net new in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Project Maximus (margin program)
parts.what: An internal profitability program rather than a product line, working on value-based pricing, utilisation and the staffing pyramid; it contributed 80 basis points of the 100 basis points of margin expansion in Q1 FY25 and is the main tool management cites for holding operating margin inside its 20%–22% guidance.

overview.what_it_does: Inox Green Energy Services is an Indian company that looks after wind farms (and now solar plants) after they are built — it does the day-to-day operations and maintenance, servicing turbines and keeping them running, with machine availability of about 96.5% as its headline quality measure. Its customers are the owners of these power projects: mostly buyers of turbines made by its parent Inox Wind (which owns about 56% of it and signs O&M contracts of 20-25 years that pass to Inox Green), plus third-party asset owners it wins through tenders and by buying up other service providers. It earns steady, annuity-like service fees tied to the size of the portfolio it maintains, so revenue grows as more megawatts are added — the portfolio went from about 90 MW at the start to roughly 3,050 MW in early 2023, 3.5 GW in late 2024, and over 13 GWp by 2026 — and management describes the business as asset-light with high margins (Q3 FY26: income of Rs.112 crore, EBITDA of Rs.53 crore, PAT of Rs.25 crore). It operates across wind and solar sites all over India and is part of the Inox GFL Group, whose other companies (Inox Wind, Inox Clean Energy) keep feeding it new projects to service.

parts.name: Wind O&M (organic / captive portfolio from Inox Wind)
parts.what: Long-term maintenance contracts on turbines supplied by parent Inox Wind, which flow automatically to Inox Green for 20-25 years once commissioned — this is the core of the business and the main engine of portfolio growth, with the parent targeting several gigawatts of execution that will add to it.

parts.name: Third-party / inorganic O&M
parts.what: Servicing wind assets that Inox Wind did not build, won either through tenders or by acquiring existing service providers — starting with a 51% stake in I-Fox Windtechnik (230 MW, bought at about a 4x multiple and said to have roughly doubled in size and profit within 12 months) and later investments to take over 6.5 GW of operating wind O&M assets from two large companies.

parts.name: Solar O&M
parts.what: A newer addition of about 3.3 GWp of solar maintenance work, picked up from KEC International and group company Inox Clean Energy, taking the company beyond pure wind.

parts.name: Value-added and refurbishment services
parts.what: Extra paid work on top of routine maintenance — refurbishment of equipment and in-house/localised manufacture of critical spares like control systems and gearboxes, which management says both adds revenue and cuts costs and supply-chain risk.

parts.name: Power evacuation / substation (common infrastructure) business
parts.what: The transmission substations and shared infrastructure at wind sites, historically capital-heavy and sitting on the balance sheet; it contributes only about Rs.3-4 crore of quarterly revenue but carried roughly Rs.16-17 crore of quarterly depreciation, and is being demerged into group company Inox Renewable Solutions (approved by NCLT by mid-2026) to leave a cleaner, asset-light balance sheet.

parts.name: Own wind power assets (SPVs) — being exited
parts.what: Legacy special-purpose vehicles that owned wind capacity, such as the 50 MW Nani Virani project, which the company said in 2023 it was selling down to become net-debt-free and move to an asset-light model.

overview.what_it_does: INOX India (which trades under the brand INOXCVA) designs, manufactures, installs and services cryogenic equipment — the tanks, cylinders, vacuum-jacketed piping and turnkey systems used to store, transport and dispense gases kept at extremely low temperatures, such as oxygen, nitrogen, argon, CO2, hydrogen, helium and LNG. It sells mostly business-to-business: industrial gas companies, LNG distributors and fuel-station operators, truck and bus OEMs, shipyards and marine customers, aerospace and space agencies, scientific research bodies like ITER in France and ISRO, and global breweries. Money comes from making and selling equipment ranging from 1-litre containers to 1 million-litre storage tanks, plus large engineered turnkey projects and installation work, with revenue recognised against an order backlog (Rs.1,043 crore as of 9MFY24). It manufactures at four plants in India (Vadodara-area sites including Savli and Kalol), with part-manufacturing and service in Brazil and service distribution into the Netherlands, and has shipped to over 100 countries — the US, Europe, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Korea, UAE and Australia being key markets, with exports roughly half the order book. FY26 revenue was Rs.1,632 crore at a 23.8% EBITDA margin; the company describes itself as debt-free and net cash surplus with high return ratios (ROCE 37%, ROE 28% in FY23).

parts.name: Industrial Gas Solutions (IG)
parts.what: The largest segment — about 65% of income in 9MFY24 and still called the biggest revenue contributor in FY26 — making cryogenic storage tanks, transport tanks and semi-trailers, IMO/ISO containers, microbulk units, vaporizers, liquid cylinders (the 'Cryoseal' brand of liquid nitrogen containers), helium dewars, cryo-bio tanks and disposable cylinders, with milestones like 2 million+ disposable cylinders dispatched to the US in FY26, 300+ transport tanks in a year, and a ~Rs.200 crore aerospace order from a US private space company.

parts.name: LNG Solutions
parts.what: About 29% of income in 9MFY24, covering LNG storage tanks and regasification systems, LNG semi-trailers (250+ on Indian roads with 85%+ market share), LCNG/LNG fuelling stations, marine fuel gas systems, vehicle-mounted LNG fuel tanks for trucks, buses and locomotives, and mini-LNG terminals — with recent wins including Cochin Shipyard marine fuel tanks, European marine tanks, and 1,500 cubic metre tanks for a Bahamas mini-LNG terminal.

parts.name: Cryo Scientific Division (CSD)
parts.what: The smallest but most technically specialised part (~4% of revenue in 9MFY24), doing turnkey cryogenic systems for research and defence — MRI cryostats (including India's first indigenous 4K helium cryostat), satellite and launch-pad facilities and cryogenic propulsion work for ISRO, a LOX tank for submarine applications, and repeat orders for cryo-lines, cryostat panels and shielding at the ITER fusion project in France.

parts.name: Beverage Keg business
parts.what: A newer segment that appears in the later calls, supplying stainless-steel beer kegs to global brewers — dispatches up 31% in FY26, with approvals and live orders from Heineken, AB InBev and Molson Coors, which management says together represent over 40% of global beer market volumes.

parts.name: Non-cryogenic equipment and turnkey projects
parts.what: Mentioned alongside the main divisions — the company also manufactures specialised non-cryogenic equipment and executes large turnkey projects including design, installation and commissioning, rather than only shipping standalone products.

overview.what_it_does: Inox Wind makes large wind turbines in India and sells them to companies that build wind power projects — independent power producers, commercial and industrial buyers, state-owned firms like NTPC, and named customers such as Aditya Birla, Amplus/Gentari, Jakson Green, First Energy and Leap Green, plus its own group company Inox Clean Energy. It earns money in two ways on each project: selling the turbine equipment itself, and, where the customer wants it, building the whole wind farm end-to-end (foundations, erection with cranes, evacuation infrastructure and commissioning) — the order book is currently split about 50:50 between these two, with management wanting equipment-only supply to rise toward 75%. After the farm is running, its 56%-owned listed subsidiary Inox Green earns recurring fees for operating and maintaining wind and solar assets. It operates only in India, with factories in Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat (including a nacelle and hub plant at Kalyangarh) and a new blade and tower plant coming up in the south; consolidated revenue was guided at over Rs. 5,000 crore for FY26 at 20-22% EBITDA margin, up from roughly Rs. 1,500 crore-scale annual revenue in FY24.

parts.name: Wind turbine manufacturing and equipment supply
parts.what: Designs and builds wind turbine generators — the 3.3 MW machine launched in FY24 and a new 4.4/4.45 MW model due to launch commercially in calendar 2026 — and sells them to project developers; this is the core of a 3.1-3.2 GW order book that gives more than 24 months of execution visibility.

parts.name: Turnkey / EPC project execution
parts.what: Builds complete wind farms for customers, covering foundations, erection, cranes and commissioning (for example a 50 MW farm handed over to NTPC in Gujarat), running across more than 25 sites for over 15 customers with each contract carrying a different scope; turnkey is about half the order book and management is deliberately shrinking it because it ties up more working capital.

parts.name: Inox Green Energy Services (O&M subsidiary, 56% owned)
parts.what: Separately listed subsidiary that services and maintains wind and solar plants for a fee, growing from a 3.2 GW portfolio in 2023 to 13.3 GWp (about 10 GW wind, 3.3 GWp solar) by early 2026 including a 6.5 GW acquisition still awaiting approvals — small in revenue (about Rs. 110-130 crore a quarter) but high margin, cash-generative and described as on track to be India's largest renewable O&M company.

parts.name: Inox Renewable Solutions (IRSL) — evacuation infrastructure / substations
parts.what: The substation and power-evacuation business being demerged out of Inox Green and merged into IRSL (approved by NCLT Ahmedabad, listing pending), which becomes the group's EPC arm and removes roughly Rs. 1,000 crore of gross block and Rs. 50-55 crore of annual depreciation from Inox Green.

parts.name: Backward integration into components
parts.what: In-house manufacture of cranes and transformers, with a stated push into power electronics, which management credits for the step-up in margins to the 20-22% EBITDA range.

parts.name: Group linkage with Inox Clean Energy (INOXGFL Group)
parts.what: Not owned by Inox Wind but the group's power-producing and solar-module arm, planning 3 GW+ of renewable capacity a year (20-30% of it wind) toward 14 GW by FY29 — expected to supply upward of 1 GW a year of repeat orders and eventually two-thirds of Inox Wind's annual execution alongside CESC.

overview.what_it_does: Intellect Design Arena is an India-headquartered (Chennai) software product company that builds and sells banking and financial-technology software to banks, credit unions, insurers, wealth managers and other financial institutions around the world — covering things like core banking, corporate/transaction banking, lending, payments, liquidity, trade finance, treasury, wealth and insurance underwriting. It makes money in four main ways: one-time software licence fees, annual maintenance contracts (AMC) on installed software, recurring 'platform' (cloud/subscription) revenue, and fees from implementation and 'digital transformation' projects; management tracks 'licence-linked revenue' (platform + licence + AMC) and annual recurring revenue as its key quality-of-revenue measures. It sells globally — the calls cite 97 countries served, offices in New York, London, Dubai, Singapore, Sydney, Toronto, Tokyo and Indian cities, and a revenue mix of roughly 37% USD, 26% INR, 14% GBP, 8% CAD and 6% EUR — with deals typically won as multi-crore, multi-year platform contracts from a tracked pipeline of 'destiny deals'. By the twelve months to December 2025 the company crossed ₹3,025 Crs of total income (up 23% year-on-year) with EBITDA of ₹709 Crs, having grown from roughly ₹2,300 Crs LTM in mid-2024.

parts.name: Wholesale Banking (formerly iGTB — Intellect Global Transaction Banking)
parts.what: Sells corporate/transaction-banking software to banks — liquidity management, corporate treasury and deposits, cash management, corporate channels, trade finance and transaction limits — and is described as the oldest and largest engine, started in 2015 and contributing about ₹1,400 Crs of the last-twelve-months revenue (Euromoney named it the world's best transaction banking software provider for 2025).

parts.name: Consumer Banking (formerly iGCB — Intellect Global Consumer Banking)
parts.what: Sells retail and commercial core banking, lending and digital engagement platforms to banks and credit unions — including full managed-service cloud deals such as Vancity, Canada's largest community credit union — and is the second engine, built up from 2018 and now contributing close to ₹1,000 Crs of LTM revenue, with active market-entry pushes into Europe, Canada and the US.

parts.name: IntellectAI
parts.what: Bundles the wealth-management and insurance businesses plus AI/machine-learning underwriting products (the SEEC platform) into one AI-led unit; deliberately seeded from 2021 and now at about ₹500 Crs of LTM revenue, with customers including large Indian banks and public-sector and wholesale insurance players.

parts.name: Purple Fabric
parts.what: The newest, fourth 'growth engine' — an 'Open Business Impact AI platform' launched in June 2025 and positioned by management as competing with Palantir in the financial domain, used for AI-led risk underwriting, claims, collections and payments; still small and pre-scale, but 14 new 'value discovery partners' joined its ecosystem in the December 2025 quarter.

parts.name: eMACH.ai
parts.what: Not a separate revenue line but the common technology platform underneath all the products — a cloud-based, composable, AI-first architecture launched in February 2023 that has grown from 300 to about 700 microservices, and which management says lets it cross-sell a second and third product to existing customers (nearly 60 of whom have assets over $100 Bn) on one shared backbone.

parts.name: GeM (Government e-Marketplace, India)
parts.what: A large Indian government e-marketplace contract that was a meaningful revenue and receivables item in earlier years — it inflated collection days (DSO of 126 versus 101 excluding GeM) — and rolled off in the December 2023 quarter, after which management reports growth on a comparable, GeM-excluded basis.

parts.name: iRTM
parts.what: A separate business line with its own CEO named on the August 2022 call, but the excerpts give no detail on its products or size, and it no longer appears among the business heads listed on the later calls.

overview.what_it_does: Indian Overseas Bank (IOB) is a government-controlled Indian commercial bank, headquartered in Chennai and majority-owned by the Government of India (92.44% shareholding), that takes deposits from the public and lends the money out. It serves over 46 million customers through roughly 3,500 branches, about 3,700 ATMs and more than 13,000 business correspondent agents across India, plus branches in four overseas countries (Singapore, Hong Kong, Thailand and Sri Lanka), and sells personal, corporate and agricultural banking along with credit cards, loans and insurance products. It earns mainly from the spread between the interest it charges on loans and what it pays depositors (net interest income of about Rs 12,574 crore in FY26, at a net interest margin of roughly 3.2-3.4%), plus fee income, gains on its bond/treasury portfolio, commission from selling priority-sector lending certificates, and recoveries on loans previously written off. As of June 2026 it had a total business mix of about Rs 6.98 lakh crore (Rs 3.76 lakh crore of deposits and Rs 3.22 lakh crore of loans) and annual net profit of Rs 5,208 crore for FY26.

parts.name: Deposits (CASA and term deposits)
parts.what: The bank's funding side — current and savings accounts (CASA, about 41% of domestic deposits, Rs 1,54,415 crore), retail term deposits (about 53%, Rs 1,83,601 crore) and a small bulk deposit slice (about 6%) — with total deposits of Rs 3,76,193 crore growing around 14-18% a year.

parts.name: RAM segment (Retail, Agriculture, MSME)
parts.what: The core lending engine and management's stated focus, making up about 83% of domestic loans, and the main driver of the bank's loan yields.

parts.name: Retail loans
parts.what: Home loans, vehicle loans, personal loans, jewel (gold) loans and deposit-backed loans to individuals; about 31% of domestic advances and the fastest-growing piece at roughly 45% year-on-year in FY26.

parts.name: Agriculture loans
parts.what: Farm and rural credit, the single largest slice of domestic lending at about 35% of domestic advances, growing roughly 40% in FY26.

parts.name: MSME loans
parts.what: Lending to micro, small and medium businesses, about 17% of domestic advances, growing about 13% overall (23.77% in core MSME), and the channel through which government-backed schemes like ECLGS (Rs 4,400 crore eligible, Rs 2,600 crore disbursed so far) are routed.

parts.name: Corporate and overseas lending
parts.what: Loans to large companies, state government entities and the four foreign branches — the remaining roughly 17% of domestic advances, concentrated in A-and-above rated borrowers and carrying very little bad debt (0.24% of NPAs).

parts.name: Treasury / investments
parts.what: The bank's bond and SLR securities book, Rs 1,19,810 crore globally as of March 2026, earning a yield of about 6.66% and contributing trading profits to non-interest income.

parts.name: Non-interest income (fees, PSLC, recoveries)
parts.what: Fee-based income of Rs 2,732 crore in FY26 plus commission from selling priority-sector lending certificates (Rs 863 crore in the June 2026 quarter alone) and recoveries from technically written-off accounts (Rs 2,252 crore in FY26) — described by management as recurring every quarter.

parts.name: Digital banking
parts.what: The delivery channel rather than a separate profit line: about 98% of all transactions now happen digitally, via the IOB Connect mobile app, WhatsApp banking, video KYC, UPI and roughly 4,100 tablet devices that open 40-50% of new accounts.

parts.name: Financial inclusion / rural banking
parts.what: Basic no-frills accounts under the government's PMJDY scheme (94.57 lakh accounts) served largely through business correspondents and the roughly 2,040 of 3,494 branches located in rural and semi-urban areas.

overview.what_it_does: Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) is India's largest oil refining and marketing company — a government-owned firm that buys crude oil (mostly imported), refines it into fuels like petrol (MS), diesel (HSD), LPG cooking gas, aviation fuel and lubricants, and then sells them across India through a network of over 42,000 retail outlets and a large pipeline and distribution system. It makes money on the gap between what crude costs and what refined products fetch (the refining margin, or GRM, reported at around $8-11 per barrel on a normalized basis in recent quarters) plus marketing volumes, selling roughly 105 million tonnes of product in FY26 on revenue of about Rs. 8.86 lakh crore and profit after tax of Rs. 36,802 crore. It also sells petrochemicals, natural gas/LNG and biofuels, and takes government compensation when it is forced to sell domestic LPG below cost (IOC's share of the Rs. 30,000 crore package was Rs. 14,486 crore). It operates almost entirely within India — refineries at Panipat, Paradip, Gujarat, Digboi and elsewhere — with a small overseas footprint through an Abu Dhabi exploration joint venture and LNG exports to Nepal.

parts.name: Refineries
parts.what: Turns crude oil into fuels at its refineries; the biggest engine of the business, running at over 100% of nameplate capacity with a record 75.5 million tonnes of crude processed in FY26, and group capacity is being expanded from about 80.8 to 98 million tonnes a year with roughly Rs. 72,000 crore of investment.

parts.name: Pipeline
parts.what: Moves crude and finished products around the country through the company's pipeline network, carrying a record 105.6 million tonnes in FY26 at about 74% utilisation — the backbone that gets fuel from refineries to selling points cheaply.

parts.name: Marketing
parts.what: Sells the fuel to end customers through petrol pumps, LPG cylinders, bulk and aviation channels; total sales hit a record 105.117 MMT in FY26 (up about 5%), with 42,818 retail outlets after 2,597 were added during the year, and management calls this the source of its national market share.

parts.name: Lubricants (lube business)
parts.what: Sells engine oils and industrial lubricants — a smaller but high-growth piece, with record sales of 905 thousand tonnes in FY26, up about 16%.

parts.name: Petrochemicals
parts.what: Converts refinery streams into plastics and chemical products such as polymers, PTA, MEG, acrylics and oxo-alcohols; sales were a record 3.396 MMT in FY26, and management wants to lift petrochemical integration from about 6% of throughput to 15% because global margins are currently weak but Indian demand is under-served.

parts.name: Gas
parts.what: Buys, imports and sells natural gas and LNG, including city gas distribution (CGD) to homes and vehicles; FY26 sales were 7,276 thousand tonnes including 188 TMT of CGD, with a mid-term Henry Hub-linked LNG supply deal signed with Trafigura and India's first LNG-by-road exports to Nepal.

parts.name: Biofuels and renewable energy
parts.what: Blends ethanol into petrol (19.97% achieved), sells compressed biogas under the IndiGreen brand, and is building green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuel, EV charging and a 31 gigawatt renewable portfolio by 2030 through subsidiary Terra Clean Limited — currently small in revenue but where a growing share of future capex is being directed, with a net-zero target of 2046.

parts.name: Exploration joint venture (Urja Bharat Pte Ltd)
parts.what: A 50:50 overseas joint venture that announced an oil discovery in an onshore block in Abu Dhabi in January 2026 — mentioned as a milestone rather than a material earnings contributor.

overview.what_it_does: Ion Exchange (India) Limited is a water treatment company: it designs and builds water and wastewater treatment plants, and separately manufactures and sells the chemicals, resins and membranes those plants run on. Its customers are mainly industrial and government buyers — refineries (it commissioned the raw water plant for IOCL's Panipat refinery, described as the largest industrial water package awarded in India), solar and semiconductor makers needing ultra-pure water, textile parks, data centres, and state water bodies such as UP Jal Nigam under the Jal Jeevan Mission — plus a smaller retail arm selling consumer water products. It makes money three ways: lumpy project/EPC contracts booked against an order book (INR 26,433 million at March 2026), repeat sales of consumable chemicals and resins, and consumer product sales; a 20-year build-and-operate contract in Oman also brings recurring revenue. Revenue for FY26 was INR 29,148 million, roughly 60-65% from engineering projects and about a quarter from chemicals, with operations across India and a growing overseas presence in the Middle East, Sri Lanka, Africa (a Malawi JV) and Europe (Portugal/Spain via the MAPRIL acquisition).

parts.name: Engineering division
parts.what: Designs, builds and commissions water and wastewater treatment systems — ultra-pure water plants, effluent treatment plants and zero-liquid-discharge solutions — for industry and government; it is the largest segment by revenue (INR 5,539 million of the INR 8,633 million quarterly total in Q4 FY26) but runs on thin single-digit margins, and its visibility comes from an order book of INR 26,433 million.

parts.name: Chemical division
parts.what: Manufactures and sells ion exchange resins, water treatment specialty chemicals and membranes (reverse osmosis, ultra-filtration, nano-filtration), including through a new technology tie-up with Germany's MANN+HUMMEL; it is roughly a quarter of revenue (INR 2,297 million in Q4 FY26) but is the profit engine, typically earning more EBIT than the much larger engineering arm, with a new plant at Roha recently fully commissioned and certified by the Water Quality Association.

parts.name: Consumer Product division
parts.what: Sells branded water-related products to household/retail customers; it is the smallest part at INR 1,047 million in Q4 FY26 and grows fast (34% year-on-year) but has consistently lost money (a loss of INR 46 million that quarter) as the company keeps spending to build scale.

parts.name: International operations and group companies
parts.what: Overseas subsidiaries, joint ventures and acquisitions that carry the same water business abroad — a 20-year design-build-own-operate-transfer contract worth OMR 73.46 million with Petroleum Development Oman, a USD 18.1 million water treatment JV in Malawi, project work in Sri Lanka and the GCC, and MAPRIL in Portugal giving a local base in Spain and Portugal; management describes this as a focused push to grow the product business in key geographies.

overview.what_it_does: Ipca Laboratories is an Indian pharmaceutical company that makes and sells medicines — both finished drugs ("formulations") and the bulk active ingredients (APIs) that go into them. Its biggest business is selling branded prescription medicines to doctors and chemists in India, where management says it ranked 16th in the industry with about a 2.09% market share (MAT March '26) and revenue of roughly INR3,817 crores in FY26; strong areas include pain (over half the domestic business), cardiovascular, diabetes, CNS, dermatology, neurology and anti-malarials. Alongside that it exports — branded/promoted medicines to Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, East Asia and the CIS; plain generics to the US, UK, Europe, Australia/New Zealand and Canada; anti-malarial drugs sold in bulk to institutions and government tenders; and APIs sold to other drug makers. It earns money on the spread between manufacturing cost and selling price, and total consolidated revenue for FY26 was around INR9,646 crores with an EBITDA margin near 20.7%.

parts.name: Domestic formulation business
parts.what: Branded prescription medicines promoted to Indian doctors through roughly 20 sales divisions with a few "power brands" each — the largest business at about INR3,817 crores in FY26, growing ~10-12% and consistently ahead of the overall Indian pharma market.

parts.name: Export formulation business – promotional (branded) exports
parts.what: Branded medicines marketed with its own sales effort in emerging markets like West/French-speaking Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, East Asia and the CIS — about INR664 crores in FY26, up ~14%.

parts.name: Export formulation business – generics
parts.what: Unbranded generic medicines sold in regulated markets including the US (about 8 products marketed, with 6-8 more planned yearly), UK, Europe, Australia/New Zealand and Canada — roughly INR1,149 crores in FY26 excluding tenders, up ~17%.

parts.name: Institutional export business (anti-malarials)
parts.what: Bulk anti-malarial supply won through institutional and tender contracts — a smaller, lumpy and shrinking line, down to about INR270 crores in FY26 from INR355 crores the year before.

parts.name: API business
parts.what: Sale of active pharmaceutical ingredients (the raw drug substance) to other manufacturers and for its own use — about INR1,396 crores in FY26, up ~10%, but carrying lower gross margins than the formulations business.

parts.name: Unichem Laboratories (subsidiary)
parts.what: An acquired drug company consolidated into Ipca's results from Q2 FY24, focused on US and European generics; management describes it as the drag on consolidated margins (EBITDA around 8%) with a hoped-for path to 18-20% through better plant utilization and new launches.

overview.what_it_does: IRB Infrastructure Developers is an Indian road company that builds highways and then charges vehicles a toll to use them. Its customer on the building side is the government — mainly the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and state authorities — which awards it road contracts under BOT (build-operate-toll), TOT (pay upfront for an existing road and collect its toll) and HAM models; on the revenue side its real customers are the millions of motorists and truckers who pay at its toll plazas on corridors such as Mumbai–Pune, Ahmedabad–Vadodara, the Hyderabad Outer Ring Road and the Ganga Expressway. Money comes in three ways: daily toll collections (which rise with traffic and with annual tariff hikes linked to wholesale inflation — e.g. an 18% hike on Mumbai–Pune from April 2023), construction (EPC) and long-term operations-and-maintenance fees billed to its own road projects and its two InvIT trusts, and distributions plus fees from its stakes in those trusts. It also recycles capital by selling mature roads into its listed trusts — management calls this the B.E.S.T. strategy (Build, Execute, Stabilise, Transfer) — which released about Rs. 4,900 crores of equity in FY26 and helped grow the asset base from Rs. 80,000 crores to Rs. 94,000 crores.

parts.name: BOT segment (toll roads owned by IRB)
parts.what: Highways IRB built or upgraded and now tolls directly on its own balance sheet, including the flagship Mumbai–Pune and Ahmedabad–Vadodara corridors; it brought in Rs. 712 crores of income in Q4 FY26, up 11% year on year, and is the steady cash-generating core of the company.

parts.name: Construction segment (EPC)
parts.what: The in-house road-building arm that constructs and widens highways — both for IRB's own projects and for the InvIT-owned ones — and is the largest single revenue line (Rs. 815 crores in Q4 FY26, though down 32% year on year), with margins guided at roughly 18–20% and an EPC order book that has shrunk to about Rs. 2,100 crores.

parts.name: InvIT & related assets segment
parts.what: IRB's income from its two infrastructure investment trusts — a Private InvIT (IRB Infrastructure Trust, 51%-owned, with GIC affiliates as partners) and a Public InvIT (~17% effective holding) — through distributions and related fees; it is the fastest-growing line, up 31% to Rs. 401 crores in Q4 FY26, with the Private InvIT alone collecting about Rs. 11.79 crores of toll per day.

parts.name: O&M (operations and maintenance) order book
parts.what: Multi-decade contracts to maintain and run the highways held inside the InvITs, which give IRB very long-dated, visible revenue — the O&M book was roughly Rs. 33,600 crores as of August 2025 and makes up the bulk of the ~Rs. 45,000 crore total order book reported in May 2026.

parts.name: TOT projects (toll-operate-transfer)
parts.what: Existing government highways IRB buys the right to toll for a long period by paying a large sum upfront — such as the Hyderabad Outer Ring Road bought for Rs. 7,380 crores over 30 years — and management says this, rather than new BOT construction, is now the main route for growing the portfolio toward a targeted Rs. 1,40,000 crore asset base.

parts.name: HAM projects (hybrid annuity)
parts.what: Roads built for the government where the authority pays IRB in instalments rather than IRB collecting toll; management describes these as lower-margin than BOT work, and one HAM asset was sold to the Public InvIT in FY26 for about Rs. 500 crores of equity value.

overview.what_it_does: IRCON International Limited is an Indian government-owned (Navratna, awarded October 2023) engineering and construction company that builds infrastructure — mainly railway lines, roads and highways, and bridges — working as an EPC contractor that takes a project from 'concept to commissioning', doing design, material procurement and construction largely in-house with a large in-house workforce. Its customers are overwhelmingly government bodies, above all the Ministry of Railways and Indian Railways, plus road/highway authorities and Coal India and its subsidiaries; roughly 45-55% of its order book comes on 'nomination' (directly awarded, mostly by railways) and the rest through competitive bidding. It earns money by billing progress on construction contracts over typical four-to-five-year build cycles (revenue is lumpy, with monsoon-hit Q1/Q2 and 60-70% of the year's work landing in Q3/Q4), and separately by owning long-term PPP/concession assets through subsidiaries and JVs that earn toll or track-usage income. About 90% of the order book is inside India with roughly 8-10% international (e.g. the Khulna-Mongla project in Bangladesh); FY26 revenue was Rs.9,502 crore with PAT of Rs.592 crore, against an order book of Rs.24,984 crore, about 2x annual revenue.

parts.name: EPC / construction (the core company)
parts.what: The main business: bidding for and executing railway, highway, bridge and related infrastructure contracts as a full engineering-procurement-construction contractor, and this is where essentially all of the roughly Rs.9,500-11,000 crore of annual revenue and the Rs.24,984 crore order book sit.

parts.name: Railways
parts.what: Management calls railways its core domain expertise and the main growth driver — including work already executed on the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor and hopes of bidding for the newly announced Dhankuni-Surat freight corridor once tenders are floated; in FY26 it submitted 107 bids worth about Rs.48,000 crore and won roughly Rs.5,000 crore of orders.

parts.name: Roads and highways
parts.what: The second leg of the construction business, done both as plain EPC work and as PPP projects, and described alongside railways as one of the two engines expected to drive growth.

parts.name: Road and highway PPP subsidiaries (SPVs)
parts.what: Of IRCON's 11 subsidiaries, about nine are special-purpose vehicles that own and operate long-term road/highway concession assets rather than just build them — the company invests equity into them and they were a drag on consolidated margins in FY26 while still under construction.

parts.name: Coal connectivity joint ventures
parts.what: Around five to seven JVs that build and then operate, under concession agreements, 'last-mile' railway lines linking Coal India's mines to the main rail network; only CERL Phase 1 is operational and it is currently loss-making, with break-even expected in roughly 18-20 months once nearby mines and a spur line come on stream.

parts.name: Ircon-Soma Tollway Limited (highway JV)
parts.what: A toll-road joint venture that has been a steady profit contributor to the consolidated results for several years, though its concession period ends in 2026-27.

parts.name: IISL (consultancy subsidiary)
parts.what: A subsidiary that does project management consultancy and some early-stage consultancy work; IRCON deliberately keeps pure standalone consultancy out of the parent company to avoid a conflict of interest with its EPC role, so this is a small, supporting piece.

parts.name: Renewable power subsidiary
parts.what: One subsidiary in renewable power, mentioned consistently across the calls as part of the group but never sized or discussed as a meaningful earnings contributor.

parts.name: International business
parts.what: Overseas construction projects such as Khulna-Mongla in Bangladesh — only about 4% of turnover and 8-10% of the order book, but management says margins are better there, helped in FY26 by roughly Rs.20 crore of foreign-exchange gains from rupee depreciation.

parts.name: IRSDC/IRFDC (railway station development JV)
parts.what: A station-development joint venture now being wound up — a liquidator is being appointed and IRCON expects to recover a significant part of its investment from around early 2026.

overview.what_it_does: IRCTC is an Indian government-owned company (a 'Mini Ratna' Govt. of India enterprise) that runs the commercial passenger-facing side of Indian Railways: it operates the online platform where railway tickets are booked, supplies food and catering on trains and at stations, bottles and sells packaged drinking water under the 'Rail Neer' brand, and sells tour and travel packages. Its customers are ordinary Indian rail passengers and travellers, and it works alongside the rail ministry, which introduces the trains (such as Vande Bharat train sets) that IRCTC caters. It earns money mainly from convenience fees and other charges on tickets booked through its site and app, from catering revenue and licence fees paid by catering licensees on trains, from selling bottled water, and from selling tour packages. It operates in India, is listed on the BSE and NSE, and in FY2025-26 reported revenue from operations of about Rs. 5,215 crores, EBITDA of about Rs. 1,666 crores and profit after tax of about Rs. 1,393 crores, having grown from about Rs. 853 crores of revenue in a single quarter of FY2023.

parts.name: Internet Ticketing
parts.what: Runs the online railway ticket-booking platform — management says roughly 89% of all reserved railway tickets in India are now booked through it — earning convenience fee and non-convenience revenue (Rs. 251 crores and Rs. 150 crores respectively in Q3 FY26 on about 14.64 lakh tickets booked per day); it is by far the most profitable segment with EBIT/EBITDA margins of roughly 76%-85%, contributing Rs. 1,536 crores of revenue in FY2025-26.

parts.name: Catering
parts.what: Supplies meals and food service on trains (including Rajdhani, Shatabdi and Vande Bharat trains) and at stations, partly through licensees who pay licence fees and partly through its own departmental kitchens and e-catering; it is the largest segment by revenue at Rs. 2,399 crores in FY2025-26 but a low-margin one (EBIT margin often in the 8%-15% range), squeezed by 5% GST on mobile catering and by newer Vande Bharat billing that carries less licence fee.

parts.name: Tourism (including State Teertha)
parts.what: Sells tour and travel packages, including pilgrimage tourism run for state governments; it lost money for nine straight quarters during the pandemic but has since become the fastest-growing segment, reaching Rs. 890 crores of revenue in FY2025-26 (up about 19% year-on-year with profit up about 36%) at EBITDA margins of roughly 16%-19%.

parts.name: Rail Neer
parts.what: Manufactures and sells packaged drinking water under the Rail Neer brand from its own bottling plants, sold largely to rail passengers; it is the smallest segment at Rs. 391 crores of revenue in FY2025-26, growing only about 3% a year, with margins swinging between small losses and roughly 13%-19% depending on plant utilisation and material costs.

overview.what_it_does: IRFC (Indian Railway Finance Corporation) is a government-owned Indian finance company — an NBFC — that exists to raise money from lenders and investors and pass it on to Indian Railways and, more recently, to companies connected with the railway ecosystem. It borrows cheaply through bonds, bank term loans, foreign-currency loans (ECBs) and instruments like zero-coupon bonds, then leases rolling stock (locomotives, coaches, wagons) and funds railway project assets under a cost-plus lease agreement with the Ministry of Railways, earning a fixed, pre-agreed spread over its own weighted-average cost of funds — historically 40 basis points on rolling stock leases and 35 basis points on project asset financing. Because its borrowing costs are among the lowest in the market and its overheads are under 0.1% of revenue, the thin spread on a very large book still produces large profits; the company reports no NPAs in nearly four decades and had roughly INR 4.85 lakh crore of assets under management at end-FY26. It operates only in India, funding Indian Railways and, since FY26 (what management calls 'IRFC 2.0'), other government-linked borrowers with backward or forward linkages to railways.

parts.name: Rolling stock leasing to Ministry of Railways
parts.what: IRFC funds locomotives, coaches and wagons and leases them to Indian Railways under a standard cost-plus lease at a consistent spread of about 40 basis points; together with project financing this was historically almost the entire book, with over 98% of AUM being direct exposure to the sovereign.

parts.name: Project asset financing / project loans to Ministry of Railways
parts.what: Loans for railway infrastructure projects that the government budget does not cover, carried at a spread of about 35 basis points; management says IRFC is the sole extra-budgetary borrowing arm for this and funded around 31.4% of the Ministry's total capex in one recent year.

parts.name: Lending to railway PSUs and SPVs
parts.what: Loans to railway-owned entities such as RVNL and IRCON, which made up only about 1.38% of AUM as of June 2022 — a small sliver next to the direct Ministry of Railways exposure.

parts.name: Railway ecosystem lending — 'IRFC 2.0' diversification
parts.what: Started April 2025, this is lending to many clients linked to railways — central PSUs, state government entities, metros, joint ventures and SPVs (examples given: NTPC and its subsidiaries, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation, Hindustan Urvarak & Rasayan) — won through competitive RFPs and open bids at margins management describes as 2x to 3x the fixed railway margin; it delivered roughly INR 74,000 crore of sanctions and INR 35,000 crore of disbursements in FY26 and is targeted to be about 40% of the business mix by 2030.

parts.name: Borrowing / treasury operations
parts.what: The funding engine behind everything else — a diversified mix of bonds (about 44% of borrowings in mid-2022), term loans (about 33%) and external commercial borrowings (about 17%), plus newer instruments like yen-denominated ECBs and zero-coupon bonds; top domestic credit ratings and sovereign-equivalent international ratings are what let IRFC quote the lowest rates and still make a margin.

overview.what_it_does: Le Travenues Technology Limited, which trades as ixigo, is an Indian online travel agency (OTA) that sells train, bus and flight tickets to everyday Indian consumers through a family of apps and websites — ixigo, ConfirmTkt and AbhiBus — with hotels and metro tickets being added more recently. Its core customer is the mass-market Indian traveller, including what management calls the 'Next Billion Users' in Tier 2, 3 and 4 towns, many of whom are booking a flight or a ticket online for the first time in their lives. It makes money by taking a cut on the tickets it sells (convenience fees and commissions on gross booking value) plus growing fees from add-on 'peace of mind' services such as ixigo Assured, Assured Flex and Travel Guarantee — in Q4 FY26 over 31% of transactions carried such an add-on. The business is almost entirely India-focused, though it also sells international flights out of India (over 20% of flights GTV by Q3 FY26); for FY26 it reported gross transaction value of about INR 18,693 crores (~USD 2 billion), revenue from operations of INR 1,228 crores and profit after tax of INR 71 crores.

parts.name: Trains
parts.what: Train ticket booking through the ixigo and ConfirmTkt apps (sold via IRCTC), historically the company's anchor business and still the OTA market leader with a 62% OTA share; it was 43% of GTV and 35% of contribution margin as of Q3 FY26, though its share of the mix is shrinking as flights and buses grow faster, and it faced volume pressure in Q4 FY26 from railway policy changes and tight seat supply.

parts.name: Flights
parts.what: Domestic and international air ticket booking, the fastest-scaling large vertical and by Q4 FY26 the biggest business by GTV at INR 2,018 crores in the quarter, supported on the supply side by GDS tie-ups with Amadeus and Travelport and 26 airlines connected via NDC.

parts.name: Buses (AbhiBus)
parts.what: Intercity bus ticket booking, acquired in 2021 when it did roughly INR 400–500 crores of annual GTV and scaled to over INR 2,400 crores in the twelve months to Q3 FY26 (about 6x), still compounding 40–50% a year and now the largest contributor of contribution margin, with management deliberately favouring growth over margin here.

parts.name: Hotels
parts.what: A new and still small line, with a hotel supply platform called HELLO for onboarding properties directly and a small on-ground team; management says it will not report hotels separately until it reaches product-market fit and meaningful scale.

parts.name: Value-added services / 'peace of mind' products
parts.what: Paid add-ons layered on top of tickets — ixigo Assured and Assured Flex, AbhiAssured free cancellation, Travel Guarantee (discounted alternate travel if a waitlisted train ticket doesn't confirm) and Flight Tracker Pro — which management now describes as the real business ('we are in the Peace of Mind business'), attached to over 31% of Q4 FY26 transactions, generally at slightly lower margin than the core ticket business in their early phase.

parts.name: AI customer-experience stack (TARA)
parts.what: In-house AI agents and chat/voice bots that handle customer support and disruption management — 4.35 million queries handled end-to-end in Q4 FY26, with 81.5% of voice and 91.1% of chat conversations resolved without a human — which management frames as the main source of operating leverage rather than a separate revenue line.

parts.name: Distribution partnerships and B2B2C
parts.what: Selling through other people's platforms and through offline agents — an exclusive tie-up powering flights, buses and trains inside PhonePe, plus Meesho, Uber (intercity buses), native apps on ChatGPT, and travelsupermall.com (TSM), a B2B2C platform that pushes travel inventory out to offline travel agents; these are described as reach and market-share levers rather than separately sized segments.

parts.name: Adjacent and ancillary offerings
parts.what: Smaller add-on businesses around the core ticket: food delivery on trains with Swiggy (40,000+ restaurants, 160+ stations), metro ticketing in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, and the AU-ixigo co-branded credit card — all described as early-traction or supporting initiatives, with no separate size disclosed.

overview.what_it_does: Jai Balaji Industries is a 24-year-old Indian steel maker, based in Kolkata, that runs fully integrated plants in West Bengal and Chhattisgarh, including a 1.1 million tonne greenfield steel facility. It converts iron ore and coking coal into finished steel products and sells them mainly to infrastructure and industrial buyers — its two flagship, higher-margin lines are ductile iron (DI) pipes used for water supply and drainage schemes such as the government's Jal Jeevan Mission and AMRUT, and specialised ferro alloys sold to Indian and overseas steel customers under long-term contracts, with exports going to more than 40 countries. It makes money on the spread between raw-material cost and the price per tonne of what it sells, so management talks in tonnes shipped, realisation per tonne and EBITDA per tonne (Q1 FY25: about INR21,000/tonne on DI pipes and INR37,000/tonne on ferro alloys versus INR5,000–7,000 on plain steel items). Revenue ran around INR1,700 crore a quarter in FY25 with EBITDA margins of roughly 14%–19%, and the company has been shifting its mix toward the two value-added lines (from about 30% of revenue in FY24 to 45%–55%, targeting 80%) while cutting net term debt from INR871 crore in FY23 to INR221 crore in FY25.

parts.name: Ductile Iron (DI) Pipes
parts.what: Large iron pipes for carrying water and sewage, sold largely into government water-infrastructure projects; this is the single biggest and most important business — roughly 30% of revenue in FY24 rising toward 45%–50%, about a 10% share of the Indian DI pipe market (targeted to reach 18%–20%), with capacity expanded from 3 lakh tonnes to 5.04 lakh tonnes in Q4 FY25 and headed to 6.6 lakh tonnes.

parts.name: Specialized Ferro Alloys
parts.what: Custom alloy grades sold to steel makers in India and abroad that fetch a premium over benchmark prices; the second pillar at roughly 20%–25% of revenue (management aimed for 35%) and the highest EBITDA per tonne of any product, with capacity going from 1.66 lakh tonnes to 1.9 lakh tonnes, though the expansion slipped to Q1 FY27 after delays with a Chinese equipment supplier.

parts.name: TMT Bars
parts.what: Ordinary reinforcement steel bars for construction — a commodity, lower-margin line (about INR6,000 EBITDA per tonne) whose capacity was raised from 2.6 to 3 lakh tonnes through low-cost debottlenecking.

parts.name: Pig Iron
parts.what: Basic iron sold on as a commodity product at roughly INR7,000 EBITDA per tonne; one of the non-core items management says has suffered falling volumes and realisations.

parts.name: Sponge Iron
parts.what: Another commodity steel input sold externally at about INR5,000 EBITDA per tonne, the lowest-margin item in the portfolio and part of the mix the company is deliberately shrinking in relative terms.

parts.name: Integrated upstream and cost-saving operations
parts.what: Not sold to outsiders but central to profitability — blast furnaces producing hot metal (capacity being revamped from 6.3 to 7.5 lakh tonnes), sinter plants (9 lakh tonnes going to 12 lakh tonnes) that substitute for costlier iron ore, a 6 lakh tonne iron ore beneficiation unit, captive power including a 35 TPH blast-furnace waste-gas boiler, and three owned railway sidings, all aimed at the lowest cost structure.

parts.name: Other Pipes and Tubes (new)
parts.what: A diversification the board approved in May 2025 to extend the existing pipe business into additional pipe and tube products; still at the proposal stage with no size given in the calls.

overview.what_it_does: Jain Resource Recycling buys scrap metal from around the world and melts and refines it into usable metal, which it then sells to industrial buyers. Its main products are copper and copper-alloy products (about 55% of FY26 revenue), lead and lead-alloy ingots (about 40%) and aluminium products (about 5%), with smaller streams of tin, plastic and, soon, antimony recovered as by-products. It earns money on the spread between what it pays for scrap and what it gets for the finished metal, with sale prices linked to LME benchmark prices and largely hedged through short futures positions to protect that margin. It buys scrap from more than 120 countries, processes it at plants in the SIPCOT industrial complex at Gummidipoondi, Tamil Nadu (head office in Chennai), and sells mostly for export (62% of FY26 revenue, chiefly to China and other overseas markets) with the remaining 38% sold in India; FY26 revenue was about INR 9,543 crore with PAT of about INR 347 crore.

parts.name: Copper and copper alloy products
parts.what: Recycles copper-bearing scrap into copper and copper-alloy products; the largest and most strategically important part of the business at roughly 55% of FY26 revenue (52% in 9M FY26), earning management-cited EBITDA of roughly INR 42,000-51,000 per tonne.

parts.name: Lead and lead alloy ingots
parts.what: Recycles lead-acid battery scrap into lead and lead-alloy ingots, contributing about 40% of FY26 revenue and described as having a faster cash-collection cycle than copper.

parts.name: Aluminium and aluminium products
parts.what: The smallest of the three main metal streams at roughly 4-5% of revenue, part of what management calls its diversified multi-metal portfolio.

parts.name: Value-added copper products (Jain Green Technologies, Unit 3)
parts.what: A new forward-integration plant making copper anodes, cathodes, wire rods, busbars/profiles and tin-silver coated products; described as the company's biggest 'profitability driver', costing about INR 95 crore in Phase 1 funded from internal accruals, with anode production started March 2026 at 800 tonnes/month and the other lines commissioning through FY27.

parts.name: Tin recovery
parts.what: Extracts tin as a by-product of lead-acid battery recycling; capacity was raised during the year from 125 to 500 tonnes per annum via an extra vacuum distillation furnace, described as already scaling and improving realisations.

parts.name: Antimony extraction
parts.what: A planned unit to separate antimony from lead-antimony bullion, called a new concept in India and a profitability driver, with about INR 20 crore capex, 1,000 tonnes/month of bullion processed for roughly 100 tonnes/month of antimony, targeted for Q3 FY27.

parts.name: Jain C&Y Circular Solutions (Ahmedabad copper scrap JV)
parts.what: A joint venture with C&Y/CNY Group to set up a 72,000 tonne-per-annum copper scrap processing plant (motor/alternator scrap, cable scrap and other scrap) yielding about 25,000 tonnes of processed copper a year; described as a volume-growth project starting operations from September 2026.

parts.name: Kuwait battery recycling investment (Abraj Al-Khaleej)
parts.what: A board-approved 25% equity stake in a Kuwaiti company to build a 2,000 tonne-per-month battery scrap plant, aimed at securing lead raw material and a Middle East presence, targeted for Q3 FY27 but delayed by shipping disruption.

parts.name: Plastic recycling
parts.what: Plastic from battery and cable scrap is currently recycled in-house at the copper and lead plants; a dedicated standalone plant on about six acres, costing roughly INR 15 crore, is planned for Q3 FY27 to support the company's zero-waste model.

overview.what_it_does: J.B. Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals ("J.B. Pharma") is an India-based drug maker that sells branded prescription medicines under its own brand names — Rantac, Metrogyl, Cilacar, Cilacar-T, Nicardia, Azmarda, Sporlac, Razel and an acquired eye-care range — to doctors and chemists across India through a large field force of medical representatives, with cardiology and other chronic therapies as its biggest area. Alongside India it exports formulations to South Africa (both government tenders and the private market), Russia/CIS, the US and other branded export markets, and it manufactures products on contract for other companies (CDMO), where management says it is a global leader in lozenges, especially herbal and medicated ones, plus liquid formulations. Money comes from selling pills, syrups and lozenges at a gross margin that has climbed from roughly 63% to about 69-70%, with operating EBITDA margins guided at 27-29%; growth comes from pushing volumes and prices on big brands, buying brand portfolios, and winning new CDMO clients. The split is roughly 58% India / 42% international; in FY26 India revenue was about INR2,461 crore, international formulations INR1,154 crore and CDMO INR445 crore. Torrent Pharma bought a controlling stake in January 2026 and a full merger was in its final stages as of the May 2026 call.

parts.name: Domestic formulations (India branded business)
parts.what: Branded prescription medicines sold to Indian doctors/pharmacies — the largest part at roughly INR620 crore a quarter and INR2,461 crore in FY26 (about 58% of revenue); management says it is the fastest-growing company among the top 25 in the Indian pharma market, with six brands in the industry's top 300 and a chronic portfolio (cardiology especially) that crossed INR1,000 crore.

parts.name: Chronic / cardiology portfolio (within domestic)
parts.what: The high-margin core of the India business — hypertension, cholesterol and heart-failure drugs like Cilacar, Cilacar-T, Nicardia, Razel and Azmarda — where the calls say J.B. ranks 8th in a roughly $3 billion Indian cardiology market and grew 19% in FY26 versus 14% for the industry.

parts.name: Acquired brand portfolios (Sanzyme/Sporlac, Azmarda, paediatrics, ophthalmology)
parts.what: Brands bought from other companies and plugged into J.B.'s sales network — e.g. the Sporlac franchise at INR122 crore growing 33% CAGR, Azmarda at about INR75 crore, four paediatric brands worth INR33 crore of sales, and an ophthalmology range added in January 2024; a meaningful growth driver but individually much smaller than the core brands.

parts.name: Trade generics
parts.what: A low-margin unbranded generics line inside India that was about 7-8% of India sales until Q3 FY26 and was then deliberately discontinued after the Torrent takeover, which is why reported India growth slowed to 2% in Q4 FY26 while the branded business still grew 8%.

parts.name: Franchisee business (within domestic)
parts.what: A smaller India channel run through franchise partners, contributing INR108 crore of revenue in Q3 FY26 and growing about 11% year-on-year.

parts.name: International formulations (exports)
parts.what: Finished medicines sold in South Africa, Russia/CIS, the US and other branded export markets — about INR306 crore in Q3 FY26 and INR1,154 crore for FY26; in South Africa management deliberately cut low-margin government tender sales so the higher-margin private market rose from 40% to about 70% of that country's business.

parts.name: CDMO / CMO (contract manufacturing)
parts.what: Making lozenges (herbal and medicated, for immunity and cough-and-cold) and liquid formulations for other companies' brands, including consumer players in Europe — around INR445 crore in FY26, roughly a quarter to a third of international revenue, described as a business where J.B. has global leadership in lozenges and which is seasonally stronger in the first half of the year.

parts.name: API
parts.what: A small side line selling active pharmaceutical ingredients (the raw drug substance), worth only about INR21 crore in Q3 FY26 — the least important of the reported categories.

overview.what_it_does: Jindal Saw Limited makes large steel and iron pipes and tubes, and sells them mostly to government water-supply projects and to oil and gas companies. Its main products are ductile iron pipes for drinking-water and sewage networks (including India's Jal Jeevan Mission and state water schemes), welded SAW pipes (LSAW/HSAW) for oil, gas and water pipelines, and seamless pipes and tubes — including higher-grade API-certified, stainless and alloy pipe — for oil and gas drilling and production. It makes money by winning tenders and contracts, holding a large order book (about USD 1 billion in 2022, USD 1.6 billion by late 2024, plus a 6 lakh tonne Saudi work order in 2026) and converting it into shipments; profitability swings with raw-material costs (steel, coal, iron ore, pig iron), the rupee, and the mix between exports and domestic sales, since exports carry higher margins. It operates plants in India (Nashik is named for seamless pipe) and, through subsidiaries and joint ventures, in Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia, selling domestically in India and exporting to the Middle East, the US, Europe and elsewhere — with standalone revenue of about INR 14,745 crore and consolidated about INR 17,987 crore in FY26.

parts.name: Ductile iron (DI) pipes / water segment
parts.what: Iron pipes for municipal and rural water supply and sewage, sold largely to government-funded water infrastructure programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission and state-level projects (some multilateral-agency funded); management describes it as the main growth driver in India in 2022 and the biggest single drag in FY26 when project execution and fund releases slowed, so it is clearly one of the largest parts of the business.

parts.name: SAW pipes (LSAW / HSAW), large diameter
parts.what: Large-diameter welded line pipe for oil and gas transmission and bulk water, sold on project contracts in India and export markets; management repeatedly points to 'large dia' wins in both water and oil and gas as a key order-book contributor, and is building dedicated 300,000 tonne-per-annum LSAW and HSAW mills in Saudi Arabia.

parts.name: Seamless pipes and tubes (carbon, stainless, alloy; OCTG)
parts.what: Higher-grade drilling and well pipe for oil and gas customers such as ONGC, including deep-sea and deepwater work; described as a newer, higher-margin basket (API-certified business earns better margins than non-API), and its importance shows in the fact that the suspension of the API monogram at the Nashik plant from January to mid-June 2026 was singled out as a material hit to quarterly results.

parts.name: Abu Dhabi operations (subsidiary)
parts.what: An overseas manufacturing base described as a ductile iron pipe facility to which a 3 lakh tonne, roughly USD 300 million seamless pipe plant is being added (commercial operation expected FY29), serving MENA energy and water customers; its results flow through the consolidated numbers and its profits swung with pig iron prices in 2022, so it is the most significant overseas operating unit.

parts.name: Saudi Arabia joint venture
parts.what: A 51:49 JV with Buhur of Saudi Arabia to build LSAW and HSAW pipe mills of 300,000 tonnes each for regional water and energy demand; still under construction with land secured and equipment LCs opened, so it contributes nothing to current earnings but is presented as a main future growth plank.

parts.name: Technology partnerships / joint ventures for oil and gas products
parts.what: A joint venture with Hunting and an exclusive technology transfer with OSI USA to make specialised oil-country tubular goods in India, mentioned in 2022 as a way to bid for ONGC tenders; described as an add-on to the pipe business rather than a large revenue line at the time.

parts.name: Iron ore pellets
parts.what: A raw-material-linked product whose prices management tracks and comments on ('a little softening on the pellet prices'), noted as a smaller swing factor that gets more than offset by the pipe business.

overview.what_it_does: Jindal Steel (listed as JINDALSTEL, formerly Jindal Steel & Power Limited) is an Indian integrated steel maker that turns coal and iron into finished steel products at two large plants — Raigarh and Angul (Odisha) — and sells them mainly to Indian construction and industrial buyers, with some exports. It makes money by selling steel tonnage: roughly 2.0–2.3 million tons a quarter in recent periods, generating about INR 15,000 crores of quarterly gross revenue, with profit driven by the gap between the realized steel price per ton and the cost per ton (dominated by coking coal and thermal coal). Its product basket runs from TMT rebar for construction to hot-rolled coil, plates and newer cold-rolled/coated products, and it also earns from by-products and from a power plant and overseas mining subsidiaries. Management is in the middle of a very large expansion program — about INR 47,043 crores announced, INR 32,925 crores spent by December 2025 — that takes steelmaking capacity to 15.6 million tons a year.

parts.name: Long products / TMT (rebar for construction)
parts.what: Construction steel bars sold into India's building and infrastructure market; the calls treat TMT pricing as demand-sensitive and seasonally weak in the monsoon, and it is one of the two main pillars of the product basket.

parts.name: Flat products — Hot Strip Mill (HRC)
parts.what: Hot-rolled coil from the Angul Hot Strip Mill, commissioned in 29 months and ramped from a standing start to about 450 kt in a single quarter against a ~3 million ton plan; it is the biggest growth driver of volumes, though management says HRC carries the lowest realization and margin in the basket.

parts.name: Plates
parts.what: Heavy steel plate made at the Raigarh plate mill; mentioned mainly as a facility whose maintenance shutdowns move quarterly production.

parts.name: Value-added flats — CRM and colour coating (CCL)
parts.what: Cold rolling and a 0.2 million tons per annum colour-coating line commissioned in January 2026, described as broadening the product portfolio and supporting higher margins.

parts.name: Steelmaking assets at Angul (blast furnaces, BOF, coke ovens, DRI)
parts.what: The upstream iron- and steel-making chain being built out — BF-2, BOF-2 and BOF-3 (3 million tons per annum, due Q4 FY26), plus coke oven batteries and a DRI unit; commissioning and ramp-up of these is the main swing factor in production, cost and capex in the calls.

parts.name: Captive coal mines
parts.what: Own coal mines such as Utkal C (started) and Utkal B1 (opened, overburden removal underway) that feed the plants and reduce dependence on bought coal, which the calls repeatedly flag as the biggest cost item.

parts.name: Power
parts.what: A 1,050 MW power plant (SBPP) acquired through the insolvency process and turned around, with two 525 MW modules commissioned/synchronized to the grid in Q3 FY26 and January 2026.

parts.name: Overseas subsidiaries (Mozambique, South Africa, Australia)
parts.what: Foreign operations that in Q1 FY23 contributed roughly INR 334 crores, INR 84 crores and INR 24 crores of EBITDA respectively; later calls describe them mainly in terms of whether their losses are shrinking, so they are small relative to the Indian steel business.

parts.name: By-products and other operating income
parts.what: Sales of process by-products alongside steel; the calls note these did not keep pace with steel revenue in Q3 FY26 because more output was consumed captively, which dragged down average selling price per ton.

overview.what_it_does: Jio Financial Services (JFS) is an Indian financial-services holding company that was spun off from Reliance Industries and listed in August 2023; it sells everyday financial products — loans, a payments bank account, merchant payment acceptance, insurance, and mutual funds — mainly to ordinary Indian consumers and to small merchants and corporate clients, delivered digitally through the JioFinance app and the wider Jio ecosystem (MyJio, JioBharat feature phones, group stores and business correspondents). It makes money the way its licensed subsidiaries do: interest on its loan book, fees on payment transactions and bank accounts, commission on insurance sold as a broker, fund-management fees on assets under management, and premium underwritten by its reinsurance venture — supplemented by treasury income on its very large capital base and dividends from the 6.1% stake it holds in Reliance Industries. Management frames the group around four customer needs — Borrow, Invest, Transact and Protect — with high-frequency payments used as a cheap acquisition and data funnel into higher-value lending, wealth and insurance. It operates only in India (plus a GIFT City fund entity for global investing), and by FY26 income from core business operations, at Rs 1,390 crore, had become the majority (54%) of net total income, versus treasury earlier.

parts.name: Lending & Leasing — Jio Finance Limited (NBFC), later called Jio Credit
parts.what: The lending arm, giving retail and corporate customers loans mainly against property (home loans) and against shares and mutual funds, plus early consumer-durable and personal loans; it is the biggest and fastest-growing part, with assets under management going from Rs 4,199 crore in Q3 FY25 to over Rs 25,700 crore in FY26 and Rs 30,667 crore by June 2026, and quarterly disbursements above Rs 11,000 crore.

parts.name: Jio Payments Bank Limited (JPBL)
parts.what: A payments bank offering savings and current accounts, UPI cash withdrawal and FASTag/toll processing, reaching customers in rural areas through roughly 7,300 business correspondents; it was originally a joint venture with State Bank of India and became a 100% subsidiary in June 2025, with deposits of Rs 544 crore in FY26 rising to Rs 617 crore — small in rupee terms but treated as a high-frequency engagement and distribution layer.

parts.name: Jio Payment Solutions Limited (JPSL)
parts.what: The merchant-payments/payment-aggregator business that onboards small merchants (in about five minutes, including via JioBharat feature phones) and runs online payment gateway and now cross-border settlement for exporters; it processed over Rs 52,200 crore of total payment volume in FY26 and Rs 19,208 crore in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Jio Insurance Broking Limited (JIBL)
parts.what: An insurance broker — it does not underwrite but sells plans from 31 insurers across motor, two-wheeler, health and life plus niche 'sachet' covers, through direct-to-customer, embedded/ecosystem and institutional corporate channels; premium facilitated was Rs 982 crore in FY26, a relatively flat and much smaller line than lending.

parts.name: Jio BlackRock Asset Management (JV with BlackRock)
parts.what: The investments arm, a 50:50 mutual-fund joint venture with BlackRock (initial commitment up to US$150 million each) that launched in FY26 and reached over Rs 15,200 crore of AUM in nine months and Rs 18,412 crore by June 2026, and has approval to set up a retail fund management entity in GIFT City so Indians can invest in global funds.

parts.name: Jio Finance Platform and Services Limited (the JioFinance app)
parts.what: The group's unified digital storefront and technology platform — an AI-driven app offering digital gold (SmartGold), a personal finance manager, UPI and bill payments, plus third-party credit cards, insurance and fixed deposits — with 25 million unique users across digital properties; management still calls it an incubation-stage venture rather than a profit centre.

parts.name: Allianz Jio Reinsurance / Jio Allianz General Insurance (JV with Allianz)
parts.what: The newest 'Protect' ventures: a reinsurance company that got approvals and started operating in March 2026 and underwrote Rs 266 crore of premium in its first full quarter, and a newly incorporated general and health insurance joint venture — both early-stage and still absorbing investment.

parts.name: Treasury and the Reliance Industries stake
parts.what: JFS holds 6.1% of Reliance Industries and a very large capital base (consolidated shareholders' equity of Rs 1.37 lakh crore, plus Rs 9,890 crore of promoter warrant money), and the resulting dividend and treasury income funds the loss-making incubating businesses — though management notes a March 2026 spike in yields hurt this income.

overview.what_it_does: JK Cement Limited is an Indian cement maker that manufactures and sells grey cement (its main product), white cement, and wall putty, branded and sold mainly through dealers to construction buyers, with a smaller "non-trade" (bulk/institutional) portion. It earns money by mining limestone, burning it into clinker at integrated plants, grinding it into cement at plants and split grinding units, and selling it by the bag — so profits swing with cement prices per bag, fuel/petcoke and diesel costs, and freight (lead distance, rail vs road mix). Its plants and markets are spread across North India (Rajasthan, Haryana, UP, Punjab), Central India (MP, UP), the South (Karnataka), the West (Gujarat) and now the East (Bihar), with some white cement also supplied from plants in the UAE. It is in a long capacity build-out — roughly 24 million tonnes in 2024 heading to 30, then a stated target of 40 million tonnes by FY28 and 50 million by FY30 — funded partly by debt (gross debt about INR5,551 crores as of June 2026); full-year FY26 net sales were about INR12,568 crores with EBITDA of INR2,318 crores.

parts.name: Grey cement
parts.what: The core business — ordinary construction cement made at integrated clinker plants and grinding units and sold by the bag across North, Central, South, West and East India; it drives almost all volume and revenue (volumes grew 19% year-on-year in the June 2026 quarter, mostly from the new Central India and Bihar capacity), and management talks about it in per-tonne terms (EBITDA of INR982 per tonne in Q1 FY27).

parts.name: White cement
parts.what: A smaller, separate and evidently higher-value product line supplied from domestic plants plus plants in the UAE, with volumes growing 11% year-on-year in Q1 FY27; management said domestic production can now meet the whole domestic demand after UAE supply into South India was disrupted.

parts.name: Wall putty
parts.what: A finishing/coating product ("JK Cement WallMaxx"-type white cement wall putty) treated as part of the white segment; the company is adding a 6 lakh tonne (0.6 million tonne) putty plant at Nathdwara, Rajasthan, expected to commission around September 2026.

parts.name: Capacity expansion projects
parts.what: Not a product but a constant management theme — greenfield and brownfield clinker and grinding units (Panna, Prayagraj, Hamirpur, Ujjain, Buxar in Bihar, Muddapur in Karnataka, and a new 7 million tonne Jaisalmer project with grinding at Bikaner and Punjab costing about INR3,630 crores for the integrated unit) that determine future volumes, capex and debt levels.

parts.name: Government incentive income
parts.what: A recurring earnings item from state-level fiscal incentives on certain plants (e.g. Aligarh), which management guides on separately and which has been falling as older incentive periods expire and GST rules change.

overview.what_it_does: JK Lakshmi Cement is an Indian cement maker: it digs limestone from its own mines, burns it into clinker at its plants, and grinds that clinker into bagged and bulk cement that it sells to builders, contractors and infrastructure projects. Its home base is Rajasthan (registered works at Jaykaypuram, Sirohi, with mines at Sirohi, Udaipur and a newly acquired lease at Nagaur), and it sells mainly across North India (Rajasthan, Haryana, western UP), the West (Gujarat, Mumbai — where a new Surat grinding station started in September 2025) and a smaller position in the East. Money comes from tons sold times the price per ton, so management talks constantly about volume, realisation per ton, the mix between dealer/retail 'trade' sales (roughly 49%–56% of volume across the calls) and lower-priced institutional 'non-trade' sales, and about pushing higher-priced 'premium' products (about 21% of trade volume in FY23, around 30% by FY25). Profit is then driven by squeezing costs — fuel (pet coke and coal), power, and freight measured as average 'lead distance' (down from ~395 km in FY23 to ~372 km) — plus greener inputs like alternative fuels and renewable power.

parts.name: Cement (the core business)
parts.what: Manufacturing and selling grey cement — roughly two-thirds blended cement and one-third OPC (ordinary Portland cement) in FY23, with a stated goal of moving blended to 72%–75% — and this is overwhelmingly where the revenue and profit come from.

parts.name: Premium products
parts.what: A higher-priced branded slice of the cement range that management deliberately pushes to lift realisation per ton; it grew from about 14% to over 21% of trade sales volume during FY23 and to roughly 30% by Q1 FY25.

parts.name: Trade vs non-trade channel
parts.what: Not a separate product but the way management splits the same cement: 'trade' means dealer/retail bags at better prices, 'non-trade' means bulk institutional sales to projects and onsite ready-mix plants — the trade share ran about 49%–56% and swings in it visibly move average realisation.

parts.name: Ready-mix concrete (RMC)
parts.what: A concrete-mixing operation that sells ready-mixed concrete to sites; it was about Rs. 52 crore of revenue in one FY23 quarter, so a small add-on next to cement.

parts.name: Non-cement revenue
parts.what: A catch-all 'other products' line — about Rs. 116 crore in a FY23 quarter (including the Rs. 52 crore of RMC) — clearly a minor contributor alongside cement.

parts.name: Udaipur Cement Works Limited (UCWL)
parts.what: A separately listed cement subsidiary that JK Lakshmi controls, whose Udaipur expansion (clinker line targeted for around March 2024, grinding a month or two later) was being ramped toward 60% utilisation by end-FY25; a merger of UCWL into JK Lakshmi was proposed at the board in mid-2024.

parts.name: Limestone mines and leases
parts.what: The raw-material base that underpins everything — reserves of roughly 15–20 years at Sirohi (lease renewal due 2030), 40–50 years at Udaipur plus an adjacent new lease, and a Nagaur lease said to support a future 5–7 million ton plant for 45–50 years.

parts.name: Grinding stations and logistics assets
parts.what: Split grinding units and in-plant railway sidings — including the Surat grinding station commissioned 22 September 2025 — that let the company grind clinker closer to customers, reach new markets and cut freight/lead distance.

parts.name: Cost and sustainability levers
parts.what: Ongoing efficiency programmes — alternative fuels and raw materials (AFR at ~12% of fuel in Q1 FY25 vs 7% the prior year), renewable power (~48% vs 39%), digital/supply-chain optimisation and headcount productivity that cut employee cost — which management treats as the main defence when cement prices are weak.

overview.what_it_does: JK Paper is an Indian paper manufacturer that makes and sells writing and printing paper (maplitho), coated paper, office/copier cut-size paper, and virgin-fibre packaging board, plus corrugated boxes through recently acquired packaging companies. Its paper goes to printers, offices, schools and courts (helped by the new education policy and offices returning to full working), while its packaging board and corrugated boxes go to FMCG, pharma and food companies that are also shifting away from plastic. It earns money by converting wood — grown through its own large plantation programme — into pulp in-house and then into paper and board, selling mainly in India (exports were around 8-10% of volume, cut back when domestic demand is strong), so profits swing with paper selling prices (NSR) versus wood, pulp, chemical and energy costs.
