It runs plants in Gujarat, Odisha and Telangana, reported consolidated revenue of about ₹6,772 crore in FY23 with a ₹1,208 crore profit, and describes itself as wood- and carbon-positive.

parts.name: Paper and packaging board (JK Paper standalone)
parts.what: The core business making writing/printing paper, coated paper, copier paper and packaging board at the Gujarat, Odisha and Telangana plants — management says roughly ₹6,000 crore-plus of the group's ~₹7,000 crore expected revenue comes from paper, including a new Gujarat board machine and pulp mill running at about 90-100% of capacity.

parts.name: Sirpur (Sirpur Paper Mills subsidiary)
parts.what: A separately consolidated, purely paper company acquired earlier and running at about 90% of its capacity, which delivered over ₹300 crore of profit in FY23 and EBITDA margins of roughly 22-23% in FY24 excluding a state incentive.

parts.name: Corrugation / corrugated packaging business
parts.what: The newest arm, built by acquiring Horizon Pack and Securipax (together described as India's largest corrugated packaging player), later Manipal Utility Packaging, and by commissioning its own Ludhiana plant in August 2023 — expected to contribute roughly ₹1,000-1,200 crore of revenue at 10-16% margins, with about ₹800 crore spent on the three acquisitions mainly to buy established customer relationships.

parts.name: Plantation / farm forestry
parts.what: The wood-sourcing activity feeding the integrated pulp mills — 8.32 crore saplings planted over 55,700 acres in FY23 and about 110 crore saplings across 6 lakh acres to date — which matters because wood is the basic raw material and its cost jumped 30-35% in FY24.

overview.what_it_does: JK Tyre & Industries is an Indian company that manufactures and sells tyres — for trucks and buses, passenger cars and SUVs, tractors/farm vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, and off-the-road industrial and mining machines. It makes money two ways: fitting tyres onto new vehicles as an approved supplier to auto makers (OEMs such as Hyundai, Kia, Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland, Mahindra, VECV, Renault), and selling replacement tyres to vehicle owners and fleets through a dealer network of brand shops, Steel Wheels centres and pit stops across India, including rural areas. Its plants (Kankroli, Banmore, Laksar and others) ran at roughly 78–85% utilisation, and profitability swings mainly with raw-material costs — natural rubber above all — which management offsets through staggered selling-price hikes, richer product mix and cost cuts. Operations are centred in India, with exports to the US and other markets plus a manufacturing and selling business in Mexico; consolidated revenue reached a record Rs.16,384 crore in FY26 with EBITDA of Rs.2,089 crore.

parts.name: TBR (truck and bus radial)
parts.what: Radial tyres for commercial vehicles, repeatedly called a critical segment for the company and a focus of capacity expansion; Q3FY26 replacement volumes grew 15% and OEM volumes 33% year-on-year.

parts.name: PCR / passenger line
parts.what: Tyres for cars and SUVs, the other segment management calls critical, including EV-approved tyres (Hyundai Creta, Tata Punch electric variants, Renault Duster) and newly launched embedded 'smart' tyres; passenger line volumes grew 16–18% year-on-year in recent quarters with premium 16-inch-and-above sizes growing 13% in FY26.

parts.name: Replacement market
parts.what: Selling tyres to existing vehicle owners and fleets through dealers — described as the steadier, promising demand driver, growing 11% in Q3FY26 and 19% (TBR) in Q4FY26.

parts.name: OEM business
parts.what: Supplying tyres as original equipment to vehicle manufacturers; lumpier than replacement (it fell ~10% in Q1FY24 on pre-buy effects, then grew 24–42% in FY26 quarters), and price increases to OEMs come with a lag.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Overseas sales from India, running around Rs.560–590 crore a quarter, roughly 15% of revenue, with volumes up 9% in Q3FY26 and 5% for full-year FY26 despite geopolitical disruption.

parts.name: Farm segment
parts.what: Tractor and agricultural tyres, including the premium 'Shresth Plus' range; volumes rose 58% year-on-year in Q4FY26 with OE volumes nearly doubling.

parts.name: OTR (off-the-road) tyres
parts.what: Tyres for industrial and mining equipment built for harsh conditions; four new types were launched in Q3FY26, a smaller but growing product line.

parts.name: JK Tornel, Mexico
parts.what: The overseas subsidiary that makes and sells tyres in Mexico and exports to the US and Latin America, contributing roughly Rs.500–680 crore of revenue per quarter (about Rs.616 crore in Q3FY26) at 8–9% EBITDA margins; described as an earlier successful turnaround acquisition.

parts.name: Cavendish Industries Limited (CIL)
parts.what: An Indian subsidiary contributing about Rs.960–1,025 crore of revenue per quarter, whose capacity utilisation JK Tyre lifted from ~30% to over 95%; it was legally merged into JK Tyre during Q3FY26 for operational and financial synergies.

parts.name: Capacity expansion programme
parts.what: Ongoing brownfield projects — Rs.1,130 crore already under way (adding ~7% capacity across TBR, ASLTR and PCR) plus a further Rs.4,980 crore approved in phases to 2029 to lift TBR and PCR capacity by 24%.

overview.what_it_does: Jupiter Life Line Hospitals runs large multi-specialty private hospitals in western India, selling in-patient and out-patient medical treatment directly to patients — everything from childbirth and newborn care to cancer surgery and organ transplants. It earns money by charging for those treatments, with revenue driven by how many beds are filled (occupancy of about 61-62% group-wide in FY26), average revenue per occupied bed per day (ARPOB of about Rs. 67,700 in FY26) and average length of stay (~3.87 days); roughly 55% of revenue is billed to health insurers, ~43% is paid out of patients' own pockets and only ~1% comes from government schemes. It ran three hospitals for most of the period covered — Thane and Dombivli in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, Pune, and Indore in Madhya Pradesh — and opened a fourth, Dombivli, in February 2026. Management stresses that every hospital is a self-built, self-owned, full-service 'hub' (no leased property, no small 'spoke' clinics), which makes it a deliberately asset-heavy business; FY26 total income was Rs. 1,499.8 crores with EBITDA of Rs. 343.3 crores (22.9% margin) and PAT of Rs. 194.2 crores.

parts.name: Thane hospital (MMR)
parts.what: The original hospital, opened in 2007 with 377 beds, now the most mature and highest-occupancy unit (about 75% in FY26) with margins management says are above 25%; growth from here is essentially only inflation-linked price increases.

parts.name: Pune hospital (Kharadi)
parts.what: A 386-bed hospital opened in 2017, running at roughly 65% occupancy, so it still has both occupancy headroom and price increases as growth levers.

parts.name: Indore hospital
parts.what: A 96%-plus owned subsidiary acquired and opened in late 2020, planned for 431 beds and expanded to 309 operating beds by January 2025; it is the least mature unit at 45-50% occupancy and grows on all three levers — price, occupancy and shifting toward more complex (higher-value) cases.

parts.name: Dombivli hospital (MMR)
parts.what: A 500-bed, 750,000 sq ft greenfield hospital built for about Rs. 425 crores and inaugurated in February 2026 with 200 beds running in Phase 1; management expects it to lose money and drag consolidated EBITDA for roughly two years before breaking even at end of year 2.

parts.name: Projects under development (Pune South/Bibvewadi, Mira Road, BKC)
parts.what: Three more owned greenfield hub hospitals in the pipeline — Pune South (500 beds, opening calendar 2028, under construction), Mira Road (~300 beds, ~Rs. 400 crores total capex, in regulatory approval) and a 400-bed quaternary hospital in Mumbai's BKC — together about 1,700 new beds in this cycle at roughly Rs. 1.5 crores per bed, taking long-term capacity toward nearly 3,000 beds.

parts.name: Payer mix (insurance / self-pay / government)
parts.what: Not a separate business but how management describes its customer base: about 55% of revenue comes from insured patients, ~43% from self-payers and ~1% from government schemes, and the company deliberately targets the well-insured western India population because insurance penetration there is far above the national average.

overview.what_it_does: JM Financial Limited is an India-based financial services group, headquartered in Mumbai and listed on the BSE and NSE, that advises companies on raising money and buying/selling businesses, lends and invests its own capital, and manages and distributes investments for wealthy and retail savers. It earns money three ways: fees and commissions from investment banking deals (IPOs, QIPs, block trades, M&A and private equity advisory), broking and wealth/asset management; interest and recovery income from loans it makes and from distressed loans it buys; and, increasingly, fees from arranging (syndicating) credit deals for outside investors rather than holding them on its own balance sheet. Its customers are Indian corporates and promoters, real estate developers, institutional and high-net-worth investors, retail investors reached through 70-odd branches and roughly 900 franchisees, and low-income home buyers. In FY26 the group reported revenue-driven profit after tax of about INR1,202 crores on a net worth of about INR10,605 crores (book value roughly INR111 per share), after a strategic pivot announced in May 2024 that shrank its wholesale lending book and shifted the group toward fee-based businesses.

parts.name: Corporate Advisory and Capital Markets (CACM) — investment banking and institutional equities
parts.what: Advises companies on IPOs, QIPs, block deals, M&A and private equity transactions and runs an institutional stockbroking desk; it is the flagship fee business, with FY26 net revenue of about INR789 crores, operating PAT of INR347 crores on only INR829 crores of capital employed (about 47% ROE), 41 capital market deals worth roughly INR95,000 crores closed in FY26, and 55 IPO filings worth about INR1,40,000 crores in the pipeline; management says it ranked #1 in QIPs in calendar 2024 and #2 among Indian banks in M&A/PE advisory.

parts.name: Wealth and Asset Management (earlier called 'Platform AWS' — Asset management, Wealth, Securities)
parts.what: Manages and distributes investments for high-net-worth clients (private wealth), mid-tier 'elite' clients and retail savers through independent financial advisers, plus retail broking, margin funding and portfolio management; wealth AUM was about INR1,10,000 crores in Dec 2024 with recurring AUM of roughly INR31,000 crores in FY26, FY26 net revenue INR775 crores and operating PAT INR132 crores, and the group is deliberately spending on 1,046 sales staff, branches and technology to grow it.

parts.name: Asset Management (mutual fund and alternative funds), reported within Wealth and Asset Management
parts.what: Runs mutual fund schemes and is launching alternative investment funds (a pre-IPO fund, a real estate fund and a credit fund); it is still small and loss-making — non-liquid mutual fund average AUM of about INR10,500 crores in FY26, mutual fund management fees of roughly INR44 crores (up 65%), and a loss after minority interest of about INR30 crores for FY26.

parts.name: Private Markets (private credit — corporate, bespoke, real estate and distressed credit — plus investments)
parts.what: Lends to and invests in companies, promoters and real estate developers, buys and recovers distressed loans through its ARC, and holds private equity fund and REIT stakes; since the 2024 pivot it is shifting from holding loans on its own books (wholesale book fell from INR7,529 crores in Mar 2024 to INR4,207 crores by Dec 2024) to originating deals and syndicating them to investors, and it delivered FY26 operating profit before tax of INR742 crores and PAT of about INR543 crores on roughly INR6,600 crores of capital employed, helped by over INR270 crores of recoveries.

parts.name: Affordable Home Loans (home finance business)
parts.what: Makes small home loans (and earlier loans against property) to lower-income borrowers through a branch network that has grown to 151 branches and over 33,000 customers; AUM was about INR3,460 crores in FY26, up 22% year-on-year, with FY26 revenue up 25%, collection efficiency near 99%, gross NPA under 1%, and management targeting 25%+ annual growth for the next three years.

parts.name: Legacy segments as reported before the FY26 format change
parts.what: Until the new segment format took effect, the group reported an Investment Bank segment, a Mortgage Lending segment (wholesale real estate lending plus retail/affordable mortgages, once the biggest piece of a INR14,670 crore loan book in Sep 2022), a Distressed Credit segment (ARC and alternative credit, about INR11,349 crores of AUM in Sep 2022), and Platform AWS; these have since been folded into CACM, Private Markets, Wealth and Asset Management, and Affordable Home Loans.

overview.what_it_does: Jana Small Finance Bank is an Indian bank, headquartered in Bengaluru, that lends small amounts to people and tiny businesses that mainstream banks tend to skip — what management calls "serving the underserved." It grew out of a microfinance lender, became a bank in 2018, and has spent the years since shifting from unsecured group loans to loans backed by collateral: home loans, small-business loans against property, gold, two-wheelers and used cars. It funds this mainly with customer deposits gathered through its branch network (Rs. 35,784 crores of deposits and 822 branches by March 2026, spread across ~25 states with deliberately low concentration in any one state), and earns its money from the gap between the high rates it charges borrowers and what it pays depositors — a net interest margin around 7.5%, plus fees. As of FY26 about 72.6% of its loan book was secured and the rest unsecured microfinance, most of which is now covered by government credit-guarantee schemes.

parts.name: Microfinance / Retail Financial Services (RFS) — unsecured advances
parts.what: Small unsecured loans to low-income, largely rural borrowers, the bank's original business and still its single biggest unsecured exposure — it fell from ~40% of loans in FY24 to ~30% in FY25 (around Rs. 8,900 crores) and to roughly 27% by FY26 after a sector-wide stress period, with 77% of it now sitting under the CGFMU/CGTMSE credit-guarantee programs.

parts.name: Affordable housing and micro housing loans
parts.what: Home loans for lower-income buyers, described in FY27 Q1 as one of the businesses "growing superbly well" and a key reason the bank relocates branches to better locations.

parts.name: MSME loans
parts.what: Lending to small and medium businesses; management lists it among the strongly growing secured lines in FY27.

parts.name: Micro LAP (loan against property)
parts.what: Small loans secured against a borrower's property; the one line that did not grow in Q1 FY27, deliberately, as the bank shifts it from third-party to direct sourcing.

parts.name: Gold loans
parts.what: Loans against gold — an incubated product management said in FY25 had "grown up" from an investment into a profitable, fast-growing business.

parts.name: Two-wheeler and vehicle loans
parts.what: Financing for two-wheelers, described alongside gold as having matured into a strong self-standing business, with vehicle loans named again as a growth driver in FY27.

parts.name: Used car loans
parts.what: A newer secured product the bank is deliberately spending money to build up, named in FY25 as the next line (with supply chain) it expects to turn into a meaningful business in a year or two.

parts.name: Supply chain financing
parts.what: Another newer, still-being-invested-in secured line, grouped with used cars as a future growth engine rather than a current earner.

parts.name: Term loans to NBFCs
parts.what: Wholesale lending to non-bank finance companies, which the bank is intentionally keeping flat because its own retail products can deliver 20–22% growth on their own.

parts.name: Branch banking and liabilities (deposits/CASA)
parts.what: The deposit-gathering side — current and savings accounts plus term deposits — which funds the lending; deposits grew 29% in FY25 and 23% in FY26 to Rs. 35,784 crores, with CASA up 31% year-on-year in Q1 FY27 and cost of funds falling to 7.46%.

parts.name: Treasury and capital markets
parts.what: Manages the bank's liquidity, borrowings and refinance lines; referenced through metrics like the CD ratio (93.3% in FY25, 82.9% including refinance) and a liquidity coverage ratio being deliberately brought down from 391% to 253%.

parts.name: Business Correspondent (BC) partnerships
parts.what: Local partner firms that originate and collect part of the microfinance book under service guarantees — about 10% of the total loan book in FY24, which management says reduces the bank's own unsecured risk.

parts.name: New / upcoming products
parts.what: Credit Line on UPI (in testing, due to go public in Q1 FY27), loans against shares and mutual funds, and foreign-exchange services under a new AD1 license — all small and not yet material.

overview.what_it_does: Jindal Stainless Limited (JSL) makes stainless steel — it melts it from scratch and then rolls and finishes it into hot- and cold-rolled sheet, coil and other flat products, which it sells mostly to Indian industrial buyers and fabricators. Its customers are sectors like automobiles, ornamental and industrial pipe & tube, railways (coaches, wagons, Vande Bharat, metro cars), lifts and elevators, white goods and infrastructure projects such as foot-over-bridges and railway cable trays, plus exports to Europe, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and other markets (exports were roughly a fifth to a quarter of sales in FY23 and have since been deliberately dialled back in favour of the domestic market). It earns money on the spread between raw-material cost (nickel prices swing the margin a lot) and selling price, measured by management as EBITDA per tonne — guided at roughly Rs 18,000–20,000 a tonne — multiplied by volume; FY26 deliveries were 2.57 million tonnes, consolidated EBITDA Rs 5,560 crore and profit Rs 3,185 crore, with net debt down to Rs 3,040 crore. Its main plants are at Jajpur (Odisha) and Hisar (Haryana), with cold rolling also at Mundra (Gujarat) and Kharagpur, total melting capacity of 4.2 million tonnes a year including 3 million in India and a newly commissioned 1.2 million-tonne melt shop in Indonesia, and a stated target of 3.5 million tonnes of sales by FY29.

parts.name: Core stainless steel manufacturing (Jajpur and Hisar, India)
parts.what: The main business: melting stainless steel and rolling it into hot-rolled and cold-rolled products for domestic and export customers — this is essentially all of the roughly 2.57 million tonnes sold in FY26 and the bulk of group profit.

parts.name: Downstream / value-added capacity (HRAP, CRAP, cold rolling)
parts.what: The finishing lines that turn crude steel into higher-priced processed sheet and coil, being expanded with a 1.1 million-tonne HRAP and 0.17 million-tonne CRAP line at Jajpur plus an extra Rs 900 crore for cold rolling at Hisar and Kharagpur, taking CRAP capacity to 2.67 million tonnes by FY28.

parts.name: Chromeni Steels Private Limited
parts.what: A 0.6 million-tonne-a-year cold rolling mill at Mundra, Gujarat, bought outright for over Rs 1,600 crore in FY25 and described in FY26 as ramping up with rising capacity utilisation.

parts.name: Indonesia melt shop (SMS) and NPI
parts.what: A 1.2 million-tonne-a-year stainless steel melt shop in Indonesia commissioned ahead of schedule, plus a nickel pig iron (NPI) operation that is ramping up — this is the overseas raw-material and melting leg of the business.

parts.name: Jindal United Steel Limited (JUSL)
parts.what: A manufacturing facility taken in as a wholly-owned subsidiary in FY23 so that, as management put it, all critical stainless steel facilities sit under one umbrella with better synergies.

parts.name: Jindal Stainless Steelways
parts.what: The service-centre subsidiary that processes and sells steel, including direct sales to vehicle and equipment makers (OEMs); one of the smaller earnings contributors within total subsidiary EBITDA of Rs 208 crore in Q1 FY25.

parts.name: Iberjindal ("Iber"), Spain
parts.what: The overseas trading/distribution arm serving European markets, whose results swing with inventory levels and European stainless prices.

parts.name: Rathi and Rabirun
parts.what: Two smaller acquired operations being ramped up from FY25 — Rathi was guided at a thinner margin of about Rs 4,000–6,000 EBITDA per tonne, well below the core business, and Rabirun's plan was still being firmed up.

parts.name: Brand and channel programmes (Jindal Saathi, Jindal Infinity)
parts.what: Not a separate profit centre but a demand-creation effort — co-branding, QR-code authentication and loyalty schemes for pipe-and-tube fabricators and retailers, now extended into consumer advertising with a brand ambassador and an IPL team tie-up, aimed at defending market share against cheap imports and counterfeits.

parts.name: Captive and renewable power
parts.what: Supporting infrastructure rather than a business line: renewable sources had reached 56% of imported power at Jajpur and Hisar by Q3 FY26, with a 315 MW solar-wind hybrid project partially commissioned in Q4 FY26.

overview.what_it_does: Jeena Sikho Lifecare (JSLL) is an Indian healthcare company that treats people using Ayurveda instead of conventional allopathic medicine, positioning itself as a mainstream hospital chain rather than a wellness brand. It runs its own network of Ayurvedic hospitals, clinics and daycare centres — 58 hospitals and 59 clinics/daycare centres, about 117 facilities in all, across 23 states and 100 cities, with roughly 2,300 operational beds — where admitted patients receive Panchakarma detoxification and rejuvenation therapy, and it separately sells its own branded Ayurvedic medicines (330+ SKUs) that patients keep taking for months after discharge. Money comes from two roughly equal streams: treatment fees for inpatient, outpatient, daycare and video consultations (paid privately, through cashless/reimbursement health insurance, and from government panels such as CGHS, ECHS and several state governments), and product sales through its centres, tele-calling and client support desks, e-commerce and now over-the-counter pharmacy retail. FY26 revenue from operations was INR801 crore, up 71% year-on-year, with EBITDA of INR349 crore and PAT of INR222 crore; the business is India-focused with an early international start in the UAE.

parts.name: Ayurveda Healthcare Services
parts.what: The hospital and clinic business — inpatient Panchakarma treatment, OPD, daycare and video consultations delivered by about 600 Ayurvedic/Naturopathy doctors and 750 wellness experts; it made up roughly 48% of FY26 revenue (54% in Q1 FY26) and management says bed occupancy has held around 57-58% for three quarters.

parts.name: Ayurveda Healthcare Products
parts.what: Branded Ayurvedic medicines and kits, 330+ SKUs made through third-party manufacturers to AYUSH standards, sold to discharged patients, through e-commerce and OTC retail; it contributed INR416 crore, or 52% of FY26 revenue, at gross margins above 85%.

parts.name: Hub-and-spoke hospital network
parts.what: Large hospitals in big cities act as hubs (about 600 beds around Delhi/Meerut, 200+ in Panvel, 150+ in Navi Mumbai) taking referrals from smaller-town clinics; setup cost is only INR3-4 lakh per bed, break-even comes at 35% occupancy, and the company plans to reach 2,800-3,000 beds within 3-4 months and 7,000-10,000 beds over 3-5 years.

parts.name: Clinics, daycare centres and franchises
parts.what: 59 clinics and daycare centres feed patients into the hospitals; only 35 of the 117 facilities are franchised — the rest have doctors on JSLL's own payroll — and JSLL supplies medicines exclusively to all of them, so product revenue and clinical control stay in-house without full capital outlay.

parts.name: OTC product launches
parts.what: A newer push to sell Ayurvedic products over the counter to healthy people, starting with the PET Yakrit Pleeha Shuddhi Kit (priced around INR960, now crossing INR10 crore in monthly sales) followed by NutriRoz, with a stated target of 16 products by December 2026.

parts.name: Health camps and client support centres
parts.what: Outreach camps and tele-calling/video-consult desks that generate demand — camps convert about 30% of attendees into inpatient admissions and bring in INR30-60 lakh of direct business each.

parts.name: Insurance and government empanelment
parts.what: Treatment is billed to all major health insurers on a cashless and reimbursement basis and to panels including CGHS, CAPF, ECHS, Air India and Air Asia plus the UP, Bihar, Haryana and Punjab state governments; management has deliberately cut back government business over slow payments, recovering about INR20-21 crore of dues, while flagging UP's new cashless Ayurveda scheme as an opportunity.

parts.name: Jeena Sikho Swadeshi Health Card
parts.what: A newly launched loyalty and referral card offering patients referral bonuses and diagnostic discounts to drive word-of-mouth, still in its trial phase.

parts.name: Research and accreditation
parts.what: Clinical trials and peer-reviewed publications (about 550 papers written last year, 400 accepted, 180+ published) plus 49 NABH-accredited facilities, used to establish evidence-based credibility for the Ayurvedic treatments.

parts.name: International expansion
parts.what: An early-stage entry into the UAE, described as just started, with no revenue figures given in the calls.

overview.what_it_does: JSW Cement makes and sells building materials in India — mainly bagged/bulk cement and GGBS (ground granulated blast furnace slag, a cement-like powder made by grinding a waste product from steel blast furnaces), plus a small amount of clinker sold to others. It earns money by manufacturing these at grinding and clinker plants and selling them by the ton: FY26 volumes were 13.96 million tons for revenue of INR6,512 crores, with cement fetching about INR4,673/ton and GGBS about INR3,682/ton in Q4 FY26. Buyers are a mix of retail/'trade' customers through a network of 13,000+ dealers (about half of cement sales) and direct institutional customers — ready-mix concrete (RMC) producers, large EPC contractors, housing developers and government infrastructure agencies (metros, airports, expressways, ports). It operates in South, West and East India, has just entered the North with a new integrated plant at Nagaur, Rajasthan (commercial operations March 2026), and has a clinker joint venture in Fujairah, UAE; it is part of the JSW Group and repeatedly stresses having the lowest CO2 emission intensity in the industry (268 kg per ton in FY26).

parts.name: Cement
parts.what: Ordinary and premium cement made by grinding clinker with slag and other materials, sold largely through dealers to retail and project buyers — the biggest line at roughly 54% of volume in 9M FY26 (2.35 million tons in Q4 FY26, up 12% year-on-year), with about 51-53% of it sold in the higher-priced 'trade' channel.

parts.name: GGBS
parts.what: Ground granulated blast furnace slag, a cementitious powder ground from steel-plant slag and sold mostly to the ready-mix concrete industry as a partial replacement for ordinary cement — about 42% of volume (5.18 million tons in FY25) and the company says it is India's single largest GGBS producer with roughly 84% market share; management treats cement and GGBS as one reporting segment and does not disclose GGBS margins separately.

parts.name: Clinker (sold externally)
parts.what: The semi-finished input to cement, produced at its own clinker units and sold to third parties — the smallest line at about 4% of volume in 9M FY26.

parts.name: Slag sourcing / JSW Steel link
parts.what: Not a revenue line but central to how it operates: it buys blast-furnace slag under long-term contracts from JSW Steel and other steelmakers, with several grinding units placed next to steel plants to cut freight — when supply was interrupted (a Dolvi blast-furnace shutdown in Q1 FY26, slag shortages in Q4 FY26) costs rose and volumes had to be rerouted.

parts.name: Fujairah clinker JV (UAE)
parts.what: A 2.31 MTPA clinker joint venture in the UAE that supplies clinker to the West India operations; it is not consolidated into the main accounts and shows up as a share of profit (INR6 crores in Q4 FY26), with a new 1.65 MTPA grinding unit in Fujairah approved at USD 39 million.

parts.name: Capacity expansion programme
parts.what: An ongoing build-out from 21.60 MTPA of grinding capacity today toward about 46 MTPA of grinding and 13.04 MTPA of clinker, via new units at Nagaur (Rajasthan), Mansa (Punjab), Sambalpur, Vijayanagar, Dolvi, Hatta and Uttar Pradesh — capex ran about INR1,962 crores in FY26 and it is the main use of cash and reason for the INR3,635 crore net debt.

overview.what_it_does: JSW Dulux (formerly Akzo Nobel India, renamed after the JSW Group bought control from Dutch parent AkzoNobel N.V.) makes and sells paints and coatings in India under the Dulux brand. Roughly two-thirds of its business is decorative paint — interior and exterior wall paint, waterproofing, floor coatings and DIY spray paints sold to homeowners and painters through a retail network of about 20,000 dealers across 5,000-plus towns, with around 16,000 tinting machines placed in shops; the rest is industrial coatings sold to businesses such as carmakers, shipowners, oil-and-gas and infrastructure projects, and steel-coil processors, plus about 4,000 B2B customers. It earns money by manufacturing paint at five plants in India and selling it at a margin, running EBITDA of roughly 14-15% on quarterly revenue of about INR 900 crore, with profitability swinging on raw-material costs (raw materials are about 55% of cost) and on how much price it can pass through. Operations are India-focused; a small colorant export business to Southeast Asia and the Middle East, the powder-coatings unit and the international research centre were carved out to the former parent as part of the ownership change, and the head office has moved from Gurugram to Mumbai.

parts.name: Decorative Paints
parts.what: House paint for consumers — premium interior emulsions (flagship brand Dulux Velvet Touch, plus a new luxury-finishes range), exteriors (Max), waterproofing, FloorPlus floor coating and the DIY 'Simply Refresh' range sold partly online; this is the largest part of the company, described in 2022 as about two-thirds of revenue, and it grew 8% by volume in Q3 FY26 and posted record volumes in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Mass, mid-tier and premium tiers within decorative
parts.what: Management splits the paint range by price tier — premium/super-premium, mid-market, and mass-economy (including the 'MEP' mass economy primer where it has been losing to new entrants); it admitted its premium products were priced 5-9% above rivals and has been cutting that premium since September 2025 to win back volume.

parts.name: Decorative B2B
parts.what: Paint sold directly to builders, projects and institutional buyers rather than through shops — a smaller piece of decorative that management called out as growing in double digits.

parts.name: Industrial / Coatings vertical
parts.what: The non-decorative side, roughly a third of the business, sold to industrial customers and split into automotive and specialty coatings, marine and protective, and coil coatings.

parts.name: Automotive and Specialty Coatings (incl. vehicle refinish)
parts.what: Coatings for vehicle makers and for repainting damaged vehicles, including a tie-up with Porsche and new wins with leading Indian OEMs; it was a weak spot in FY25 but grew across the board in Q4 FY26, with mid-market vehicle refinish still under pressure.

parts.name: Marine and Protective
parts.what: Paint for ships and for protecting steel structures, with an order book in oil, gas and infrastructure and dry-dock/ship work including jobs for the Indian Navy; management called out one of its highest-ever revenue months in March 2026, and a big Navy order in a prior year created a high base.

parts.name: Coil coatings
parts.what: Coatings applied to metal coil used in buildings and infrastructure — a fast-growing line that won marquee projects such as Navi Mumbai Airport, though a couple of coil customers were retained by the former parent in the carve-out.

parts.name: Powder Coatings and International Research Centre (carved out)
parts.what: A powder-coatings business and an R&D centre that used to sit inside the company but were moved to an unlisted AkzoNobel entity as part of the ownership change; together with ceased colorant exports (Dramatone/Acotone) this removed about INR 200 crore of annual revenue, roughly INR 25 crore a quarter.

parts.name: Colour and innovation centres
parts.what: A global colour centre and a low-cost innovation centre in Bengaluru that developed products for India and other Asian markets under the old parent.

overview.what_it_does: JSW Energy Limited is an Indian electricity generation company (part of the O. P. Jindal Group, listed in Mumbai) that builds and runs power plants and sells the electricity they produce. It earns money mainly by selling power under long-term Power Purchase Agreements to government and state buyers such as SECI, NTPC, SJVN, UPPCL, Tamil Nadu's TANGEDCO and Rajasthan discoms, plus group-captive and industrial customers including sister company JSW Steel, and by selling the remaining untied 'merchant' power on the day-ahead power exchanges at prevailing spot tariffs (about Rs 3.86/unit through FY26, rising to Rs 5.10/unit in Q1 FY27, with management claiming a ~20% premium to exchange averages). Its fleet mixes coal-fired thermal, wind, solar, hydro and battery storage, spread across many Indian states — Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Odisha, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka and the seven states of the acquired O2 Power platform. Installed capacity grew from about 7.7 GW in late 2024 to roughly 14.6 GW by July 2026, with another 14 GW under construction (all tied to long-term PPAs) and a target of 30 GW of generation plus 40 GWh of storage by 2030 backed by roughly Rs 1,30,000 crore of planned capex; FY26 EBITDA was a record Rs 11,041 crore.

parts.name: Renewable energy generation (wind, solar, hybrid)
parts.what: Wind and solar farms — including hybrid and FDRE projects, agrivoltaics and floating solar — sold mostly under long-term PPAs to SECI and similar buyers; this is now the biggest slice of the company at roughly 61% of the 14.6 GW installed base, hugely boosted by the Rs 12,468 crore acquisition of the 4.7 GW O2 Power platform (blended tariff Rs 3.37/unit) announced in December 2024.

parts.name: Thermal power generation (coal-based)
parts.what: Coal-fired baseload plants totalling about 5.7 GW — including the 1,800 MW operational KSK Mahanadi in Chhattisgarh bought through insolvency proceedings, the Utkal (Ind-Barath) plant in Odisha, the imported-coal Vijayanagar plant tied up with JSW Steel, and a 300 MW Maruti Clean Coal plant being acquired — described by management as regaining prominence as reliable, dispatchable, contracted capacity, with 3,200 MW being built at Salboni and 1,800 MW of brownfield expansion optionality at KSK.

parts.name: Hydro power
parts.what: Run-of-river hydro plants — Karcham-Wangtoo, Baspa, the newly built 240 MW Kutehr project and the 150 MW Tidong plant bought from Statkraft — which management says make JSW Energy the largest private independent power producer in Indian hydro, and which generated 13-16% above design energy in FY26.

parts.name: Energy storage (battery and pumped hydro)
parts.what: Grid-scale storage to firm up intermittent renewable power, with locked-in capacity of 29.6 GWh — 3.2 GWh in batteries and 26.4 GWh in what management calls the 'remunerative' pumped-hydro space — an area they say they are well ahead of the market on, though one early 1 GWh SECI battery project was put on hold after the regulator refused to adopt its tariff.

parts.name: Merchant / short-term power sales
parts.what: The untied portion of generation sold on power exchanges and through back-to-back short-term contracts; management has deliberately shrunk this exposure to roughly 1.1 GW (about 8% of capacity, heading to 5%) by signing new PPAs, while noting it still delivers attractive 'dark spreads' when coal prices are low.

parts.name: Equipment manufacturing / vertical integration
parts.what: In-house making of key power equipment to cut cost and supply risk rather than as a standalone revenue engine — a 5 GWh battery assembly plant in Pune (commissioned Q4 FY26, first external order about Rs 440 crore), wind blade factories at Halol and Chitradurga, a partnership with SANY for wind turbines, a raised 10.7% stake in the Toshiba JSW turbine-generator JV, and the pending purchase of GE Power India's boiler business.

overview.what_it_does: JSW Infrastructure is an Indian ports company that gets paid to load, unload, store and move cargo — mainly coal, iron ore, containers and liquid products — through the seaport berths and terminals it owns or operates under long-term government concessions. Roughly half its cargo comes from its own parent group's factories (JSW Steel plants at Dolvi, Vasind, Tarapur and elsewhere) and the other half from outside "third-party" customers, with the third-party share rising from 36% of volumes in FY24 to a record 52% by Q1 FY26. It makes money on a per-tonne cargo-handling basis plus vessel-related charges (about 17-18% of revenue is dollar-denominated), and it runs at high margins — around 52% EBITDA — handling 58.2 million tonnes in the first half of FY26 for Rs. 2,686 crores of revenue, Rs. 1,387 crores of EBITDA and Rs. 758 crores of net profit. Its assets sit along both Indian coasts (Jaigarh, Dharamtar, Paradip, Mangalore, Ennore, PNP, Goa/South West Port, Tuticorin, JNPA, Kolkata) plus liquid-storage and operations contracts in the UAE, and it is expanding capacity from 177 million tonnes a year today to a targeted 400 million tonnes by FY30.

parts.name: Port business (ports and terminals)
parts.what: The core operation — cargo-handling berths and terminals at Jaigarh, Dharamtar, Paradip (separate coal and iron ore terminals), Mangalore, Ennore, PNP, South West Port, Tuticorin and JNPA — which brought in Rs. 1,086 crores of the Rs. 1,314 crores total revenue in Q1 FY26 at a 51.7% operating EBITDA margin, making it the overwhelming bulk of the company.

parts.name: Group (captive) cargo vs third-party cargo
parts.what: Management splits every tonne into cargo from its own JSW group companies and cargo from outside customers; third-party volumes have grown fastest (48% year-on-year in Q2 FY25) and reached 52-54% of the mix, and management treats this shift as the key measure of the business becoming less dependent on the parent.

parts.name: Liquid storage and terminals
parts.what: Tank storage and liquid-cargo handling — a 465,000 cubic metre liquid storage facility at Fujairah in the UAE bought for $187 million (described as a major world bunkering hub), a 2 million tonne LPG project at Jaigarh, and a new liquid terminal at JNPA that was nearing commercial start-up in late 2025.

parts.name: Overseas operations and maintenance contracts (UAE)
parts.what: Paid contracts to run other owners' port facilities at Fujairah and Dibba in the UAE; Fujairah was on track to beat its minimum guaranteed cargo volumes, which entitles JSW to a share of the extra profit.

parts.name: Logistics business (Navkar Corporation and multimodal assets)
parts.what: An inland container and rail-linked logistics arm built around the acquired Navkar Corporation — 81,000 TEUs of EXIM container volume and 275,000 tonnes of domestic cargo in Q1 FY26 on Rs. 138 crores of revenue — plus NCR Rail Infrastructure (won through insolvency proceedings) and a new Rs. 380 crore multimodal logistics park and inland container depot at Kudathini, Ballari; still small today but targeted to reach a Rs. 8,000 crore top line by FY30.

parts.name: Greenfield port development
parts.what: Three brand-new ports being built at once — Keni in Karnataka, Murbe in Maharashtra and Jatadhar in Odisha — together about 93 million tonnes a year of capacity in their first phase; management says no other Indian port company is developing three greenfield ports simultaneously.

parts.name: Brownfield expansion of existing ports
parts.what: A Rs. 2,359 crore programme of new berths, civil and mechanical work and a railway siding at Jaigarh and Dharamtar, expected to add roughly 27 million tonnes a year of handling capacity by March 2027.

parts.name: Winning privatised government terminals (PPP / landlord-port model)
parts.what: Bidding for terminals that central-government-owned "major ports" are handing to private operators — described as the company's single biggest growth opportunity since major ports hold over half of India's capacity — with a recent win being a 30-year concession to redevelop and run the 6.3 million tonne container terminal at Netaji Subhash Dock, Kolkata.

parts.name: Iron ore slurry pipeline
parts.what: A 302 kilometre pipeline to pump iron ore in slurry form instead of trucking or railing it, with 218 km welded and 195 km lowered as of October 2025 and completion targeted for March 2027.

overview.what_it_does: JSW Steel makes and sells steel — both flat products (hot-rolled and cold-rolled coil, galvanised, electrical steel, tinplate) and long products (beams, rails, structural sections, special engineering steel) — mostly in India, where it sold about 30 million tonnes in FY26 and booked consolidated revenue of over Rs.51,100 crores in the March 2026 quarter alone. Its customers are Indian industrial and construction buyers: automotive makers (priced on quarterly contracts), packaging, alloy engineering, infrastructure and general manufacturing, plus retail buyers, with roughly half of retail sales sold under its own brands. It earns money on the spread between steel selling prices and input costs — iron ore and coking coal together are about 60% of cost of goods sold — so it is pushing hard on 'captive' mines it owns itself to secure raw materials and cut logistics costs, and on higher-priced value-added products (management targets keeping these above 50% of the mix). Operations are overwhelmingly India-centric across multiple plant sites (Vijayanagar, Dolvi, Kadapa, Raigarh, and a new Odisha site at JSW Utkal), with small overseas businesses in the United States and Italy, and management is spending heavily — Rs.1,26,000 crores of approved capex over 4–5 years — to grow capacity toward 62 million tonnes by FY32.

parts.name: Indian steel operations (Vijayanagar, Dolvi, Kadapa, Raigarh, JSW Utkal)
parts.what: The core business: large integrated steel plants across India that ran at 96% capacity utilisation in Q4 FY26 and produced the bulk of the ~30 million tonnes sold in FY26, with Vijayanagar being expanded by a further 5 million tonnes to 25 million tonnes, which management says would make it the world's largest single-location steel plant.

parts.name: Value-added and special products (VASP) / downstream
parts.what: Higher-priced finished steel — galvanised, electrical steel, tinplate, cold-rolled, structural products — where downstream capacity ran at 95% utilisation in Q4 and management is adding about 3 million tonnes more capacity between FY28 and FY29 to keep VASP above 50% of the mix.

parts.name: Long products
parts.what: Beams, rails, structural sections and special engineering steel aimed at India's infrastructure build-out, expanded via a 1 million tonne structural mill at Kadapa (targeted FY29), a beam-and-rail expansion at Raigarh, and the acquisition of BMM Ispat, a 0.9 million tonne long-products plant in Karnataka bought for about Rs.6,500 crores that can be doubled to 1.8 million tonnes cheaply.

parts.name: Raw material / mining (iron ore and coking coal)
parts.what: Self-owned mine supply to feed the steel plants — 25 iron ore mines (13 operating, ~1.7 billion tonnes of resources) that covered about one-third of iron ore use in Q4, plus coking coal from Mozambique (MdR), a 30% stake in Australia's Illawarra mine and Indian mines/linkages; the goal is 50% captive supply of both iron ore and coking coal by FY31.

parts.name: JSW JFE joint venture (BPSL business)
parts.what: A 50-50 joint venture with Japan's JFE Steel, formed by end-March 2026, into which JSW put its BPSL steel business — it removes roughly Rs.37,000 crores of debt from JSW's balance sheet (about Rs.30,000 crores done by March) and is targeted to grow to around 10 million tonnes of capacity; its volumes are tracked separately and are excluded from FY27 guidance.

parts.name: POSCO joint venture
parts.what: A newly signed joint venture with South Korea's POSCO to build a brand-new 6 million tonne integrated steel plant in Odisha, partly to supply POSCO's existing 2 million tonne cold-rolling plant in Maharashtra with locally made steel instead of imports from Korea.

parts.name: Overseas operations (USA and Italy)
parts.what: Small foreign plants — a 1.5 million tonne Ohio operation and a Plate & Pipe Mill in Texas, which together turned to $36 million of EBITDA in FY26 from a $35 million loss the prior year, plus Italian operations that made EUR 16.4 million of EBITDA — clearly minor next to the India business.

parts.name: JSW One (online platform)
parts.what: An online steel sales and financing platform in which JSW holds about 61%; its steel volumes grew 50% year-on-year, gross merchandise value reached Rs.6,200 crores (up 57%, with over Rs.2,000 crores driven by its credit offerings), and it turned profitable for the first time in Q4.

overview.what_it_does: Jubilant FoodWorks runs quick-service restaurant chains, selling pizza, fried chicken, doughnuts, coffee and Chinese-style food to everyday consumers who order for delivery, dine-in or takeaway. It operates franchised international brands — chiefly Domino's Pizza — under master-franchise rights in India, Turkey, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, plus its own brands, and makes money mainly from food sold at company-owned stores, supported by its own ordering app, delivery riders and in-house 'food tech' commissary factories that supply the stores. In Turkey, where roughly 88% of stores are run by franchisees, it earns instead by supplying and servicing those franchise partners, so management reports both 'system sales' (all end-customer sales including franchise stores) and its own revenue. As of the latest call it operates close to 3,600 stores across five brands and six countries (~2,530 of them in India), with consolidated quarterly revenue of about Rs. 24.4 billion, EBITDA margin around 20.5%, and growth driven by opening 230–250 new stores a year toward a stated goal of a 5,000-plus store business.

parts.name: Domino's India (India segment)
parts.what: The core business by far — around 2,530 pizza stores across 400-plus Indian cities, delivering roughly Rs. 18 billion of the group's Rs. 24.4 billion quarterly revenue, with delivery the main and fastest-growing channel and dine-in/takeaway the acknowledged weak spot.

parts.name: Turkey business (DP Eurasia) — Domino's Turkey
parts.what: About 700-plus Domino's stores in Turkey, overwhelmingly franchisee-run and therefore 'asset-lite'; acquired and consolidated from FY25, it now runs at high margins, generates steady cash and pays dividends back to the parent to service the debt raised to buy it.

parts.name: COFFY (Turkey)
parts.what: The group's coffee-shop chain in Turkey, which crossed 100 stores in 2024 and keeps adding stores (18 in one recent quarter); still small in sales terms versus Domino's Turkey but described as a key growth brand.

parts.name: Popeyes (India)
parts.what: The fried-chicken chain, grown from a Bangalore launch to 73 stores, now posting high double-digit like-for-like growth and called out by management as an emerging new growth engine, though still loss-making enough to drag group margins.

parts.name: Dunkin' (India)
parts.what: The doughnut-and-beverage chain, a small part of the portfolio where management is adding a handful of stores and pushing beverages like bubble tea to get it to positive restaurant-level profitability.

parts.name: Hong's Kitchen (India)
parts.what: The company's own Chinese-food QSR brand, described as India's first, at roughly 33 stores with entry-price items around Rs. 99 — the smallest brand and, with Popeyes and Dunkin', part of the 'new business' drag on profits.

parts.name: Sri Lanka and Bangladesh operations
parts.what: Smaller overseas Domino's markets that management reports as delivering high double-digit top-line growth and improving profitability, but which are not broken out with meaningful revenue figures on these calls.

parts.name: Supply chain / 'food tech' factories
parts.what: In-house commissary plants running a complex multi-temperature forward and reverse supply chain that make and distribute dough and ingredients to the store network — not sold separately, but described as a core cost and quality advantage.

parts.name: App, data and advertising
parts.what: The own-brand ordering apps and loyalty programme (over 20% year-on-year growth in monthly transacting users) that cut reliance on third-party platforms, plus a small but new advertising income stream from post-order page ads, which crossed 10 active clients in one recent quarter.

overview.what_it_does: Jubilant Ingrevia is an India-listed chemicals maker (part of the Jubilant Bhartia Group, traded as JUBLINGREA) that manufactures industrial and specialty chemicals, vitamin/nutrition ingredients and bulk chemical intermediates from plants at Gajraula, Bharuch, Nira and Greater Noida. It sells business-to-business to pharmaceutical, agrochemical, nutrition/animal-feed, cosmetics and personal care, oil-field, industrial and, more recently, semiconductor and electronics customers in India, Europe and the rest of the world. It makes money by selling these chemicals in volume — earning on the spread between raw material/energy costs and selling prices, which it passes through to customers with a lag — and increasingly by contract manufacturing (CDMO) where it makes intermediates to a customer's own patented process under multi-year agreements. Quarterly revenue runs around Rs. 1,100–1,300 crore, split roughly evenly between higher-margin Specialty Chemicals plus Nutrition on one side and lower-margin Chemical Intermediates on the other, with management targeting a bigger share from the specialty side under its "Pinnacle 345" growth plan.

parts.name: Specialty Chemicals
parts.what: Makes pyridine and picoline derivatives (management calls itself the world's #1 and only scaled non-Chinese player), chloro-pyridines, fine chemicals and diketene derivatives sold mainly to pharma and agrochemical customers; it is the largest and most profitable segment at about Rs. 533 crore revenue and 26% EBITDA margin in the June 2026 quarter, versus Rs. 382 crore back in mid-2022.

parts.name: CDMO (contract development and manufacturing, sits inside Specialty Chemicals)
parts.what: Builds dedicated GMP and non-GMP plants to manufacture intermediates for pharma, agrochemical and semiconductor innovators using the customer's own technology — including a five-year deal described as one of India's largest agro CDMO contracts — with a funnel of 100-plus molecules worth about Rs. 3,500 crore of peak revenue potential and 25-plus molecules confirmed.

parts.name: Nutrition & Health Solutions
parts.what: Sells niacinamide (vitamin B3) for animal feed, food and cosmetics, choline chloride and choline bitartrate, and vitamin/nutrition premixes; revenue was about Rs. 243 crore in the June 2026 quarter (Rs. 790 crore for FY26) at roughly 15% margins, with the 2026 acquisition of Remidex Pharma added to push further into human nutrition and premixes.

parts.name: Chemical Intermediates (Acetyls)
parts.what: The bulk-volume commodity arm making acetic anhydride — where it is the domestic market leader and a growing supplier in Europe — plus ethyl acetate and propionic anhydride, sold heavily into paracetamol and agrochemical makers; revenue is comparable to Specialty (about Rs. 524 crore in the June 2026 quarter) but at much thinner margins that swing with acetic acid prices.

overview.what_it_does: Jubilant Pharmova is an India-listed, diversified specialty pharmaceutical company that mostly makes its money in the United States and in US dollars, with roughly 5,000 people across India and North America. It sells radioactive imaging drugs and runs a network of 46 radiopharmacies that deliver them to hospitals, sells allergy treatment extracts to US allergy clinics, manufactures sterile injectable medicines under contract for large innovator drug companies, does contract drug-discovery research and makes active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) for other drug firms, and sells its own generic medicines in the US and other regulated markets. Revenue therefore comes from a mix of selling its own specialty products and being paid a fee to research or manufacture for other pharma companies. In FY2026 revenue was about Rs. 8,280 crore with EBITDA of Rs. 1,326 crore (a 15.9% margin), and it operates 6 FDA-regulated manufacturing plants (2 each in Canada, the US and India), research centres in Bengaluru, Noida and France, and the 46-site radiopharmacy network; it is also spending money to expand injectable capacity in Spokane (US) and Montreal (Canada).

parts.name: Radiopharmaceuticals / Radiopharma (part of Specialty Pharmaceuticals)
parts.what: Makes and distributes radioactive drugs used to image the body — SPECT products (like MAA, DTPA, Sulfur Colloid, Mertiatide), PET products, the Ruby-Fill heart-imaging system and MIBG — and delivers them through the second-largest US network of 46 radiopharmacies; management calls it the largest segment at over 45% of company revenue, with target margins of 38–40%, though FY2026 was hurt by a shortage of SPECT cold-kit supply.

parts.name: Allergy Immunotherapy (part of Specialty Pharmaceuticals)
parts.what: Sells allergenic extracts used to treat allergies in the US, where it is the second-largest player and the sole supplier of venom immunotherapy extracts; it has grown steadily and operates above pre-COVID volumes, and management wants to add adjacent new products to regain outright leadership.

parts.name: CDMO Sterile Injectables (contract manufacturing)
parts.what: Fills and finishes injectable medicines to order for many of the world's largest innovator pharma companies from plants in Spokane (US) and Montreal (Canada); it was the biggest driver of FY2026 revenue growth, is doubling capacity with new isolator fill-finish lines, and has 10-plus products (about 80% complex biologics, including one of the world's largest oncology products) in tech transfer on Line 3, expected to reach $80–90 million of peak revenue.

parts.name: CRDMO — Drug Discovery Services
parts.what: Provides end-to-end contract drug-discovery and development research to biotech and large pharma customers from research centres in Bengaluru, Noida and France, covering chemistry, DMPK, discovery biology and clinical trial data management; it grew 15% in FY2026 to more than Rs. 650 crore and management says demand is supported by the industry patent cliff.

parts.name: CRDMO — CDMO-API / custom manufacturing
parts.what: Manufactures active pharmaceutical ingredients, increasingly as custom manufacturing for innovator clients rather than commodity supply; it runs at about a 15% EBITDA margin today with spare capacity, and management expects innovator custom-manufacturing revenue to start showing up in FY2027 and lift margins.

parts.name: Generics
parts.what: Sells its own off-patent medicines across many therapy areas into the US and other regulated markets, plus a branded generics push in India; it was badly hit in FY2023 by US price erosion (notably sartans) and a US FDA import alert on the Roorkee plant, but management says the business has since been turned around and grew in FY2026.

parts.name: Jubilant Therapeutics (Proprietary Novel Drugs)
parts.what: An in-house research effort developing its own new cancer and auto-immune drugs — such as JBI-802, a dual LSD1/HDAC6 inhibitor in Phase I/II for advanced solid tumours, and a brain-penetrant PRMT5 inhibitor — with two molecules in clinical trials; it is a long-term bet rather than a revenue contributor today.

overview.what_it_does: Just Dial runs India's largest local search platform: consumers use its website and app (85-87% of traffic is mobile) to find local businesses and services near them — restaurants, hardware shops, AC repair, tutorials and so on — searching a free database that grew from about 32.8 million listings in mid-2022 to 48.8 million by March 2025, drawing roughly 148 to 191 million unique visitors a quarter. It makes money not from users but from the small and medium businesses in that database, which pay for 'paid campaigns' (advertising subscriptions that give them visibility and leads), sold by a large in-house sales and telesales force of roughly 13,000 people; about 613,000 campaigns were active at March 2025, at around INR 2,200-2,300 per campaign per month in the big cities and about INR 1,100 in smaller ones. Subscriptions are mostly annual and paid upfront (with some monthly bank-debit plans), so cash is collected first and booked as revenue over the following 12 months — quarterly revenue rose from INR 186 crores in Q1 FY23 to INR 289 crores in Q4 FY25 at a roughly 29% EBITDA margin. It operates only in India, and separately earns very large interest income — INR 87-109 crores a quarter, often more than the operating profit — on a treasury portfolio of cash and bonds that had grown to INR 5,279 crores by March 2025.

parts.name: Core local search business (listings and paid campaigns)
parts.what: The whole operating business: a free searchable directory of local businesses that attracts consumer traffic, monetised by charging those businesses for paid advertising campaigns — this is essentially 100% of the INR 289 crores of quarterly operating revenue management discusses.

parts.name: Active paid campaigns
parts.what: The count of merchant advertising subscriptions running at any time — the key volume driver, growing from about 484,000 in June 2022 to 613,290 in March 2025, with growth in revenue coming from a mix of more campaigns plus price/realisation increases.

parts.name: Top 11 cities vs rest of India
parts.what: Management splits the business geographically: the 11 largest cities are about 40% of campaigns but roughly 56-64% of revenue, while smaller towns are cheaper (realisations were about 48-49% of big-city levels in 2024, up from 40-42% a few years earlier) and are the stated catch-up opportunity.

parts.name: Traffic / listings database
parts.what: The free consumer side — unique visitors (191.3 million in the March 2025 quarter, 87% mobile) and total listings (48.8 million) — which management treats as the raw material that 'leads monetisation' rather than a revenue line of its own.

parts.name: Collections, deferred revenue and realizable value
parts.what: Because customers pay upfront for a year, management tracks cash collected (INR 340 crores in the March 2025 quarter), deferred revenue on the balance sheet (INR 558 crores) and 'realizable value' of new sign-ups as the leading indicators of future reported revenue.

parts.name: Treasury / other income
parts.what: A very large pile of cash and bonds — INR 3,740 crores in mid-2022 rising to INR 5,279 crores by March 2025, partly from a INR 2,000 crore promoter infusion in 2021 — yielding about 7.2% and producing INR 87-109 crores a quarter of other income, an amount comparable to or larger than the operating profit; it has sat undeployed for years, with a dividend policy only 'expected' as of the April 2025 call.

parts.name: New initiatives
parts.what: Referred to in the July 2022 call as new products being rolled out to users 'in a phase-wise manner' with focus on user experience and broader product, service and geographic coverage; no revenue is attributed to them and they drop out of the later calls, where management says the focus is entirely on the core business.

overview.what_it_does: Jupiter Wagons Limited (NSE: JWL, formerly Commercial Engineers & Body Builders) is an Indian engineering manufacturer whose core business is building freight railway wagons and the parts that go into them, sold to Indian Railways and to private companies that own their own rakes (steel, cement, auto and defence customers). It makes money by winning large manufacturing contracts and tenders, executing them out of factories in Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Odisha and elsewhere, and reporting an order book that it converts to revenue over following quarters — FY26 consolidated total income was about INR 2,961 crore with EBITDA of INR 363 crore (12.4% margin) and PAT of INR 166 crore, entering FY27 with an order book of INR 4,675 crore. Over time it has bought and partnered its way into the components that sit inside a wagon — wheelsets and axles, braking systems, brake discs, track crossings — so that it supplies itself rather than importing, and has added adjacent businesses in truck load bodies, shipping containers and battery energy storage. Management now describes it as a diversified mobility and infrastructure solutions company spanning rail, mobility, logistics and clean energy, mostly domestic with a growing export/partnership angle into Europe.

parts.name: Freight wagons
parts.what: Designs and manufactures railway freight wagons for both Indian Railways tenders and private buyers — historically the dominant revenue line (INR 4,000 crore of a INR 4,700 crore order book in 2022), with management claiming 60-70% share of the private wagon segment and over 100 private rakes delivered in FY24.

parts.name: Wheelsets and axles (Jupiter Tatravagonka Railwheel Factory / erstwhile Bonatrans India)
parts.what: Makes and machines wheelsets and axles for freight wagons, LHB coaches, metro systems and Vande Bharat trains; acquired in 2024, it crossed INR 500 crore of revenue in FY26 at roughly 17% EBITDA margin, and a shortage of bought-in wheelsets was the single biggest constraint on the company's own wagon output in FY26.

parts.name: Odisha greenfield wheelset project
parts.what: A new fully integrated wheelset plant under construction meant to remove the wheelset shortage and serve exports (including a long-term supply deal with European wagon maker Tatravagonka), with partial production expected by end-FY27 and full commissioning targeted by end-FY28.

parts.name: Braking systems (DAKO-CZ tie-up and subsidiary Stone India)
parts.what: Supplies brake systems for passenger coaches and freight wagons; Stone India received RDSO approval for its freight brake system with commercial production due July 2026, which management says completes full backward integration of the core railroad product range.

parts.name: Brake discs (KOVIS joint venture)
parts.what: A JV making brake discs and castings for Indian Railways and for export to Europe — described early on as roughly a INR 1,000 crore Indian market, and still cited in FY26 as a steady growth product.

parts.name: CMS crossings
parts.what: Cast manganese steel track crossings, including newer weldable crossings that let trains run at higher speeds; JWL is an Indian Railways-approved source and won an early large weldable-crossing order (about 4,000 sets, ~INR 127 crore), with railways buying roughly 20,000 crossings a year.

parts.name: Commercial vehicle load bodies and containers
parts.what: Builds load bodies for India's major commercial-vehicle OEMs and is one of India's leading ISO/shipping container manufacturers; a smaller line historically (~INR 60 crore of the 2022 order book) but growing, with a INR 10,000 crore government PLI scheme for container manufacturing named as a tailwind.

parts.name: Jupiter Electric Mobility (clean energy / eLCVs)
parts.what: The newer clean-energy arm covering electric light commercial vehicles, auxiliary battery systems for Vande Bharat trains, a cell-to-battery line in Indore, and containerised Battery Energy Storage Systems; it added 110 MW of BESS orders to the FY27 book and management aspires to build it into a INR 1,000 crore revenue business in 3-4 years.

parts.name: Passenger rolling stock (planned)
parts.what: A not-yet-started segment: the company says it is in advanced discussions with a leading European partner and is preparing to enter passenger mobility in FY27 as a new growth avenue.

overview.what_it_does: Jyothy Labs is an Indian consumer-goods (FMCG) company that makes and sells everyday household and personal products under its own brands — laundry detergents and fabric whiteners, dishwashing bars/liquids, mosquito repellents, and neem-based soaps. It sells to ordinary Indian households through a wide retail distribution network (management cites reaching about a million retail outlets, with a deliberate push into rural stockists and van operations), plus modern trade, CSD, e-commerce and quick commerce; north and east India are described as its core markets for insecticides, and south India as strong for some fabric brands. It earns money on the margin between what it pays for raw materials (LABSA, SLES, soda ash, palm oil, packaging — roughly 50-60% of inputs are crude-linked) and the shelf price of high-frequency, low-ticket packs, so profits swing with commodity costs, price/grammage competition and advertising spend (typically 8-9% of revenue). FY26 revenue was INR2,944 crores (up 3.5% in value, 6% in volume) with a 15.3% EBITDA margin and PAT of INR333 crores; the company says it is debt-free with about INR1,000 crores of cash.

parts.name: Fabric Care (main wash + post wash)
parts.what: Laundry products — detergent powders, bars and fast-growing liquid detergents under Henko, Ujala IDD, Mr. White and Morelight (plus the new Dr.Wool), alongside post-wash Ujala Supreme fabric whitener and Ujala Crisp & Shine; it is the company's biggest and best-performing engine, growing 8% in value and 9.5% in volume in FY26 with liquid detergents nearly doubling.

parts.name: Dishwash
parts.what: Utensil-cleaning bars, powders and newer liquids under the Exo and Pril brands (including a bio-enzyme variant launched in Q4 FY26); a large, under-penetrated category for the company that grew about 6% in volume in FY26 but fell 1.3% in value as competitors cut prices and gave extra grammage, squeezing its segment margin.

parts.name: Household Insecticides (HI)
parts.what: Mosquito-repellent coils, liquid vaporizers and a newly launched Maxo aerosol, concentrated in north and east India (about 75% of segment sales) and highly weather-dependent; it is the smallest and problem segment — sales fell 1.3% in FY26 but management deliberately shifted the mix away from coils (liquid vaporizers now ~55% of the portfolio), cutting losses from INR25 crores to about INR5 crores and targeting a full turnaround by end-FY27.

parts.name: Personal Care
parts.what: Essentially the 100-year-old Margo neem soap franchise (Margo Original Neem, Margo Neem Naturals and newer variants), marketed on natural/neem credentials to younger consumers via influencers and social media; it recovered strongly after GST-related disruption, growing 20% in value and volume in Q4 FY26 and 5% in value for the full year.

parts.name: Sales channels and distribution
parts.what: Not a product segment but repeatedly flagged as the core asset — direct distribution reaching roughly a million retail outlets with rural stockists and vans described as a competitive moat and 'barrier to entry', supplemented by modern trade, e-commerce and quick commerce, which management says are growing strongly and becoming an increasingly important part of the mix.

overview.what_it_does: Jyoti CNC Automation builds and sells CNC (computer numerical control) metal-cutting machine tools — the precision machines that factories use to cut and shape metal parts — from its plants in Rajkot, Gujarat and Strasbourg, France. It sells these machines directly to manufacturers: aerospace and defence firms (ISRO, BrahMos, MBDA, Tata Sikorsky, large European aerospace players), auto and auto-component makers (Bharat Forge, Bosch), general engineering shops, electronics manufacturing (EMS) companies, and die-and-mould makers. It makes money by taking machine orders into an order book and recognising revenue as machines are built and delivered, with build cycles running 3-6 months for entry-level machines and up to 12-18 months for large complex ones; FY26 consolidated revenue was about INR 599 crores in Q4 and the closing order book was INR 4,732 crores. It is vertically integrated (own foundry, machine shop, sheet metal, paint, assembly), sells mainly in India through roughly 29 sales and service centres, and exports via subsidiaries in France, Germany, Canada and Turkey.

parts.name: Entry-level machines (roughly up to INR 50 lakh)
parts.what: Lower-priced CNC machines with a 3-6 month build cycle, supplied mostly to EMS, automobile/auto-component and general engineering customers.

parts.name: Mid-level machines (roughly INR 50 lakh to 2 crores)
parts.what: Mid-priced machines with a build cycle of around 9 months; management describes Jyoti as present across the full value chain of entry, mid and high-end products.

parts.name: High-end machines, including 5-Axis and multi-tasking
parts.what: Large, complex high-precision machines with 12-18 month build cycles, aimed mainly at aerospace and defence; the 5-Axis multi-tasking machine was developed with IIT Chennai under a Department of Heavy Industries scheme, and these are described as the company's most significant technology milestone.

parts.name: Huron (France subsidiary, acquired 2007)
parts.what: A French machine-tool maker at Strasbourg (46,000 sq m, 120-machine capacity, doubled in November 2025) that supplies precision 5-Axis machines to global aerospace and defence customers and acts as the group's technology hub; an export-control investigation there caused a INR 67 crore revenue deferment in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Aerospace and defence end-market
parts.what: The largest single end-market — 39-45% of revenue across FY25 and FY26 and about 38-41% of the order book (roughly INR 1,900 crores) — served with high-precision machining solutions.

parts.name: Auto and auto components end-market
parts.what: Consistently around 23-28% of revenue and about 20% of the order book, including EV-oriented products such as the VST 160 machine launched in 2022.

parts.name: General engineering end-market
parts.what: Around 20-23% of revenue and about 19% of the order book, and one of the two segments management says picked up fastest in FY26 order intake (31% of FY26 intake).

parts.name: EMS (electronics manufacturing services) end-market
parts.what: A newer market entered with the purpose-built 'Tachyon' product developed from 2015-2021; it was about 16% of the March 2025 order book but around 4% by March 2026.

parts.name: Die and mould and other sectors
parts.what: A small residual slice, roughly 2-5% of revenue and order book.

parts.name: R&D — Leonardo Da Vinci Centre and software products
parts.what: An in-house R&D centre set up in 2008 with 140+ engineers that has produced 200-plus product variants plus the '7th SENSE' Industry 4.0 platform, the 'PreciProtect' AI collision-prevention system and the 'Huma' control panel.

parts.name: Electronics / mechatronics build-out (new)
parts.what: A stated push beyond mechanical into in-house servo motors, servo drives, sensors, PLCs and controllers, intended to cut import dependence and later support industrial automation, robotics and semiconductor equipment — described as future strategy rather than current revenue.

parts.name: Manufacturing capacity and expansion
parts.what: Two vertically integrated Rajkot plants (253,000 sq m) running above 100% utilisation at peak, with installed capacity of 6,000 machines a year being expanded to 16,000 by around September 2026 — management calls this the main driver of the next growth phase.

overview.what_it_does: Kajaria Ceramics makes and sells ceramic and vitrified tiles in India — floor and wall tiles in sizes from small ceramic tiles up to large glazed vitrified tiles and four-foot-by-eight-foot slabs — under its own brand. It earns money by manufacturing tiles at its own plants (North at Gailpur, South at Srikalahasti and near Hyderabad, and units in Morbi, Gujarat, plus joint ventures there and a new plant in Nepal), topping that up with tiles bought in from outside makers, and selling almost entirely through a network of dealers who display the product in their showrooms; management repeatedly stresses that 'what is visible is sold.' Demand comes from Indian home building and renovation, real-estate projects and government housing/infrastructure schemes, with particularly good traction in tier-II and smaller cities rather than the metros. Alongside tiles it sells bathroom fittings, tile adhesives and, until it was shut in FY26, plywood; revenue runs at roughly Rs 1,100–1,400 crore a quarter, and natural gas/fuel cost is the single biggest swing factor on its margins.

parts.name: Tiles
parts.what: The core business — ceramic floor and wall tiles, glazed vitrified tiles (GVT) and large slabs, made at company plants and joint ventures plus outsourced supply, accounting for the overwhelming majority of revenue (about Rs 1,212 crore of Rs 1,373 crore consolidated revenue in Q4 FY26) and volumes of roughly 23–27 million square metres per quarter.

parts.name: Bathware
parts.what: Bathroom products (sanitaryware and fittings) sold under the same brand and dealer network — a small but steadily growing side business, moving from about Rs 71 crore a quarter in FY23 to Rs 117 crore in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Adhesives
parts.what: Tile adhesives and related fixing materials, run as its own division under a dedicated head — the fastest-growing part off a tiny base, from about Rs 15 crore in Q1 FY25 to Rs 44 crore in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Plywood
parts.what: A small plywood business that grew from roughly Rs 5 crore to Rs 20 crore a quarter in FY23 and then stagnated around Rs 18 crore, and which the company closed down during FY26 — management cites 'absence of Ply sales due to closure of that division' as a drag on Q3 FY26 revenue.

parts.name: Joint ventures and acquired units in Morbi
parts.what: Stakes in and acquisitions of tile plants in the Morbi cluster in Gujarat (such as the Keronite unit, 6 million square metres of GVT) plus buyouts like South Asian Ceramics near Hyderabad, used to add cheap capacity and cut delivery time to nearby markets; profits from JVs are reported separately from the main operating profit.

overview.what_it_does: Kalyan Jewellers is an Indian jewellery retailer that sells gold jewellery and studded (diamond/stone-set) jewellery to everyday retail shoppers, largely for weddings and festivals such as Diwali and Akshaya Tritiya. It makes money by running a large chain of branded showrooms — some owned by the company, some run by franchise partners under a FOCO arrangement where the partner puts up the store and inventory — and earns a retail margin on the jewellery sold; a small amount also comes from gold coin sales to retail and corporate customers. Most of the business is in India, split between its home South Indian markets and the faster-growing non-South regions (non-South was 49% of revenue in Q1 FY25 and by FY26 was growing faster than South), plus a Middle East operation and small pilot showrooms in the U.S. and U.K. In FY26 the group reported consolidated revenue of about INR 35,740 crores and profit after tax of about INR 1,350 crores, up from INR 3,333 crores of quarterly revenue and INR 108 crores of quarterly profit back in Q1 FY23.

parts.name: India business (Kalyan showrooms — own and franchise/FOCO)
parts.what: The core chain of Kalyan-branded jewellery showrooms across India, run both as company-owned stores and as franchise (FOCO) stores where partners fund the store and inventory — this is by far the biggest part, at roughly INR 8,990 crores of the INR 10,275 crores consolidated revenue in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Middle East business
parts.what: Kalyan showrooms in the Middle East serving local and tourist demand, a much smaller and thinner-margin piece at about INR 1,074 crores of revenue and INR 21 crores of profit in Q4 FY26, with some stores being converted to franchise to pay down regional debt.

parts.name: Candere (e-commerce / omnichannel brand)
parts.what: A separate digital-first jewellery brand, now a wholly-owned subsidiary, that has been built into an omnichannel business with 110 physical stores as of Q3 FY26; still small in absolute terms (INR 131 crores of revenue in Q4 FY26) but growing very fast — 160% revenue growth in FY26 — and it turned profitable from the second half of FY26 after years of small losses.

parts.name: Franchise showroom expansion
parts.what: Management describes signing up franchise partners as a distinct strategic engine — the partner funds store inventory while Kalyan books the sale up front, which lets the chain expand without tying up its own cash; started as a pilot in FY23 (first store in Aurangabad) and by FY26 is a standing pipeline with plans for roughly 150 new showrooms across Kalyan, Candere and a new regional brand in FY27.

parts.name: New international markets (U.S. and U.K.)
parts.what: Small pilot showrooms outside India and the Middle East — the first U.S. store was targeted before Diwali FY25 and the first U.K. Kalyan showroom opened in FY26 — funded out of free cash flow (about INR 300 crores went to Candere expansion plus these pilots in 9M FY26) and not yet a meaningful revenue contributor.

parts.name: Gold coin sales
parts.what: Sales of plain gold coins to retail and corporate buyers, explicitly called out as a very small sliver of the business — about INR 13 crores, or 0.46% of total revenue, in Q1 FY23, with no bullion sales in that quarter.

parts.name: New regional brand
parts.what: A further jewellery format mentioned in the FY26 year-end call as part of the FY27 store-opening plan alongside Kalyan and Candere; the calls give no revenue or size detail for it yet.

overview.what_it_does: Kansai Nerolac Paints is an India-listed paint and coatings maker (NSE symbol KANSAINER), majority-owned by its promoter Kansai Paint Co., Ltd. of Japan, which supplies much of its technology. It makes money two ways: selling decorative paints, waterproofing and construction chemicals and wood finishes to households, painters, architects and building projects through a dealer/retail network it keeps expanding (3,500 dealers added as of December 2025, 600-plus branded Shoppe/shop-in-shop outlets), and selling industrial coatings directly to manufacturers — above all car, two-wheeler, three-wheeler, commercial-vehicle and tractor makers, where management says it is the market leader.
