It manufactures in India across eight plants (expansions cited at Vizag, Jainpur and Hosur) and keeps 200–300 technical staff stationed on customers' production lines. Growth is tied to Indian housing/repainting demand, monsoon and festive timing, government infrastructure spending and vehicle production, while raw-material costs move with crude and the rupee; recent quarters show low-single-digit revenue growth amid heavy new competition in decorative.

parts.name: Decorative
parts.what: Paints and coatings for homes and buildings sold through retail dealers, plus the newer premium 'Paint+' range that management says now contributes more than 10% of decorative sales; this is the larger, more competitive side of the business and the focus of most of the calls.

parts.name: Decorative – Retail
parts.what: The core over-the-counter business where Nerolac is the number-two brand nationally, supported by painter and architect loyalty programmes, branded experience stores and heavy advertising (TV jingle, Asia Cup/World Cup campaigns).

parts.name: Decorative – Projects & Institutional
parts.what: Bulk supply to builders, institutions and construction projects through a dedicated on-ground team now covering 80-plus towns; started from a small base, grows in double digits and is described as growing faster than the industry, though its share of decorative was still below 10% as of early 2025.

parts.name: Decorative – New Businesses (construction chemicals, waterproofing, wood finishes)
parts.what: Adjacent products like waterproofing and repair chemicals that Nerolac had no presence in until roughly 2021-22; salience has crossed 10%, it grows in strong double digits, and it was expanded by acquiring Nerofix and Perma — management sees big headroom since only about three in ten buildings currently use construction chemicals.

parts.name: Services (paint-as-a-service / influencer programmes)
parts.what: A painting-service and architect/interior-designer programme that generates digital leads and executes jobs in 150-plus cities; it now contributes more than 5% of decorative business, the 'critical mass' target management had set.

parts.name: Industrial – Automotive (OEM)
parts.what: Coatings supplied directly onto vehicle assembly lines for passenger cars, two- and three-wheelers, commercial vehicles and tractors, where Nerolac is the market leader and is still gaining share; demand jumped roughly 20% year-on-year after the October 2025 GST cuts, and management expects support from bigger SUVs (more paintable area), OEM capacity expansion and vehicle exports.

parts.name: Industrial – Auto Refinish
parts.what: The after-market side, selling repair paints to car body shops, with a push to win premium 'A-class' body shops and convert them from solvent-based to waterborne systems; described as stable rather than fast-growing.

parts.name: Industrial – Performance Coatings (liquid and powder)
parts.what: Non-automotive industrial coatings — coil coating, fusion-bonded epoxy powder, general industrial for construction equipment and pre-engineered buildings, plus powder coatings for auto ancillaries, appliances and furniture; management has deliberately exited low-end, low-margin work here to raise the premium mix, and wins depend on long approval cycles.

overview.what_it_does: Karur Vysya Bank is an Indian commercial bank, headquartered in Karur, Tamil Nadu and listed on the NSE and BSE, that takes deposits from the public and lends the money out at a higher rate. Its customers are mainly retail households, farmers, small and medium businesses (MSMEs) and, to a smaller extent, larger corporates, served through a branch network (including newer "lite" branches and an open-market sales channel) plus digital channels. It makes money chiefly from net interest income — the spread between what it pays on deposits and what it earns on loans and investments, running a net interest margin of roughly 3.7%-4.3% — plus fee and other non-interest income; management steers the bank on three stated metrics: growth, profitability and asset quality. As of June 2026 total business was about INR 2,27,267 crore, split roughly 54% deposits (INR 1,22,587 crore) and the rest advances (INR 1,04,680 crore).

parts.name: RAM verticals (Retail, Agriculture, MSME/Commercial)
parts.what: The bank's core lending engine and stated focus area — granular, mostly secured loans that make up about 86% of total advances and grew 18% year-on-year in FY26.

parts.name: Retail advances
parts.what: Loans to individuals — jewel (gold) loans, mortgages, housing loans and personal loans — about 27% of the loan book, growing 25% in FY26 and 23% year-on-year by Q1 FY27, led by mortgage and retail jewel loans; mortgage-focused branches were raised from 144 to 175.

parts.name: Agriculture
parts.what: Farm lending at about 25% of the loan book, of which roughly 91%-92% is agri jewel (gold-backed) loans at a loan-to-value around 55%-64%, growing about 19% in FY26 with LTV monitored through automated branch alerts.

parts.name: Commercial / MSME (Small Business Group and Business Banking Group)
parts.what: Working-capital and business loans to small and medium enterprises — the largest single slice at about 35% of advances, grew 11.6% in FY26, now sold through a relationship-manager model across 77 branches with products like a GST surrogate loan and an open term loan.

parts.name: Corporate and institutional banking
parts.what: Lending to larger companies — about 14% of advances; shrank for a period as the bank walked away from low-yielding business, then returned to 12% growth in FY26 (20% including credit substitutes) via commercial real estate, capital-market participants and EPC/infrastructure clients.

parts.name: Credit substitutes
parts.what: Bond-like exposures to existing, externally A-rated corporate customers used instead of plain loans because the pricing is better — INR 969 crore added in FY26 and INR 171 crore in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Liability business (deposits, CASA and NRI)
parts.what: Raising current, savings and term deposits — 54% of total business, with retail households supplying 72% of deposits; run through a dedicated acquisition channel, 24 CASA product variants and separate desks for corporate salary, institutional, NRE, government, trade/forex and business correspondents, with FCNR (B) deposits used to court NRI customers.

parts.name: Transaction Banking Group
parts.what: Digital plumbing for corporate and MSME clients — API-based real-time banking, bulk payments for payroll and vendor/B2B settlement, and automated trade finance and supply-chain workflows; described as supporting portfolio diversification and big client relationships rather than as a large earner on its own.

parts.name: BNPL (buy-now-pay-later) partnership book
parts.what: Small consumer credit sourced through an outside partner, INR 798 crore outstanding at March 2026; it shrank in FY26 after the partner changed management and household debt levels rose, and grew 2% in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Co-lending with NBFCs
parts.what: Loans made jointly with non-bank lenders, deliberately shrunk to about INR 249 crore because it was not adding to return on assets, and treated as secondary to the bank's own organic lending.

parts.name: Microfinance (MFI)
parts.what: A deliberately tiny book of INR 173 crore, just 0.18% of the portfolio, now with government (CGFMU) guarantee cover and guardrails after stress in the segment.

parts.name: Treasury and investments
parts.what: Manages the bank's securities portfolio and liquidity — contributes yield on investments and occasional mark-to-market write-backs to non-interest income, and was reorganised under the new RBI investment-classification rules from April 2024 (P&L neutral, +INR 81 crore to reserves); the bank has no overseas or GIFT City presence.

overview.what_it_does: Kaynes Technology is an Indian electronics contract manufacturer — what the industry calls an ESDM/EMS player — that builds electronic assemblies for other companies' products rather than selling anything under its own brand. Its core work is designing and assembling printed circuit boards (PCBAs) and complete electronic boxes for customers in automotive and EV, railways, industrial, aerospace, defence and medical-type end markets, described by management as 'high mix, high value' work with variable volumes, plus support across the whole life of a product from concept through post-manufacturing and end-of-life. It earns money by winning firm, non-cancellable customer orders (order book about INR 90,000 million as of Q3 FY26) and recognising revenue as it builds and ships against them; FY26 consolidated revenue was INR 3,626.4 crore, up 33% year-on-year, at a 15.8% EBITDA margin and 10% PAT margin. It is headquartered in Mysore with plants across India (Mysore, Manesar, Chamarajanagar, Hyderabad, Sanand, a new PCB plant at Chennai), sells to 300-plus customers in 24 countries, and has bought its way into North America via August Electronics.

parts.name: Core EMS / PCBA business
parts.what: The original and still-dominant business: assembling printed circuit boards and electronic sub-systems to customer designs across automotive, EV, industrial, railway and aerospace verticals — management says nearly all current order-book additions are EMS orders, and the flagship Mysore plant alone crossed INR 10,000 million of revenue in FY26.

parts.name: Smart meters / power distribution products
parts.what: Makes electricity smart meters (and is targeting gas and water meters) for AMISPs — the companies that win state utility metering contracts — built up via the October 2024 acquisition of Iskraemeco India and a new Hyderabad factory; management said it was roughly 10% of sales at the time, possibly 12–15% at peak execution, and it carries a heavier working-capital cycle than core EMS.

parts.name: OSAT (semiconductor assembly and test)
parts.what: A new chip packaging and testing plant at Sanand, Gujarat, backed by government incentives under the India Semiconductor Mission (FSA approval received) — Unit 1 is operational and ramping, Unit 2 commercialises in Q2 FY27, with management citing revenue visibility of over INR 25,000 million across the next five years.

parts.name: HDI PCB manufacturing
parts.what: A roughly INR 1,500 crore plant coming up at Chennai to make the bare high-density, multi-layer circuit boards themselves — a backward-integration move aimed at defence, aerospace and complex industrial customers, which management argues can pull through about INR 13,500 crore of follow-on EMS work from the same clients.

parts.name: August Electronics (North America)
parts.what: An acquired US operation being integrated to give Kaynes a North American customer base and higher-margin specialist capability such as RF and microwave assemblies.

overview.what_it_does: KEC International is an Indian engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor: it wins tenders to design and build large infrastructure — power transmission lines and substations, buildings and factories, water pipelines, railway and metro systems, oil and gas pipelines and solar/wind projects — and also manufactures and sells hardware such as transmission towers, poles, cables and conductors from its own factories in India, Dubai, Mexico and Brazil. Its customers are government power utilities (PGCIL, state electricity boards), private transmission developers bidding under the TBCB route, Indian Railways and metro authorities, and private industrial and real-estate clients. It makes money by executing these turnkey projects against a large order book (about INR 36,000 crore at FY26 year-end, plus L1 positions, giving six to seven quarters of visibility), booking revenue as work progresses; margins are thin — roughly 7% EBITDA and 2-3% net on FY26 revenue of INR 23,506 crore — so profitability turns on commodity prices, labour availability and how fast clients pay. Roughly two-thirds of revenue comes from India, with the rest spread across the Middle East (about 27% of order book), Africa, the CIS, the Americas, SAARC and Australia.

parts.name: Transmission & Distribution (T&D)
parts.what: Builds high-voltage power lines and substations (including 765 kV, GIS/AIS and HVDC) and supplies towers in India and overseas; by far the biggest and fastest-growing part, at INR 15,883 crore or 68% of FY26 revenue and about 70% of new orders, with an order book plus L1 of over INR 26,000 crore.

parts.name: SAE Towers
parts.what: The overseas tower-manufacturing arm with plants in Mexico and Brazil that supplies towers, hardware, poles and monopoles across the U.S., Mexico and Brazil (and earlier did EPC work in Brazil); revenue of INR 1,800 crore in FY26, up 36%, with an order book plus L1 above INR 2,600 crore — a past problem area that management says is now profitable and much less indebted.

parts.name: Civil
parts.what: Turnkey construction of buildings and factories — residential high-rises, industrial plants, hospitals, data centres, metals and mining facilities, defence and water pipeline projects; the second-largest business, described repeatedly as a key growth driver, with an order book plus L1 of over INR 10,000 crore, though revenue (around INR 900-1,000 crore a quarter) has been held back by labour shortages and slow payments on water projects.

parts.name: Railways / Transportation
parts.what: Overhead electrification, gauge conversion, metro power supply, ballastless track and signalling work, including the KAVACH train collision avoidance system (611 route km done, 1,836 more under way) and automatic block signalling; a smaller unit of roughly INR 350-470 crore a quarter with an order book plus L1 above INR 3,000 crore, where management is deliberately bidding selectively and focusing on finishing existing jobs.

parts.name: Cables and Conductors
parts.what: Manufactures and sells power and specialty cables plus transmission conductors and railway products (signalling cables, contact and catenary conductors) to T&D, railway, metro, solar and metals customers and increasingly for export; revenue of roughly INR 360-420 crore a quarter, doubling as a supplier to KEC's own railway and T&D projects.

parts.name: Oil & Gas Pipelines
parts.what: Lays cross-country oil and gas pipelines for government and private clients, now including a first international project in Africa and approval to bid for Saudi Aramco; the smallest business at about INR 90-130 crore a quarter, still being built up by acquiring the pre-qualifications needed to bid for bigger jobs.

parts.name: Renewables
parts.what: Builds solar PV plants on an EPC basis — including a 625 MWp project in Rajasthan and a 600 MWp project in Karnataka — and has begun moving into wind, with an order book of over INR 1,300 crore when first broken out; a newer, small but strategically emphasised growth engine tied to India's energy transition.

overview.what_it_does: KEI Industries is an Indian manufacturer of electrical wires and cables — everything from house wiring sold to retail consumers to low-tension, high-tension and extra-high-voltage (up to 400 kV) power cables used by industry and utilities. It makes money three ways: selling to institutional/B2B customers (power transmission and distribution utilities, solar and thermal power projects, metros and railways, real estate and construction, oil and gas, data centres), selling through a dealer/distribution network of about 2,125 active dealers to the retail market, and exporting cables to markets including the Middle East, UAE, Australia, Spain, the UK, the Caribbean and the United States. It also takes on turnkey EPC (engineering, procurement, construction) contracts and runs a small stainless steel wire business. Revenue was roughly INR11,746 crores in FY26 (up about 21%) with profit after tax of about INR918 crores; manufacturing plants are in Rajasthan (Bhiwadi, Chopanki, Pathredi), Silvassa/Chinchpada and a large new plant at Sanand in Gujarat.

parts.name: Sales through distribution network (B2C / dealer sales)
parts.what: House wires and cables sold through an all-India dealer network (about 2,125 active dealers as of March 2026) — the largest and fastest-growing part of the business at INR6,349 crores in FY26, roughly 54-56% of total sales and growing about 25-29% a year.

parts.name: Domestic institutional cable sales (B2B, wires and cables)
parts.what: Direct sales of low-tension and high-tension power cables to Indian industrial and infrastructure customers — INR2,688 crores in FY26; together with EHV and exports this institutional bucket is about 40-42% of sales.

parts.name: Extra high-voltage (EHV) cables
parts.what: High-end cables for power transmission at very high voltages (management cites 220 kV to 400 kV, first Indian supplier of 330 kV cable to Australia and the only Indian firm qualified in the UK National Grid framework) — a small but fast-growing and prestigious line at INR559 crores domestically in FY26, up 82%.

parts.name: Export sales
parts.what: Cables shipped to overseas customers in the Middle East, Australia, Spain, the UK, the Caribbean/West Indies and the US — INR1,833 crores in FY26, up 45%, which management wants to take to roughly 20% of total sales.

parts.name: EPC (engineering, procurement, construction) other than cable
parts.what: Turnkey project contracts, including donor-funded overseas work (an ADB-funded Nepal project and a World Bank-funded Gambia project were in the order book) and EHV cable-laying projects — a small line at INR311 crores in FY26, and a shrinking share of the company.

parts.name: Stainless steel wire division
parts.what: A separate small manufacturing line making stainless steel wire, essentially flat at around INR212 crores a year — under 2% of sales.

parts.name: House wire division / manufacturing capacity
parts.what: The plants themselves (Bhiwadi, Chopanki, Pathredi in Rajasthan; Silvassa/Chinchpada; and the new Sanand plant in Gujarat) are the engine of growth — Sanand cost about INR2,000 crores, started phase-1 production in December 2025, and is expected to add roughly INR5,000-6,000 crores of annual sales once fully ramped by around FY29.

overview.what_it_does: KFin Technologies is an Indian record-keeping and back-office services company — a registrar and transfer agent (RTA) — that keeps track of who owns what across financial products. It does the paperwork, record-keeping, technology platforms and investor servicing for mutual funds, alternative investment funds, pension schemes and listed/unlisted companies, so its customers are financial institutions (asset managers, fund houses, custodians, corporates) rather than retail investors directly, even though it maintains the individual investor accounts (folios) on their behalf. It earns fees largely linked to the assets under management of the funds it services, plus per-client, per-transaction and per-mandate charges for corporate registry work, IPO handling, fund accounting and technology/data products — so revenue moves with market levels as well as with new client wins. Started in 1985 and listed on NSE and BSE in December 2022, it operates across India and increasingly overseas — Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand and beyond, plus GIFT City — with management saying nearly 40% of revenue now comes from businesses outside domestic mutual funds.

parts.name: Investor Solutions – Domestic Mutual Funds
parts.what: Acts as the transfer agent for Indian mutual fund houses — maintaining investor folios, processing purchases, redemptions and SIPs, and providing related technology — and is the company's single biggest business (about 68% of revenue in FY23, still the dominant line but down to roughly 60% by mid-2026), serving 24-26 of India's ~41-46 asset managers with roughly a third of industry AUM and about 40% of SIP flows.

parts.name: Issuer Solutions (corporate / share transfer registry)
parts.what: Maintains shareholder registers for listed and unlisted companies and runs IPOs, corporate actions and corporate events for them; management calls it a mature business alongside mutual funds, with clients growing from about 5,100 in FY23 to over 10,500 by March 2026, roughly 50-52% market share of NSE/Nifty 500 companies by market cap, and it handled around 80% by market cap of IPOs in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: International / Global Fund Solutions
parts.what: Sells the same transfer-agency and fund-administration services to asset managers, trusts and custodians outside India — Malaysia (over 50% share of AMCs there), Philippines, Thailand and elsewhere — and is described as one of the company's biggest bets, boosted by the October 2025 acquisition of Ascent Fund Solutions (about $22 million of annualised revenue at low margin initially), with international revenue growing over 30% organically and nearly 200% including Ascent.

parts.name: Alternatives (Alternative Investment Funds)
parts.what: Provides combined transfer agency, fund accounting and value-added services to AIFs and private funds in India and GIFT City on a proprietary multi-currency, multi-asset platform; it grew from 348 funds in FY23 to 716 funds by March 2026, about a 38% share of AIFs by fund count, with over ₹1.4 trillion of AUM as of early 2025.

parts.name: National Pension System / Central Recordkeeping Agency (Pensions)
parts.what: Operates as one of the licensed central record keepers for the National Pension System, maintaining pension subscriber accounts — a small business in revenue terms that only broke even around late 2024, but management values it as a sticky, non-market-linked hedge; share went from zero in 2017 to roughly 10% by 2025, growing about 3-3.5x faster than the industry and now the second-largest CRA.

parts.name: Technology, data and value-added products
parts.what: Sells software and data services to its financial clients — data lake contracts for asset managers (eight signed by end-2024), fund accounting (via the Hexagram acquisition), CRM, mobility and cloud solutions — described as over 20 products launched, generating direct fees while also helping clients grow, which feeds back into KFin's asset-linked revenue.

parts.name: Global Business Services
parts.what: An outsourcing arm doing back-office work for specific clients — mortgage processing, finance & accounting outsourcing and general ledger accounting for Middle Eastern banks — mentioned as a distinct business line in the early calls but not sized, and it gets little airtime in later calls.

overview.what_it_does: KIMS (Krishna Institute of Medical Sciences) runs a chain of private multi-specialty hospitals in India, selling in-patient treatment (surgeries and admissions, including complex work like organ transplants, neurosurgery, cardiac, cancer and orthopaedic care) and out-patient doctor consultations to individual patients. It earns money per patient treated — the calls track revenue as beds occupied times average revenue per occupied bed (ARPOB) and average revenue per patient (ARPP) — with bills paid by patients in cash, by health insurers, and by government schemes such as Aarogyasri. It started in and is still anchored in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (about 3,600 beds across those two states in 2022) and has since spread to Maharashtra, Karnataka and Kerala, reaching 25 hospitals across 5 states by early 2026, with a Chennai hospital under construction. Growth comes from building new hospitals, adding beds at existing ones, recruiting senior consultants, and buying existing hospitals such as Sunshine.

parts.name: In-patient (IP) business
parts.what: Admitted patients having surgery or treatment — the main revenue driver, measured by IP volumes, occupancy and length of stay; volumes were about 61,000 in a single quarter (Q3 FY26) and grew roughly 15% over FY26.

parts.name: Out-patient (OP) / OPD consultations
parts.what: Walk-in doctor consultations that also feed admissions and tests; about 4 lakh consultations in FY24, rising to roughly 5.85 lakh in a single quarter by Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Telangana cluster (Hyderabad/Secunderabad, Kondapur, Kompally)
parts.what: The original home market and largest cluster, including the flagship Secunderabad unit doing robotic and transplant work, with about 600 beds added at Kondapur and a new 6 lakh sq ft Secunderabad building being built over 2-3 years.

parts.name: Andhra Pradesh cluster (Guntur, Ongole, Nellore, Vizag/Seetamadara)
parts.what: The other core home-state cluster of tier-1 and tier-2 town hospitals; two new Guntur units, a Vizag unit, a cancer block at Ongole and a mother-and-child unit at Nellore were added in FY26.

parts.name: Sunshine Hospitals (acquired)
parts.what: A majority-stake acquisition completed in FY23 that brought a nationally known orthopaedics franchise; it came in at a lower 17.8% EBITDA margin than the rest of KIMS but management repeatedly says it has since improved as expected.

parts.name: Maharashtra cluster (Nagpur, Nashik, Thane, Sangli)
parts.what: The main out-of-home-state expansion: Nagpur was the first and turned around to roughly 20% EBITDA on about INR18 crore monthly revenue, followed by Nashik, a 290-bed Thane (Mumbai) hospital on 99-year leased land, and Sangli.

parts.name: Karnataka / Bangalore cluster (Mahadevapura, Electronic City, PES)
parts.what: Newest big-city cluster, commissioned in 2025 with a dedicated cluster CEO; ARPOB is high (above INR76,000) but it is the largest source of current EBITDA losses, expected to turn EBITDA-neutral through FY27.

parts.name: Kerala (Kollam)
parts.what: A single new hospital opened in 2025, part of the FY26 batch of seven new units that lifted revenue but dragged margins.

parts.name: Mature units vs newer units
parts.what: Management's own split of the P&L: in Q4 FY26 mature hospitals produced about INR862 crore of the INR1,085 crore revenue at roughly 28.5-30% EBITDA margin, while units under one year old contributed about INR224 crore of revenue but eroded EBITDA and pulled the group margin down to 19.9%.

parts.name: Specialty centres of excellence
parts.what: High-end clinical programmes management highlights as the brand's pull — organ transplants (over 430 renal, 120 liver and 100 heart-and-lung transplants in 2025), neurosciences (10,000+ brain tumour surgeries), oncology, renal and gastro sciences, robotic surgery (500+ in 2025) and equipment like Gamma Knife and Tulsa Pro.

parts.name: Fertility centres and KIMS Cuddles (mother and child)
parts.what: Smaller newer formats — fertility centres opened at Hyderabad and Guntur and a mother-and-child unit at Nellore in FY26; the calls give no separate revenue figures for them.

overview.what_it_does: Kirloskar Brothers Limited (KBL) is an old, family-run Indian engineering company that designs, manufactures and sells pumps and pumping systems — from small retail pumps used by farmers and households to large engineered pumps for industrial projects. It sells to a wide mix of end users: agriculture and irrigation, water and waste-water supply schemes, building and construction, industry, oil and gas, power stations (coal and nuclear), and marine and defence. It makes money by selling equipment in two ways — large 'made-to-order' and 'engineered-to-order' pumps that sit in an order book and are billed as they are built and dispatched, and standard 'made-to-stock' small pumps sold through a long-standing dealer and distributor network on cash terms (no order book) — plus a growing spares, maintenance and subscription-style service business that brings repeat revenue. Roughly 60-65% of sales come from India (including its own foundry at Kirloskarvadi) and the rest from overseas units in the UK, USA, Netherlands, South Africa and Thailand; FY26 consolidated revenue was about Rs.4,538 crores with EBITDA margin around 13.7% and PAT of about Rs.377 crores.

parts.name: Standalone / domestic pumps business (India)
parts.what: The core Indian operation that designs and builds pumps across small, medium and large ranges at plants including the Kirloskarvadi foundry; it is the biggest single piece of the group, contributing roughly two-thirds of consolidated revenue (about Rs.2,828 crores in FY26) with a domestic order book of about Rs.2,468 crores, up 30% year-on-year.

parts.name: Small pumps / retail business
parts.what: Standard off-the-shelf pumps made to stock and sold through generations-old dealers to farmers and households on cash terms; management says it carries no order book, and its dispatches were hurt in FY26 by weak monsoon-linked demand and by Jal Jeevan Mission funding not reaching dealers (JJM itself is only about 4-5% of revenue but matters a lot to the water segment).

parts.name: Made-to-order / engineered-to-order project pumps
parts.what: Large, customised pumps for irrigation, water supply, industry, oil and gas, power and marine and defence, booked only against confirmed orders with advances or letters of credit; this is where the visible order book and much of the recent growth sits, with management calling out building and construction, marine and defence, oil and gas, power and water/irrigation as the strongest areas.

parts.name: International business (Kirloskar Brothers International B.V. and subsidiaries)
parts.what: Overseas manufacturing and selling units — SPP Pumps UK, SPP USA, the Dutch entity, South Africa and Kirloskar Brothers Thailand — serving oil and gas, water management and industry; it accounts for roughly a third of revenue, grew 7% in FY26, and its order book was about Rs.1,481 crores, up 21% year-on-year.

parts.name: Spares, maintenance and subscription/service platform
parts.what: Aftermarket parts, servicing and a subscription platform sold mainly through the international business, valued by management because it brings recurring revenue, upfront cash and closer customer contact; described as a business the company wants to scale up rather than a major revenue line today.

parts.name: Karad Projects and Motors Limited (KPML)
parts.what: A domestic subsidiary making motors and doing project work that management described as growing healthily (revenue up 27% in H1 FY23); it also absorbed the group's Kolhapur Steel business in 2024 to simplify the structure.

parts.name: Kolhapur Steel Limited
parts.what: A small steel/castings subsidiary that was being turned around with rising revenue and production, and whose entire stake KBL sold to Karad Projects and Motors in FY25 to tidy up the group structure.

parts.name: Kirloskar Ebara Pumps Limited (KEPL)
parts.what: An associate company (not fully consolidated) run as a joint venture-style pump business under Rama Kirloskar; it shows up in KBL's accounts as share of associate profit and is lumpy — one delayed Rs.100 crore order pushed it to a loss of about Rs.5 crores in Q1 FY25.

overview.what_it_does: Kirloskar Oil Engines (KOEL) is an Indian engineering and manufacturing company that designs and builds diesel and alternate-fuel engines, and the products built around them — mainly diesel generator sets for power backup (its range goes up to 1500 KVA, with newer CPCB 4+ emission-compliant and natural-gas models) and engines sold to other manufacturers who put them into tractors, construction equipment, self-loading mixers, fire-fighting pump sets, marine and defence applications. It also makes and sells water pumps and farm mechanisation equipment for households and farmers, and separately runs a lending business, Arka Fincap. Money comes from selling engines, gensets and pumps to builders, real estate and hospitality projects, data centres, industrial OEMs, dealers and retail customers, plus a steady stream of spare parts, service and annual maintenance contracts, and interest income at Arka. It is centred on India (its market share and unit volumes are quoted against the Indian diesel generator market) but is deliberately pushing overseas — the Middle East, South Africa, UAE — with international gross sales crossing INR1,000 crores in FY26 against standalone net sales of INR5,604 crores.

parts.name: Power Generation (Power Gen)
parts.what: Sells diesel and gas generator sets for power backup to real estate, services, hospitality, data centres and retail buyers; it is the single biggest business line, at INR603 crores in the December 2025 quarter (up 44%), and KOEL says it sold upwards of 50,000 units in FY26 in a roughly 179,000-unit Indian DG market.

parts.name: Industrial
parts.what: Supplies engines to other equipment makers — construction and mining machinery, tractors, self-loading mixers, fire-fighting pumps — and to defence, nuclear, marine and railway customers; it generated INR1,444 crores of revenue in FY26, growing 22% for the year.

parts.name: Distribution & Aftermarket
parts.what: Sells spare parts and service through channel partners and is moving from just supplying parts to managing the whole ecosystem via annual maintenance contracts; roughly INR238 crores in the December 2025 quarter and growing steadily in the low-to-mid teens.

parts.name: International business
parts.what: Exports and locally-built operations in markets such as the Middle East, UAE (fire-fighting) and South Africa (industrial); management distinguishes exporting from genuinely 'being international' (hiring and possibly assembling locally), and wants international to reach 30% of the total, having crossed INR1,000 crores of gross sales in FY26.

parts.name: B2C — Water Management Solutions (later renamed Fluid Dynamics / Kirloskar Fluid Dynamics)
parts.what: Makes and sells water pumps and electric motors under the KOEL and LGM brands to households, farmers and dealers — over 1 million pumps sold in FY26 — and was transferred into subsidiary LGM by slump sale in October 2025; it runs at roughly INR249 crores a quarter, far smaller than B2B.

parts.name: B2C — Farm Mechanization
parts.what: Sells farm equipment to agricultural customers through channel partners and some exports; it is the smallest and most inconsistent line, described as growing in FY23 but in degrowth by FY25.

parts.name: Financial Services — Arka Fincap
parts.what: A separate lending arm that earns interest income, now pivoting toward small-ticket retail loans (used vehicles, loans against property) through 137 branches; assets under management were INR7,947 crores with INR69 crores of profit in FY26, contributing about INR227 crores of revenue in the December 2025 quarter.

parts.name: Kirloskar Advanced Systems Private Limited
parts.what: A newly incorporated subsidiary announced in May 2026 to pursue systems-integration work beyond the traditional engine business, aimed at key accounts in sectors like defence; it is a start-up effort with no revenue disclosed.

overview.what_it_does: Kirloskar Pneumatic (KPCL) is a Pune-based Kirloskar Group engineering company that designs and manufactures industrial compressors and the complete packaged systems built around them — air compressors, refrigeration compressors and cooling packages, and gas compression packages for oil, gas, CNG, biogas and hydrogen. It sells business-to-business to industrial customers such as dairy, food processing, fisheries, cold chain and ice plants, pharma, chemicals and fertilizers, cement, metals, mining, power plants, textiles, tyre makers and city gas/CNG station operators. Revenue comes mostly from building and shipping equipment and large engineered packages against a project order book (roughly INR1,900 crores of orders on hand entering 2026, on FY26 total income of INR1,786 crores), plus a growing annuity-like operations-and-maintenance service business on its installed base. It is overwhelmingly a domestic Indian business — exports were only about INR140 crores in FY26, mainly CNG packages to the Middle East/North Africa — and management stresses in-house manufacturing at Hadapsar, Nashik and Saswad, own patents (128+ IPs filed) and import substitution as its edge.

parts.name: Air Compressor Division (ACD)
parts.what: Makes air and gas compressors — the Tezcatlipoca centrifugal compressor (the standout product, 115 ordered in FY26, sold into metals, power, pharma, tyres and textiles), reciprocating and screw compressors, plus the new Hydrino oil-free machine; management says it is roughly 18-20% of the business.

parts.name: Refrigeration Compressors and Systems
parts.what: The largest part at roughly 40-45% of the business: ammonia reciprocating compressors (KC/KCX range) that dominate cold chain and ice plants, Khione refrigeration packages sold to dairy, pharma, fisheries and concrete, the new Tyche semi-hermetic compressor replacing European imports, and large engineered process-refrigeration projects.

parts.name: Process Gas Systems (PGS) / Gas Compression
parts.what: Roughly 35-40% of the business, supplying upstream, midstream and downstream gas compression packages, CNG station and booster packages (including exports to the MENA region), and biogas (Jarilo) and hydrogen packages — the most volatile part, hit by nearly two years of slow oil-and-gas order finalisation before picking up in early 2026.

parts.name: O&M (operations and maintenance) service business
parts.what: Services the company's own installed base, notably managing over 1,000 CNG filling stations across India; described as steadily growing with the installed base, though no revenue figure is given.

parts.name: Precision Engineering Division
parts.what: A new unit set up in FY26 selling forgings, castings and precision-machined components made on spare capacity at the Nashik and Hadapsar plants; still small and a non-reportable segment, with management declining to say much until it proves it is not one-time work.

parts.name: Zephyros commercial air conditioning (new segment)
parts.what: An in-house-developed commercial air conditioning package aimed at an Indian market management sizes at over INR5,000 crores, applied for under the government PLI scheme, with demonstrator units running at its own plants and commercialisation planned for the first quarter of FY27.

parts.name: Systems & Components (India) Private Limited (subsidiary)
parts.what: A process-refrigeration company in which KPCL bought a 55.26% stake in early 2025; small — about INR9 crores of sales in a quarter — and only recently turned profitable, meant to widen KPCL's reach in the process refrigeration market.

overview.what_it_does: KNR Constructions (KNRCON) is a Hyderabad-headquartered civil construction contractor that builds infrastructure — mainly highways and roads, plus irrigation works, water pipeline schemes and, more recently, mining development — for government customers such as NHAI/MoRTH and various state governments, with a small share from private clients. It earns money in two ways: as a plain construction contractor paid a fixed contract price for building the asset (EPC), and by winning Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) road concessions where it puts its own equity into a project company (SPV), builds the road itself, and then earns construction revenue plus annuity/toll cash flows, and later sells the completed SPV — for example the December 2025 agreement to sell four HAM SPVs to Indus Infra Trust for about INR 1,543 crores against roughly INR 567 crores invested. Revenue visibility comes from an order book that stood at about INR 8,586 crores in mid-2022, dipped to INR 4,922 crores by mid-2024, and recovered to about INR 11,903 crores by March 2026 (including newly won HAM projects), typically executable over roughly 2-3.5 years. Its work is concentrated in southern and central India — Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala — with one toll road in Bihar and stated ambitions in Maharashtra and the northeast.

parts.name: EPC road projects
parts.what: Straight construction contracts where a government body pays KNR to build or widen roads, flyovers and bridges (e.g. a INR 319 crore iconic bridge for Musi Riverfront Development Corporation, a INR 50 crore Hyderabad flyover); roads were about 29% of the order book in December 2025 and 49% by March 2026.

parts.name: HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) road projects
parts.what: Road concessions won by KNR and housed in its own subsidiary SPVs, which then award the construction to KNR — so-called 'captive' order book (44% in 2022, 37% in 2024, 16% in Dec 2025, 39% in Mar 2026); it requires KNR to inject equity (INR 734 crores invested of a revised INR 952 crores as of March 2026) and is the company's most capital-hungry business.

parts.name: Irrigation projects
parts.what: Construction work on state irrigation and lift-irrigation schemes (Palamuru, Kaleshwaram and JV packages), which was about 26% of the order book in 2022 and has shrunk to roughly 14-19% by 2025-26, and which management flagged as a payment-delay problem (about INR 850 crores outstanding in mid-2022).

parts.name: Pipeline projects
parts.what: Water/pipeline-laying contracts, mostly for state government clients, forming a smaller slice of the order book — around 22% in mid-2024, 12% in December 2025 and 7% by March 2026.

parts.name: Mining projects
parts.what: A newer diversification into mining development work that had become the single largest order-book component by late FY26 — about 40% in December 2025 and 30% in March 2026 — though management excludes it when quoting the order book's execution period.

parts.name: Toll / operating road assets and asset monetization
parts.what: Completed concessions generate cash — the Bihar Muzaffarpur-Barauni project collected about INR 10-12 crores of toll per quarter — and finished HAM SPVs are sold to infrastructure trusts (KNR Palani alone brought INR 205 crores of consideration plus INR 90 crores of upstreamed cash against INR 64.4 crores invested), recycling capital back into new projects.

parts.name: JVs, associates and arbitration claims
parts.what: Income also comes from joint ventures and associate companies outside the main contracting business — for instance a INR 60.8 crore arbitration award from the Patel KNR joint venture and a INR 14.5 crore dividend from associate Patel KNR Infrastructures, both booked in Q1 FY25 — which are lumpy and can materially swing a quarter's profit.

overview.what_it_does: Kotak Mahindra Bank is an Indian bank that runs as what management calls a "financial conglomerate" — the Bank itself plus 19 wholly owned subsidiaries — serving customers almost entirely in India. It takes deposits (current and savings accounts, term deposits; CASA ratio around 43%) and lends that money out as home loans, SME and business loans, car and tractor loans, commercial-vehicle finance, microfinance, credit cards and personal loans, plus corporate/wholesale lending. Its main earnings come from the spread between lending rates and its low cost of deposits (net interest margin roughly 4.5%–5.75% over the period), topped up by fee income from general banking, distribution of investment and insurance products, and syndication. Alongside the Bank, the group sells life insurance, mutual funds and alternate assets, stockbroking, investment banking and custody services — these subsidiaries have contributed roughly 30%–33% of consolidated group profit, with the Bank supplying the other ~67%–70%. Management targets loan growth of 1.5x–2x India's nominal GDP and repeatedly stresses a "fortress balance sheet" (group capital adequacy above 22%).

parts.name: Consumer Bank
parts.what: Retail deposits and retail lending to individuals — savings/current accounts, mortgages (growing ~18% a year and called a key driver), secured consumer loans, working capital and business loans, plus digital account offerings 811 and 811 Super for mass-market "Core India" customers; this is the engine behind the low-cost CASA deposits that underpin margins.

parts.name: Private Bank / Solitaire (High Net Worth and affluent)
parts.what: Wealth propositions for rich and affluent customers, gathering assets under management across mutual funds, discretionary portfolios (NDPMS) and AIFs, and driving CASA balances, SIPs and card spends — described as showing consistent good AUM growth.

parts.name: Unsecured retail (credit cards, personal loans, microcredit)
parts.what: Credit cards, personal loans and micro-credit; deliberately shrunk and then grown back only "gradually and responsibly" after an RBI technology embargo halted new card issuance and after credit stress from over-leveraged borrowers — down from about 11.3% of assets in FY25 to a stable ~8.9% of net advances by FY26.

parts.name: Commercial Bank
parts.what: Lending to smaller commercial customers — commercial vehicles, construction equipment, agri and tractor finance, and microfinance (MFI) — a segment that saw slow industry growth and credit strain in FY25; Kotak calls itself the leader in Tractor Finance, growing about 16% year-on-year.

parts.name: SME
parts.what: Loans to small and medium businesses, run across three verticals (commercial bank agri/working capital, consumer business loans, and wholesale SME); management calls SME "the backbone of Kotak" — a book of about ₹1.16 lakh crore growing ~17–18% year-on-year.

parts.name: Wholesale / Corporate Banking
parts.what: Lending and banking services to large corporates and institutional clients; a significant contributor to asset growth in FY25, though a slower corporate book held back advances growth in Q4FY26.

parts.name: Kotak Mahindra Prime (car finance NBFC)
parts.what: A non-bank finance subsidiary doing car finance; separately capitalised with capital adequacy above 28%.

parts.name: Kotak Mahindra Investments (NBFC)
parts.what: A second non-bank lending subsidiary, contributing around ₹100 crore of quarterly profit in FY23 and also capitalised above 28%.

parts.name: BSS Microfinance (business correspondent)
parts.what: A microfinance business-correspondent entity acquired in 2017 that originates small loans for the group; earned ₹297 crore post-tax in FY23 versus ₹83 crore the prior year.

parts.name: Kotak Life Insurance
parts.what: Life insurance manufacturer; FY23 profit crossed ₹1,000 crore (up from ₹425 crore), embedded value ~₹12,500 crore and VNB margin 38.8%, with solvency of 2.83x against a 1.5x regulatory minimum.

parts.name: Asset Management (Kotak Mahindra AMC and trustee company)
parts.what: Runs mutual funds and, increasingly, alternate assets for Indian savers; the domestic mutual fund entities made about ₹555 crore in FY23 and asset management grew 58% year-on-year in Q2FY25, benefiting from the "Savers to Investors" shift.

parts.name: Capital Markets (Kotak Securities, Kotak Capital / investment banking, institutional equities and custody)
parts.what: Stockbroking for retail investors, institutional equities and custody services for foreign investors, and investment banking/deal syndication; profits fell in FY23 on a market slowdown, jumped 52% year-on-year in Q2FY25, and in FY26 investment banking was muted while retail brokerage held up on domestic flows.

parts.name: General Insurance
parts.what: Kotak General Insurance was part of the group but a transaction on it produced a one-off booked profit in Q1FY25, after which it is treated separately from the ongoing quarterly profit comparisons.

parts.name: Product verticals (Tractor Finance, CV, CE)
parts.what: Tractor finance, commercial vehicles and construction equipment are run as standalone product lines across the group rather than inside a customer segment; tractor finance is described as a market-leading business growing ~16% year-on-year.

overview.what_it_does: KPI Green Energy is an Indian renewable power company (part of the KP Group, with in-house EPC expertise since 2008) that builds and runs solar, wind and hybrid solar-wind power plants, mainly in Gujarat. It makes money two ways: it builds plants for industrial and commercial customers who want their own captive power — earning a one-off construction/sale fee of roughly Rs. 4.25–4.50 crore per MW plus an ongoing land-lease and operations-and-maintenance fee of about Rs. 10 lakh per MW per year — and it owns plants itself, selling the electricity under 25-year power purchase agreements to state utilities such as GUVNL, which gives it steady, high-margin annuity income. Alongside this it takes third-party EPC and balance-of-plant construction orders (for example from GSECL and Adani Green) and is moving into battery storage, floating solar, green hydrogen and power trading. Revenue has grown fast — from Rs. 647 crore in FY23 to Rs. 2,742 crore in FY26, with PAT of Rs. 509 crore in FY26, an installed capacity of about 1.62 GW and an installed-plus-upcoming portfolio of roughly 6.26 GW.

parts.name: CPP (Captive Power Producer)
parts.what: Builds solar/wind/hybrid plants that are sold to industrial and commercial clients for their own captive use, then leases them the land and runs the plant for a recurring O&M fee of about Rs. 10 lakh per MW per year; this was historically the bigger revenue earner (about 85% of FY23 revenue, Rs. 550 crore) and stands at roughly 3.69 GW of installed plus upcoming capacity by March 2026.

parts.name: IPP (Independent Power Producer)
parts.what: KPI owns and operates its own solar, wind and hybrid plants and sells the electricity under 25-year PPAs with state utilities like GUVNL — a smaller share of revenue but far higher margin and the source of long-term annuity income; the portfolio is about 2.57 GW installed plus upcoming and is expected to generate over 390 crore units of electricity a year.

parts.name: EPC / Balance-of-Plant contracts for third parties
parts.what: Uses its engineering and construction arm to build plants for outside customers — recent examples being a 152 MW floating solar contract from GSECL at Kadana Dam and balance-of-plant supply and site services for Adani Green totalling 534 MW at Khavda (later cited as 1.13 GW), sitting within an order book of about Rs. 6,000 crore that carries price-escalation clauses to protect margins.

parts.name: Battery Energy Storage (BESS)
parts.what: A newer line: a 445 MW / 890 MWh standalone battery project awarded by GUVNL with viability gap funding needing roughly Rs. 1,000–1,100 crore of investment at an expected 13–14% IRR, plus a further 120 MW / 240 MWh project — described as a key future growth segment rather than a current earnings driver.

parts.name: Land bank and power evacuation infrastructure
parts.what: Owns a large land bank (6,275 acres as of June 2025) and transmission/evacuation capacity of over 3.2 GW at 11 kV and 66 kV, which management presents as the enabling asset base that lets it site and connect both CPP and IPP projects quickly; land carried at only about Rs. 83 crore in the books versus a stated much higher current value.

parts.name: Power trading
parts.what: Recently obtained an interstate trading licence from CERC and an intrastate licence from GERC, allowing it to buy and sell power on exchanges and through bilateral contracts across India for better realisations — described as new and still small.

parts.name: Emerging segments (green hydrogen, EV charging, floating solar, offshore wind, pumped storage)
parts.what: Early-stage areas backed by three MOUs with Delta Electronics India covering storage, green hydrogen, EV charging and solar inverters; management lists these as future capability-building rather than material revenue today.

parts.name: Sundrops Energia (subsidiary)
parts.what: A subsidiary that did Rs. 586 crore of revenue with Rs. 130 crore PBT and Rs. 97 crore PAT in FY26 and is being prepared for its own IPO (DRHP stage).

parts.name: International expansion (Botswana)
parts.what: An MOU with the government of Botswana for up to about 5 GW of renewable generation and storage (cited as roughly Rs. 36,000 crore of investment), with an initial 500 MW targeted within a couple of years — a stated ambition, not yet an operating business.

overview.what_it_does: Kalpataru Projects International (KPIL) is an India-based engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor — it wins fixed-scope infrastructure and construction contracts, then designs, buys the materials for, and physically builds them for clients such as power grid utilities (e.g. PGCIL), state water departments, oil & gas majors (e.g. Aramco in Saudi Arabia), metro rail authorities, railways, and private property developers. Revenue is recognised as projects are executed against a large order backlog, so the order book is the main indicator of future sales: FY26 consolidated revenue was INR 27,143 crores off an all-time-high order book of INR 65,457 crores, with consolidated PBT margins of about 4.9% and PAT of INR 1,031 crores. Its biggest business by far is power transmission & distribution, followed by buildings and factories, with smaller water, oil & gas, urban infrastructure and railway units. Roughly speaking it works across India and international markets including the Nordics (subsidiary LMG Sweden), the Middle East, Africa, South America and Brazil (subsidiary Fasttel), and it is exiting non-core assets such as road toll SPVs and an Indore real estate project to put capital back into EPC. The company is the merged entity of the erstwhile Kalpataru Power and JMC Projects, combined from FY24.

parts.name: Transmission & Distribution (T&D)
parts.what: Builds power transmission lines, substations and HVDC systems for utilities in India and overseas; the flagship and largest business, with revenue crossing INR 10,000 crores in FY25, +25% growth in FY26 and an order book of INR 28,572 crores at end-FY26 — management calls itself a global leader here.

parts.name: Buildings & Factories (B&F)
parts.what: Constructs residential towers, airports, data centres, hospitals and industrial plants — increasingly on 'design-build' contracts where KPIL does the design too; the second-largest business, with FY26 order inflows of INR 11,460 crores (up ~40%) and an order book of INR 18,295 crores.

parts.name: Oil & Gas
parts.what: Builds oil and gas infrastructure, mainly in the Middle East and anchored by Saudi Aramco projects; small but the fastest-scaling unit — revenue INR 1,758 crores in FY25 after doubling, then up another 55% in FY26, and management calls it a future major growth engine.

parts.name: Water
parts.what: Executes water supply and pipeline work, largely government Jal Jeevan Mission schemes (including UP JJM); the problem child — INR 2,112 crores of FY26 revenue, the only unit that shrank, held back by delayed government payments, so the company is finishing existing jobs and bidding cautiously despite a ~INR 9,500 crore order book.

parts.name: Urban Infrastructure
parts.what: Builds elevated and underground metro rail, tunnels (including TBM tunnelling in Kanpur and Bhopal) and elevated roads; a mid-sized unit that grew 49% in FY26 on metro execution, with FY26 order wins of about INR 2,000 crores.

parts.name: Railways
parts.what: Rail infrastructure work; a small, deliberately shrinking-focus unit — about INR 1,019 crores of revenue in FY25 and 9% growth in FY26 — where management bids selectively because competition is intense.

parts.name: International subsidiaries (LMG Sweden, Fasttel Brazil)
parts.what: Overseas T&D arms — LMG serves Sweden and the Nordics and has been a strong performer (FY25 revenue +79%, order book INR 3,535 crores), while Fasttel Brazil underperformed and KPIL wound up all its Brazilian projects and took a full provision on that exposure in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Non-core assets (road SPVs, Indore real estate)
parts.what: Legacy toll-road holding companies and a leftover real estate project that management is selling off rather than growing — the Vindhyachal road asset was divested in January 2026 at about INR 799 crores enterprise value (over INR 600 crores net cash), with the Indore inventory being fully monetised by March 2026, freeing capital for the core EPC business.

overview.what_it_does: KPIT Technologies is an India-headquartered (Pune) software and engineering services firm that works almost entirely for the automotive and wider mobility industry — it writes, integrates and validates the software that goes inside vehicles, covering things like powertrain and electrification, vehicle middleware and electronic architecture, connected/cloud services, digital key and other in-car features, and after-sales systems. Its customers are vehicle manufacturers (OEMs) — passenger car makers plus, more recently, truck and off-highway/commercial vehicle makers — with whom it runs long, deep engagements; management ranks its top accounts as 'Diamond' and 'gold' clients and says Tier-1 suppliers were never a focus. It earns money by billing these clients for engineering programs, historically on a per-person time basis but increasingly on fixed-price contracts (66% of revenue in Q3 FY26 versus 59% a year earlier), with new business reported as deal wins/TCV each quarter; EBITDA margin has run around 18.5%–21%. It operates across three main regions — the USA, Europe and Asia (mainly Japan, Korea and India) — with a recent push into China, and it has bought companies (Somit Solutions, Technica, Caresoft, N-Dream) to add depth and reach.

parts.name: Feature development and integration
parts.what: Builds and integrates individual vehicle software features for OEM programs; described as a core revenue line growing about 20% year-on-year in FY23, and the kind of hands-on delivery work that underpins the bulk of the business.

parts.name: Architecture and middleware
parts.what: Designs the underlying electronic/electrical architecture and middleware layer of the vehicle's software; it was the fastest-growing practice in FY23 (up 73% year-on-year) and was boosted by the Technica acquisition, and management calls it a main growth driver alongside powertrain.

parts.name: Cloud-based connected services
parts.what: Software connecting vehicles to the cloud and related connected-car services; grew 49% year-on-year in Q3 FY23 and was cited as the second-biggest contributor to growth in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Powertrain (including electrification)
parts.what: Software for how the vehicle is driven and powered — covering conventional engines, hybrids, electric and pilot hydrogen systems; a long-standing growth engine, though management says its growth is no longer the highest of the four areas.

parts.name: Vehicle engineering
parts.what: Added mainly through the Caresoft acquisition, this goes beyond software into benchmarking and cost reduction of the whole vehicle — including what management calls one-of-a-kind 'software benchmarking' — aimed at OEMs' biggest pain point, cost.

parts.name: After sales
parts.what: Solutions helping OEMs earn revenue over the vehicle's life rather than only at the point of sale; described as one of KPIT's fastest-growing areas and one where it has built strong solutions.

parts.name: Trucks and off-highway / commercial vehicles
parts.what: A deliberate expansion beyond passenger cars decided in FY25, helped by the Caresoft acquisition; it grew 18% year-on-year in FY26 and led Q4 FY26 growth at 11.6%, versus passenger cars which had been the main engine earlier (up 26.4% year-on-year in Q2 FY25).

parts.name: Solutions and products (the 'next pivot')
parts.what: Selling largely pre-built offerings that need only some per-customer customisation rather than pure people-based project work — management says this now accounts for 21% of the total pipeline and is the reason fixed-price mix and revenue per person are rising.

parts.name: AI initiatives
parts.what: A newer investment area with two AI wins already in customer production programs, a Microsoft partnership (KPIT named a 'frontier partner'), an agentic-solutions agreement with a leading CRM company, and a dedicated CTO for AI; spending on it is over and above the roughly USD 3.8 million per quarter of other business investment.

parts.name: Geographies (USA, Europe, Asia/China)
parts.what: Revenue is reported across three regions because most clients are global: Europe led Q3 FY26 deal wins followed by the USA, Asia (Japan, Korea, India) drove Q2 FY25 growth, and China is a new but strategically important market where KPIT has landed two OEM engagements that are still small in revenue.

overview.what_it_does: K.P.R. Mill is an Indian textile manufacturer based around Coimbatore/Tirupur in Tamil Nadu that runs a vertically integrated chain: it spins cotton (and viscose) yarn, knits and processes fabric, and stitches finished garments — mainly basic cotton knitwear — which it sells largely to overseas retail buyers, with roughly 50% of garment sales going to Europe, about 20% to the US and about 15% to Australia, plus a small share in Asia. It makes money by selling yarn and grey fabric to outside customers while using most of its own yarn and processed fabric internally to make garments, where margins are highest (garments around 21–27% versus yarn at about 12–14%); management says value additions like full-body printing, fabric and garment printing and embroidery have lifted EBITDA per piece from about INR30 to INR40. Alongside textiles it runs a sugar business (KPR Sugar Mill) that crushes sugarcane and increasingly converts sugar syrup and molasses into ethanol, which management describes as the higher-margin end of that chain and which supported group profits when textile demand was weak. It also generates its own power — sugar co-generation plus wind and rooftop solar — consuming most of it captively and selling the surplus co-gen power. Blended group EBITDA margin ran around 23% and management repeatedly calls textiles the core business.

parts.name: Garments
parts.what: Stitches and exports mainly basic cotton knitwear to buyers in Europe, the US and Australia, running at roughly 40 million pieces a quarter (about 150 million a year) at around INR185 per piece with a standing order book of about INR1,000 crore — described by management as the segment that supports overall performance, earning about 21–27% margins.

parts.name: Yarn / spinning (textile)
parts.what: Spins cotton yarn (about 14,600 tons and INR391 crore of sales in one quarter) plus a new INR100 crore vortex spinning mill for viscose yarn; margins here swing with cotton prices, running about 12% against a stated sustainable 17–18%, and much of the output feeds the company's own garment units.

parts.name: Fabric (knitting, processing and printing)
parts.what: Knits fabric and runs processing/printing operations, selling only grey fabric outside (about 2,285 tons for roughly INR66 crore in a quarter) while processed and printed fabric is kept for in-house garment use; a INR50 crore debottlenecking added about 20% processing capacity, described as value addition for own consumption.

parts.name: Sugar
parts.what: Crushes sugarcane and produces sugar and molasses through KPR Sugar Mill; sugar and ethanol together brought in about INR619 crore over nine months of FY23 (of which sugar sales were about INR115 crore in the quarter discussed), at a blended sugar-segment margin of around 25%.

parts.name: Ethanol
parts.what: Converts sugar syrup and molasses into ethanol, the higher-margin use of the sugar stream; capacity was being expanded from 130 KLPD to 250 KLPD for INR150 crore (taking both units together to roughly 5 lakh litres a day), expected to add about INR200 crore of revenue gross, or about INR100 crore net of the sugar and molasses it displaces.

parts.name: Power (co-generation, wind and solar)
parts.what: Produces about 32 crore units of co-generation power, of which around 12 crore units are used in sugar production and the balance sold in the market, plus about 11 crore units of wind and solar (including a 12 MW / INR50 crore rooftop solar plant) that is entirely consumed captively and saves roughly INR12 crore a year.

parts.name: Ethiopia garment operation
parts.what: An overseas garment manufacturing facility set up in Ethiopia that management says is no longer feasible after Europe and the US withdrew the tax concession, and the company is now focused on Indian expansion only.

overview.what_it_does: KRBL Limited is an Indian rice company — it buys paddy from farmers in Punjab, Haryana, Western Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and parts of Madhya Pradesh, mills and ages it, and sells the rice under its own consumer brands, chiefly basmati rice under the 'India Gate' brand (which management calls the world's No. 1 basmati rice brand) plus the Unity brand and a growing non-basmati range. It describes itself as the world's largest rice miller and basmati rice exporter, selling both inside India through general trade, modern trade and e-commerce (about 3.2 lakh retail outlets, reaching roughly 1.2 crore urban households) and overseas, mainly to the Middle East (Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, UAE), plus the EU, UK and the United States. It makes money on the spread between what it pays for paddy and what it gets for packed and bulk rice, so profits swing with crop quality, paddy prices, government export policy, and freight and geopolitical conditions on Middle East shipping routes. India is by far the bigger side of the business — around Rs. 4,000 crore of domestic revenue in FY24 against Rs. 1,345 crore of exports, out of total income of Rs. 5,482 crore.

parts.name: India / Domestic business
parts.what: Sells branded packaged rice to Indian households through distributors, general trade, modern trade and e-commerce; it is the largest part of the company (roughly Rs. 4,000 crore in FY24, about Rs. 1,104 crore in Q3 FY26 excluding power) and management claims clear market leadership with ~37.8% share in general trade, 39.3% in modern trade and 41.2% in e-commerce.

parts.name: Branded basmati (India Gate and other brands)
parts.what: The core premium product — aged basmati rice sold in consumer packs — described as the world's No. 1 basmati brand; it drives most domestic sales but was flat in Q3 FY26 as loose and regional players competed harder and raw material prices fell.

parts.name: Unity brand
parts.what: A separate, lower-priced rice brand aimed at the mass market that grew more than 100% year-on-year to about Rs. 150 crore in a single quarter (Q1 FY23), so a fast-growing but much smaller piece than India Gate.

parts.name: Branded non-basmati rice
parts.what: Ordinary (non-basmati) rice sold under KRBL's brands, treated as a completely separate commodity from basmati in price and market terms; it is the fastest-growing domestic line, up 35% over nine months of FY26 and 9% in Q3 FY26, though still smaller than basmati.

parts.name: Export business (branded)
parts.what: Sells packaged branded rice overseas through country distributors, especially in the Middle East, with management repeatedly flagging distributor changes (for example rebuilding a lost 40-year Saudi relationship) as a swing factor; total exports were Rs. 1,345 crore in FY24 and Rs. 1,276 crore over nine months of FY26, up 21% year-on-year.

parts.name: Bulk export segment
parts.what: Lower-margin, unbranded, large-volume rice shipments to overseas buyers; management deliberately pulls back here when payment risk in markets like Iran and Iraq rises, which it says cost roughly Rs. 600 crore of export revenue in FY24 and cut Q3 FY26 exports to Rs. 357 crore from Rs. 563 crore a year earlier.

parts.name: Power
parts.what: A small energy-generation activity whose revenue management explicitly strips out when reporting domestic sales ('domestic revenue, excluding power'), indicating it is a minor side stream rather than a core business.

parts.name: New products / portfolio expansion
parts.what: An effort to add products beyond core rice, with a stated target of about 10% of revenue from new products within two financial years (as of FY23), so currently a small contributor.

parts.name: Procurement, milling and manufacturing base
parts.what: Buying paddy directly from farming belts and milling it — management stresses sourcing low-moisture, high-recovery paddy to protect margins, and mentions long-term consolidation of operations at Panipat for scale and cost efficiency.

overview.what_it_does: KRN Heat Exchanger and Refrigeration is an Indian manufacturer, founded in 2017 and based at Neemrana in Rajasthan, that makes heat exchangers — the aluminium and copper tube coils that move heat inside cooling equipment, including condenser coils, evaporator coils and water coils. It sells almost entirely business-to-business to OEMs (original equipment makers) who build air conditioning and refrigeration equipment, with named customers including Daikin and Schneider Electric; management said on the Aug-2025 call that the business is 100% B2B and that it deliberately stays out of the low-margin aftermarket for its established products. It makes money by manufacturing to customer specification and repricing quarter-on-quarter against copper LME, aluminium LME and the USD-INR rate, so it says it passes on close to 100% of raw material moves, and it typically carries 2 to 2.5 months of metal inventory. It sells mainly in India (about 81% of revenue in Q2 FY25) with the rest exported to markets including the UAE, US, Canada, Italy, Germany and France; consolidated total income for FY26 was Rs.609.81 crores, up 38.06%, with net profit of Rs.76.47 crores, and it listed on the NSE and BSE in October 2024.

parts.name: Heat exchangers and coils (fin and tube) — the core business
parts.what: The original product line of aluminium and copper tube heat exchangers, condenser coils, evaporator coils and water coils sold to HVAC and refrigeration OEMs; this is the bulk of revenue and management describes the company as having started from 'four heat exchanger products', with the old plant running at 100% capacity by late 2024.

parts.name: KRN HVAC Products Private Limited (the new Neemrana facility)
parts.what: A wholly-owned subsidiary whose new plant began commercial operations on 31 May 2025 and adds roughly six times the old facility's capacity; it won a PLI (production-linked incentive) approval for white goods worth Rs.141.72 crores, added 40-plus new customers in a single quarter, and management expects only about 50% utilisation in FY27, so it is the main growth engine but still ramping.

parts.name: New refrigeration products
parts.what: Wire and tube condensers, roll bond evaporators, frost-free evaporators and skin condensers — components for refrigerators, made at the new facility; these are new enough that KRN is selling some of them into the aftermarket while it settles machines, manpower and quality systems.

parts.name: Bar and plate heat exchangers
parts.what: A different construction type of heat exchanger added as a new product with the new capacity, aimed at bringing in customers the existing fin-and-tube range did not serve.

parts.name: Complete (finished) products — dry air coolers and ammonia evaporators
parts.what: A step up from selling components to selling whole units used in industrial cooling and refrigeration; described as part of the move toward a 'more integrated offering' rather than sized separately in the calls.

parts.name: Bus air conditioning
parts.what: Entered during FY26 as a strategic move from component supplier to full system supplier, helped by in-house heat exchangers, tubing and FRP; it contributed about Rs.10 crores in FY26 and management is targeting at least a 15% market share, so it is small today but flagged as a meaningful future avenue.

parts.name: Data centre cooling
parts.what: Currently supplied with the same fin-and-tube coils used in chillers and dry coolers, this was about 18.7% of Q4 FY26 revenue, up roughly 2.7 percentage points quarter-on-quarter, with long lead-time orders booked six to seven months out and two new export customers — described as the fastest-growing end market.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Sales outside India, roughly 19% of revenue in Q2 FY25 and about Rs.100 crores in the latest year, driven by the UAE, US, Canada and Italy with early traction in Europe; the company reported an export order book of over Rs.120 crores including data centre orders.

parts.name: Thermotech Research Laboratory
parts.what: A separately identified testing lab held under a subsidiary, set up under an MoU with AHRI and described as the first AHRI-approved lab in India; it earns no meaningful revenue yet and exists to certify products for Indian, European, American and UAE customers and eventually support patents.

parts.name: Products under development
parts.what: Micro-channel heat exchangers (MCHX), expected in the portfolio by end of 2026 or early 2027, and plate heat exchangers for liquid-cooled data centre CDUs, still at the study stage — neither contributes revenue today.

overview.what_it_does: KSB Limited makes and sells pumps and valves in India — everything from small household and farm pumps to large engineered pumps for power plants, refineries and water utilities, plus gate/globe/check and ball valves and (through associate MIL Controls in Kochi) control valves. Its customers are industrial and infrastructure buyers such as Thermax, BHEL, L&T, NTPC, HPCL/BPCL, NPCIL, ISGEC, Veolia, Wabag and municipal corporations, reached both directly and through a network of 800-1,100+ authorised dealers, 14 branches, four zonal offices and 350+ service centres. It earns money by selling equipment against orders (a mix of standard catalogue pumps and project-specific engineered pumps) and by an ongoing after-sales stream of spare parts, repairs, field service and pump replacement. Established in 1960 and headquartered in Pune, it operates six manufacturing plants plus its own foundries across Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Kerala; it is part of the German KSB group, sells mainly in India (with Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan served as neighbouring markets) and exports about 17% of order intake, with CY2025 revenue of about ₹26,957 million and profit before tax of about ₹352 crore.

parts.name: Standard pumps (Water Pump Division, Sinnar)
parts.what: Makes standard and domestic pumps — submersible, openwell and mini-monobloc, dewatering — for irrigation, farmhouses, drinking water and building use; management calls this the largest and fastest-growing slice, roughly 48% of 2025 order intake.

parts.name: Engineered pumps (Industrial Pump Division, Pimpri and Energy Pump Division, Shirwal)
parts.what: Builds project-specific pumps such as high-pressure multistage, API 610 process, FGD and boiler recirculation pumps for power, oil and gas, petrochemical and process plants; about 19% of 2025 order intake and the source of the large project orders.

parts.name: Valves Division (Coimbatore)
parts.what: Manufactures gate, globe, check and ball valves used across energy, industry, water and wastewater, including for export to China after a regulatory audit; about 18% of 2025 order intake, described as steady, with associate MIL Controls in Kochi adding control valves.

parts.name: SupremeServ (aftermarket)
parts.what: The after-sales unit at Chinchwad selling spare parts, repairs, field service, modernisation and replacement pumps, plus a training academy and central warehouse; about 15% of 2025 order intake and a recurring revenue stream on the installed base.

parts.name: Nuclear business
parts.what: Supplies primary coolant pumps, motors, spares and mechanical seals to NPCIL — one Kaiga 5 & 6 order alone was about ₹5,000 million; a long-gestation business held separately in reporting, with roughly ₹12,816 million of orders on hand at December 2025, about half the total order book.

parts.name: Solar pumps business
parts.what: Sells solar pumping products, now including an in-house-made solar controller, largely to state government buyers like Dakshin Gujarat, Maharashtra Energy and Haryana Renewable; small but the fastest-growing line at a stated 112% order intake CAGR.

parts.name: Water and wastewater
parts.what: Non-clog submersible and end-suction pumps, vertical turbine pumps and valves for municipal and industrial sewage, effluent, stormwater and drainage; the biggest market area at 29% of sales, growing at a stated 30% CAGR with breakthrough orders from Kolkata, Amritsar and Navi Mumbai.

parts.name: Building services / firefighting
parts.what: Hydro-pneumatic systems, FM/UL-certified firefighting pumps and HVAC pumps for commercial buildings, airports, metros, hospitals and data centres; about 8% of sales but called a sunrise segment growing at 68% CAGR.

parts.name: Foundry (Vambori) and KSB Tech
parts.what: Supporting units — cast-iron and stainless steel foundries producing castings mainly for KSB's own pumps and valves, and KSB Tech in Pune, a captive engineering and IT services centre serving the worldwide KSB group.

overview.what_it_does: Kaveri Seed Company Limited (KSCL) is an Indian company that breeds, produces and sells packaged hybrid and research seeds to farmers — mainly cotton, rice (both hybrid and 'selection'/research paddy), maize, bajra/millet, sunflower, mustard and vegetables. It makes money by selling branded seed packets through a dealer/distributor channel across Indian states such as Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, plus a small but fast-growing export business into international markets where it is registering its seeds. Its own in-house R&D breeds the hybrids it sells (management says it has 200+ hybrids in its portfolio and spends roughly 5%-10% of revenue on R&D plus capex), so profits depend on getting new products accepted while controlling the cost of growing the seed crop, which it cannot always pass on to farmers because cotton seed prices are government-controlled. The business is highly seasonal and monsoon-linked — the June quarter is by far the biggest — with FY26 revenue of about Rs. 1,304 crores, net profit of about Rs. 283 crores, and a debt-free, cash-on-books balance sheet.

parts.name: Cotton (hybrid BT cotton seed)
parts.what: Sells hybrid cotton seed packets at a government-capped MRP; historically the single largest crop at more than 35% of the portfolio, but it shrank sharply (volumes -35% in Q1 FY25) due to lower acreage, illegal/unapproved BT seed competition and high production cost, and management expects a recovery led by new hybrids whose share of cotton volumes jumped from 10.3% to 30.05% in FY26.

parts.name: Hybrid rice
parts.what: Hybrid paddy seed sold in markets like Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand; a core growth crop with FY26 revenues up 18.3% even though Punjab — described as one of its largest hybrid rice markets — imposed restrictions.

parts.name: Selection rice / research paddy
parts.what: Non-hybrid 'selection' or research paddy varieties bred in-house; a steadily growing segment with FY26 volumes up about 2.4% and revenues up 9.8%, and research paddy volumes up 51% in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Maize
parts.what: Hybrid maize seed, called the key growth driver of FY26 with volumes up 18.8% and revenues up 40.2%; new products rose from 40% to 52% of maize volumes, and demand swings with commercial maize grain prices and rabi/spring sowing in states like Bihar, UP, Punjab and Madhya Pradesh.

parts.name: Bajra / millet
parts.what: Pearl millet seed where new products already make up the bulk of volumes (75.8% in Q1 FY25), with growth expected in summer and rainy millet in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.

parts.name: Vegetable seeds
